Sports.title: Chelsea's breakthrough star, London City's Halloween fan... and the Man United supporter named after Eric Cantona! The young stars to watch in England's World Cup qualifiers against Greece
Sports.content:
Five years into her reign, Sarina Wiegman knows exactly what it takes to keep her Lionesses ticking. After a four-goal thumping by Spain prior to the summer break, the Dutch coach opted to wield the axe and bring in the young guns. Wiegman, who has regularly been praised for her transparency with her players over her selection decisions, chose to leave out two of her most trusted stalwarts in Chloe Kelly and Ella Toone for these two-legged semi-final World Cup qualifiers. Whether this was a tactical ploy to light a fire under the duo amid tepid starts to their club seasons, or a warning sign to the rest of the squad not to rest on their laurels, it remains to be seen. Either way, there was no holding back. ‘I think the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch,’ Wiegman said. ‘We expect a bit more and we know they can bring more.’ An injury to Lucy Bronze has thrown a lifeline to the returning Toone, but the future remains uncertain for the pair who played significant roles in helping England claim back-to-back Euros wins last year, despite Kelly’s right boot having been the deciding factor in both of those triumphs. Yet with one keen eye on next summer’s World Cup, Wiegman has already cranked up the gears ahead of what many believe will be her last tournament in charge. Freya Godfrey and Lexi Potter are among the young stars hoping to make their mark with England in their World Cup qualifiers against Greece Indeed, there is a new guard champing at the bit, waiting to usurp their heroes and book a seat on the plane to Brazil, should they get there, of course. Many of these youngsters point to the fact that Michelle Agyemang, who is still sidelined with an ACL injury, showed last summer that the status quo is there to be disrupted. Here, Daily Mail Sport’s women’s football reporter, TARA ANSON-WALSH analyses the three young stars to watch in the upcoming World Cup qualifiers against Greece… 1) Lexi Potter At just 20, Lexi Potter is the latest young star off Chelsea’s production line, her impressive start to the season earning a first senior call-up from Wiegman. Asked about that intensifying spotlight, a smiley, slightly overawed Potter told the media at her first Lionesses camp earlier this week: ‘I don’t really like to read into anything I see in the media. ‘I like to keep my feet on the ground. All my team-mates have been making fun of me and making comments. Keira has been calling me a baller and I’m like “please, stop”.’ A deep-lying midfielder, the Epsom-born player broke through the ranks at Chelsea’s academy before spending two seasons at Crystal Palace between 2023 and 2025. At Palace, she was credited by former coach Laura Kaminski with helping the side secure promotion. Calm on the ball and blessed with a strong passing range, Potter’s tactical astuteness is of a different pedigree. She received the highest of praise from Walsh, one of England’s best players, earlier this year: ‘She's probably going to be better than me, to be honest. ‘I don't mean to put too much pressure on her with that, to be fair, but the way we see the game is very similar. We both see football in a very tactical way and I've really enjoyed playing with her so far.’ She added: ‘When Lexi's playing alongside me, she makes me feel really comfortable and she gives me the freedom to (get forward), and we've got a great partnership.’ Lexi Potter has been rewarded for her strong start to the season at Chelsea with a call-up Keira Walsh claimed earlier this year that Potter is 'probably going to be better than me' Potter returned to Chelsea for last season, and after spending a lot of it on the bench, she made a case for herself to head coach Sonia Bompastor over the summer – and the Chelsea coach answered. Such was the composure that Potter showed on her debut alongside Walsh that Bompastor rewarded her with a further two starts. The pair have shown a natural chemistry while working together on the pitch, with Walsh given more freedom to roam forward, trusting that there are capable feet to mop up behind her should she need it. That composure was monumental in keeping rivals Arsenal quiet in Chelsea’s 1-0 victory at Stamford Bridge last month. After the match, Chelsea’s French head coach Bompastor said: ‘For her age, the way she has been performing, I think it’s great. I think people were looking forward to this game to see in this big occasion if she was able to repeat and sustain the performance, and she proved that today. ‘For a player as young as her, being able to bring that impact into the game, out of possession, in possession, it's great news for England. I wish she could be French.’ 2) Freya Godfrey For those who regularly follow the WSL, Freya Godfrey is one they will know well. A pacy, exciting young winger with the world at her feet. Yet to Lionesses fans, the 21-year-old is still a relative unknown, having failed to make her debut despite receiving her first call-up by Wiegman last November. Godfrey joined London City Lionesses from Arsenal last year and had a terrific debut season, ending as the club's 2025-26 Players' Player of the Season after scoring six goals and providing four assists in their maiden WSL campaign. There were warning signs that she could be displaced by one of her team’s many expensive new recruits when she was left out of the opening matchday squad against Manchester United. Yet Godfrey has clearly shown enough in training to stake a claim in Eder Maestre’s starting XI for three of London City’s last four games and to get the nod once again from Wiegman. While there has been stiff competition ahead of her on the right wing, with Beth Mead, Jess Park and Lauren James all able to play in that position, Godfrey’s newfound deployment at No9 for London City could set her in good stead for winning her first cap during this camp, should Wiegman look to rest Russo at any point. And she has been learning from the best, feeding off the nuggets of information World Cup winner Alexia Putellas has been handing out this season. Godfrey was London City Lionesses Players' Player of the Season last year and has retained a spot in the team despite expensive summer arrivals The 21-year-old looks in good stead to win her first England cap during this camp ‘As a young player it’s so incredible to have her around every day,’ Godfrey said of the two-time Ballon d’Or winner. ‘She’s very caring, she wants you to develop and she’ll put a lot of faith in you and have a lot of conversations with you. ‘She’s very good at one-to-one speaking, if she sees something, she’ll say it, so I think I’ve developed a lot (playing alongside her).’ Charismatic and funny, Godfrey has been open about the fact that she genuinely enjoys speaking to the media, unlike some of her peers, speaking with maturity about the importance of ‘feeling like my opinion is valued’. She opened up about her desire to dress up for Halloween as her favourite character from the video game Fortnite, but has been shut down by ‘the Spanish’, who ‘want to go sexy… typical.’ ‘I'm not going to embarrass myself and go as a banana while everyone else looks great,’ she adds. While there is no doubt that the priority is always to win football games, in terms of the marketability of the Lionesses, Godfrey has that bit of stardust that will stand her in good stead for the future. 3) Erica Meg Parkinson Lastly, but certainly not least, Erica Meg Parkinson is another to keep an eye on this window after the 18-year-old returned to camp just a few months after she was handed a shock call-up in March. A player full of flair and close ball control, Parkinson is an exciting attacking midfielder to watch, and she has adjusted well since moving from Portugal’s top flight to America in the summer, turning down a plethora of enquiries from European clubs, including the WSL, in the hope of more game time. ‘I feel like the NWSL does a good job at bringing in young players and giving them the minutes that they need, and I felt like that was what I needed at that time,’ she said on Tuesday, a worrying indictment of the lack of opportunities afforded to young players in this country. For Parkinson, though, North Carolina Courage have certainly provided that. Their reliance on the youngster has grown to the point where she was forced to withdraw from the U20s World Cup in order to help guide her club through its play-off matches. One of the more amusing anecdotes from Parkinson, who grew up in Singapore and whose parents are Japanese and English, related to the origins of her first name. ‘My dad’s a huge Man United fan, so we basically became a huge Man United family and I was named after Eric Cantona,’ she said. Erica Meg Parkinson, who revealed she is named after Man United legend Eric Cantona, would become England's youngest debutant should she feature for the Lionesses ‘It was a pretty good player to be named after, except for the karate kicks. And my brother was named after Denis Law. I don’t think my mum had much of a say but it kind of worked out because we both play football now.’ Wiegman has been known to make her young players wait for their first appearance, although she broke that mould with Lucia Kendall getting a first start in her first call-up against Australia last year. If Parkinson were to make an appearance in one of the Lionesses’ upcoming World Cup qualifiers, she would become England’s youngest debutant by some distance. Euros heroine Michelle Agyemang currently holds that record, having been aged 19 years and 64 days when she came off the bench to score 41 seconds into her debut against Belgium last April. If Agyemang is anything to go by, the future is certainly bright for these young Lionesses.

Sports.title: England shoot themselves in the foot AGAIN as Argentina swoop for defence guru Shaun Edwards - Steve Borthwick and the RFU have missed a golden opportunity for much-needed coaching shake-up and this grave error will come back to haunt them
Sports.content:
England shoot themselves in the foot AGAIN as Argentina swoop for defence guru Shaun Edwards - Steve Borthwick and the RFU have missed a golden opportunity for much-needed coaching shake-up and this grave error will come back to haunt them

Shaun Edwards has signed with Argentina for next year’s World Cup, ending any chance the Wigan-born defence guru will join Steve Borthwick’s England set-up.

Edwards, 59, is the most decorated coach in rugby history and has won seven men’s Six Nations titles. He left a trophy-laden stint with France earlier this year and is currently working with England’s women’s side on a consultancy basis.

Edwards being under the RFU’s umbrella – albeit on a short-term basis – had raised the tantalising prospect of him transferring across to the country’s men’s team ahead of the 2027 global showpiece in Australia, especially after he told Daily Mail Sport last month he wanted to join the England set-up full-time: ‘I’m a proud Englishman and everybody loves to represent their country, don’t they? I’m no different.’

But that won’t be happening now. It is understood Edwards is disappointed there was no long-term offer to stay with England, though he is now looking forward to a new challenge in South America.

Edwards will begin his work with Argentina in time for their Nations Championship games away to Ireland, Italy and France next month. He has won more than 50 trophies across his playing and coaching career, and previously held successful backroom roles with Wasps, Wales and the British and Irish Lions before helping turn France into the northern hemisphere's dominant force.

With Argentina, he will work under the guidance of their head coach and former fly-half Felipe Contepomi and joined by Mario Ledesma, who will work with the team's forwards. Ledesma was previously head coach of the Pumas between 2018 and 2022. ‘I am delighted to join Felipe Contepomi, his coaching staff, and the Argentine team later this month, staying on through next year’s World Cup in Australia,’ Edwards said. ‘I have always admired the skill and quality of Argentine players and I hope to contribute some of my international experience to the team over the coming year.’

Shaun Edwards, widely regarded as one of the best defence coaches in world rugby, has slipped through England's fingers again

The 59-year-old has been in the RFU building for the last few weeks as a consultant for the Red Roses, but he will now join Argentina

Analysis: The RFU has shot itself in the foot again - letting Edwards slip away is a grave mistake

by Alex Bywater

By letting Shaun Edwards slip through their own net after finally getting him in an England tracksuit, the RFU has shot itself in the foot a year out from the next World Cup.

Edwards has a reputation for being the best in the world at what he does - and has the medals to prove it. It is barely believable and bordering on criminal that the RFU has not capitalised on what was a glorious opportunity to finally bring Edwards on board full-time without even having to pay compensation to another employer.

It is a grave mistake and represents rugby negligence at the heart of the organisation. Edwards’ aura, experience, no-nonsense methods and winning record would have been perfect for England right now as they look to get back on track after a stuttering 2026 so far and try to catch up with the game’s leading sides South Africa, France and New Zealand. His signing would also have been a good PR play for the RFU.

What a shame it is that the organisation hasn’t had the foresight to do it. It says a lot about Bill Sweeney, the RFU chief executive, and Borthwick as head coach that they haven’t grasped the nettle and offered Edwards a role. It was there on a plate.

Only this week, England’s current defence coach Joe El Abd confirmed he will be leaving his role after the World Cup, and is expected to take up a role at French Top14 side Clermont Auvergne.

If that's the case, Borthwick should have thanked his good friend and former room-mate at the University of Bath El Abd for his services, but told him in no uncertain terms that if he’s not with England for the long haul, he can move on now. El Abd should have been gone this month with Edwards replacing him.

It's Borthwick's prerogative to choose who he wants to work with. But it's impossible to ignore the fact that allowing Edwards to join another of England’s rivals will prove to be a huge error.

Let’s be honest here. England’s current set-up is badly underperforming. Earlier this year, the national team – which remains packed with talent – produced its worst-ever Six Nations with a fifth-place finish and a first loss at the hands of Italy. The environment is absolutely ripe for shaking up and the current coaching set-up is inexperienced at international level. Edwards would have been the perfect addition.

Edwards has brought in trophies wherever he has been, starting at Wasps and then bringing glory to Wales (left) and France (right)

Joe El Abd has just announced he will leave his role as assistant coach and is expected to move to Clermont. He should have been told to go now, with Edwards in to replace him

Edwards would have challenged Borthwick and his current assistants and made changes. Instead, England's loss is Argentina's gain

He would have challenged Borthwick and his current assistants and made changes. England’s women’s players have already spoken in glowing terms of the impact Edwards has made on them even in such a short time. He has done that wherever he has gone. Just think of what Edwards could have done with England’s men’s players across the next 12 months. Alas, those players and supporters will never know what might have been.

The RFU are understood to be happy with their men’s coaching team, having won 12 games in a row in 2025 before what they admit was a poor Six Nations. That was followed by a summer of two wins from three matches. There is also a feeling at the RFU that changing their backroom team a year out from a World Cup would be disruptive - though, of course, Borthwick himself replaced Eddie Jones as head coach just nine months before the most recent global showpiece.

Edwards not joining England is Argentina’s gain. The Pumas have plenty of talent, but sometimes lack structure and cohesion – qualities Edwards brings in spades, even if there have been suggestions in some quarters he is not now the force he was.

Argentina have a relatively easy World Cup task, having been drawn in Pool C alongside Fiji, Spain and Canada before likely facing Chile, Samoa or Tonga in the last 16 and then Ireland or Scotland in the quarter-finals. With Edwards in their camp, you never know what might happen for Argentina, who have reached the semi-finals in three of the last five World Cups.

England have, instead, decided to stick and not twist despite Edwards being keen to stay with them. The RFU’s failure to sign Edwards will undoubtedly go down badly with England supporters who were keen to see him work with his home nation. They are right to be annoyed. What a wasted opportunity.

Sports.title: Mercedes boss Toto Wolff hits out at 'lunatics hiding behind screens' who claim he favours Kimi Antonelli over George Russell: 'They should watch Teletubbies instead'
Sports.content:
Mercedes boss Toto Wolff hits out at 'lunatics hiding behind screens' who claim he favours Kimi Antonelli over George Russell: 'They should watch Teletubbies instead'

Toto Wolff has called internet trolls ‘lunatics’ and ‘hilarious’ for claiming that his Mercedes team are biased against George Russell and instead favour Kimi Antonelli.

The Silver Arrows boss was speaking ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix, which takes place on Sunday, and disputed all accusations of favouritism in the treatment of his two drivers, saying: ‘I don’t know what is going on. Do they think I have a button which says, “George engine failure now?”’

The Austrian’s defence came before a decent sprint qualifying in which Max Verstappen took a fine pole under Singapore’s lights. Russell was second best, Charles Leclerc third – and Antonelli seventh.

Russell is 84 points back from his team-mate Antonelli with a possible seven races remaining, depending on whether the final rounds in the Middle East go ahead at the end of November and start of December, given the conflict in the region.

Wolff continued: ‘Sometimes when I read what people write, I find it hilarious. These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they are abusing the team. I have zero understanding and respect for those who come up with these things.

‘Rather than watching Formula One, they should do Teletubbies or Mickey Mouse.

Toto Wolff has rubbished claims of favouritism within the Mercedes camp ahead of this week's Singapore Grand Prix

‘I have always tried to be the most balanced and transparent with the drivers. I look it as my challenge to keep it that way, always – and it was not easy with Lewis (Hamilton) and Nico (Rosberg) back in the day.

‘Integrity and respect are important for me. We have had Kimi since he was 11. He’s an integral part of the team.

‘It is very nice to see him grow into a position where he is fighting for the championship at such a young age, with the talent he has.

‘George has been with us since he was 17. He is someone I feel a lot of emotion and compassion for. We are very close.

‘We spent a lot of time with Carmen (Russell’s fiancée) and Susie (Wolff’s wife) off the track.

‘We travel together. We have coffee together. That is why it is annoying to have lunatics with no understanding of how the relationship works coming up with these kinds of accusations.

Kimi Antonelli is the runaway favourite for the championship while George Russell is snapping at his heels in second

‘Most important is that George and Kimi know how the team is.’

As for his pole, Verstappe, who was victorious in Malaysia last weekend, but has never won in Singapore, said: ‘It’s always close here. As for your lap, you’re pushing as hard as you think is possible, close to the walls in places.

‘Once we bolted on the soft tyres, it felt like the car was coming alive, but I did not expect this. Of course, I’m happy to be first.

‘We have been stronger in the last few races, but this track still highlights a few little weaknesses in the car, but we manage to drive with them as well as possible.’

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri will start the sprint fourth with his team-mate Lando Norris fifth and Hamilton sixth for Ferrari.

Sports.title: Attack coaches explain why PREM is now a try-fest with Saints and Bristol leading the way - and how it could help England: Tackle height changes, dynamic back threes, the cat-and-mouse maul and the jackal clampdown
Sports.content:
Attack coaches explain why PREM is now a try-fest with Saints and Bristol leading the way - and how it could help England: Tackle height changes, dynamic back threes, the cat-and-mouse maul and the jackal clampdown

One of Brendan Venter’s early moves as returning Saracens boss was to blast an intimidating chorus of howling wolves over the sound system as his players ran out for their first home game of the season against Sale on Sunday.

It was a nod to the club’s period of dominance, before the salary-cap scandal, when their gameplan was defined by their feared ‘Wolfpack’ defence. Venter is a trendsetter – not a trend follower – and he has ambitions to break the PREM’s cycle of attacking supremacy. The eccentric South African may be on a one-man crusade.

In the opening 10 games of this season, the winning team has scored 38 points on average. The number of tries is higher than ever and, if you ask PREM attack coaches, that should be a fillip for Steve Borthwick’s England.

Tweaks to the game’s laws mean 97 per cent of points now come from tries and conversions. Kicking for three points no longer stacks up. Northampton and Bristol lead the way with their high-intensity attacks but their rivals are catching up.

So, what has led to the PREM becoming a try-fest? Is it good for England? And can Venter stop it?

RULE CHANGES

‘There are loads of little governance changes that have made the game quicker,' Northampton attack coach Sam Vesty tells Daily Mail Sport.

Tommy Freeman of Northampton goes over to score in what has been a try-fest of a PREM season so far

Louis Rees-Zammit of Gloucester is top try-scorer with four so far

‘For example, a few years ago, you could stand with one foot off the pitch and one foot on to catch the ball and it would be out. You get a breather. They switched that rule so it's impossible to take the ball out now. Therefore, the ball's on the pitch for that little bit longer, there's more fatigue and more space to go and attack.

Tackle height plays a part too.

‘If you tackle high, you are now highly sanctioned,' Vesty adds. 'Therefore, people are tackling a bit lower. If you tackle lower, the player being tackled has their hands free and the ball is available to offload easily.

‘Plus, historically, people would say you're overplaying if you had the ball around the halfway line. But now we say keep playing because you're going to create something. It’s more productive to have the ball deeper on the pitch than it is to kick it away.

‘And then there's the offside line. It is being refereed more harshly than it has been previously. Therefore, there's a little bit more space.

'If you think 10 years ago, when Saracens were winning lots of stuff, a lot of that would have been based on a high kick game and a very good defence. The game has changed a lot since then and it’s refereed very differently as well.’

Freddie Steward of Leicester offloads the ball in the tackle. The lower tackle height means it is easier for players to keep the ball alive

ATTACKING INTENT

Financial pressure put the brakes on PREM clubs recruiting the biggest and most powerful players. Many instead moved to France or Japan in search of bigger salaries. There are fewer bulldozing carriers and a greater premium on movement, skill and sleight of hand. High-possession teams are thriving.

‘I watch all the line breaks and tries in the league every week,’ says Gloucester attack coach James Lightfoot-Brown, who has been named in the England A management team for this autumn.

‘There's a real intent to score from every possession, which maybe you wouldn't have seen before. Firstly, you have to credit the cohesion and the accuracy.

'Defences have not just stopped defending. Now teams are attacking with 15 players. Look at some of the movements off the ball from the back three to create numbers and then some of the speed off the floor from forwards.

‘There’s a desire to work. Modern back three players don't just stand on the wing anymore. When we played Exeter two weeks ago, Manny Feyi-Waboso was everywhere. Popping off nine, popping up on the other wing.

'We want to see the number on the back disappear from a back-three perspective when we have the ball. How quickly can we get an overload? How quickly can we get our best players on the ball?

'There are different nuances. These guys are no longer just runners. They can link, they can pop up on shoulders and get an additional pass or an offload. Northampton are the best at it. They are so fluid. If players want to get to the next level, they’ve got to get involvements.'

Exeter winger Manny Feyi-Waboso does not stick to the touchline but roams the park to get his hands on the ball

Rees-Zammit celebrates going over for another try

Bath’s new attack coach, Mike Prendergast, agrees.

‘Teams are looking for space and playing to edges,' he says. 'When you get into that opposition 22, a lot of tries are being scored on the edges. That’s quite an interesting trend.

‘There’s a huge amount of speed here. England have got a lot of very good, quick back-three players. I’ve seen that first hand over the last couple of weeks, including some of our own players at Bath.

'There are some exceptional athletes, especially out wide. A lot of the ball in play has been quite high in the first two rounds, which is great in terms of a spectacle.’

Teams have also been adapting their selection to maximise player output. Louis Rees-Zammit, for example, is the league's top try-scorer with four and has been prolific since he was shifted back to the wing by Bristol from full-back.

RISK-TAKING

‘Teams are taking more risks,' Lightfoot-Brown continues. 'They are running from deep and putting defences under pressure all the time. We used to see a couple of phases of probing, seeing what the defence is going to do.

'There's no probing going on at the moment. Teams are trying to score or they're kicking the ball. There's no middle ground, which makes for an exciting product.’

The warm weather conditions have promoted ball-passing and fast-track pitches which also help explain why 94 tries have already been scored.

‘The time of the year has an effect,’ says Prendergast. ‘The good weather means we’ve generally been playing with dry balls.'

'The time of the year has an effect,’ says Bath coach Mike Prendergast. ‘The good weather means we’ve generally been playing with dry balls'

BROKEN-FIELD BONUSES

The bulk of attacking opportunities now come from broken-field situations.

Last season, 29.3 per cent of attacking chances came from kick returns and 16 per cent from turnovers. Attack coaches have been encouraging their teams to react to unstructured defences, with harsher officiating of the breakdown ensuring the attacking team has the advantage.

‘Referees are not rewarding negative defensive actions as much as they used to,’ adds Lightfoot-Brown. ‘It’s becoming very clear that the jackal attempt has to be a genuine positive action. No hands on the floor.

'It can't just be a post-tackle effort to slow up the ball. We always want to reward good defensive work on the floor, but they’re not letting teams cynically slow things down.’

CAT AND MOUSE MAUL

But the most significant change this season has been around the maul. Defending forwards now have less freedom to disrupt the set-piece play, which means they have to commit more players to stop the drive. The byproduct has been additional space to attack.

‘The maul has come back into the game,’ says Prendergast. ‘Outside of the 22, the maul probably went away. Now we’re seeing a lot of mauls around the halfway line and up.

'The forwards coaches are looking to get it moving forwards or moving in towards the 15 so you can create space on the edge. The defence has to put numbers in to negate it or keep numbers out on their feet.

'It’s a bit of cat and mouse at the moment and everyone is trying to figure it out. It’s certainly something teams are looking to exploit.’

Nathan Michelow of Saracens controls the maul during the match against Leicester Tigers at Welford Road

SO, IS IT GOOD FOR ENGLAND?

Bigger collisions, better jackallers and stronger set-piece all change the game at international level but there seems to be a consensus that the level of PREM attacking play should boost the national side.

‘People follow what has been successful,’ says Vesty. ‘People look at the way Bordeaux and Toulouse keep the ball alive and score loads of points. The high tempo game has been successful so people go after that.

Marcus Smith scores a try for England - but can the PREM's attacking instincts rub off on Steve Borthwick's national team?

‘New Zealand are playing in a quite PREM style at the moment. Because the Springboks have so much power, if you try to take them on at that you are going to come second.

'The All Blacks have been high speed and high possession and they look really good at it. People talk about high numbers of phases but if you do it well then you don’t need loads of phases. They would rather have a crack as a first option and use a kicking game to move up the field as almost a second option.

‘The PREM is a better product but we need to make sure it doesn't become a basketball-style try-fest. The beauty of the game is that you can win in a lot of ways. If it just turns into a basketball, you score, we score, you score type affair, it gets a bit boring. We’re not there yet but we need to be mindful.’

As autumn descends and Venter gets his claws in deeper, the PREM will find out if the Wolfpack can make defence fashionable again.

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher and Mark Goldbridge trade 'policeman fraud', 'sell-out' and 'punditry career' jibes in awkward start to Gary Neville's big-money new podcast slate
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher and Mark Goldbridge trade 'policeman fraud', 'sell-out' and 'punditry career' jibes in awkward start to Gary Neville's big-money new podcast slate

Gary Neville's upgrade to his Overlap podcast empire appears to be off to a rocky start after pundit Jamie Carragher and YouTuber Mark Goldbridge exchanged jibes moments into the debut of their new show.

Carragher and Goldbridge went head-to-head at the start of a launch show for the Overlap Daily, the expansion of Neville's podcast network.

Liverpool legend Carragher was quick to scrutinise Goldbridge, who has risen to fame in recent years with his outspoken views on Manchester United on his YouTube channels.

Carragher highlighted Goldbridge's real name – Brent Cleminson – and the lingering claims that he is actually a Nottingham Forest supporter in the opening exchanges on the show.

'Are you going to be yourself on the show? I keep reading that you're not going to be yourself, you've sold out,' Carragher quipped, prompting laughter from Neville.

Goldbridge responded: 'I was actually thinking on the way up, you know, your punditry career is a bit like your playing career, isn't it?'

Mark Goldbridge and Jamie Carragher are pictured on Gary Neville's new 'Overlap Daily' show

Carragher referred to Goldbridge by his real name - 'Brent' - and questioned his background

'Go on, have you got your lines ready and all that? I've got my lines ready for you,' Carragher replied.

'Used to be a policeman, didn't you?'

After Goldbridge responded 'yeah' Carragher joked the presenter was a 'fraud' to provoke more laughter from Neville.

'This is why I'm here, for the Man City stuff,' Goldbridge said, referencing the recent independent commission decision to find City guilty of financial rule breaches, which the club has appealed.

'Yeah, but you are the biggest fraud though, aren't you, when you think about it?' Carragher continued, with Goldbridge responding 'Why's this?'

'Your name's Mark, but it's really Brent, and you say you're a Man United fan, but you're really a Nottingham Forest fan,' Carragher said.

'You know what I mean, you want to start with that?'

The exchange continued with Goldbridge referencing Carragher wearing an Everton kit, having supported the club as a youngster, before ultimately becoming a club legend at their arch rivals Liverpool.

Neville's The Overlap, majority owned by Global, earlier this year paid a seven-figure sum for Goldbridge's The United Stand and That's Football YouTube channels.

The move has seen The United Stand be extended to include 'Stick to United', which will feature former players and journalists, with the show fronted by Goldbridge and Wayne Rooney.

Goldbridge's That's Football was also rebranded to Overlap Daily as part of the deal, with the YouTuber continuing to broadcast his watchalongs on the channel.

He was also confirmed as host of the Overlap Daily's Friday show, with Carragher, Joe Hart and Peter Schmeichel set to be regular co-hosts.

Sports.title: Keely Hodgkinson defends her 'sexy' all-black running catsuit which feels like she's 'wearing nothing' - despite being banned from using it at Olympics
Sports.content:
Keely Hodgkinson defends her 'sexy' all-black running catsuit which feels like she's 'wearing nothing' - despite being banned from using it at Olympics

Keely Hodgkinson's team has admitted her all-black Nike catsuit is a 'statement piece' but insists the outfit is not a gimmick and can help her run faster.

The Olympic 800m champion debuted the suit at the all-female Athlos meet last month in London.

Hodgkinson's suit has a tight hood over her head with a gap for her ponytail and covers her in the sleek material from palms to ankles – except for her almost entirely bare back – and covered in strategically placed, small iridescent spikes.

The British star admitted following the race, which she won in one minute and 56.40 seconds, that she wanted to feel 'a little bit sexy' while wearing the suit.

Hodgkinson's coach Jenny Meadows has now revealed that Hodgkinson, who she described as a 'fashion icon', had first revealed the suit to her and her husband and fellow coach Trevor Painter at the start of the year in South Africa.

'Nike had been speaking to Keely about the suit, Keely is an innovator herself. She's always wanted to do things differently, she's a big lover of fashion,' Meadows told Athletics Weekly.

Keely Hodgkinson's team have admitted her all-black Nike catsuit is a 'statement piece' but insisted the outfit is not a gimmick

Hodgkinson reportedly claimed it felt like she was 'wearing nothing' while running in the catsuit

The Olympic 800 metres champion wore the suit for the first time at the all-female Athlos meet last month in London.

'She shouted over: "Trev and Jen. What do you think of this?"

'My initial reaction was like: "Oh, you've got to be brave to wear that". And Trevor was kind of like: "Yeah, you look Catwoman. Go for it. It's so you".

'Nike were so respectful of us as coaches because they obviously wanted us to be really, really comfortable with it.

'Because at the end of the day, we think about performance and it's not just what you look like.

'You've got to think: Is it faster or is it just a gimmick?

'You've actually got to walk out in front of an audience the first time and you've got to win in that thing. It's a statement piece.'

Hodgkinson initially planned to wear the suit at the London leg of the Diamond League, but opted to delay the unveiling after suffering a knee injury in a fall in the build-up to the event.

The star had tested the suit in the United States and believed it had helped her to move despite inflammation.

Hodgkinson said post-race that she wanted to feel 'a little bit sexy' while wearing the suit

Keely Hodgkinson will not be allowed to wear her all-black Nike catsuit at the Olympics in 2028

'She was literally like: "Guys in this speed suit, I can run",' Meadows said.

'She says it feels like she's not wearing anything. She says: 'Honestly, it feels just so light. I can flow.'

The one-of-a-kind super suit, which seemingly takes inspiration from Cathy Freeman's iconic Sydney 2000 number, was engineered by Nike specifically for Hodgkinson.

When asked if she and all her competitors will be wearing the style in LA in two years' time, Hodgkinson gave an answer that suggested it could be a possibility.

'We might know some things that people don't,' Hodgkinson said last month. 'It was a test out there. This is not something we haven't seen before.'

Hodgkinson, though, will be unable to wear the Nike gear, due to Team GB's partnership with Adidas which spans back to the Los Angeles 1984 Olympics.

British athletes are required to wear the team racing kit when competing for the nation at the Games. 'Technical' kit, such as running spikes, are an exception to the rule.

If Nike does roll out the full-body 'Zero-Distraction Speed Suit' to its other athletes, and World Athletics ratifies it for use at the Olympics, then Hodgkinson may indeed watch her competitors take to the track in the eye-catching black catsuit she brought back to life. But she wouldn't be able to race them in it.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

This article originally appeared in The Athletic.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

YouTube YouTube , which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies. You can use the buttons below to amend your preferences to enable YouTube cookies or to allow those cookies just once.
