Welcoming the new members, Yilwatda said: “Let me welcome all of you to our great party and thank you for taking this decisive action. You are not just changing a platform, but you are coming in to join us in reinforcing our belief in President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and his Renewed Hope Agenda.”

He then went through what he described as Tinubu’s record of backing northern politicians, starting in 2007.

“If anybody has worked for the unity of Nigeria, it is President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, in 2007, supported Atiku to become the president of Nigeria because he believed then that power should move from the South to the North,” he said.

Yilwatda said Tinubu did the same in 2011 with the present National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu, who ran as a presidential candidate under the Action Congress of Nigeria ACN.

“He supported and sponsored his network to ensure that he became the president of Nigeria. He’s from the North,” he said.

In 2015, he said, Tinubu “stood behind President Buhari” with the argument that “For the unity of Nigeria and social cohesion, power should move back to the North because we lost President Yar’Adua.”

He added that in 2019, “when a lot of the northern elders and politicians left Buhari, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu stood for him and led a reconciliation committee that brought Nigerians together to support President Buhari.”

Yilwatda told the defectors that Tinubu had also delivered for the North, citing road and rail projects.

“Most times, they deceive you. They say, ‘What has President Bola Ahmed Tinubu done for the North?’ They keep on saying that,” he said.

He listed the Abuja–Kaduna–Kano road, the Kano–Maiduguri road, and rail links from Kano to Maradi and from Kaduna to Kano, among other projects he said are under way.

“Why did he spend that kind of infrastructure in the South? He’s doing it for us, and we said he has done nothing for us,” he said.

Yilwatda also took on the opposition’s record and promises. He said he had heard Atiku say that the president had blocked all the ports.

“We forgot when we opened those ports long ago. They don’t even read the news. They don’t even follow what’s happening in the country,” he said.

On the opposition’s pledge of a N500 per litre discount on oil, he said it would cost about N20 trillion a year, “about half of our budget as a country.” He argued that government does not have the crude to give, since about 60 per cent of Nigerian oil production is under joint ventures in which the Federal Government holds only part. “How do you make a promise of what you don’t have?” he asked.

He also made claims about the privatisation of public assets. He said that the Aluminium Smelting Company in Akwa Ibom was built for about $3.5 billion, and “Atiku sold it for less than 130 million US dollars, less than four per cent of the total cost of building the company.”

He said the steel companies at Ajaokuta and in Delta were each built for about $1.5 billion and the Delta one was sold for $30 million.

“Away with that man that sold out the future. 3.5 billion for just less than 130 million, 1.5 billion for 30 million,” he said.

The party also presented the candidates who defected. A party member, Dr. Princess Aslam Aliyu, said she had brought 12 African Democratic Congress (ADC) House of Assembly candidates into the APC about two weeks ago. On Friday, she presented 11 House of Representatives and House of Assembly candidates from the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and the ADC.

She said their candidacies were “verifiable on the INEC portal and INEC records”, referring to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

“These are not merely defections; they are clear demonstrations of confidence in President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, and the Renewed Hope Agenda as a pathway to national recovery.

“In two weeks, we are bringing 23 opposition candidates back to the APC. If politics is a contest of influence, then our scoreboard currently reads two-zero in our favour,” she added.

Earlier, National Secretary of the party, Sen. Ajibola Basiru, said the APC was not aiming to turn Nigeria into a one-party state.

“So, most of the time, when they say APC wants to turn Nigeria into a one-party state, we are not. That’s not our aspiration,” he said.

He added that if that is what the party’s hard work produces, “we cannot deny that because we have a functional secretariat.”

Basiru also criticised the ADC vice-presidential candidate, Rotimi Amaechi, over his reported comments on the seaport project in Ogun State.

“And yesterday, I heard Rotimi Amaechi saying that we should not have done a seaport in Ogun State because we are only doing a seaport in Ogun State because the president wants to make money from it.

“How can you say that a developmental project, which is being embarked on in support of a leading economy, should not have been done because we want to politicise it?” he asked.

On fuel subsidy, he said: “We are not going back to subsidy. It’s gone and gone forever.” He also defended the student loan scheme, the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), saying more than 1.4 million students had benefited. He faulted former senator Dino Melaye for criticising the N20,000 monthly allowance paid to beneficiaries, saying students’ fees are paid in addition to it.

World.title: 2023 election loss led me to become pastor — Banky W
World.content:
Nigerian singer, filmmaker and politician Bankole Wellington, popularly known as Banky W, has said his defeat in the 2023 House of Representatives election left him heartbroken and prompted him to seek a new direction, eventually leading him into pastoral ministry.

Banky W disclosed this while reflecting on his first anniversary as a pastor in the United States, where he said the electoral setback forced him to surrender his plans to God and reconsider his purpose.

“In 2023 I lost an election. And while the experience inspired me in many ways, it also broke my heart into a million little pieces,” he wrote on Instagram.

The entertainer said he turned to God after the election to seek direction and surrender his ambitions.

“When the dust settled, I took those pieces back to God. And I surrendered,” he said.

According to him, the experience made him question whether he should focus on leadership, entertainment, business or ministry.

However, he said he eventually realised that he did not have to choose one path at the expense of the others.

“And somewhere along the way, I realised that I was asking God to choose between things He had never asked me to separate,” Banky W said.

“It wasn’t either/or. It was all of the above.”

He added that his transition into pastoral ministry had changed his understanding of purpose, saying he now saw his responsibilities as expanding rather than narrowing.

“Turns out, God wasn’t trying to put me in a box. He was expanding my assignment,” he said.

Banky W explained that he now combines his responsibilities as a pastor and professor with his work as a filmmaker, musician and entrepreneur.

He also recalled joking about his possible future in ministry, saying he had previously insisted that the letter “P” in his name, P. Banks, stood for professor rather than pastor.

“I used to joke that the ‘P’ in P. Banks stood for Professor, not Pastor. I guess God heard and said, ‘Why not both?’” he wrote.

The singer also spoke about the challenges of travelling regularly between Lagos and the Washington, DC, Maryland and Virginia area to manage his various responsibilities.

“Constantly travelling back and forth between Lagos and the DMV isn’t always easy. But has it been worth it? Absolutely,” he said.

Reflecting on the past year, Banky W said the experience had taught him that setbacks could lead to unexpected opportunities.

“One year later, I’m reminded that sometimes what feels like the end of your story is really just God turning the page,” he said.

“The election didn’t go the way I hoped. But God’s plans for my life are bigger than the plans I had for myself.”

Banky W contested the 2023 House of Representatives election to represent Eti-Osa Federal Constituency in Lagos State on the platform of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP). He lost to Thaddeus Attah of the Labour Party.

World.title: DSS Arraigns Terrorism Suspect, Court Orders Detention in Kuje
World.content:
A Federal High Court in Abuja has remanded a terrorism suspect, Muhammad Ibrahim, at the Kuje Correctional Centre until November 16, 2026, fixed for the beginning of his trial.

Ibrahim was arraigned by the Department of State Services, DSS, on a four-count charge of terrorism-related activities, unlawful possession and transportation of ammunition, failure to disclose information about gun-running activities, and identity fraud.

He is accused of conveying 170 rounds of AK-47 live ammunition concealed in a cooler to one Imrana Halilu in Dankama village, Katsina State, in February 2025.

The DSS also accused Ibrahim of knowingly providing logistical support to terrorist groups by transporting the ammunition in furtherance of terrorist activities.

In another count, the defendant was accused of failing to disclose information about gunrunning activities to law enforcement or security officers, despite allegedly possessing information that could assist in the apprehension and prosecution of those involved.

The fourth charge is that Ibrahim, described in the charge as a Nigerien citizen, fraudulently obtained a Nigerian National Identity Management Commission identity card linked to a National Identification Number (NIN).

The alleged offences are said to contravene provisions of the Terrorism (Prevention and Prohibition) Act, 2022, and the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) Act, 2015.

Following the defendant’s plea, Justice Salim Ibrahim adjourned the matter to November 16, 2026, for the commencement of trial.

World.title: Foundation Inaugurates New Facilities at Ogun School, Boosts Learning Environment
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare

Codix Group, through its charity arm, Codix Charity Foundation, Wednesday inaugurated new and upgraded educational facilities at Isanbi Comprehensive Secondary School, Ilishan-Remo, Ogun State, in an effort aimed at improving the learning environment and supporting student welfare.

The intervention comprises two new classroom blocks, 10 desktop computers, new tables and chairs, eight toilet facilities for students and teachers, and the refurbishment of the junior school principal’s office.

Speaking at the inauguration, the Ogun State Commissioner for Education, Science and Technology, Prof. Abayomi Arigbabu, described the project as a demonstration of the positive impact of government-private sector collaboration in advancing education.

Arigbabu said education remained the bedrock of sustainable development, stressing that meaningful progress in schools required active synergy between government and visionary private sector partners.

He also emphasised the role of the alumni in supporting the development of their former schools, describing the intervention as evidence of the enduring bond between old students and their alma mater.

“This landmark gesture beautifully exemplifies how deeply old students cherish their alma mater and remain an integral, devoted part of its growth and success for generations,” he stated.

He commended the Executive Chairman and Group Chief Executive of Codix Holdings Limited, Mr. Sammy Ogunjimi, and his team for setting what he described as a remarkable benchmark in corporate social responsibility.

In his remarks, Ogunjimi said the intervention was inspired by his personal connection to the school and his conviction that education is one of the most important investments society could make in its future.

Recalling his years at the institution, he said his experiences and memories of the school motivated him to give back to his alma mater.

According to him, “Creating an enabling environment for learning was essential to helping young people develop their potential.”

The chairman said the foundation’s intervention formed part of its broader commitment to supporting communities through initiatives focused on human capital development and improving the welfare of young people.

“Better learning environments can inspire students, strengthen their confidence and create opportunities for them to participate more effectively in the future economy,” Ogunjimi said.

Also speaking, the representative of the Olofin of Ilishan-Remo and Baale of Ago-Ilara, Dr. Muftau Oyegunle, commended Ogunjimi, the Board of Trustees, Codix Group and Codix Charity Foundation for the intervention.

He described the transformation at the school as a demonstration of what could be achieved when corporate citizenship was combined with community development.

World.title: We Are Changing Story to Development in Niger Delta, Says Ebie
World.content:
Sylvester Idowu

Chairman of the board of the Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC), Mr Chiedu Ebie, has said the commission will continue to transform the renewed hope agenda of the Federal Government into reality in the region with its development projects across the region.

Ebie, in a statement by his media aide, Jerome-Mario Utomi, reflected on the massive electrification jobs, road rehabilitation projects, educational scholarship provision and several other development driven initiatives of the commission in the region.

The statement read: “The Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC) is increasingly emerging as a critical instrument for translating President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda into tangible development across the Niger Delta, with its growing portfolio of infrastructure and human-capital projects offering a compelling narrative ahead of the 2027 general election.

“From roads and bridges to electricity, scholarships, youth empowerment and digital skills acquisition, the commission’s interventions are strengthening the Federal Government’s development footprint in a region whose stability and prosperity remain vital to Nigeria’s economic growth.

“This development featured prominently during a recent visit by the NDDC Governing Board Chairman, Mr Chiedu Ebie; Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer, Chief Samuel Ogbuku; and Executive Director, Corporate Services, Hon. Ifedayo ‘Abena’ Abegunde, to President Tinubu. The delegation briefed Mr. President on the commission’s programmes and achievements.

“At the heart of the NDDC’s strategy is a commitment to align its operations with the Renewed Hope Agenda, translating policy objectives into projects that directly improve the lives of the people.

“Ogbuku has in like manner reaffirmed this commitment, by noting that the commission’s priority is to deliver development, complete abandoned projects and accelerate infrastructure delivery in line with the president’s directives.

“The figures provide an indication of the scale of the task. According to the commission, its project database contains more than 21,000 projects and programmes, with over 9,000 completed across its 13 mandate states and 18 development sectors.

“Among its flagship interventions is the 1.2-kilometre Kaa-Ataba Bridge in Rivers State, linking Khana and Andoni Local Government Areas. The bridge is expected to ease transportation difficulties, connect previously underserved communities and stimulate commerce. Its completion reflects the administration’s emphasis on turning inherited infrastructure commitments into functional assets.

“Other strategic projects, including the Benin-Sapele Expressway, Kaa-Ataba Road and Bonny Ring Road, further demonstrate the importance of sustained investment in regional connectivity.

“Beyond infrastructure, the NDDC’s Light Up the Niger Delta initiative deploys solar-powered streetlights to improve security, encourage night-time economic activities and support community stability. Education, postgraduate scholarships, school facilities and targeted empowerment programmes for women, young people and persons with disabilities also feature prominently in its development agenda.

“These interventions reinforce a fundamental political reality: government performance becomes meaningful to citizens when policies translate into visible improvements in their daily lives.

“Ebie, the Governing Board Chairman, has at different times and places stressed the importance of communicating development outcomes and ensuring that communities experience the benefits of government programmes. His position underscores the need for projects that citizens can see, use and evaluate, particularly in a region long burdened by infrastructure deficits.

“By linking the Commission’s interventions to the broader transformation objectives of the Tinubu administration, Ebie has also advocated sustained support for the President’s Renewed Hope Agenda ahead of 2027. The underlying argument is straightforward: continuity becomes more persuasive when it is supported by measurable results and projects that address longstanding community needs.

“Ogbuku has equally made his political position clear. In November 2024, while dismissing speculation that he intended to contest the Bayelsa governorship election, he declared that his priority was to serve the Niger Delta and support President Tinubu. He indicated that, if he had a political ambition, it would be to work for the President’s re-election in 2027.

“His emphasis on service delivery is significant. Political endorsements may communicate loyalty, but completed projects provide the tangible evidence that can make a government’s development claims credible.

“In April 2026, NDDC’s leadership/management again briefed President Tinubu on progress with the Commission’s legacy projects, attributing the achievements to the support of the Presidency and reaffirming the directive to complete projects for the benefit of Niger Delta residents.

“The commission’s partnerships, including collaboration with Nigeria LNG Limited on strategic infrastructure, also show how institutional cooperation can expand development opportunities and accelerate project delivery.

“As the 2027 elections approach, the NDDC’s performance could strengthen the Tinubu administration’s appeal in the Niger Delta. Better roads can reduce travel costs and improve the movement of goods; reliable electricity can support businesses; and scholarships and digital skills programmes can widen opportunities for young people.

“These benefits matter in a region central to Nigeria’s oil and gas economy, where development, investment and peace have national implications.

“The political implications are clear. While the NDDC’s performance alone cannot determine the outcome of the 2027 elections, sustained delivery can provide President Tinubu with a stronger development record to present to voters in the region.”

With Ebie providing board-level leadership and Ogbuku driving management and project execution, the commission has an opportunity to demonstrate that the Renewed Hope Agenda can produce practical results where they matter most.

“Ultimately, the strongest argument for continuity is performance. As NDDC continues to sustain its momentum, completes strategic projects and expands opportunities for Niger Delta communities, its achievements could become a significant asset to President Tinubu’s 2027 re-election campaign,” he said.

World.title: Gbemi Olateru-Olagbegi Returns with Season 2 of ‘The Fashion Roundtable’
World.content:
Media personality and entrepreneur Gbemi Olateru-Olagbegi has returned with Season 2 of The Fashion Roundtable, a talk show dedicated to real, unfiltered conversations with key players shaping Nigeria’s fashion industry. The new season premiered on Thursday, October 8, 2026.

Season 2 builds on the show’s mission to look beyond the glitz and glamour. It offers creative minds an intimate space to share their behind-the-scenes stories while documenting the complexities and business realities of the industry.

Speaking on the show’s return, creator and host Gbemi Olateru-Olagbegi shared, “Season 2 is about going deeper. Fashion in Nigeria is a business, a craft, and a community, but the people behind it rarely get to tell their full story.”

This season, the media personality will have conversations with a wide range of professionals from designers and retailers to photographers, publicists, and agents, including renowned designer Weizdhurm Franklyn, Sharon Ademefun, Deco, acclaimed photographer Kola Oshalusi, PR and communications experts Njideka Akabogu and Elizabeth Osho, Beth Model Management founder Elohor Isiorho, and fashion influencer Ozinna Anumudu, to “talk honestly about what it takes to build and sustain a career in this industry.”

The premiere episode aired at 6pm, with new episodes released weekly across major streaming and podcast platforms, including YouTube, Apple Podcasts, and Spotify.

World.title: Emee Freda Returns to Felabration as an Artiste in Her Own Right
World.content:
Freda Francis, popularly known as Emee Freda, will return to the New Afrika Shrine in Lagos for Felabration 2026, 12 years after beginning her journey there as a dancer and backup singer for Afrobeat musician Femi Kuti.

This time, she returns as a singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist with a growing catalogue of music and a career spanning dance, acting, modelling and fashion.

“I’m returning to the Afrikan Shrine as a matured artiste to honour Fela and Femi, not as a student anymore. I am coming with so much love,” she said.

Her return resonates with this year’s Felabration theme, “Who Are You?”, drawn from Fela Anikulapo-Kuti’s 1971 album, Fela’s London Scenes. For Emee, the question offers an opportunity to reflect on an artistic journey defined by versatility and reinvention.

Her musical foundation was laid at the Performing Arts, Entrepreneurship, Fashion and Technology Innovations (PEFTI) academy in Lagos, where she studied Music Technology and Production. She subsequently gained live-performance experience as a backup singer and dancer at the Shrine and through performances with the Robots Band.

Emee began releasing music officially in 2015 with the singles “Peace and Confession” and “God of Bad Boys and Girls”. Her reggae and conscious-music sound earned her exposure on platforms including Jamaica’s Reggae Revolution Show, Future Atlas Radio in Florida and Kriss Radio in London. Other releases include “Arise”, “Babylon City” and “Tragedy”.

Her latest single, “Story”, marks a shift towards Afrobeat. Produced by Mr Dehniece Etukudo of Audio Factory, the song has received radio and club rotation. Her earlier single, “Ekondo”, was produced by Lemmy Jackson.

Beyond singing, Emee plays the guitar and has demonstrated proficiency with the flute and saxophone. In 2018, she founded Planet 9, a live band that has performed at events including the Nigerian Reggae Festival in Lagos, Industry Night Lagos and Christmas Unplugged in Akwa Ibom.

Her creative pursuits also extend to fashion and acting. She contested in the Most Beautiful Girl in Nigeria pageant in 2012, was named Model of the Year in a reality television competition organised by Deji Bakare in collaboration with Silverbird Television the following year, and later walked at Nigerian Fashion Week. She also featured in television productions including This Life and Super Story.

At Felabration, Emee is expected to perform some of her newer songs, bringing her journey full circle at the venue where she began developing her craft.

For the artiste, the return represents more than a performance. It is an opportunity to honour the experience that shaped her while presenting the artist she has become—one whose creative identity continues to evolve beyond the roles with which she first became known.

World.title: SERAP, Deputy Director’s Appeals Against ₦101m Defamation Judgment Stalled Over Late Filing of Brief
World.content:
The planned hearing of appeals filed by the Incorporated Trustees of the Socio-economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) and its Deputy Director, Kolawole Oluwadare, against a ₦101 million defamation judgment was stalled at the Court of Appeal, Abuja, on Friday following the late filing of one of the appellants’ briefs.

The appeals are against a May 5 judgment of the High Court of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), which held that SERAP and Oluwadare defamed two officials of the Department of State Services (DSS) through a false publication made on September 10, 2024.

At Friday’s proceedings, the first appeal, marked CA/ABJ/CV/1114/2026 and filed by SERAP, was heard by a three-member panel of the appellate court presided over by Justice Danlami Senchi.

However, when the second appeal, marked CA/ABJ/CV/1105/2026 and filed by Oluwadare, was called, his lawyer, Hannah Ayanwale, told the court that the appeal was not ripe for hearing.

Ayanwale explained that her client had only filed his brief on Thursday and served it on the respondents on Friday morning, shortly before the court commenced sitting.

The disclosure reportedly angered the justices, who expressed displeasure over the lawyer’s failure to inform the court earlier that Oluwadare’s appeal, which is a sister appeal to SERAP’s, was not ready for hearing.

The court, however, set aside the proceedings earlier conducted on SERAP’s appeal, holding that the two appeals, having emanated from the same judgment, ought to be heard together.

It subsequently adjourned the hearing of both appeals until October 13 and ordered the respondents to file their briefs on October 12, while the appellant is to file a reply brief before the next adjourned date.

The appeals arose from a suit marked CV/4547/2024, filed by two DSS officials, Sarah John and Gabriel Ogundele, who accused SERAP and Oluwadare of making false claims on the organisation’s website and social media platforms.

The claimants alleged that the defendants published claims that they invaded SERAP’s Abuja office on September 9, 2024, and subjected its officials to harassment.

In his May 5 judgment, Justice Halilu Yusuf of the High Court of the FCT held that the claimants had presented sufficient evidence to establish all the ingredients of defamation.

The judge rejected the defence of justification raised by SERAP and Oluwadare, ruling that they failed to provide evidence that their publications were not based on falsehood.

He noted that terms such as “invasion,” “forceful entry” and “harassment” were used inaccurately, adding that the defendants had admitted during the trial that the DSS officials did not forcefully enter SERAP’s premises or brandish any weapon.

Justice Yusuf held that the publications injured the claimants’ reputations in their professional capacities and standing in society.

“Having been unable to establish invasion and harassment, the defence of justification fails. There is no doubt that the publication affected the claimants mentally and psychologically,” the judge said.

He stressed the need for SERAP and its officials to exercise care and due diligence before releasing information to the public.

The judge added that, in exercising their right to publish information on social media, the defendants should be mindful of the rights of others, particularly government agencies and their officials.

Justice Yusuf also dismissed the defendants’ objection to the competence of the suit, holding that the claimants had the requisite locus standi to institute the action and that the court had jurisdiction to hear it.

He further held that the claimants did not have to be expressly named in the publication for defamation to be established.

According to the judge, the defendants failed to take steps to remove the allegedly injurious publication after the claimants complained about its inaccuracy.

The court consequently found the publications defamatory and awarded ₦100 million in damages against SERAP and Oluwadare, in addition to ₦1 million as the cost of prosecuting the suit.

Justice Yusuf also ordered the defendants to publish a public apology on SERAP’s website, X handle, two national daily newspapers and two television stations.

He further ruled that the judgment sum would attract 10 per cent interest per annum from the date of the judgment until full payment.

World.title: Chinese Embassy Explains One-China Principle to Nigerian Media Executives
World.content:
The Chinese Embassy has explained its One-China Principle, urging the Nigerian media to distinguish between reporting on Taiwan and descriptions that suggest the island is a sovereign country separate from China.

Speaking during a meeting with media executives in Lagos, Mr. Xu Fan, Director of Bilateral Relations and Commerce at the Chinese Consulate General in Lagos,

said China’s position on Taiwan was rooted in historical records, international agreements and the diplomatic framework established after the Second World War.

He cited United Nations General Assembly Resolution 2758 of 1971 and Nigeria’s diplomatic recognition of the People’s Republic of China, while maintaining that the One-China Principle remained the political foundation of diplomatic relations between Beijing and Abuja.

Fan noted that Nigeria reaffirmed its commitment to the principle during President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s state visit to China in September 2024.

He clarified that China did not object to Nigerian media reporting on Taiwan but was concerned about terminology that could be interpreted as recognising the island as a sovereign state.

The explanation prompted a robust exchange with Nigerian media executives, who stressed the importance of editorial independence and the need to preserve the freedom of journalists to report issues in the public interest.

The discussion, which also examined Nigeria-China relations, trade, investment and media cooperation, underscored the importance of dialogue between Chinese diplomatic institutions and Nigerian media organisations.

The session was convened by Hon. Peter Ogbonna Eze, representative of Buffalo and Bay Media, and featured Ambassador Anderson Madubike, a former Nigerian High Commissioner to Australia, former Consul General in Shanghai, China, and former Chargé d’Affaires to South Africa.

Earlier, Eze described Nigeria-China relations as a partnership that had expanded beyond traditional diplomatic engagement to encompass infrastructure, trade, education, technology, agriculture, investment and people-to-people exchanges.

He urged media organisations to report the relationship with accuracy, balance and context, stressing that informed public discourse was essential to maximising the benefits of bilateral cooperation.

“The media does not merely report events. It shapes how societies understand countries, people, policies and opportunities,” Eze said.

Madubike, on his part, drawing on his diplomatic experience, described Nigeria-China relations as robust, citing the extensive diplomatic, commercial and infrastructure ties between the two countries.

He said the media had a critical role in sustaining diplomatic relations by shaping public perceptions, providing reliable information and promoting mutual understanding.

“Diplomacy opens doors, but the media helps to keep those doors open,” he said.

According to him, treaties and government agreements alone cannot sustain long-term relationships between nations without public understanding and engagement.

The diplomat also stressed the importance of reporting the human dimension of Nigeria-China relations, including the experiences of Nigerian students, entrepreneurs and traders in China, as well as Chinese investors, engineers and business operators in Nigeria.

He noted that credible information about markets, regulations, infrastructure, incentives and investment opportunities could encourage business partnerships and strengthen economic ties.

The interaction also featured concerns about the trade imbalance between Nigeria and China, import dependence and complaints by Nigerian traders that some Chinese businesses were competing with them in the retail market.

Responding, Xu acknowledged the concerns but argued that the solution should involve establishing clearer regulatory boundaries between wholesale and retail operations rather than excluding Chinese businesses from Nigeria.

He said the Chinese Embassy had engaged Chinese traders, market authorities and other stakeholders to explore practical solutions.

Xu also advocated a shift from a relationship dominated by trade in finished products towards greater Chinese investment in local manufacturing.

He said Chinese companies could establish more factories and production facilities in Nigeria to create jobs, transfer skills and contribute to the country’s industrial development.

The Chinese diplomat disclosed that bilateral trade reached approximately $28 billion in 2025, describing the figure as evidence of the growing economic relationship between both countries.

He also said China had become Nigeria’s largest market for engineering contractors, its second-largest export market and China’s third-largest trading partner in Africa.

Xu further highlighted China’s decision to extend zero-tariff treatment to 53 African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations, including Nigeria.

He said the policy presented opportunities for Nigerian agricultural products, including sesame, cashew nuts and cocoa, to gain greater access to the Chinese market, subject to applicable rules of origin, inspection and quarantine requirements.

He urged Nigerian businesses to improve product quality, strengthen branding and take advantage of opportunities in the Chinese market.

The issue of illegal mining involving some Chinese nationals in Nigeria also featured prominently in the discussions.

Xu distinguished between law-abiding Chinese businesses and individuals involved in illegal activities, insisting that violations of Nigerian law were unacceptable to the Chinese government and diplomatic authorities.

He said the Chinese Embassy and relevant authorities were cooperating with Nigerian institutions by providing information and supporting efforts to identify Chinese nationals involved in illegal mining.

According to him, the Chinese government would not shield individuals found to have violated Nigerian laws.

Participants also called for deeper Chinese investment in manufacturing, technology transfer, industrial development and local value addition, arguing that bilateral cooperation should deliver more benefits to Nigeria beyond infrastructure development and the importation of finished goods.

The discussion highlighted the need for a partnership that promotes local production, employment, skills development and technological advancement.

On media freedom, Nigerian executives reiterated that editorial independence remained a fundamental principle of journalism and that disagreements over sensitive diplomatic issues should be addressed through dialogue, clarification and the right of reply.

In his concluding remarks, Xu described Nigerian media organisations as “partners and friends, not enemies.”

He offered to strengthen cooperation with Nigerian media through professional exchanges, training programmes, seminars, media delegations and other institutional initiatives.

He said Chinese authorities would continue to facilitate opportunities for Nigerian journalists to visit China, experience its development and gain a deeper understanding of its society, culture, economy and political system.

Xu also invited participating media organisations to propose practical joint initiatives, including media programmes, publications and professional exchange projects.

The engagement highlighted the opportunities and challenges in Nigeria-China relations, particularly the need to reconcile diplomatic sensitivities with the principles of editorial independence and responsible journalism.

Participants agreed that sustained dialogue, accurate reporting and stronger people-to-people engagement were essential to building mutual trust and ensuring that the bilateral relationship delivered greater benefits to both countries.

World.title: UNICEF Launches ‘Neem Tree Dialogue’ to Protect Children
World.content:
John Shiklam in Kaduna

The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has launched ‘The Neem Tree Dialogue’, an initiative aimed at preventing violence against children and promoting positive parenting in five communities in Zaria, Kaduna State.

Speaking at the launch yesterday in Zaria, UNICEF’s Chief of Field Office, Kaduna, Dr. Gerida Birukila, said the initiative would strengthen families and mobilise communities to protect children from abuse, neglect and exploitation.

“We cannot build peaceful, prosperous and resilient communities while children continue to experience violence, neglect, exploitation, and deprivation,” she said.

Birukila said positive parenting requires families to recognise children as individuals with rights, dignity, potential, and voices.

“Positive parenting is not simply about changing how parents discipline their children. It is about transforming the way families understand children, as individuals with rights, dignity, potential, and voices that deserve to be heard,” she said.

She also called on traditional institutions to use their influence to challenge harmful practices and promote child protection.

Birukila maintained that the protection of children is not the responsibility of government or development organisations alone, but a shared responsibility of families, communities, traditional and religious institutions, government and society as a whole.

She described the ‘Neem Tree Dialogue’ as a platform for communities to discuss harmful practices and agree on practical actions to protect children.

“Let this Dialogue similarly become a space where communities come together, listen to one another, challenge harmful practices, and agree on practical actions to protect their children.

“When we invest in positive parenting, we invest in children. When we protect children, we strengthen families. And when we strengthen families, we build peaceful and resilient communities,” she said.

Also speaking on the initiative, the UNICEF Child Protection Specialist, Dr Willy Mamah, said the project is expected to engage at least 1,000 parents in Gelesu, Tudun Wada, Zaria City, Samaru and Kongo communities through storytelling, dialogue, parenting sessions and other creative approaches.

Mamah said the initiative was inspired by a book written by a grassroots lawyer and advocate, Maryam Marwa Abdu.

He explained that the project was designed to take the issues raised in the book beyond fiction and into communities where parents, traditional and religious leaders, young people and other stakeholders could discuss practical solutions to challenges affecting children.

“The Neem Tree Dialogue is a community action initiative using storytelling and dialogue to promote positive parenting, prevent violence against children, including child marriage, and strengthen the agency of girls and boys,” he said.

According to Mamah, the initiative was a collaboration involving the Kaduna State Ministry of Justice, Women and Children Rights Empowerment Foundation, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA), the National Orientation Agency (NOA), and UNICEF.

He said parenting remained an important component of UNICEF’s programme of cooperation with government, adding that preventing violence against children required strengthening families and the wider community systems surrounding them.

“Our approach recognises something fundamental: if we want to prevent violence against children, we must strengthen the family and the community systems that surround the child,” he said.

Mamah said the parenting component would focus on positive communication, quality time with children, emotional literacy, constructive conflict resolution, and knowing when and where to seek help.

He stressed that the initiative was not intended to tell communities what to think, but to create a safe space for them to examine harmful practices, reaffirm positive values, and develop solutions they could own.

Mamah urged stakeholders to support the initiative, stressing that child protection was a responsibility shared by the entire community.

World.title: ‘The Devi Show’ ends after six years: What’s next?
World.content:
South African investigative journalist Devi Sankaree Govender announced that The Devi Show will be coming to an end, but she hinted that it will not be completely disappearing from our screens. What’s next for the journalist?

‘THE DEVI SHOW’ ENDS AFTER SIX YEARS

Six years later, after catching “crooks”, corrupt indiviudals and more, Devi Sankaree Govender announced that The Devi Show will have it’s final episode on Sunday. While The Devi Show is ending on TV, Devi hinted that she will be transitioning from TV into the digital space, as streaming sites grow in popularity.

“Join me for my final episode of #Devi #Sunday as I transition from linear TV into the digital space,” she said.



“And we end, in grand style, with one of our most prolific ‘characters’. Leopards seldom change their spots – and so it was with #GeorgeWebb, who made his 1st appearance as ‘the tenant from hell’ way back in 2020. We confront him for the 5th time.”

FROM LINEAR TELEVISION TO DIGITAL SPACES

She explained the jump from linear television into the ditial space in an Instagram post. Take a look…

“After 30 years on television (imagine!) I’m getting ready for a whole new escapade. I’ve had the privilege of telling extraordinary stories, interacting with super-cool South Africans and confronting a few rather interesting characters (you know The Ones). For the past six years on eTV, The Devi Show has been such a special part of that journey. On Sunday, 11 October, we’ll be wrapping up our television chapter,” she wrote.



“But … relax – I’m not disappearing off your screens. The world is changing, and so is the way we connect. I want to meet you where you are and explore new possibilities,” she continued.

“To everyone who has watched and trusted me with your stories, thank you! To my dear crooks – don’t celebrate too early – I’m moving to a bigger space and I have very interesting plans for us,” she continued.

World.title: ‘I’ll be very happy after the match’: Rulani divided over loyalty for Sundowns/Pirates
World.content:
Pyramids FC coach Rulani Mokwena says he is divided on which team to support ahead of the MTN8 final between Mamelodi Sundowns and Orlando Pirates.

Mokwena, who has coached both teams, claims he will be a happy man on Saturday after the final whistle.

The two giants of South African football, clash at the Moses Mabhida on Saturday evening,



“It’s very difficult for me to decide who I think will win, but I’ll be very happy at the end, for sure,” Mokwena told SAFJA members.

“At the end of the game, I’ll be very happy because if Sundowns win, I would be very, very happy. And if Orlando Pirates win, I will be very, very happy too, ” said the former Sundowns head coach.

Rulani coached both Sundowns and Pirates

Mokwena was assistant coach in the late 2010s at Downs before moving to Orlando Pirates where he was promoted head coach for a short stint. He returneed to Sundowns and in 2022, he was made head coach, winning several league titles.



The 39-year-old coach said the only time he was against both teams, was when he was on the opposing bench.

“The only time I don’t want Pirates or Sundowns to win is when I’m sitting, and I’m competing on the opposite bench. That’s the only time,” Mokwena added.

“When I was at Pirates, I wanted to win every time against Sundowns, even though I am a Sundowns fan. When I was at Sundowns, when we played Pirates, I wanted to win every time we played against them, even though I’m an Orlando Pirates fan.”

World.title: Navi Pillay says Donald Trump ‘will never’ win Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
: South African judge Navi Pillay has taken aim at US President Donald Trump, declaring that he will never win the Nobel Peace Prize after securing the prestigious award herself. Image: Centre for Human Rights/University of Pretoria

South African judge Navi Pillay has declared that US President Donald Trump will never win the Nobel Peace Prize, describing his failure to secure the award as an indictment against him.

Pillay, 85, made the remarks in an interview on Friday, 9 October, after being named the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner for her contribution to international law and human rights.

“The fact that Trump never got the Nobel Prize and never will is an indictment against him,” she said.



Pillay also challenged Americans to consider what their president’s actions say about the values they want their country to uphold.

“There’s a message that all Americans should take on board,” she said.

She questioned whether Americans wanted to stand for justice, fairness and impartiality, values she believes are cherished across the world, or support Trump’s approach to international affairs.

Pillay accused the US president of using sanctions, punishment, deportations and arrests against people and foreign leaders whose views or actions he opposed.

Her criticism follows Trump’s repeated public claims that he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize for his diplomatic efforts to resolve international conflicts.

Trump administration sanctions International Criminal Court

Pillay’s criticism coincided with a major announcement from Washington on Friday.



Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Navi Pillay's reaction in her first interview after being named 2026 Laureate.#sabcnews pic.twitter.com/TA3lR9H2R0 — Sherwin Bryce-Pease (@sherwiebp) October 9, 2026

The Trump administration imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), where Pillay previously served as a judge.

According to a report, the measures could prevent American companies from providing financial and other services to the court, which investigates and prosecutes war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the decision, saying Washington would not allow the court to prosecute Americans.

Rubio described the ICC as a “rogue court” and accused it of exceeding its authority.

The court’s deputy prosecutor, Nazhat Shameem Khan, condemned the sanctions, warning that they threatened international law. She insisted that the court would continue its investigations and prosecutions.

Navi Pillay jokes about sharing Nobel Prize with Trump

Earlier on Friday, Pillay drew laughter while receiving a standing ovation at the Nuremberg Palace of Justice in Germany.

“If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump,” she joked.

Amnesty International Secretary-General Agnes Callamard shared footage of the moment on X.

Pillay was attending an international legal conference when the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that she had won the prestigious award.

The committee recognised her decades of work strengthening international law and holding those responsible for serious international crimes accountable.

Pillay previously served as the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and held senior positions at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the ICC.

More recently, she chaired a UN commission investigating alleged violations of international law in Gaza.

Ramaphosa congratulates Navi Pillay

President Cyril Ramaphosa has congratulated Pillay, describing the award as recognition of her lifelong commitment to justice, human dignity and peace.

“She has served humanity with principle and the belief that the world can and should be a better place,” Ramaphosa said.

The president praised Pillay’s contribution to international law, which began during apartheid when she represented political activists, including Nelson Mandela.

Pillay joins Albert Luthuli, Archbishop Desmond Tutu, Mandela and FW de Klerk among South Africa’s Nobel Peace Prize laureates.

The United Nations Human Rights Office also welcomed the announcement.

Spokesperson Shabia Mantoo described Pillay as a committed defender of human rights and said the recognition was especially significant at a time when international human rights protections faced mounting pressure.

The Sharks and the Cheetahs also start their EPCR Challenge Cup seasons next weekend.

The competition begins on 16 October with reigning champions Union Bordeaux Begles travelling to Gloucester Rugby.

New signing Haashim Pead could be included after his debut against the Sharks off the bench in the URC.
