World.title: South Africa: Zuma Remains in Hospital as Conflicting Reports Emerge Over His Health
World.content:
Former South African president Jacob Zuma has remained at a private hospital in Pietermaritzburg. However, there have been conflicting accounts about his health following his admission.

The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party said Zuma had attended a routine medical check-up, a procedure he undergoes twice a year, and reassured supporters that he was "healthy and in good spirits".

According to News24, his brother Khanya said that Zuma was unwell and remained in hospital. He said the situation was concerning and that the family was praying for Zuma's recovery.

The 84-year-old former president is set to testify before the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) cases inquiry in two weeks.

Zuma was president from 2009 to 2018.

He now leads the uMkhonto weSizwe Party. His hospitalisation comes as his party continues its campaign activities for the local government elections on 4 November.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Home Affairs Withdraws Asylum Directive After Soweto, Durban Unrest

The Department of Home Affairs has withdrawn a directive on the intake of asylum applications following violent anti-immigration protests in Soweto and Durban, where at least 24 vehicles were torched and foreign-owned businesses were looted. The directive was introduced after a July Constitutional Court ruling that allowed asylum seekers to apply for protection regardless of how they entered South Africa or whether they missed immigration deadlines. However, mounting pressure on refugee reception offices, concerns over staff safety and threats to public order prompted the department to reconsider its approach. Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi welcomed the withdrawal, saying it creates an opportunity for further consultation without undermining the court judgment. The ruling remains in force, and asylum applications must still be assessed individually. Police are investigating cases of vandalism, assault and public violence as authorities remain on alert for further unrest.

Yemen Conflict Escalating, Endangering African Economies, Regional Stability



Fears are mounting over Africa's economic stability, maritime trade and humanitarian situation due to the conflict involving Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. Fears of further disruption to world trade have been raised by the alleged seizure of Yemen's Perim Island by the Houthis. The island lies near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. If the strait becomes impassable, shipping companies may be forced to divert vessels around the southern tip of Africa, increasing transport costs, insurance premiums and consumer prices. African economies are already grappling with fuel and fertiliser shortages linked to disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also triggered a humanitarian crisis, with at least 3,700 refugees reportedly crossing from Yemen into Djibouti since September 10, mostly women and children. Djibouti faces additional pressure because of limited water resources, while neighbouring Ethiopia is particularly vulnerable because it relies on Djibouti's ports for about 95% of its imports and exports. Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region and escalating tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea could further destabilise the Horn of Africa and threaten shipping through the strait. African countries have called for a United Nations-led diplomatic solution. Ports in Kenya and Tanzania could benefit from increased shipping activity if vessels continue to avoid the Red Sea.

Ethiopia's Humanitarian and Food Crisis Worsens as Tigray Conflict Flairs

Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region is exacerbating an already dire humanitarian crisis that has seen millions of people face food shortages after years of conflict, displacement and drought. Four years after a peace deal was signed in 2022, communities are still struggling to recover from the effects of the unresolved territorial disputes, limited reconstruction and reduced international aid. About 44% of Tigray's prime agricultural land remains inaccessible to displaced residents, and erratic rainfall and prolonged dry spells have wiped out crops and grazed away livestock grazing areas. Regional assessments have reported the destruction of over 252,500 hectares of planted crops, dire conditions in 140 districts, and the threat of starvation and disease to over 3.5 million livestock. Some 3.9 million people require urgent food assistance, with millions more still in need of adequate support. Renewed hostilities since late September have further disrupted humanitarian operations through air strikes, damage to infrastructure, telecommunications blackouts, and closure or seizure of regional airports. Aid deliveries are either suspended or delayed, and the looting in Mekelle has destroyed the critical supplies, vehicles and medical equipment of humanitarian organizations. These losses have disrupted services for healthcare and support for displaced people and vulnerable children, including children living with HIV. Humanitarian workers are calling for an immediate pause in fighting and safe access for food, medicine, fuel and cash to reach affected communities, warning that continued disruption could push the region towards famine.

At Least 84 Kenyans Killed or Missing in Russia-Ukraine War

At least 84 Kenyans have been killed or remain missing in connection with the Russia-Ukraine war, according to figures released by Kenya's Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs. The government has identified 354 Kenyan nationals as having become involved in the conflict, including 77 reportedly on the front lines, 38 in military camps and 52 whose locations remain unknown or unclassified. Another 34 are hospitalised, 62 have been repatriated, and five are being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine. One Kenyan is in detention, while another has completed their military contract. Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said Ukrainian authorities confirmed the five prisoners of war on September 3, adding that Kenya is seeking to have them recognised as potential victims of human trafficking because some reportedly enlisted after receiving misleading employment offers. The government is pursuing their release and repatriation while investigating the deaths and disappearances of other nationals, including four whose remains are reportedly in Ukrainian custody. Kenya also says it secured Russia's inclusion of Kenyan nationals on a "Stop List" during a diplomatic visit in March, a measure intended to prevent further recruitment. Mudavadi has urged families to report missing relatives promptly to help authorities verify cases, trace their whereabouts and provide assistance. The government says it will continue diplomatic efforts and strengthen preventive measures against deceptive recruitment.

Guinea-Bissau Elections Face Delay

Guinea-Bissau's planned presidential and legislative elections, scheduled for December 6, could be delayed after Prime Minister Ilídio Vieira Té said the conditions necessary to hold the polls had not been met. Following a meeting with transitional President and junta leader General Horta N'Tam, Té said political parties were not adequately prepared to contest the elections and that several needed to renew their leadership structures. The National Electoral Commission also warned that organising the polls on the scheduled date would not be technically feasible, although no formal postponement has been announced. The elections form part of a 12-month transition programme introduced after the military seized power on November 26, 2025, just days after presidential and legislative elections were held but before their results were declared. The takeover halted the electoral process and led the junta to schedule new elections for December 2026. Political tensions have since intensified, particularly after the authorities barred former president Umaro Sissoco Embaló from returning from exile earlier this month, citing national security and public order concerns. Embaló had intended to contest the presidential election. The junta has also faced opposition over constitutional changes approved in an August 30 referendum that strengthen presidential powers and alter the country's political and electoral framework. With no new election date announced, uncertainty remains over the country's political transition and the restoration of civilian democratic rule.

Close 

Wajir Patient Tests Negative for Ebola, Positive for Malaria

Kenya's Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale has confirmed that a patient in Wajir County who was being assessed for a possible Ebola infection has tested negative for the virus and positive for malaria. The patient, who was receiving treatment at Habaswein Sub-County Hospital in Wajir South, was started on antimalarial medication after laboratory results confirmed the diagnosis. The findings have eased concerns about a possible second Ebola case as Kenya strengthens surveillance following its first confirmed imported case, involving a Kenyan citizen who had lived in the Democratic Republic of Congo for seven years and died in Nairobi on October 6. The deceased patient travelled from the DRC through Uganda before boarding Jambojet flight JM8523 to Nairobi on October 3, and laboratory tests confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease. Health authorities are tracing family members, healthcare workers and passengers who may have been exposed, while strengthening screening at points of entry and preparedness at designated treatment facilities. Wajir Governor Ahmed Abdullahi has called on residents to stay calm and not circulate unverified information. The Ministry of Health says Kenya is not experiencing an outbreak of Ebola on a large scale. Authorities continue to encourage good hygiene, prompt medical attention for concerning symptoms, and strict infection prevention measures among healthcare workers. Members of the public can access official health information through the Ministry's toll-free line, 719. The Wajir patient's negative result is separate from the confirmed imported case in Nairobi, and surveillance efforts remain ongoing.

World.title: South Africa: Home Affairs Withdraws Asylum Directive After Violent Anti-Immigration Protests
World.content:
Chaos erupted in Durban city centre during a march by hundreds of anti-immigrant protesters.

The Department of Home Affairs (DHA) has withdrawn a directive on the intake of asylum applications following violent anti-immigration protests in Durban and Soweto, as the government seeks to find a way to implement a Constitutional Court ruling without further escalating tensions.

The directive, issued on 28 September, followed a July judgment by the Constitutional Court in the Scalabrini Centre of Cape Town case. The ruling struck down provisions of the Refugees Act that prevented some asylum seekers from accessing the application process on procedural grounds before their claims could be assessed on their merits.

The judgment allows asylum seekers to apply for protection regardless of how they entered South Africa. However, it does not automatically grant applicants refugee status or permanent residence, as each claim must still be assessed in accordance with the law.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Home Affairs said the directive was introduced as an operational measure to implement the court order but was issued by the department’s director-general without the knowledge of the minister or other political office-bearers.

The department said the implementation process had presented unforeseen challenges, with Refugee Reception Offices overwhelmed by the number of people seeking to submit asylum applications within days of the directive being issued.

It also raised concerns about the safety of departmental officials and the potential impact on public safety and order.

The department will now develop a revised operational approach to ensure compliance with the Constitutional Court’s judgment while addressing the challenges experienced at its offices.

The withdrawal of the directive does not overturn the court ruling, and Home Affairs has yet to announce details of its revised approach.

The development follows violent protests in Durban and Soweto during which vehicles were torched, and businesses vandalised amid growing opposition to immigration and the processing of asylum applications.

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi has welcomed the department's decision, describing it as a relief that creates an opportunity for further consultation.

World.title: South Africa: Four Killed in Germiston Shack Fire - South African News Briefs - October 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Four Killed in Germiston Shack Fire

Four people, including three children aged two, five and seven, have died in a fire that destroyed 12 shacks at the Marathon informal settlement in Germiston, Gauteng, reports EWN. Ekurhuleni Emergency Management Services spokesperson William Ntladi said the victims' bodies were found beneath the rubble. Ntladi said the scene has been handed over to the South African Police Service (SAPS) for investigation, rehabilitation and the removal of the deceased. The cause of the fire remains unknown and is under investigation.

R10 Billion Bill Adopted to Help Stabilise Fuel Prices

The Standing Committee on Appropriations has adopted the Second Special Appropriations Bill, which proposes withdrawing R10 billion from the National Revenue Fund to help stabilise fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, reports SABC News. Committee chairperson Mmusi Maimane said that consumers should receive immediate relief from fuel price volatility. The Bill will soon be tabled in the National Assembly for consideration.

Govt Warns Against Asylum System Abuse

The government has warned foreign nationals that those who do not qualify for asylum or refugee status will be deported, following the Department of Home Affairs' resumption of asylum application processing, reports EWN. Minister in the Presidency Khumbudzo Ntshavheni said the process would help identify undocumented migrants and those attempting to misuse the system. The announcement comes amid heightened tensions over immigration, with protests turning violent in Durban’s CBD and Soweto, leaving about 20 vehicles torched.

World.title: Nigeria: American Lobbying Firms Disagree Over $57m U.S. Lawsuit Against Tinubu
World.content:
DCI Group has rejected allegations in a $57 million US lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu and others, while Femi Fani-Kayode's office says he has not been formally served.

American lobbying firm DCI Group has rejected allegations made by Washington-based lobbyist Karl Von Batten in a $57 million lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu, the Federal Government of Nigeria, former aviation minister Femi Fani-Kayode and the firm.

DCI has been hired by the Nigerian government for lobbying activities in the United States, while Mr Von Batten is doing the same work for former Vice President Atiku Abubakar.

Mr Fani-Kayode's office also told PREMIUM TIMES that he had not been formally served with the court papers and maintained his earlier denial of the allegations.



The case, filed at the United States District Court for the District of Columbia on 28 September, concerns allegations of defamation and a conspiracy to kidnap and physically harm Mr Von Batten. The claims are disputed and have not been established by a court.

DCI, Fani-Kayode respond

In an email to PREMIUM TIMES on Wednesday, Craig Stevens of DCI Group dismissed the allegations.

"Mr. Von Batten's allegations are so far past unfounded that they reach the point of the absurd," Mr Stevens said.

He said DCI's work for the Nigerian government focused on strengthening relations between Nigeria and US policymakers and referred the newspaper to the firm's disclosures under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

Mr Stevens did not address the specific allegations individually.

Mr Fani-Kayode's office, responding separately, answered "No" when asked whether the former minister had been formally served. It also confirmed that he stood by his earlier denial of the allegations.

Mr Fani-Kayode had previously indicated that he would pursue a $100 million counterclaim against Mr Von Batten.

Asked whether the counterclaim had been filed or lawyers instructed to commence proceedings, his office replied: "All in good time."

The response did not confirm any filing.

What the lawsuit alleges

The US federal court docket identifies the case as Von Batten v. Tinubu et al., No. 1:26-cv-03374, before Judge Randolph D. Moss.

The defendants include President Tinubu, the Federal Government of Nigeria, Mr Fani-Kayode, DCI Group AZ, LLC, and 10 unidentified persons.

In a public announcement, Von Batten-Montague-York said it was seeking $36 million jointly from President Tinubu and the Nigerian government, $3 million from Mr Fani-Kayode and $18 million from DCI.

The firm alleged that the defendants were involved in efforts to defame, kidnap or physically harm Mr Von Batten over his advocacy concerning US government records relating to President Tinubu.

Close 

The publicly accessible docket records the filing and issuance of summonses, although this does not establish that the defendants have been formally served.

PREMIUM TIMES has requested the complete file-stamped complaint and exhibits to examine the allegations and the damages sought.

Presidency, others yet to respond

PREMIUM TIMES contacted the Presidency through Bayo Onanuga, Special Adviser to President Tinubu on Information and Strategy, seeking its response to the allegations, confirmation of any formal service and its position on the court's jurisdiction.

The enquiries were sent by email and WhatsApp, followed by telephone contact and reminders.

The newspaper also contacted Mr Atiku's ADC campaign to establish whether the former vice president or his representatives knew about the lawsuit before it was filed and whether they endorsed its allegations.

The campaign was further asked about the status of Mr Atiku's $1.2 million lobbying agreement with Mr Von Batten's firm, payments made and their source.

Mr Von Batten was separately contacted for the full complaint, supporting documents and his response to the denials by DCI and Mr Fani-Kayode. PREMIUM TIMES also sought clarification on the alleged threats, the damages claimed and whether the incidents had been reported to US law-enforcement authorities.

During a telephone call to his firm's office on Thursday, an answering-service representative took the reporter's contact details and said the enquiry would be forwarded.

By the time this report was filed, the Presidency, the ADC campaign and Mr Von Batten had not provided substantive responses.

World.title: Kenya: U.S. Report Flags Kenya's Failure to Act On Officials Linked to Human Trafficking
World.content:
Nairobi — Kenya has failed to report meaningful enforcement action against public officials and recruitment agencies allegedly linked to human trafficking, with a new United States report warning that official complicity continues to undermine the country's efforts to prosecute the crime.

The 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report said Kenyan authorities investigated three Ministry of Labour officials suspected of accepting bribes to facilitate potential trafficking involving migrant workers travelling to the Middle East, but highlighted broader concerns over alleged collusion between public officials and recruitment networks.

The report also found that the government had not reported action against recruitment agencies allegedly owned by government employees and suspected of facilitating trafficking, with authorities frequently pursuing lesser offences such as failure to register recruitment companies.



"Corruption and official complicity in trafficking crimes remained significant concerns, inhibiting law enforcement action during the year," the report stated.

The findings raise questions about accountability within institutions responsible for regulating overseas recruitment and protecting Kenyans seeking employment abroad.

Media reports cited in the assessment indicated that more than 10 per cent of Kenyan government officials held ownership interests in private employment agencies, including firms recruiting migrant workers for jobs overseas, creating potential conflicts of interest.

Observers also alleged that criminal syndicates colluded with law enforcement and immigration departments at border checkpoints and airports to transport trafficking victims into and within Kenya.

The report further cited allegations that some Kenyan embassy officials in Saudi Arabia demanded sex or cash payments from women seeking government assistance to escape abusive employers and return home.

The allegations come against the backdrop of declining anti-trafficking prosecutions and convictions.

Kenya convicted six traffickers in 2025, down from 21 in 2024, while prosecutions fell from 44 cases to 14.

The government investigated 43 trafficking cases during the year, compared with 42 in 2024.

The report also detailed allegations involving the fraudulent recruitment of more than 1,000 Kenyan men to fight for the Russian military in the war against Ukraine, with officials reporting that Kenyan and Russian officials had colluded with illicit recruiters to facilitate the recruitment.

Despite the concerns, Kenya remained on Tier 2 in the US assessment, which recognises significant efforts to combat trafficking while finding that the government has not fully met the minimum standards for eliminating the crime.

Close 

The report credited Kenya with identifying more victims, repatriating citizens exploited in overseas online scam operations, and securing its first civil judgment against a fraudulent recruiter.

However, it said persistent concerns over official complicity continued to hamper law enforcement and victim identification, while protection services for adult survivors remained limited.

World.title: South Africa: Navi Pillay's Nobel Win Draws Attention To Her Work Defending Media Freedom And Beyond
World.content:
Navi Pillay speaking at the South African National EditorsÂ Forum (SANEF) Nat Nakasa Award for Courageous Journalism in 2022.

Recognised by the Norwegian Nobel Committee for her efforts to promote peace and international law, Navi Pillay is being celebrated by African media, legal and civil society voices for a career advancing justice, accountability and human rights — including the right to report freely and safely.

Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize, announced on Friday, 9 October, is drawing attention to her support for media freedom and a career spanning some of the most consequential developments in international human rights law.

The South African jurist has backed initiatives to strengthen legal protections for free expression and promote a free and pluralistic information space.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Pillay is the fifth South African to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, following Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela and F. W. de Klerk.

Announcing the Nobel, Norwegian Nobel Committee chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes linked Pillay’s early legal work under apartheid to her later role in international justice, from defending Nelson Mandela and others who opposed apartheid to serving as a judge in major international cases.

The committee said she had helped strengthen the international legal order and institutions responsible for holding perpetrators of serious crimes accountable. It also highlighted the uneven application of international law and the ability of powerful states and leaders to evade responsibility.

“Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence," the committee said.

Pillay’s win is particularly being celebrated by the media fraternity in Africa, most of whom are citing her efforts in defending media freedom.

Reacting to the announcement, Moky Makura, executive director of Africa No Filter said Pillay “embodies African agency”.

“For decades, she has worked tirelessly to create the change she wants to see in the world. This Nobel Prize shines a well-deserved spotlight on her extraordinary contribution. It is a reminder that African progress is not always about what is happening, but also about what the world is failing to see,” Makura said.

Churchill Otieno, president of The African Editors Forum (TAEF), also said Pillay’s record held particular significance for journalists because of its emphasis on accountability and the right to report freely.

“From her struggle against apartheid to her work in international human rights and law, she has shown that peace cannot endure without accountability,” Otieno said.

“For us journalists and media workers, her record also speaks directly to the right to report freely and safely. As UN High Commissioner, she called for journalists to be protected from political interference and physical threats. Her recognition affirms that defending human dignity, press freedom and the rule of law takes courage, especially when powerful interests resist scrutiny.”

In February 2025, Pillay delivered the keynote address at the launch of South Africa’s Free Expression Legal Network in Johannesburg. Developed by the South African National Editors’ Forum (SANEF), the Press Council, the Campaign for Free Expression and other organisations and legal experts, the network connects journalists and others facing legal threats over their expression with support, including legal representation.

Information and digital rights activist Izak Minnaar notes that Pillay had actively supported the network and advanced media freedom initiatives internationally.

“As the only South African on the global Information and Democracy Commission, she has been spearheading initiatives to support media freedom in South Africa and beyond,” Minnaar explained.

Anton Harber, director of the Henry Nxumalo Foundation, said Pillay had been particularly consistent in defending independent journalism.

“Navi Pillay has stood firm on many human rights issues, but has had particularly clear, strong and consistent views in defence of media freedom and the importance of independent journalism.”

“Whenever called upon to defend the media, she has been quick to stand up and be counted, even when it was not an easy thing to do. Her prize will be celebrated by journalists,” Harber added.

At the network’s launch, Pillay stressed the value of collective action. “If you clap with a single hand, nobody yells for you. But if a lot of people form a network clap, they will be heard,” she said, according to SANEF.

In its statement congratulating her, SANEF recalled Pillay’s call for governments to promote a free press that can “combat disinformation, build public trust and advance the promotion and protection of human rights.”

She also emphasised the need to protect those who help journalists expose wrongdoing. “I would say that such action must also protect media sources and whistle-blowers,” she said, according to SANEF.

Pillay served on the International Commission on Information and Democracy, convened by Reporters Without Borders in 2018. The 25-member commission developed principles for protecting freedom of expression and democratic debate in the global information space. Its declaration described information and communication as a common good and called for freedom, pluralism and reliable information.

President Cyril Ramaphosa said the award recognised Pillay’s contributions to peace and human dignity in South Africa and internationally.

“She has served humanity with principle and the belief that the world can and should be a better place,” Ramaphosa said.

Mameltwe Sebei, president of the General Industries Workers Union of South Africa (Giwusa) and an attorney at Lawyers for Human Rights, described the Nobel as recognition of Pillay’s legal career serving oppressed and marginalised people.

Her work defending anti-apartheid activists and involvement in international cases concerning atrocities, including the Rwanda genocide and the occupied Palestinian territory, made the award a source of pride for South Africans, he said.

“Most importantly, this should affirm our commitment to the principles of justice that underpin the work of any lawyer who stands on the side of the oppressed,” Sebei said. “She represents that type of jurist, that type of lawyer, and this Nobel Peace Prize is a well-deserved recognition of that.”

South Africa’s parliamentary Portfolio Committee on International Relations and Cooperation also described the award as a source of national pride, citing Pillay’s contribution to international justice and accountability for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

Na’eem Jeenah, Senior Researcher at Mapungubwe Institute for Strategic Reflection (MISTRA) and political analyst said the award carries significance beyond South Africa.

“This then is an honour not only for South Africa but for the whole of Africa, a continent that is battling with its own conflicts and violations of international law,” Jeenah said.

While he believes the Nobel Prize would not change conditions for Palestinians nor stop the violence in Gaza, it “adds to the body of moral and legal evidence against Israel, including several UN reports (including on genocide), and the ICJ genocide case”.

Born on 23 September 1941 in Clairwood, Durban, to a family of Indian Tamil descent, Pillay grew up under apartheid. She graduated from the University of Natal with a bachelor’s degree in 1963 and an LLB in 1965.

In 1967, she became the first Black woman to open her own law practice in Natal, now KwaZulu-Natal. She represented political detainees and exposed abuses including torture and solitary confinement. In 1973, she successfully challenged restrictions preventing political prisoners from accessing legal counsel, according to South African History Online.

After earning postgraduate law degrees at Harvard University, she became the first Black woman appointed to South Africa’s High Court in Natal in 1995. She also participated in the Women’s National Coalition during the country’s constitutional transition and co-founded Equality Now, an organisation campaigning for the rights of women and girls.

In 1995, Pillay joined the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, established to prosecute those responsible for the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. She became its president in 1999, serving until 2003.

A landmark case during her time on the tribunal was the trial of Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former local official convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity. The tribunal’s 1998 judgment established that rape and other forms of sexual violence could constitute acts of genocide when committed with the intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part.

Pillay later served in the International Criminal Court’s Appeals Division from 2003 to 2008. She became United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in 2008, serving until 2014, a period that included the Arab Spring uprisings and the Syrian civil war.

Close 

Her later work included international proceedings and investigations into alleged serious crimes. In December 2019, she was appointed an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over alleged genocide against the Rohingya minority. The court confirmed its jurisdiction and ruled the application admissible.

From 2021 to 2025, Pillay chaired the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel.

In September 2025, the commission concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel rejected the conclusion. The finding was made by a UN commission of inquiry, not a final judgment by an international court.

The commission’s work highlighted a central challenge for international law: translating findings of serious violations into consequences for those responsible, particularly when powerful states are involved.

The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) said the award underscored the importance of international law at a time when its institutions face growing pressure.

“Throughout her long career, Navi Pillay has set a high moral example, speaking out and standing up for justice, accountability and the rule of law,” said SIPRI director Karim Haggag.

Haggag said the award also recognised the institutions Pillay had served, warning that powerful states were increasingly resorting to power politics and transactionalism while international law and its institutions faced attack.

South African investigative organisation Open Secrets also welcomed the award, saying it affirmed the importance of international law and its promise of holding human rights abusers to account.

Pillay was a panellist at the first People’s Tribunal on Economic Crime in the arms trade, convened by Open Secrets and civil society partners in 2018. The tribunal sought accountability for arms companies and politicians in the aftermath of apartheid and State Capture.

The announcement also prompted a lighter moment. Reacting to the news in Nuremberg, Pillay joked with supporters, “If you clap a little bit louder, I may share this prize with Trump,” according to an amateur social media clip.

World.title: Liberia: 'Stop Following America' - Sirleaf Urges Liberians
World.content:
MONROVIA — Former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf has urged Liberia to reduce its dependence on the United States for policy direction and embrace homegrown solutions that reflect the country's development priorities and national interests.

Sirleaf said Liberia must break away from longstanding patterns of dependency and take greater responsibility for shaping its future through policies, institutions and development strategies suited to its own circumstances.

"We have to stop following the United States of America. Let's join the new era of sovereignty, respectability," the former president declared.



Her remarks signal a call for greater national ownership of Liberia's development agenda, particularly in a changing global environment where countries are increasingly reassessing their political and economic relationships.

Sirleaf made the statement during a brief interview with journalists on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, following her participation in a one-day symposium organized by the Governance Commission on 3rd Street in Monrovia.

The symposium, held as part of activities marking Good Governance Month, was organized under the theme, "Promoting Good Governance Through Accountability and Transparency in Liberia."

The observance was established by presidential proclamation in keeping with the Governance Commission's founding Act of October 9, 2007.

Speaking to journalists, Sirleaf emphasized the need for Liberia to rethink traditional approaches to governance and development, arguing that the country must adapt to changing global realities rather than continue relying on policies and systems developed elsewhere.

Her comments come against the backdrop of Liberia's longstanding diplomatic, historical and development relationship with the United States, a partnership that remained particularly strong during her 12-year presidency.

Sirleaf, who served from January 2006 to January 2018, became Africa's first elected female head of state after defeating George Manneh Weah in Liberia's 2005 presidential runoff election.

Her administration inherited a country devastated by years of civil conflict and prioritized post-war reconstruction, international debt relief, infrastructure development, institutional reforms and the restoration of Liberia's international standing.

During her presidency, the United States remained one of Liberia's major development and diplomatic partners, providing substantial assistance in governance, economic recovery, health, education and security-sector reform.

Sirleaf also maintained close relationships with successive American administrations.

In March 2006, shortly after assuming office, she addressed a joint session of the United States Congress, highlighting Liberia's recovery efforts and appealing for continued international support.

Then-U.S. President George W. Bush visited Liberia in February 2008, while his successor, Barack Obama, hosted Sirleaf at the White House in 2010 and 2015.

The relationship became particularly significant during the 2014-2016 Ebola epidemic, when the United States provided major emergency assistance to Liberia, including medical personnel, logistical support and resources to help contain the outbreak.

Her administration also secured substantial international debt relief and development assistance as part of efforts to rebuild Liberia's economy and strengthen public institutions.

Against this historical background, Sirleaf's latest remarks represent a notable emphasis on national self-reliance by a former president whose administration benefited significantly from close American cooperation.

However, her statement did not explicitly call for Liberia to abandon its diplomatic relationship with Washington or reject international partnerships.

Close 

Rather, her comments focused on the need for Liberia to exercise greater independence in determining its national priorities and developing solutions to its governance and economic challenges.

The former president did not outline specific policy changes or identify particular American-supported programs that Liberia should reconsider.

Nevertheless, her remarks raise broader questions about how Liberia can balance its longstanding relationship with the United States against the need to strengthen domestic institutions, promote economic self-reliance and exercise greater control over its development agenda.

For a country whose reconstruction and development efforts have depended heavily on international assistance, Sirleaf's message places renewed attention on the distinction between maintaining strategic partnerships and relying on external powers to shape national policy.

Her central argument is that Liberia must increasingly take ownership of its future while engaging international partners on terms that reflect its own priorities and interests.

World.title: One type of sleep linked to dramatically lower risk of dementia, Parkinson's and 81 other diseases
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Not all stages of sleep are equal in terms of benefits for the brain.

Greater amounts of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were associated with lower risks of 83 diseases, including dementia, Parkinson’s disease and heart failure, new research has shown.

Additionally, greater amounts of deep sleep were associated with lower risks of seven conditions.

THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS

That’s according to a study of 95,559 adults who wore wrist accelerometers continuously for seven consecutive days and nights. Researchers in China used deep-learning algorithms to analyze REM sleep, deep sleep, light sleep, total sleep duration, wakefulness after sleep onset and sleep irregularity.

They then looked at health records to assess associations with more than 1,000 diseases over a nearly nine-year follow-up period.

Greater REM sleep was associated with a significantly lower risk of several diseases, including Parkinson’s (80% lower relative risk), dementia (46% lower risk) and heart failure (26% lower risk).

Greater deep sleep was associated with lower risks of seven conditions, including type 2 diabetes and major depressive disorder.

MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS

Sleep duration was also found to be highly linked to disease outcome. Six to eight hours per night was found to be the "sweet spot" that was associated with the lowest risk for 69 diseases. In contrast, sleeping fewer than five hours per night was linked to an increased risk of 37 health conditions.

The study also found that greater night-to-night sleep irregularity and more wakefulness during the night were associated with higher risks of several conditions, including anxiety and substance use disorders.

The findings were published Sept. 17 in the journal PLOS Medicine.

"I think what is important is the total duration of sleep, and the percentage that REM takes up," Oki Ishikawa, M.D., pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine expert at Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital, told Fox News Digital.

"The average percentage of REM sleep in this study population was about 20%, and generally 20-25% is considered normal per sleep cycle."

5-STEP SLEEP RESET COULD PROMOTE HEALTHY WEIGHT LOSS, NUTRITIONIST SAYS

Ishikawa, who was not involved in the study, said he does not believe that a higher amount of REM sleep alone will not necessarily lower the risk.

"Normal sleep pattern and duration are associated with aspects like maintenance of good immune function and memory, so I think the important message here is to try and get a sufficient amount of sleep in general."

Disrupted sleep may sometimes be an early warning sign of disease rather than simply a cause, according to Dr. Chelsie Rohrscheib, head sleep expert at Wesper, a sleep analysis company in New York.

"Conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, dementia and heart failure can begin affecting sleep years before they are diagnosed," Rohrscheib, who also was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.

"At the same time, poor sleep may contribute to disease progression, so the relationship likely works both ways."

DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID

The researchers noted some limitations of the study. Because it was observational, it could only show an association and could not prove that increasing REM or deep sleep directly prevents disease.

"Sleep was measured for only one week using a wrist device, which is less accurate than a clinical sleep study for identifying sleep stages," Rohrscheib said.

"Some health information was collected years earlier, medications that can affect sleep were not fully considered, and some medical diagnoses may have been missed."

As the participants were all from the UK Biobank, the study population was also less diverse and generally healthier than the overall population, so the findings may not apply equally to everyone, Rohrscheib noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Overall, changes in sleep may provide important clues about underlying health, but this study cannot determine whether poor sleep is a cause, an early symptom, or both," she concluded.

Rohrscheib also cautioned that while wrist-worn sleep trackers are generally good at estimating sleep stages, they are not 100% accurate.

CLICK HERE TO 

"Without a formal in-lab sleep study, it's impossible to know how much time the participants spent in REM and other sleep stages," she said.

More research is needed to determine whether increasing REM or deep sleep can help prevent certain diseases, the researchers said.

"If you get about seven to nine hours of uninterrupted sleep, you most likely have the opportunity to cycle through REM in a sufficient way."

Future studies could also explore whether the relationship between sleep stages and disease risk varies by age, sex, overall health and other individual characteristics.

Both experts recommended following general sleep hygiene practices, such as maintaining an optimal environment (dark, cool and quiet), keeping a consistent sleep schedule, and avoiding sleep-disrupting substances such as alcohol and caffeine.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"If you have other sleep pathologies like sleep apnea … treating that would be a great way to optimize the amount of REM sleep," Ishikawa advised.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

While it can be difficult to measure REM sleep without a wearable, he said the best gauge is whether one feels refreshed upon waking and doesn’t feel sleepy during the day.

"If you get about seven to nine hours of uninterrupted sleep, you most likely have the opportunity to cycle through REM in a sufficient way."

World.title: Who is Navi Pillay? Nobel Peace Prize winner's UN record renews fierce antisemitism accusations
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The decision to award the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to former U.N. human rights chief Navi Pillay sparked fierce backlash Friday from Jewish advocacy groups and U.N. watchdogs accusing the South African jurist of longstanding anti-Israel bias and defending antisemitic rhetoric.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee honored Pillay, 85, for her contributions to international law and efforts to hold perpetrators of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide accountable.

But her selection immediately reignited controversies surrounding her leadership of U.N. investigations into Israel, her defense of a fellow commissioner accused of antisemitism and positions she expressed before being appointed to investigate the Jewish state.

ICC PROSECUTOR WHOSE NETANYAHU WARRANT FUELED MAMDANI ARREST THREAT IS FIRED OVER SEXUAL MISCONDUCT

"Navi Pillay is indeed a world leader – an individual at the forefront of the international spread of the poisonous forms of antisemitism that beset the 21st century," Anne Bayefsky, president of Human Rights Voices and director of the Touro Institute on Human Rights, told Fox News Digital.

Bayefsky accused Pillay of having "perfected the art of perverting legal and universal standards of human rights to demonize and delegitimize Jewish self-determination." "This award stands as a testament to human wrongs," she added.

The Nobel Committee offered a sharply different assessment of Pillay's legacy, praising her lifelong commitment to international justice and describing her career as an example of courage and integrity in defending the rule of law.

ISRAEL VINDICATED BY GAZA NUTRITION DATA AFTER ‘BLOOD LIBEL’ STARVATION CLAIMS, UN ENVOY SAYS

Who Is Navi Pillay?

Born in Durban, South Africa, in 1941, Pillay built her career challenging apartheid-era discrimination, becoming the first non-White woman appointed to South Africa's high court. She later served as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court.

From 2008 to 2014, she served as U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights. In 2021, she was appointed to chair the U.N. Human Rights Council's open-ended Commission of Inquiry investigating alleged violations in Israel and the Palestinian territories.

In September 2025, the commission concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, a finding Israel rejected as politically motivated and biased. The commission's conclusion was not a ruling by an international court.

Geneva-based U.N. Watch condemned Friday's Nobel announcement, accusing Pillay of breaching the impartiality expected of international investigators.

UN CHIEF BACKS OFFICIAL WHO REPOSTED ANTI-ISRAEL ACTIVIST'S CLAIMS AMID CALLS FOR INVESTIGATION

"We are shocked that the Nobel committee honored Navi Pillay," Executive Director Hillel Neuer said. "Her troubling record on antisemitism and gross breach of ethics in presiding over a notorious UN commission utterly disqualifies her from such an award."

Neuer pointed to a June 2020 manifesto that Pillay signed calling on governments to "Sanction Apartheid Israel," along with a June 2021 letter urging President Joe Biden to punish Israel following its conflict with Hamas.

U.N. Watch argued that the positions raised questions about her impartiality before she accepted the commission's chairmanship in July 2021.

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres offered a sharply different assessment Friday, congratulating Pillay on the Nobel Peace Prize and praising her decades-long career in international justice, including her leadership of the U.N. investigation into Israel.

"For decades, she has been a champion of international law and human rights, and a steadfast, independent voice of justice amidst some of the most historic international legal cases of our time," Guterres said in a statement.

Guterres highlighted her different roles including chairing the commission investigating Israel and the Palestinian territories, declaring that Pillay had demonstrated "that the force of law must prevail over the law of force and that defending human rights is the surest safeguard against injustice."

NORWAY FACES BACKLASH OVER 'DEEPLY RACIST' PROPOSAL TO JAIL CITIZENS FOR WEST BANK BUSINESS

Another controversy erupted in 2022 when fellow commissioner Miloon Kothari suggested that social media criticism of the investigation was controlled by the "Jewish lobby" and questioned Israel's U.N. membership.

The remarks were condemned by U.S. officials, including then-state department antisemitism envoy Deborah Lipstadt. Pillay defended Kothari, arguing his comments had been taken out of context. Kothari subsequently apologized, calling his language inappropriate and insensitive.

The controversy also reached Germany, where Berlin's mayor withdrew support for a planned event honoring Pillay in 2022, and the event was canceled, according to The Times of Israel.

Bayefsky also recalled the 2009 U.N. anti-racism conference in Geneva, when Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad delivered an inflammatory speech attacking Israel. While Western diplomats walked out, Pillay remained seated.

However, Pillay subsequently condemned his address, saying she joined the secretary-general in "utterly deploring the speech," according to the U.N.'s official transcript.

The Nobel Committee, meanwhile, defended Pillay's legacy, crediting her with strengthening international law at a time when the institutions responsible for enforcing it face increasing political pressure.

Pillay's selection highlights the divide between supporters who celebrate her contributions to international justice and critics who contend that her record on Israel undermines the universal human rights principles she championed.

The Dream and Valkyries come into tonight with a chance to close out their series, but they must do it on the road as a visiting team.

ATLANTA DREAM ADVANCE TO WNBA PLAYOFFS SEMIFINALS FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2018 WITH GAME 2 WIN

Dream vs Liberty, 7:30 pm ET

It is a bit hard to believe the Dream are even in this position. They were terrible two years ago. Last year, they improved, but didn't win a playoff series. Breanna Stewart continues to be dominant, and Sabrina Ionescu led the way in Game 1, but they need to both be on if they want to stop this Dream attack. Now that the series is shifting to New York, the team should get a bit of a boost, and I think they will win this one. The Liberty are a team of champions and won't go out without a fight. World.title: Thousands flood Brussels streets as anti-austerity protests erupt into clashes with police
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Thousands of demonstrators poured into the streets of Brussels on Friday, at times clashing with police officers, to protest the Belgian government's budget-tightening measures and the overall rise in the cost of living.

Dozens of protesters, most of them young and dressed in black with masks over their faces, were seen throwing rocks and firecrackers at police at the central Brussels railway station, The Associated Press reported.

They also set several fires, with photos showing a man lighting an electric scooter ablaze.

MAY DAY PROTESTS ACROSS EUROPE AND ASIA TURN INTO ANTI-AMERICAN, ANTI-ISRAEL POLITICAL BATTLEGROUNDS

Riot police responded by deploying tear gas canisters and shooting water cannons, tactics that dispersed the crowds. The chaos in the streets contributed to increased traffic across the Belgian capital.

Police said the unrest was caused by people unaffiliated with the anti-austerity demonstration, which drew an estimated 30,000 participants, the AP reported.

Two of Belgium’s largest labor unions organized Friday’s daylong national strike, with a separate public-sector walkout planned for Monday. Union leaders also distanced themselves from the unrest, saying those responsible were not affiliated with their movement.

THINK YOUR STATE IS EXPENSIVE? NEW DATA REVEALS WHERE AMERICANS FACE THE HIGHEST COST-OF-LIVING

Union members and their supporters were dressed in red or green as they marched peacefully throughout the city.

Marie Gobert, a single mother and social worker, came to Brussels from Namur for the march, telling the AP she "cannot make ends meet."

The rising cost of schools, public transport and train tickets is what preoccupies her the most.

FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE

"You can feel the social tension, you can feel anger starting to simmer everywhere," Gobert said. "The education system is being dismantled, and when young people want to speak out, no one listens to them."

This summer, Belgium’s French Community government raised standard university tuition by roughly 43% this academic year, from €835 to €1,194, as part of a broader austerity program.

In June, there were clashes between protesters and police in Brussels over dissatisfaction with the tuition hike and other issues with the French-language education system, including overcrowded classrooms and difficulty accessing study materials.

This week, hundreds of students took to the streets of the eastern Belgian city of Liège. Local media reported that 107 students were arrested.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

World.title: Trump sets up committee to investigate Fed Governor Lisa Cook over mortgage fraud allegations
World.content:

President Donald Trump has set up a committee to investigate Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook over allegations she made false statements on mortgage documents, the same accusations Trump has cited for over a year in a bid to remove her from office.

Trump attempted to remove Cook in August 2025, triggering a lengthy legal battle that culminated in the Supreme Court blocking her firing in June 2026. In a 5-4 ruling, the court ruled she had not been given adequate time to respond to the allegations against her.

This newly-formed committee appears to be the process the White House has settled on to give Cook a chance to advocate for herself, as she will be allowed to submit a written statement ahead of her first scheduled hearing on Nov. 5, 2026.

WHO IS LISA COOK? THE CENTRAL BANK GOVERNOR AT THE HEART OF THE SUPREME COURT’S TRUMP-FED SHOWDOWN

Her statement must be received by the committee at least three days ahead of the hearing, which will unfold at the White House and will last no more than four hours, according to a notice dated Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, but released on Friday by the Trump administration.

At the hearing itself, Cook will be able to "present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations," the White House said. In turn, lawyers with the Department of Justice will question her.

The hearing will be closed to the public but will be transcribed.

EXPLAINED: HOW LISA COOK’S THREE HOME LOANS BECAME CENTRAL TO TRUMP’S FIGHT OVER HER FEDERAL RESERVE SEAT

Three White House staffers, including National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett, will serve as members of the committee. Hassett was one of Trump's top picks to replace Jerome Powell as Fed Chair before he ultimately settled on Kevin Warsh.

The White House said it expects Cook to submit another written statement after the hearing, after which the committee will make a recommendation to Trump on whether there is adequate cause to remove her from her post.

The White House revisited its effort to fire Cook in August, sending her a letter informing her that Trump was once again considering terminating her.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

This time, Cook was given 21 days to respond. Her attorneys submitted a letter to the White House on Aug. 26 denying that she had committed mortgage fraud.

The White House alleged that Cook claimed homes in Atlanta and Michigan as her primary residence on separate mortgage agreements and later rented out the Atlanta property.

Cook's attorney said the Atlanta designation was an inadvertent mistake, arguing that she sought financing for it as a vacation home and consistently identified Michigan as her "primary" or "permanent" residence.

World.title: Food pantries overwhelmed by Trump cuts
World.content:
“There’s a decent chance we could run out,” said Likens, who runs the food pantry in Dunlow as director of community outreach for Cabwaylingo Presbyterian Chapel, a small brick church he attended growing up.

“I don’t want them to sit in that line and not get anything,” he said. “But I don’t have a lot of extra food these days.”

Increasingly, the job of feeding the nation’s hungry is falling on the shoulders of everyday Americans like Likens, who have become the last bulwark against hunger in a land of plenty.

Likens and others on the front lines of feeding their neighbors say they face unprecedented challenges brought on by Washington. Food distribution programs are getting less food from federal programs to feed the hungry after cuts by the Trump administration. At the same time, restrictions on food stamps from the Republicans’ “big, beautiful bill” have driven up demand, while rising gas prices because of the Iran war have cut into the budgets of households and food banks alike.

Bill Likens, director of community outreach for Cabwaylingo Presbyterian Chapel, grew up hungry in Dunlow. Now he works to make sure that doesn't happen to other kids. Mike Belleme for NBC News

The challenges extend far beyond Appalachia. An NBC News survey of 48 of the largest food banks across 35 states and Washington, D.C., found that nearly three-quarters said more people are showing up at their doors over the past year, from workers on their lunch breaks to older adults overwhelmed with medical expenses. At the same time, more than 80% said the food and funding they received through the U.S. Department of Agriculture had dropped and they were struggling with higher fuel costs for transporting food.

In Maine, Good Shepherd Food Bank said the USDA cut the amount of food it received from 13 million pounds to 9 million pounds in one year. A Michigan food bank, Forgotten Harvest, said it’s handing out less food to make sure there is enough to go around: one bag of potatoes instead of two, two tubs of yogurt as opposed to six.

“People are facing multiple hits to their budgets,” said Poonam Gupta, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute, a think tank that researches social and economic issues. “It is really difficult to find a way to continue affording a healthy and nutritious and balanced diet when you just have these constant hits.”

Food banks’ struggles started in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term when officials cut a $400 million Covid-era program to supply food banks with food from local farmers and paused an estimated $500 million in other planned food purchases by the USDA. Funding from Congress for a separate decades-old program to supply food banks with emergency food assistance has increased over the past several years, but many food bank leaders said they’re still getting less overall than during the Biden administration.

We want to hear from you Have you been affected by changes to the SNAP/food stamp program? Share your story here.

Trump also signed into law the new restrictions on who can receive Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, or food stamps, requiring nearly all able-bodied adults not caring for young children to work, volunteer or go to school at least 80 hours a month. Since the law was enacted, more than 5 million people, including at least 1 million children, have lost their food benefits.

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly defended the administration’s policies, saying Trump is “uplifting every American’s financial situation” through tax cuts and efforts to increase jobs and business investments.

“President Trump is strengthening SNAP for the Americans who need it by ensuring these programs are sustainable for future generations,” Kelly said, including measures to “crack down on waste, fraud and abuse.”

World.title: Mike Ditka, legendary Chicago Bears coach, dies at 86
World.content:
Legendary Chicago Bears coach Mike Ditka, who led the team to its only Super Bowl victory in 1986, has died, his family announced.

He was 86.

“It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka,” the family said in a statement Friday.

“While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears’ Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family,” the statement said. “Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever.”

The Bears released a statement saying Ditka’s impact on the team as “a player, coach, and proud icon and ambassador for our organization, is immeasurable.”

Ditka, the statement said, “created a lifetime of cherished memories in the hearts and minds of Bears fans that will last for generations.”

Ditka, who was inducted into the pro football Hall of Fame in 1988, was remembered by the organization’s president Jim Porter as a player who “brought an unrivaled level of toughness to an era already defined by physicality.”

“He brought that same philosophy to his coaching,” Porter said in a statement.

Tough and pugnacious, Ditka personified the hard-hitting team he led to a 46-10 thrashing of the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XX and was called “Iron Mike,” both because of his gruff demeanor and because he hailed from a steel town in western Pennsylvania.

Ditka, who was born Michael Dyczko on Oct. 18, 1939, became a beloved figure in the Windy City and the embodiment of Chicago’s blue-collar, tough-guy identity.

In the years after the Bears won the Super Bowl, Ditka was immortalized by “Saturday Night Live” in the “Bill Swerski’s Superfans” sketches, which featured a group of fans singing his praises to the point of absurdity with tick Chicawgo ayccents.

“If I may shift gears for a moment gentlemen, coach Ditka vs. The Hurricane, who would win?” the Bill Swerski character says in one skit.

“Ditka! Ditka!,” the others reply.

The oldest of four children, Ditka was the son of a welder of Polish and Ukrainian stock who changed his name to make it easier to pronounce.

But growing up in the town of Aliquippa, Ditka excelled at the all-American sport of football and that earned him a scholarship and a ticket out of town to the University of Pittsburgh, where he initially planned to study dentistry.

Mike Ditka when he was an All-American tight end with the University of Pittsburgh in 1960. AP

Instead, Ditka excelled on the gridiron and in 1961 he was drafted by the Bears as a tight end. There, Ditka redefined a position that mostly consisted of blocking for rushers by becoming a scoring machine who racked up a dozen touchdowns in his first season and was named Rookie of the Year.

Ditka was a star on the 1963 Bears championship, in the pre-Super Bowl era, and a pro-bowler in each of the five seasons he played for “Da Bears.” He also gained some infamy by decking a fan who ran out on the field in the middle of a championship game broadcast on national TV.

“Ditka has been trained since high school to knock down anything that moves,” famous Chicago newspaper columnist Mike Royko wrote in Sept. 1966. “The young man flew into the air. He was limp when he landed and shaky when the police led him away.”

Unable to reach a contract agreement with Bears owner and coach George Halas, Ditka signed with the Houston Oilers in 1987 for the then-princely sum of $300,000.

Halas, Ditka said disparagingly, “threw nickels around like manhole covers.”

Ditka went on to play for the Dallas Cowboys, where in 1972 he caught a touchdown pass in their 24–3 victory over the Miami Dolphins in Super Bowl VI.

After retiring in 1973, Ditka was hired by the Cowboys as an assistant coach. And during his nine seasons there, Dallas made the playoffs eight times, won six division titles, three NFC championships, and a Super Bowl victory in 1977.

“Ditka was the first man enshrined in Canton who had won Super Bowls as a player, assistant coach and head coach,” the Hall of Fame said in a statement.

World.title: With all eyes on Texas Senate race, James Talarico has vanished from the campaign trail
World.content:
The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now.

But in the final push, when campaigns believe most voters are finally tuning in, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has been off the trail for in-person events in the state for 12 days.

His campaign says he has the flu and is expected to be back in action this weekend.

While he has appeared virtually at a forum, Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser, and, according to the virtual remarks he gave to the Hispanic Business Council the next day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care.

It has all prompted a stream of fodder from his opponent, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose campaign is calling on Talarico to produce a photo of himself with a newspaper showing today’s date.

“We have a simple request: proof of life,” Paxton campaign spokeswoman Madison Cercy said. “James Talarico wants to represent 31 million Texans in the U.S. Senate, but for 12 days, he’s hidden from every one of them. There’s a reason they call it ‘Texas Tough,’ and it’s not because Texans hide at the first sign of trouble. If James Talarico is too fragile to face Texans, he has no business asking for their vote.”

While some Texas Democrats are shrugging it off, it is causing some consternation.

“He’s, like, really sick. Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.”

At the Hispanic Business Council event, Talarico appeared virtually and was blowing his nose and coughing through the event.

“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico said at the time. “I’m running a fever, and I’m my most contagious right now. And I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe.”

Talarico’s absence is undoubtedly a curveball for Democrats who believe his best asset is connecting with potential voters in person. It is also a turnaround for Talarico, who had been visible in the early days of the campaign as Paxton was off the trail.

“After holding more than 100 public events and shaking tens of thousands of hands, James came down with the flu but will be back on the trail this weekend,” Talarico spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement. “Ken Paxton has been ignoring Texans this entire campaign, and his priorities are clear: he doesn’t answer to the people of this state — he answers to his billionaire megadonors and special interests.”

Democratic political strategist Ed Espinoza said some supporters he has spoken to noted Talarico’s absence from in-person campaign events and lamented that they wanted to make sure other people were seeing enough of him.

Espinoza, though, said he didn’t think that would be a problem.

“Look, he’s got, like, $80 million of ads going right now. So I think that’s pretty good scale for him at the moment,” Espinoza said. “He may be recovering at home, but he is still everywhere.”

Espinoza said he’d rather Talarico be off the trail and recovering now rather than be hampered even closer to the election.

Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder said Paxton “caught a little bit of a break” with Talarico’s absence.

“It’s certainly not ideal, but we want to make sure he does everything he needs to to make sure that he’s healthy and ready to go. We’re in the homestretch, and it sounds like he’s on the mend, and that’s great news,” Scudder said. “He’s a phenomenal candidate, he’s been working really hard for a long time, and everyone gets sick every now and then.”

To Talarico’s great fortune, distractions have abounded. A steady flow of damaging audio featuring Paxton saying that President Donald Trump’s midterm convention wasn’t helpful or that cuts to “mandatory spending” were inevitable has grabbed public attention.

At the same time, both Paxton and Trump have hit Talarico for being off the trail.

“You haven’t seen him in a couple of weeks,” Trump said Wednesday at a rally in San Antonio. “I hear the guy has disappeared. Nobody knows. You know where he is? He’s sick, because he’s forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”

After the rally, Trump posted a demand on social media that Talarico show up in person to debate Paxton.

“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able, one of the best Attorney Generals in the Country, and will soon be, hopefully, a United States Senator representing the Great People of Texas!” Trump said on Truth Social.

It was a twist, given that Talarico has repeatedly called on Paxton to debate. Though he’s not on the trail yet, Talarico did respond over social media:

“President Trump just said Ken Paxton should debate,” Talarico wrote. “I agree. Ball’s in your court @KenPaxtonTX.”

World.title: Trump establishes panel to probe Fed governor Lisa Cook in latest attempt to fire her
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Friday signed an order directing the attorney general and other top federal officials to establish a committee to investigate Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, in his latest attempt to fire her.

“By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, I hereby establish a committee of inquiry (Committee) to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa D. Cook made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments,” read a presidential memorandum posted to the White House website.

It said that the committee would “investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is ‘cause’ for Governor Cook’s removal.”

“Governor Cook may submit a written position statement to the Committee regarding the allegations,” the memorandum said.

The unprecedented White House announcement comes after a top White House official in August wrote a letter to Cook, saying that Trump was considering removing her from the Federal Reserve board.

The White House memorandum said that Cook “shall appear at the hearing and be examined by the Committee,” as well as “present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations.”

The committee is set to meet Nov. 5 for the hearing, two days after the midterm elections. No president has ever fired a top Fed official.

“In light of the President’s repeated statements that he has already decided to fire Governor Cook — regardless of the facts and evidence — we have grave doubts that this ‘hearing’ is a legitimate one that would conform to the law,” said Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, Cook’s attorneys.

“But if it is anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board.”

Lowell and Eisen said they have engaged with the White House to determine if this is a “genuine” process and that Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.”

The memo follows a Supreme Court ruling in June, which allowed Cook to remain in her job for now. But the justices did not permanently block Trump from removing Cook, instead ruling that she had the right to an opportunity to defend herself.

Trump’s latest move stems from allegations first leveled against Cook in August 2025 by Federal Housing Finance Agency chief Bill Pulte. Trump amplified those allegations on social media and, citing a “criminal referral” he said Pulte had sent to the Justice Department, attempted to remove her from the Fed’s board.

Pulte alleged that Cook committed mortgage fraud, however documents obtained and reviewed by NBC News later revealed that Cook declared that the property in question was to be used as a “vacation home” and not her primary residence.

The Federal Reserve declined to comment on Friday’s developments.

Other top Trump administration officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, reportedly have similar mortgage situations.

Former Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin have all called more than one property their “primary residence” on mortgage applications, according to a report last year from ProPublica.

Cook, a governor on the Federal Reserve’s board, has a permanent vote on interest rates. Trump and Pulte’s attacks on Cook came amid a long-running pressure campaign by the administration to get the U.S. central bank to cut interest rates.

“President Trump is convening an illegitimate show trial in his dangerous quest to illegally take over our nation’s central bank,” said Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, which oversees the Fed.

“Instead of playing judge in a kangaroo court of his own making, Trump should end the war in Iran and cancel his chaotic tariffs,” Warren said.

Trump also recently resumed his attacks on another Fed governor, Jerome Powell. Trump claimed Sept. 30 that the former chairman was complicit in cost overruns for a construction project at the central bank’s headquarters. However, an inspector general’s report found no wrongdoing.

Trump responded to the report by writing on social media, “He should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY! If he doesn’t resign, he should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government, for either corruption or incompetence.”

Following the post, Attorney General Todd Blanche told Bloomberg News, “We’re not reopening a criminal investigation into him.”

Powell has remained on the Fed’s board despite the end of his term as chair, breaking with tradition. As long as Powell remains on the board, the Trump administration is denied the opportunity to name a new board member of the president’s choice.

Cook has consistently maintained that she did nothing wrong.

Just weeks ago, Cook’s lawyer told the White House for a second time that, “There is no legal basis for President Trump to remove Governor Cook for cause.”

“An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing,” Abbe Lowell said Aug. 26. “These attacks on Governor Cook are not about real estate paperwork; they are an attempt by President Trump to force the Federal Reserve to bend to his will.”

Lowell said he and Cook were prepared to continue to fight “any illegal attempt to remove Governor Cook.”
