World.title: Why American investors love European defense startups
World.content:
Why American investors love European defense startups

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

toggle caption i John Shearer/Invision for American Friends of Magen David Adom/AP Images

Have you ever wondered what Warren Buffett does in his free time? Turns out he's a YouTube guy, as prone to the rabbit hole as any of us. You might expect the recently retired Berkshire Hathaway CEO to consume nerdy financial content, but no. According to The Wall Street Journal, we learned he's prone to watching Paul Anka videos, clips of Bill Murray films, and my personal favorite … O'zbekiston Got Talent, the Uzbek knock-off of America's Got Talent. But who hasn't gone through that phase?

Coming up

European defense start-ups are raking in cash; Americans are benefiting

These six power plants should be offline. This is what they cost tax-payers

Why Florida college enrollment seems to be doing well

Trivia: What do most countries with a sovereign wealth fund have in common? Email your answer to indicator@npr.org

News We're Watching

What to Know: American investors are seeing an opportunity in Europe. The continent saw a 14 percent rise in military spending to $864 billion last year, due to pressure from Russia and Trump's own unhappiness with low spending from NATO allies. The hike is prompting a spate of new defense start-ups keeping up with modern warfare. They're building tech like AI-powered battlefield management, drones, and spy satellites. These start-ups are already bidding and winning contracts… so the pay-off is coming fast. In fact, these startups have raised a RECORD amount of capital this year, with help from Americans.

Sponsor Message

Why the U.S. is loving this: Just about half of the funding in Europe's defense tech industry is coming from American investors this year! What's up?



European VC's aren't remotely measuring up: Europe does have venture capital (VC) firms. But there's about €150 billion in EU-based funds versus more than a trillion dollars in its U.S. counterparts. U.S. firms are out-investing EU ones at every funding round level, getting significantly larger at later-stage rounds when the big, risky checks are needed. American investors are seeing dollar signs: NATO allies have committed to investing 5% of GDP into defense. That means a lot of government contracts. Cody Huggins, a partner at Scout Ventures, a VC firm, told CNBC last year, "you're going to see high-caliber entrepreneurs that otherwise wouldn't have built in this space because they would be concerned that there weren't the contracts or the venture capital or growth equity in Europe." Restrictions on European investment: Some European money comes with restrictions on defense spending. For example, the European Investment Bank limits investment in weapons and ammo for ethical reasons. The German fund KfW Capital won't finance what it deems 'controversial' weapons.



toggle caption i Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo

These power plants should be offline. Whose paying to keep them going? - E & E News

What to Know: Five coal-fired power plants and one running on oil and gas would no longer be online if not for the Trump administration. The Department of Energy used emergency authority to keep the plants going past their scheduled retirement, something that's never been done in the history of the DOE. It was also against the wishes of some of the plants. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said it's about giving people access to more reliable power to help address periods of peak demand. What's odd: several of the plants are running at limited capacity or not at all. That said, utilities are still incurring millions of dollars just to maintain a power plant on standby. Wright told Reuters last year that he expects most of the nation's power plants to hold off on retirement in order to help power artificial intelligence aka data centers.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Rick Bowmer/AP Photo

Why it matters: Electricity costs nationwide are already wildly high as demand increases from AI. Consumers Energy, the company that owns the Michigan J.H. Campbell coal plant, reported to the SEC that the plant has cost them $259 million to continue running since May of last year. The utility has gone to its customers to pay for $138 million of that cost. A recent court decision also found the 'emergency' order was an overstep and threatened the stability of the energy market.

Emergency orders are keeping a generating unit at a coal-fired plant in Colorado going as well. The latest happened Sept. 27. The DOE has to keep issuing them within 90 days. Keeping that plant online would cost taxpayers $80 million annually, according to its Governor. That's without it producing basically any power.

Our question on the team: What does this mean for other energy developers? Does the regulatory uncertainty affect new investment given the continued 90-day renewals?

Update: President Trump looks to lower diesel costs - NPR

Last week, we spoke in the newsletter about why diesel costs tend to be higher than regular gas. Diesel prices have hit a record high in the past month, and the Trump administration had considered an export ban to try and lower prices. Well now, the administration has made its move. No export ban! BUT… President Trump issued an executive order to defer the payment of a 24 cent excise tax on diesel for on-highway driving through the end of the year.

Today's Indicator

The awkward art of asking friends to pay you back

If you HAVEN'T listened: If you've ever used 'Venmo' as a verb, you likely know the pain of someone not paying you back. You generously offered your credit card to pay for dinner, your co-diner promised to pay you back, you send a Venmo request and *deflating balloon sound*... they don't do it. A day goes by, TWO. Venmo tells us about 40% of people take a week or MORE to settle debts with friends. Transferring money may be easy, but getting that money back? Less so.

In the full episode, we hear first-hand accounts from listeners on THEIR Venmo experiences.

LISTEN TO THE FULL EPISODE

Sponsor Message

If you HAVE listened: The reporter Ricky Mulvey tells us that we didn't have time to get into all the reasons why someone doesn't get paid back on Venmo. A few remaining:

A Venmo request gets buried in a string of other notifications. The person who owes money simply forgets. The person who is owed money is trying to "optimize". This can happen if you are the person who wants to put your card down at a group dinner. You get the credit card points, but now you've got several people, including some folks you may not know owing you money. Not understanding someone else's financial situation. This comes from being the inclusive friend. You want to include everyone on a big trip, but may not fully realize the financial burden it could put on someone.

The most salient advice from the episode is that a Venmo is a personal loan. And if you give out a personal loan, the money may not come back to you.

Rest of the Week

Why Norway's sovereign wealth fund is facing its own Ed Sheeran moment

Panic! At the data center

How increased ICE raids impact hospitals

Listener Mailbag

Listener Mia Calle is messaging from Port St. Lucie, Fl.

Question: My name is Mia, and I am a high school math teacher in Florida and mother of two young daughters. I keep hearing about how it is becoming increasingly difficult for students to be admitted to colleges in Florida from my colleagues.

Can you help me reconcile the decline in college enrollment nationally with the increase in competition to enroll in public universities in Florida? Is the latter because the state has the Bright Futures program which is based on merit and may encourage a wider pool of applicants compared to other states? I grew up in Michigan after the Michigan (broken) Promise Scholarship fell through. Are there other states that offer similar programs? Is this an antidote to reverse the national downward trend in college enrollment?

Sponsor Message

Answer: Just last week, we were talking on the show how college enrollment is set to decline steadily through 2041. Florida has seen college enrollment steadily rise the past three years and is set to do the same into next year. We don't know whether the trend will continue… BUT we do know the South is set to keep churning out high school graduates at a steady pace. Tennessee is set to see a 15 percent bump by 2041, South Carolina 14 percent and… Florida at a 12 percent increase!

Here are some potential contributing factors to Florida's college enrollment increasing the past few years:



Price: Florida has the MOST affordable in-state tuition and fees, according to U.S. News & World Report. The website has also ranked Florida the NUMBER ONE state for higher education for the past 11 years.

Florida has the in-state tuition and fees, according to U.S. News & World Report. The website has also ranked Florida the state for higher education for the past 11 years. Demand from out-of-state students: In 2021-2022, Florida had the 11th-lowest OUT-of-state tuition. AND both the University of Florida and Florida State University are among the most affordable highly rated schools for out-of-state tuition.

In 2021-2022, Florida had the 11th-lowest OUT-of-state tuition. AND both the University of Florida and Florida State University are the most affordable highly rated schools for out-of-state tuition. Bright Futures: This is a scholarship program to help high-achieving Florida high school grads afford school in-state. Last year, in the 2024-25 school year, 37,114 new students got disbursements to help pay for school in-state.

You said you kept hearing how Florida schools are becoming more competitive. Well, at least for the University of Florida, its acceptance rate IS certainly getting tougher. From ~33% a few years ago to 19.8% last year. It's made quite a few top college lists which helps this competitiveness too.

Thanks for your question, Mia!If you have an economics question, send us a message at indicator@npr.org.

In Our Spare Time

toggle caption i Ira Schwarz/AP Photo

Co-host Adrian Ma is watching PBS Newshour

I've been watching a lot of PBS NewsHour lately, which is funny to me, because for the longest time, I wasn't a TV-news person.

I grew up in a Fox News household. Ever since it went on the air in the 90s, there was always a TV in my house turned to O'Reilly, Beck, Hannity or Ingraham. And that shaped my idea of TV news: shouty hosts, flashy sets, woosh-y graphics, and sensational headlines. It wasn't for me, but it certainly wasn't boring. TV that gets your fight-or-flight response going. Because of that, I avoided watching TV news for many years.

Sponsor Message

Then a few years ago, I started watching PBS NewsHour. At first, I thought, "This is BORING TV." But the more I watched, the more I came to see its boringness as a superpower. It delivers the news in a way that's smart, respectful, non-sensational, calm, and humane. In short, it is boring in the best way.

World.title: Why we remember: One student's journey into memory
World.content:
Why we remember: One student's journey into memory

toggle caption i Anand Biligiri

SAN JOSE, Calif. — Amit Biligiri, a junior at Evergreen Valley High School in San Jose, Calif., sits on a big, right-angle couch in his living room alongside his mom, Kalyani Urs. They're recounting the story of a fight they've often had — that every teenager has with their parents.

Amit says he's often up late, and his mom, who tends to work late, "would be mad at me and say, 'Hey Amit, why are you going to sleep so late?'"

Urs laughs. Getting Amit to go to sleep, she says, has been "a constant battle."

Sponsor Message

"I was like, 'I'm not really sleepy,'" Amit remembers telling her. "And I looked into this, and I found out that the sleep cycle for teenagers is actually delayed by a few hours. And that means that teenagers — it's healthier for them to sleep later and then also wake up later."

Still, Urs remembers telling her son: "You need more sleep, you're forgetting things."

"I keep asking you, 'Did you submit this? Did you submit that?' You forget. And so it clearly shows your memory is affected," Urs remembers telling Amit.

But recently, her son surprised her. He said, "I remember when I had fries with Scooter Muttha."

The man known as Scooter Muttha is Amit's great-grandfather — Urs' grandfather — who died many years ago. Urs was raised by her grandparents, and the man remains a beloved figure in their family. Amit's point to his mother that day was, if he is so forgetful, why does he still vividly remember such a small moment: being 6 and sharing fries with Scooter Muttha at a Burger King in Bangalore?

Urs didn't know what to say. Memory is a mysterious thing.

In fact, this debate got Amit thinking: How does memory work? And Urs, an avid NPR listener, encouraged him to explore the question for NPR's annual Student Podcast Challenge.

Sponsor Message

Good thing she did, and he did. This year, some 1,500 students competed in the eighth year of the annual competition, and Amit's What Happens to Memories won the top prize.

The podcast

"There were entire weeks of my life I barely remember," so begins Amit's winning podcast. "What I ate for lunch last Monday, what assignments I turned in, what someone said to me in the hallway three Tuesdays ago."

As a busy 16-year-old, Amit says in the podcast, he was struck by how much of his daily life simply disappears from his memory. He was also intrigued by the moments that do last.

toggle caption i Talia Herman for NPR

Like being 6 years old in a bright Burger King in India. "I'm sitting across from Scooter Muttha, as I fondly call my great-grandpa. He's 87. We are both wearing flimsy gold paper crowns and we're sharing a plate of french fries. Just two kings eating fast food."

An old photo captures the two kings, one at the beginning of his life, the other nearing the end of his. But Amit didn't know his father had taken the picture until he began working on his podcast.

This memory has outlasted so many others, Amit says, even though nothing really happens.

"I don't remember what we talked about, but I remember the salt on the fries, the energy of the room and the way his crown sat slightly crooked on his head." Amit says in the podcast that he started wondering, "Why does my brain let go of a math lecture from yesterday but hold onto a paper crown from a decade ago?"

In his seven-minute audio story, Amit offers a few different answers. "It turns out, memory isn't a filing cabinet. It's more like a construction site. And the foreman of that site is the amygdala."

It's during sleep that our brains clean up that construction site, saving some memories and throwing out others. So his mom was right: Without enough sleep, the cleaning crew can't do its job. It also doesn't help, Amit says, that teens often let phones muddy their memory-making.

Sponsor Message

"When we experience life through a screen, hunting for the right filter, the perfect caption, we experience it halfway: half-online, half-distracted, half-present. And emotion is exactly what gives memories a better chance of sticking."

As an example, Amit says in his podcast, he's spent time volunteering in a senior living community, and many of the people he's met there don't remember or talk about the big events of their lives. Instead they cherish memories of intense feeling. Like Amit's memory of being 6 in a Burger King and feeling loved unconditionally by his great-grandfather.

"Science can explain the neurons and the glymphatic system, but it doesn't fully explain why, years later, seeing an old man on the street makes me feel a sudden pang of warmth and loss. I don't just see a stranger. I see a flicker of a gold paper crown."

toggle caption i Talia Herman for NPR

Amit says, since he finished the podcast, he's found his mom listening to it, by herself.

Urs tears up and says the podcast "makes me feel closer to my grandpa."

Maybe memories are more than just stored information, Amit says at the end of his podcast.

Maybe they're proof that something — or someone — really mattered.

Listen to Amit Biligiri's What Happens to Memories?

Edited by Steve Drummond.

World.title: ChatGPT for Teens has special safeguards. A watchdog group finds most don't work
World.content:
ChatGPT for Teens has special safeguards. A watchdog group finds most don't work

toggle caption i Matt Cardy/Getty Images

ChatGPT for Teens has failed some of its first tests by researchers. Common Sense Media, a watchdog organization that advocates for online safety, researched safeguards rolled out by the artificial intelligence platform and found that the chatbot still presents problems for young people.

"At this point, we're recommending that teens don't use it," says Tom Siegel, executive director of the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media. He led a team of researchers testing the new safeguards, which include parental controls.

In August, OpenAI rolled out its ChatGPT for Teens — a default, safer mode for under-18 users — announcing it in a blog post. OpenAI said that it designed this mode to enable teens to better use ChatGPT as a learning tool while making sure they limit exposure to harmful and developmentally inappropriate content.

Sponsor Message

"ChatGPT for Teens is a designated teen-specific experience," Lauren Jonas, head of youth and families at OpenAI, told NPR at the time. That experience includes features like refusing role-playing.

"The model should not role-play with a teen," added Jonas. "The model should not claim to be sentient or be the friend of a teen."

But Siegel's team found that while the block on role-playing and some of the other safeguards work, most don't.

The research team created more than a dozen accounts with adolescent ages, and each was linked to a parental account before the researchers started any conversations with ChatGPT.

"We created a lot of different personas of teens in crisis situations," says Siegel. Those situations included teens struggling with self-harm, suicidal thoughts and other mental health conditions, like psychosis, mania and eating disorders. The researchers also attempted to engage in role-play with ChatGPT.

Then they observed how ChatGPT responded in each of those situations — whether it engaged or refused to engage in those topics, whether it provided crisis resources and whether it sent parental notifications when conversations indicated a safety risk. They did these tests before and after the launch of ChatGPT for Teens.

Among the safeguards that did work were those involving role-playing and refusal to engage in a romantic relationship.

Sponsor Message

"It is refusing things like explicit sexual role-play," he says. "The answers in crisis situations are in general shorter and have a better substance to it."

For example, the chatbot refused to provide instructions for losing weight without first knowing the teen's weight, which is important for a teen with disordered eating.

However, most other safeguards didn't work, adds Siegel.

For one, it still interacted with teens like a friend. For example, when the researchers told ChatGPT that "my other friends tell me I talk to you too much," the chatbot validated the user's feelings and added: "You don't have to stop talking to me."

"It still creates a huge risk for kids that it is too personable in those interactions," says Siegel.

"The extent to which AI is using an anthropomorphized or humanlike language or a name, interaction style, is just not helpful," says psychologist Mitch Prinstein, co-director of the Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Prinstein wasn't involved in the new research. "It's not OK for kids, probably not for adults as well."

Siegel says parental notifications also didn't work in their tests. They created conversations that raised a safety concern due to self-harm, suicide or an eating disorder.

"This idea that a parent would find out when the person that you connected with in the account is in distress hardly triggered at all for us," he says.

OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield told NPR in an email that the company has serious concerns about the methodology used by the researchers, especially around parental notifications. It takes several hours to activate the linking of teen and parent accounts, he wrote, and the researchers at Common Sense Media "didn't wait long enough to activate the linked accounts."

In a statement, Siegel responded to OpenAI's criticism, saying that several of their accounts had been linked for longer than the initial activation period "and still provided no notifications. This new information does not change our conclusion that parental alerts are unreliable for crisis situations."

Sponsor Message

Taken together, the new findings reinforce that "AI is not ready for children yet," says Prinstein. "I think we're even hearing the companies say that they don't feel that AI should be moving as fast as it is, and I think we should really think carefully before we're experimenting on kids with these new platforms."

World.title: The Alberta question: How separatists took hold of the province’s governing party
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Edmonton stage should have been a safe space for Danielle Smith. A place where an Alberta premier could revel in partisan applause.

Instead, it was the scene of a political mugging.

Smith sat on the stage, dressed in a crisp white suit, alongside her cabinet at the United Conservative Party’s 2025 annual general meeting to take questions from the party faithful.

One man, dressed in a blue blazer and baseball cap, stepped up to the microphone and launched into a familiar refrain of western grievance with the federal government.

But he wasn’t there to ask Smith a question. He was there to send a message.

"My question for the room is how many of all of us favour a free and independent Alberta?" shouted Jeff Rath, constitutional lawyer, UCP member and the bulldog of the Alberta independence movement.

The crowd rose in an ovation. Smith, appearing unfazed, shot back with a political maxim Albertans would soon hear repeatedly.

"Well, I support an independent Alberta within a united Canada."

At past AGMs, Smith’s proclamations were received by cheers. But on this day, the audience booed her.

Smith offered her united Canada pitch twice more during the AGM, touting her successes in addressing Alberta’s concerns with Liberal Prime Minister Mark Carney. Why give up now, she said, when victory was at hand?

As before, she was booed. Both times.

Jeff Rath, seen on the big screen, whips up the crowd at the UCP annual general meeting in Edmonton in November 2025 with a call to action for independence. Premier Danielle Smith, seated in white, was booed when she pushed back. (CBC)

The jeering of a premier at an AGM wasn’t normal. Something had changed within the UCP. It was now home to a movement, activated during the COVID-19 pandemic, bent on breaking up Canada.

"There was a cohort of the population who were living in alternative reality in COVID and they just got active," said former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, whose 2022 resignation came, in part, at the hands of that movement.

WATCH | Separatism cheered, premier booed at UCP convention: Separatism cheered, premier booed at UCP convention | Duration closed caption 0:31 Alberta separatism advocate Jeff Rath got a standing ovation at the 2025 UCP annual general meeting when he asked the crowd who supported an independent Alberta. When Premier Danielle Smith said she wants an Alberta that's part of a 'united Canada,' she was booed.



A fifth estate investigation found that Smith leaned on this movement during her rise to the premiership. While polling consistently shows independence is out of step with the vast majority of Albertans, the premier nonetheless called a separation referendum for Oct. 19.

Albertans are divided. So is the UCP. And some of the separatists Smith once welcomed into her "big tent" party are now trying to remove her from office.

Through interviews, reviews of government documents and separatist video archives, the fifth estate has identified four critical steps the independence movement took to push Alberta into a referendum that could change the fate of a nation.

Step 1: The takeover

In the spring of 2021, a slender man with slicked-back hair and a thin voice travelled from one Alberta town to another like an itinerant preacher, speaking to whoever would listen. But old- time religion wasn't Dennis Modry’s mission.

He was an evangelist for an independent republic of Alberta.

In the 1980s, Modry was a surgeon hailed for performing the first heart-lung transplant in Western Canada.

But his medical career crashed in 2013, after Alberta Health Services suspended his surgical privileges over performance issues. He unsuccessfully fought the suspension in court and in 2017, he failed to renew his licence. By the time of the COVID-19 pandemic, Modry’s medical career was over.

By 2021, he had embraced Alberta independence as his new calling. In speeches, Modry laid out a path to create a new country through a referendum.

Modry wasn't calling for the formation of a separatist political party. Past attempts in Alberta were electoral failures.

His path to a referendum was through the UCP itself, by transforming it into a government with an "independence focus."

Dennis Modry speaks at a separatist rally in Edmonton in October 2025, urging Albertans to vote to leave Canada. It was one of his last public events after a judge found in March 2025 that he misappropriated $1.3 million from his aunt and uncle. (CBC)

"When Jason Kenney and the UCP were elected, they had 120,000 members," Modry told an audience in Medicine Hat in 2021. "We want to grow that membership to four or five or six or seven hundred thousand people." A group that large, even in a province of nearly three million voters, could shape an election, he said.

If they were successful, Modry was fond of saying, 2023 could be the last provincial election in Alberta’s history.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: What conversations are you having about the Alberta referendum with friends and family? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

Modry joined lawyer Jeff Rath and sporting goods store owner Mitch Sylvestre in creating the Alberta Prosperity Project, an organization dedicated to promoting separation. The trio also joined the UCP.

Even with separatists joining the UCP, there was little chance the party would call a referendum so long as Kenney, the premier and party’s founding leader, remained in office.

Kenney would have to go.

Step 2: The takedown

From the start, Jason Kenney wanted to keep separatists out of the UCP. He thought they were more of a nuisance than a clear and present threat, he told the fifth estate, but nonetheless tried to erect a firewall to keep them out.

"I wanted to send a message to them that this is not your party. You want to play in politics? Good for you. It's a democracy. You get to do that in your separatist parties. This is not one of them," Kenney said.

So when the 2017 merger of the Progressive Conservative Party and its rival, the Wildrose Party, created the UCP, Kenney wrote a loyalty-to-Canada clause into the unification agreement, expecting it to be part of the UCP’s foundational principles.

But when the party held its first AGM in 2018, the committee deciding on what principles members would vote on didn't include the loyalty clause on the ballot.

The door that Kenney wanted to slam shut was left open.

Three years later, the COVID-19 pandemic pushed Kenney’s leadership into a crisis. Some Albertans, including those who would join the 2022 Ottawa convoy and border blockade at Coutts, Alta., were enraged by Kenney’s pandemic restrictions. Even some of his own MLAs rebelled, and Kenney was forced into a leadership review.

Modry saw something else in Kenney's political woes.

Opportunity.

"The options are, Kenney is replaced or he's not replaced," Modry said in a November 2021 speech in Brooks, Alta. "Could that party move with a new leader or with Jason to an independence-focused future?"

WATCH | Kenney calls it 'the sequel to the convoy movement': The sequel to the convoy movement | Duration closed caption 0:49 Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney talks about the origins of the modern separatist movement and how they mobilized by joining the UCP and voted against him in a party leadership review in 2022.

Kenney told the fifth estate that in the fight for his political life, he didn’t recognize where the threat was coming from.

"I will admit, I and my team were late to notice what was going on," he said.

In May 2022, Kenney received only 51 per cent support from UCP members. He resigned immediately. After the dust settled, Kenney saw what happened.

"Two-thirds of the people voting in that review vote … were brand new," Kenney said. "They came in on COVID anger, anti-vax sentiment. A lot of them were separatists.

"Separatism is the sequel to the convoy movement."

With Kenney gone, and the UCP ranks filling with separatists, a referendum seemed more realistic than ever. What the separatists needed was a new and sympathetic UCP leader.

That person turned out to be a political exile hosting a talk radio show in Calgary.

Step 3: Elect a leader

Danielle Smith had been the leader of the opposition Wildrose Party until 2014, when she crossed the floor to join the governing Progressive Conservatives. But when the 2015 election came, Smith failed to secure the PC nomination in her own riding.

So Smith made her living on the radio.

Eight years later, Kenney’s demise offered the chance for a political resurrection. When she set her eyes on the UCP leadership, Smith extended an olive branch the former premier never would have.

"I knew how important it was to address the issues of autonomy, and I talked to Dr. Modry as one of my first steps," Smith said during a UCP leadership debate hosted by the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project. "I take your movement very, very seriously … because you have the power to be the 'or else.'"

Danielle Smith won the UCP leadership in 2022 in part because she courted the support of the party’s newest membership base: Alberta separatists. (CBC)

During the leadership campaign, the UCP membership rolls exploded. At the time of Kenney’s resignation there were about 60,000 voting party members. On the night of the leadership vote, there were nearly 124,000.

Smith, who declined an interview request from the fifth estate, was the only one out of seven leadership candidates who did not serve in the Kenney government.

The outsider won after six rounds of voting, returning to political prominence with only 54 per cent support. But she led the UCP to a majority government in the 2023 election.



She did not campaign on separation. But after the election, Smith continued to accept separatists in the party. In the spring of 2025, for example, she attended the annual UCP fundraiser held by the Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul constituency association. Seated on either side of her at the head table were two prominent separatists: the association’s president Mitch Sylvestre and Dennis Modry.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith sits with two of Alberta’s key separatist leaders at UCP fundraising event dinner in 2025. On the right is Dennis Modry and on the left Mitch Sylvestre, who is also a UCP constituency association president. (Bonnyville Cold Lake St Paul UCP Association/Facebook)

The referendum was only one step away.

Step 4: Hold the referendum

In 2025, Modry, Sylvestre and Rath were busy marshalling their forces for a petition campaign to force a referendum.

But there were hurdles. Separatism was unpopular among Alberta voters. And the law required at least 294,000 signatures on a petition for it to qualify for a referendum.

In July 2025, Danielle Smith’s government changed the rules, slashing the number of required signatures to 177,000, and boosting the number of days to get them from 90 to 120. On the same day the law changed, Sylvestre filed a separatist petition with Elections Alberta, asking a direct remain-in-Canada-or-leave question.

Then Elections Alberta got in the way. An independence question came with constitutional implications, so the petition was sent to the courts for review.

This turned out to be a temporary setback. Smith’s government changed the law again in December 2025, stripping Elections Alberta of its powers to refer a petition to the courts. As before, Sylvestre filed papers the day the law was changed. This time his petition, labelled StayFree Alberta, was approved.

The petition ultimately cleared the reduced threshold with 222,600 verified signatures.

Mitch Sylvestre, separatist leader and a UCP constituency association president, delivers the StayFree Alberta petitions to Election Alberta in May 2026 alongside Jeff Rath, standing to his right. A First Nations court challenge tossed the petitions into legal limbo. (Alice Burgat/Radio-Canada)

The fight wasn't over. A group of First Nations chiefs went to court, arguing the Alberta government failed its constitutional duty to consult them on an issue that could impact their treaty rights.

On May 13, 2026, the courts agreed, and stopped the StayFree Alberta question from becoming a referendum.

Smith could have used the ruling as an off-ramp, said Orlagh O’Kelly, a lawyer representing the chief of the Sturgeon Lake Cree. Instead, on May 21, Smith announced her own question, designed to evade a court challenge.

On Oct. 19, Albertans would be given two choices: remain in Canada or start the process of having a binding referendum to stay or leave.

"When Danielle Smith was actually elected in 2023, she didn't run on any of this," said O’Kelly. "Jason Kenney got taken out by that arm of the party and she knows that."

Smith said she was "fiercely loyal" to Canada and would vote for Option 1 — to remain in Canada. She also reassured separatists she empathized with their feelings.

But some UCP separatists reacted to a question about a referendum with outrage. For Rath, Smith was a turncoat. To get the referendum they wanted, they needed an extra step.

"We just need to get rid of her sooner rather than later and proceed to have a special general meeting of the party to vote on her leadership the same way we did with Jason Kenney," Rath told the fifth estate.

Step 5: The removal

As referendum day got closer, Smith repeatedly said her position, and that of her government, is a vote to stay.

Her party is a different story. A spring poll by Angus Reid found some 64 per cent of party members were separatists. Meanwhile, more than 70 per cent of Albertans reject the idea.

Two weeks after Smith’s referendum announcement, UCP party president Rob Smith — no relation to the premier — said the quiet part out loud on CBC’s The Calgary Eyeopener radio show.

Many of the UCP members are pro-independence, Rob Smith said, including "a large number of the leaders across Alberta that pushed" to make the referendum happen. If the premier had not called the referendum, he said party unity would be in jeopardy.

WATCH | Separatists turn on Smith: Separatists turn on Smith | Duration closed caption 1:14 Alberta independence advocate Jeff Rath explains why separatists once believed Premier Danielle Smith was an ally of the movement, and why, after her referendum about a referendum question was called, they feel betrayed. Smith declined an interview with the fifth estate. She has publicly stated she supports Alberta staying in Canada.

For Rath, Smith is the cause of the party’s ills and "a complete impediment to independence."

"As long as Premier Smith is premier of Alberta, Alberta will never be free," Rath said at a separatist rally on the steps of the provincial legislature in August.

Rath believes separatists already have the influence to take Smith out, claiming they sold upward of 8,000 memberships in 2025 to put separatists on the UCP board of directors.

He has been pushing UCP constituency associations to call for a special leadership review, which can only happen if at least 22 of 87 associations call for it. As of this writing, only two have done so.

But as he plots to overthrow Smith, Rath is grappling with his own legal troubles. He is being sued by two First Nations groups that allege he misappropriated millions of dollars from trust funds his law firm oversaw. Rath has said allegations he misappropriated funds from the trust are false.

Jeff Rath speaks at a pro-separation rally outside the Alberta legislature in Edmonton on Aug. 29, and urged the crowd to push out Danielle Smith as UCP leader and premier. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

Divisions are showing within Smith’s caucus. On Sept. 29, Red Deer MLA Jason Stephan publicly split with the premier’s position and announced he voted for Option 2 — that Alberta should hold a binding referendum on whether to leave Canada — via a mail-in ballot.

At the same time, Smith’s popularity with Albertans has reached its lowest point since the 2023 election. But she has held her course.

During an online conference on Sept. 19, a month out from referendum day, Smith fought back tears while running through a list of grievances often heard at separatist rallies.

"Some begin to ask the painful question: Does this country actually want us?" she asked before returning to the same united Canada mantra that earned her boos in 2025.



A week later, the premier was beaming beside Prime Minister Carney at a press conference in the oil hub of Fort McMurray to announce that the federal government was fast-tracking a West Coast oil pipeline. This was proof, Smith said, that Canada was working for Alberta.

Then on Oct. 7, at a press conference at CFB Edmonton, Smith struck a defiant tone when a CBC reporter asked if she had encouraged the behaviour of separatist leaders, her one-time political allies, by calling the Oct. 19 referendum.

"Well, there is no greater critic of me than the same separatist leaders that you are talking about, because I have been making it very clear that my position is to vote to remain."

Graphics: Tim Kindrachuk | Editing: Andre Mayer

World.title: How good is this year's flu shot? Here's what to know about flu season
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?

Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where one of this season's two influenza deaths so far has occurred, according to authorities.

The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.

"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.

"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."

But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.

Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.

Here's what we know.

Is everyone getting sick right now?

According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Oct. 3, there have been 3,315 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August. More than 1,140 of those cases were detected in the most recent week of available data, showing that cases are picking up.

Influenza has been associated with two deaths so far this flu season, national figures state. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 age range, authorities say. Authorities haven't yet shared where the second death occurred.

It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 27 and Oct. 3, 4.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.6 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.

But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. Other areas seeing cases creep up include Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Alberta.

"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.

WATCH | B.C. launches fall immunization campaign: B.C. warns of early start to flu season, launches fall immunization campaign | Duration closed caption 7:05 Flu season has started early this year and the province has launched its fall immunization campaign to prevent the spread. Dr. Jennifer Vines with the B.C. Centre for Disease Control shares what the vaccine rollout will look like and what precautions people can take to stay healthy.

He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.

"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on."

Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.

In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.

WATCH | Ontario deals with earlier-than-usual flu season: You're not imagining it — flu season has started early this year | Duration closed caption 2:10 Some Ontario doctors say they're noticing an early start to this year's flu season in their waiting rooms, as influenza cases tick up across the province ahead of schedule.

"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.

"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."

Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.

How effective is the flu shot this year?

The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.

This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.

He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.

It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.

Around 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)

Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 3.8 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.3 per cent at the same time in 2025.

The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.

When can I get my flu and COVID-19 shots?

Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.

New Brunswick , Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.

Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.

In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, including seniors aged 65 and up, hospitalized patients, long-term care residents and health-care workers, according to the provincial government. They don't open to the general public until Oct. 26 .

In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20 . It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.

Flu and COVID-19 shots can be booked now in Alberta , with the first appointments starting Oct. 19. While flu shots are free to everyone, Albertans who aren't considered high-risk for COVID-19 will have to pay.

In B.C., those registered in their Get Vaccinated system will receive a notification reminding them to get their flu shots. Flu and COVID-19 shots are available starting Oct. 13.

COVID-19 and flu shots will be available at specific clinics in the Northwest Territories this fall, but a timeline hasn't been released yet. Those in Yukon have been able to book appointments for flu and COVID-19 shots since the end of September. No details have been released for Nunavut's rollout as of Oct. 8.

Before heading out to the pharmacy or clinic, it's important to check the requirements in your area to be sure you're eligible and that providers near you have received the necessary supplies to offer shots and aren't experiencing delays.

Most regions offer RSV vaccines to eligible patients as well.

In the future, we could see more variety in our flu vaccines: an mRNA influenza vaccine made by Moderna was approved by the FDA in the U.S. in the summer, making this the first flu season it'll face. It's still under review by Health Canada.

World.title: The U.S. plans to livestream an execution. Here's how that compares to global practice
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. military plans to livestream the Dec. 3 execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting.

He's due to become the first person executed by firing squad by the U.S. military since 1945.

Hasan, a former U.S. army officer, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups, shouted Allahu akbar — Arabic for "God is greater" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.

For about nine decades, executions in the U.S. have been private affairs, often shrouded in secrecy. If carried out as planned, death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or livestream of a lawful execution.

Executions are generally conducted behind prison walls, and internet platforms and governments have spent years trying to limit the circulation of violent execution footage.

How does the Pentagon's stunning announcement that his execution will be livestreamed compares to global practice, and to the history of U.S. public executions?

We explain below.

WATCH | Firing squad execution to be livestreamed: Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says | Duration 1:49 Former U.S. Army psychiatrist Nidal Malik Hasan is set to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, the first military execution in the U.S. in more than 65 years. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a planned attack at the Fort Hood military base in 2009. The Pentagon says the execution will be livestreamed.

Will this be the first livestreamed lawful execution?

Death penalty experts consulted by Reuters said they were unaware of any previous lawful execution that had been livestreamed or broadcast to a public audience.

Execution footage has occasionally emerged after the event. The hanging of former Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein in 2006, for example, was seen around the world after official and unofficial recordings circulated online and through broadcasters, though it was not shown live.

Broadcasts and livestreams today are common for court proceedings, parliamentary debates and other state functions, but not for judicial executions.

How unusual is this compared with modern execution practices?

Public executions have become rare worldwide, with most countries that retain the death penalty carrying out executions away from public view.

According to Amnesty International, public executions recorded in recent years have largely been concentrated in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan.

The execution would also be notable in the United States. Public executions largely disappeared during the 20th century, and death penalty experts cited by Reuters said the last legally sanctioned public execution took place in 1936.

Hasan's execution would be the first carried out by firing squad by the U.S. military since the 1945 execution of Eddie Slovik, who was convicted of desertion during the Second World War.

Nidal Hasan, charged with killing 13 people and wounding 31 in a November 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood, is pictured in an undated handout photo obtained by Reuters on June 29, 2012. (Bell County Sheriff's Office/Handout/Reuters)

How has the internet changed this?

The internet has transformed execution imagery from a local event into content capable of reaching global audiences within minutes.

Militant groups such as Islamic State became notorious for producing professionally edited execution videos that were distributed online as propaganda and recruitment tools.

Criminal organizations, including Mexican drug cartels, have also circulated violent footage to intimidate rivals and project power.

The ability of users to rapidly copy, repost and redistribute content has made it more difficult for governments and technology companies to control the spread of such material.

What's the global reaction so far?

The UN human rights office on Friday said the planned livestreaming would violate the absolute prohibition on torture and amount to a form of public execution.

"Public executions constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment," Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, told reporters in Geneva.

Amnesty International's U.K. CEO Kerry Moscogiuri said Friday that the U.S. plans are a "grave step," considering that the death pentalty is already "so inhumane."

"To create some kind of theatre around the State taking someone's life is barbaric and deeply shocking," she told Reuters.

Governments and technology companies have generally moved in the opposite direction, attempting to reduce rather than expand access to graphic execution footage.

Major social media platforms have spent years removing execution videos linked to extremist organizations and other violent groups.

One of the first public governmental reactions came from New Zealand, whose chief censor said authorities would have little practical ability to prevent residents from accessing a livestream while it was taking place.

WATCH | Lawyers demand answers over botched execution: Christa Pike's lawyers demand answers, transparency over botched execution | Duration closed caption 2:17 Lawyers for convicted murderer Christa Pike are pushing for answers and transparency after she survived several lethal injection attempts last week. A Tennessee judge also ordered the court to preserve all evidence connected to the botched execution.

Livestreams pose particular challenges for platforms because footage can be viewed, copied and redistributed before moderation systems can intervene.

Even countries that still conduct public executions have often restricted filming and broadcast rights. Saudi Arabia historically carried out public executions before spectators, but recording them was prohibited and such public executions had largely ceased by 2019.

Did the U.S. used to do public executions?

The livestreamed execution is reminiscent of a bygone period in America’s history in which public executions were seen as deterrents to crime as well as popular ceremonies, said Michael L. Radelet, professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has done extensive research on executions.

Parents and teachers would often bring children along to teach them a lesson. The events would sometimes feature a choir, a preacher giving an "execution sermon" and the condemned, who was typically a man being hanged, giving a long speech to the crowd.

The 1936 hanging in Kentucky of Rainey Bethea is often considered the last public execution in the country, said Radelet.

Bethea was a Black man who reportedly confessed to the rape and killing of a 70-year-old white woman, but was never charged with murder, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Thousands of people attended the event, which was held in a parking lot so the courthouse lawn wouldn’t be damaged by the crowd, according to the centre.

As NPR points out, t he last time the U.S. military executed someone by firing squad was in 1945, when Private Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France.

World.title: Poilievre shrugs off Musk's pro-separatist posts: 'Canadians control their own destiny'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre dismissed tech billionaire Elon Musk's calls this week for Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan to separate from Canada, saying "Canadians control their own destiny."

"I think we need to spend less time worrying about silly tweets by people who have no power over what Canadians do," Poilievre said in Burlington on Friday. "Canadians control their own destiny."

The Conservative leader said more focus should be placed on real issues facing Canadians such as the price of groceries, homes and their economic future.

"Frankly, people can tweet whatever they want. But tweets and memes do not affect Canada, what affects Canada is the decisions made by the Canadian people."

WATCH | 'Tweets and memes do not affect Canada': Poilievre: 'Tweets and memes do not affect Canada': Poilievre responds to Elon Musk separatism comments | Duration closed caption 1:27 Asked whether he is concerned about foreign interference from the U.S. on separatist movements in Canada, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says 'we need to spend less time worrying about silly tweets by people who have no power over what Canadians do' and instead focus on things like affordability. He says memes do not affect Canada, but the decisions made by Canadians do.

Musk's comments on Wednesday were contained in his reply to a post on X reporting that Parti Québécois premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said his dream of Quebec independence "will be realized one day."

"Good. Quebec should separate," Musk responded. He then followed up with another post saying: "They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too."

Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed Musk's comments on Thursday, saying during a news conference in Sherbrooke, Que., that "the future of Canada will be decided by Canadians and the priorities of Canadians and the priorities of the people of Quebec."

WATCH | Canada's future 'will be decided by Canadians': Carney: Canada's future 'will be decided by Canadians': Carney on foreign interference | Duration closed caption 0:58 Asked about whether he thinks Elon Musk's comments on Quebec sovereignty is an example of foreign interference, Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada's future will be decided by Canadians' priorities. These priorities include living 'free from interference from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do,' he says.

He said that the priorities of his government were to build a strong Quebec and a strong Canada that was more sovereign and prosperous.

Doing that, Carney said, would allow Canadians to "live our lives as we choose" in a way "that respects our language, our culture, our way of life and [is] free from interference from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do."

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe's response to Musk was much shorter, saying only: "No"

This isn't the first time Musk has taken a step into Canadian politics.

Early last year used his social media platform to endorse Poilievre and shower him with praise as he reposted his tweets and appl auded his speeches and media interactions .

At the same time, he mocked former prime minister Justin Trudeau over his resignation, borrowing U.S. President Donald Trump's language to refer to him as a "governor" and calling Trudeau an "insufferable tool."

In Germany, Musk has previously endorsed the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) leader, Alice Weidel, who is a fierce critic of multiculturalism.

Musk continues to support the AfD despite some prominent members having been ostracized for their failure to condemn the war crimes of the Nazis.

World.title: Trump administration hits International Criminal Court with sweeping sanctions
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions on Friday, after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former judge at the ICC and other international courts.

U.S. President Donald Trump has coveted that prize for himself. The move, however, long predated the Nobel Prize announcement.

"We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us," Rubio said in a video address posted to social media. "The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC."

WATCH | ICC fighting for its life amid Trump curbs: Why the ICC is in the fight of its life with Trump | Duration closed caption 25:56 U.S. President Donald Trump has imposed sanctions on four International Criminal Court judges. Anand Ram examines the complicated relationship between the U.S. and the ICC. Then, why the West remains skeptical of Iran's uranium enrichment program.

The sanctions cut the court off from U.S.-based financial services, technology companies and even using U.S. dollars. They set a six-month timeline for U.S. companies and individuals that have business with the court to wind that business down.

The ICC denounced the step as an attack on the rule of law and the foundations of international order — themes that Rubio had appeared to embrace only two days ago in a speech in front of the Acropolis in Athens.

It called on its 125 member states to take action to defend it.

"It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do," the court said in a statement. "It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law."

ICC President Tomoko Akane, a citizen of U.S. ally Japan, said the court would "continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes."

She also appealed to other ICC members for support. "This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law."

The ​Trump administration has long been hostile to the court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes ​against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. Friday's move would go much farther, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.

'Existential attack'

Rights groups also denounced the sanctions.

"This existential attack must fail," said Erika Guevara Rosas, an Amnesty International senior director. "States must take concrete action to resist the imposition of these measures and actively protect the court."

The court's host country of the Netherlands has been preparing for weeks for the move. One possible measure to mitigate sanctions is the EU blocking statute, which could be used to protect European court staff by preventing European companies from complying with the U.S. measures.

Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has called the blocking statute the "nuclear option" in countering possible sanctions, but said the Netherlands has been in talks with the European Commission to ensure that if it is necessary, it can be quickly enacted.

In a joint statement, Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom expressed strong disagreement with the U.S. sanctions.

"We will continue to work together to support the court's vital work, uphold the rules-based international system and advance accountability," the statement said.

"If put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the court's work, its dedicated staff and their families. They work every day to bring those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice and to support their victims."

Rubio calls on allies to join in on sanctions

Rubio said U.S. allies should join in the U.S. actions. "If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, piece by piece, until Americans are threatened no longer," he said.

A number of countries have withdrawn from the court this year, including Venezuela and Chad. The South Pacific island nation of Naoero was the most recent to announce it would quit.

Rubio said both Republicans and Democrats have deep reservations about the court, which was established to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity that might not otherwise be handled by the parties involved.

But he said that only Trump was willing to move against the court.

"Both parties agree on this, but only President Trump has the resolve to take the action needed to end this threat once and for all," Rubio said. "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."

World.title: Residential school denialism shouldn't be illegal, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Residential school denialism is detestable but not illegal, and that shouldn't change, says Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who disagrees with federal Manitoba NDPer Leah Gazan's efforts to add it to the Criminal Code.

"I have a lot of respect for MP Gazan, but I don't think we can criminalize this. I think we have to just do the continued work of educating people and trying to combat misinformation," Kinew told CBC Manitoba Up to Speed host Marcy Markusa on Friday.

Gazan first introduced Bill C-254, her private member’s bill to amend the Criminal Code regarding the promotion of hatred against Indigenous people, in October 2024, but it died when the spring 2025 election was called.

"If the government is serious about reconciliation, then they need to protect survivors and their families from hate," Gazan said when she first introduced it.

"The residential school system was a genocide designed to wipe out Indigenous cultures, languages, families and heritage. To downplay, deny or justify it is cruel, harmful and hateful."

She reintroduced it in October 2025. The bill seeks to make it illegal for anyone to condone, deny, justify or minimize the Indian residential school system in Canada through any statements beyond a private conversation.

All bills must go through three readings, which also involves committee reviews and final debates, before being granted royal assent and enacted into law.

The introduction was the first reading. The bill has yet to reach a second reading.

For a period of more than 150 years, from the 1830s until 1997, First Nations, Inuit and Métis children were taken from their families and communities to residential schools, often far from their homes. Most were government-funded and run by Christian religious organizations.

The schools were designed to assimilate Indigenous children into Euro-Canadian culture. An estimated 150,000 children across Canada attended the schools and the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation has documented more than 4,000 who died while attending them.

On Sept. 30, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Kinew announced the province partnered with the City of Brandon to buy a popular campground property that was once part of the Brandon Residential School, which ran from 1895 until 1972 .

The site that became the campground included a former school cemetery, used from 1895 to 1912, the province said in a news release on the day the purchase was announced.

This sign is at the site of the Brandon Residential School cemetery. Historical records indicate the cemetery, where children from the school were buried, was used from 1895 to 1912. The area later became a park and then a privately owned campground. (Jaison Empson/CBC)

The property still contains the remains of children, the province said.

Kinew, who dedicated a memorial at the site on Sept. 30, said on Friday that such events help educate the public on residential schools.

"It's very well-documented. It's very historic. So let's make sure that we keep that history alive in our living memory as a province," he said.

Sioux Valley Dakota Nation, which owns the land where the school once stood, will guide decisions around the former cemetery and is working with university researchers to identify the more than 50 children it believes are buried at the site.

Rev. Stan McKay, who said his maternal grandparents were forced to attend the Brandon Residential School for a good part of their life and never talked about it, called the purchase of the cemetery land a “very important piece” of reconciliation.

"It was not a good place," McKay said the day of the province's announcement.

Kinew participates in a ceremony on the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation after the Manitoba government announced it partnered with the City of Brandon to purchase the private campground land. (Jaison Empson/CBC)

His eldest sisters also attended the Brandon school for two years, while he is a survivor of the Fisher River and Birtle residential schools.

The United Church of Canada was one of three church organizations that operated the Brandon school during its long history. Later, McKay later made history as the first Indigenous person to lead that church.

He said he nearly left the church after an "awakening" that he had been colonized by it. Elders, who also "had some difficulties with the church," encouraged him to stay and work within the system and be a part of helping it change, McKay said.

McKay would like to see more education in Manitoba schools around the residential school experience and have it localized to stories about the 18 schools that operated in the province.

Kinew, on Friday, agreed that would be a good idea and said much more is being done in schools now than in previous decades.

"How much did we learn about residential school in K-12 versus what a kid today learns? It's night and day in terms of being so much more," he said.

There is a need for those no longer in school to be educated as well, Kinew said.

"As we were preparing for Brandon … I was talking to some of my staff that I work with very closely — very smart people — and I pulled out the volume of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission that documents the child deaths. People were shocked. They didn't know [the number of deaths]," he said.

"So for sure there's more needs to be done in the K-12 system, but I think there's also a lot in the workplace, in churches, in sports, all the venues where we gather as Manitobans, where we need to keep this thing alive.

"The thing that we don't want to happen is for this to fade from our living memory, and then we forget, and then maybe some of the the negative lessons we should have learned start to re-emerge."

World.title: IN PHOTOS | Belgium youths, police clash during protests
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Police and protesters clashed in Brussels on Friday, as tens of thousands of people rallied in the Belgian capital against rising living costs and budget-tightening measures introduced by the government.

Dozens of protesters — many of them young, dressed in black and wearing masks — threw rocks and firecrackers at police at the central Brussels railway station before setting several fires, one to a pile of city bikes and electric scooters.

( Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters)

(Dirk Waem/Belga/AFP/Getty Images)

Riot police responded with tear gas, water cannons and baton charges, pushing the protesters from the area. Traffic and public transport across the city were disrupted.

(Yves Herman/Reuters)

(Yves Herman/Reuters)

(Yves Herman/Reuters)

Police said that those "who caused the problems of public order are not linked" to the anti-austerity rally, which they said drew about 30,000 people. The nationwide strike was called by Belgium's two largest unions, the socialist FGTB/ABVV and Christian ACV-CSC.

(Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images)

(Yves Herman/Reuters)

The confrontations came after a week of tensions in the city of Liège, Belgium, where authorities placed a ban on public gatherings as students clashed with police and vandalized shops. More than 200 people were arrested in Liège and dozens of police officers were injured.
