Where to Watch El Chavo Legally in the US

On 9 October 2026, Amazon’s US Prime Video store listed El Chavo inside its ViX Premium add-on channel. ViX is the streaming service of TelevisaUnivision, the Spanish-language group that owns the Univision and UniMás networks.

ViX itself added the series in September 2024, with 273 episodes, according to Señal News and La Nación. TelevisaUnivision scheduled the US launch on ViX and UniMás for 23 September 2024.

The Amazon listing shows the show as part of a paid add-on but prints no price. In July 2025 La Nación, the Buenos Aires daily, quoted ViX Premium at US$5.99 a month with ads and US$8.99 without.

The same report listed an annual plan at US$59.99 and said the first five episodes were free. Check the current price on the sign-up page before subscribing, because streaming prices change often.

TelevisaUnivision also returned the show to broadcast television. In July 2025 La Nación listed weekday slots on Univision at 7 p.m. ET and on UniMás at 8 p.m. ET.

Broadcast schedules shift, so check local listings for the current slot. Uploads by individuals on free video sites are not among the licensed options listed here.

Netflix began offering the series on 11 August 2025 in markets it did not list. US subscribers should search the app rather than assume it is there.

Why the Show Vanished From Television in 2020

At the start of August 2020, Roberto Gómez Fernández announced on X that his father’s programmes would stop airing worldwide. He said the decision had not been taken by the family.

The contract under which the series was broadcast expired in July 2020 and neither side renewed it, Minuto60 reported. The two sides were Grupo Chespirito and Televisa, the Mexico City broadcaster that aired the shows for decades.

Reports at the time described a split in ownership. Televisa controlled the recorded episodes, while the Gómez family held the commercial rights to the characters.

Without a new contract, the archive went dark. Minuto60 said the shows left the air in more than 20 countries, including Mexico and Brazil.

Florinda Meza, the creator’s widow and the actress behind Doña Florinda, was later blamed online for the impasse. In October 2023 she denied it, saying a buyer had tried four times to acquire the rights.

How the Show Came Back on ViX, Univision and Netflix

Meza broke the news of a return on 7 September 2024, the trade site Tavi Latam reported. UniMás, a TelevisaUnivision channel, was first to confirm it with a promotional video.

In Mexico, ViX added all episodes on 18 September 2024. The free-to-air channel Las Estrellas began airing two episodes each weekday at 1:30 p.m. on 16 October.

Netflix then acquired broadcast rights of its own and announced the series on 24 July 2025. The post came as HBO Max aired the final episode of a biopic about Gómez Bolaños.

Minuto60 reported that Netflix offered the series with translations into more than 50 languages. That reach could take El Chavo far beyond its traditional Spanish-speaking audience.

The Cast Behind the Vecindad

Gómez Bolaños wrote the scripts and played El Chavo himself, an adult in the role of an eight-year-old. Several other adult actors also played children.

The HBO Max press materials for the 2025 biopic name the real actors behind the main roles. María Antonieta de las Nieves played La Chilindrina, and Édgar Vivar played both Señor Barriga and Ñoño.

Ramón Valdés played Don Ramón, Rubén Aguirre played Profesor Jirafales and Angelines Fernández played La Bruja del 71. Profesor Jirafales is the schoolteacher, and Don Ramón is the neighbour forever behind on rent.

Two real cast members appear under invented names in the biopic. The actress behind Doña Florinda becomes “Margarita Ruiz”, and the actor behind Quico becomes “Marcos Barragán”.

Minuto60 reported that Meza’s character was renamed for legal and image-rights reasons. Meza herself called the series a distorted version of the story, Metro Puerto Rico reported.

The Chespirito Biopic and the Fight Over the Story

“Chespirito: Sin querer queriendo” premiered on 5 June 2025 on Max, the US-based streaming service now called HBO Max. The title borrows El Chavo’s catchphrase, roughly “without meaning to, meaning to”.

The eight episodes were written by the creator’s children, Roberto and Paulina Gómez Fernández, with literary editing by Juan Pablo Balcázar. Rodrigo Santos directed alongside Julián de Tavira and David “Leche” Ruiz.

Pablo Cruz Guerrero plays Gómez Bolaños in a story running from childhood to fame, says HBO Max’s Latin American press office. THR3 Media and Perro Azul produced it as a Max Original.

Because the family wrote it, the series doubles as Grupo Chespirito’s version of events. It arrived while Meza was pursuing legal action to claim a share of the legacy, Minuto60 reported.

Televisa’s wider weight in Mexican business and politics is covered in who dominates Mexico. The country’s longer arc is told in Mexico’s history explained.

A Legacy Measured in Stadiums and Stamps

In 1977 the live “Show de Chespirito” twice filled Santiago’s 80,000-seat stadium on one Sunday, Grupo Chespirito says. In 1983 it sold out New York’s Madison Square Garden twice on a single Sunday.

By 1995, when the last “Chespirito” episode was recorded, the company counted 300 million viewers worldwide. An animated El Chavo series followed in 2006 with more than 100 episodes.

Mexico’s postal service, the Servicio Postal Mexicano, issued stamps of El Chavo and El Chapulín Colorado in 2006. On 29 March 2012, about 10,000 people attended a tribute at the Auditorio Nacional in Mexico City.

Televisa broadcast that tribute in more than 17 countries at once, according to Grupo Chespirito. Gómez Bolaños died in Cancún on Friday, 28 November 2014, aged 85, of respiratory problems, El Financiero reported.

Televisa held a farewell at its San Ángel studios the next day. On Sunday, 30 November 2014, a public tribute with his body present was held on the field of the Estadio Azteca.

What It Means for US Readers

The US Census Bureau counted about 68 million Hispanic residents on 1 July 2024, roughly 20% of the population. For many of their families, El Chavo was shared childhood television.

That makes the show a common reference in many Latino households. Knowing its characters helps other Americans follow the jokes, memes and nostalgia that still circulate.

For viewers, the legal US route runs through ViX, directly or via its Prime Video add-on channel. Netflix availability in the US should be checked in the app before assuming it is there.

The saga also shows the commercial pull of a 1970s archive: ViX licensed it in 2024 and Netflix in 2025. More on the country is on the Rio Times Mexico page.

What Is Not Known

Netflix has not said publicly whether its 2025 release includes the United States. Current US prices for ViX Premium and its Prime Video channel could not be confirmed with the platforms.

The financial terms of the 2024 agreement and the length of the new licences have not been published. Whether Univision and UniMás still air the show daily in October 2026 is also unconfirmed.

It is not known whether HBO Max offers the biopic to US subscribers. No court outcome of Meza’s legal claims over the legacy could be confirmed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Chavo del Ocho about?

It is a Mexican sitcom about El Chavo, an eight-year-old orphan living in a Mexico City courtyard. Roberto Gómez Bolaños created it in 1971 and played the boy himself.

Where can I watch El Chavo del Ocho legally in the US?

On 9 October 2026, Amazon’s US store listed it in the ViX Premium channel on Prime Video. ViX, TelevisaUnivision’s streaming service, has carried the series since September 2024.

Why was El Chavo taken off the air in 2020?

The broadcast contract expired in July 2020 and neither Televisa nor Grupo Chespirito renewed it. Televisa held the recordings, while the Gómez family held the commercial rights to the characters.

Is El Chavo del Ocho on Netflix?

Netflix said the series would arrive on 11 August 2025. It did not name the countries covered, so US availability is unconfirmed.

What is the Chespirito biopic called?

It is “Chespirito: Sin querer queriendo”, an eight-episode HBO Max series that premiered on 5 June 2025. Pablo Cruz Guerrero plays Roberto Gómez Bolaños.

When did Chespirito die?

Roberto Gómez Bolaños died in Cancún on 28 November 2014, aged 85. A public tribute followed at Mexico City’s Estadio Azteca two days later.

Sources: Grupo Chespirito, chespirito.com (official timeline and character profiles); HBO Max Latin America press office, “Sin querer queriendo”, 5 June 2025; Amazon Prime Video US, ViX Premium channel; US Census Bureau, Hispanic Heritage Month 2025; Señal News; La Nación; El Imparcial; Minuto60; El Financiero; Metro Puerto Rico; Tavi Latam (all accessed 9 October 2026).

World.title: Peru Natural Resources Explained 2026
World.content:
PERU · NATURAL RESOURCES

Key Facts — The country An Andean nation of 34.2 million people, per the 2025 census.

— The metals Third in world copper output, second in silver and zinc.

— The money Mining earned US$62.7 billion in 2025, two thirds of exports.

— Beyond mines Camisea gas, anchovy fishmeal, Amazon forests and fresh fruit exports.

— Who profits Mostly foreign miners, the treasury and producing regions.

— The cost Illegal gold mining strips Amazon forest and spreads mercury into rivers.

Metals pay most of Peru’s bills abroad, while gas, fish, fruit and forests complete a resource map with heavy costs.

Peru resources start with copper, gold, silver and zinc, but the country also sells gas, fishmeal, fruit and coffee abroad. Mining alone brought in US$62.7 billion of exports in 2025, about two thirds of the total, by central bank figures.

That makes Peru one of the main suppliers of the metals behind US power grids, electric cars and electronics. This guide explains what Peru holds on land and at sea, who extracts it, who profits and what it costs.

Peru Resources at a Glance

Peru is a country of 34.2 million people, according to the 2025 national census by INEI, the national statistics institute. Its territory runs from a dry Pacific coast over the Andes to the Amazon basin.

Each of those three zones holds a different kind of wealth. The coast has fish, farms and ports, the Andes hold the metals, and the Amazon holds forests, gas and oil.

Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Peru sold US$94.0 billion of goods abroad in 2025, says the Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCRP), the central bank. Mining products made up US$62.7 billion of that, or 67 percent.

The share has grown in 2026 as metal prices climbed. From January to August, mining exports reached US$57.5 billion out of US$77.4 billion, or 74 percent.

Oil and natural gas added US$3.3 billion in 2025, and fish products about US$4.65 billion. Farm goods, led by fresh fruit, brought in about US$14.5 billion.

Active mining and exploration sites cover only about 1.5 percent of Peru’s territory, says MINEM, the Ministry of Energy and Mines. Their weight in exports, taxes and jobs is far larger, as Rio Times coverage of Peru’s booming mining exports has shown.

Copper, Silver and Zinc Lead the Metals

Copper is Peru’s biggest earner. MINEM recorded output of 2,769,794 tonnes in 2025, a record and 1.2 percent above 2024.

The US Geological Survey (USGS) ranks Peru third in world copper output in 2025, behind Chile and the Democratic Republic of Congo. It puts Peru’s copper reserves at 85 million tonnes, close to a tenth of the world total.

Three operators each mined just under 15 percent of the national total in 2025. They were Southern Peru Copper, Las Bambas and Cerro Verde, MINEM data show.

Southern Peru belongs to Southern Copper, which is controlled by the Mexican conglomerate Grupo México and listed in New York. Las Bambas, in Apurímac, is run by MMG, a Hong Kong-listed miner controlled by the Chinese state group China Minmetals.

Cerro Verde, near the city of Arequipa, is majority-owned by Freeport-McMoRan of Phoenix, Arizona. Quellaveco, in Moquegua, is run by the London-listed Anglo American with Japan’s Mitsubishi as partner.

Most of the metal leaves as concentrate, a powder of crushed and processed ore, rather than as refined copper. The USGS estimates Peru refined only about 340,000 tonnes at home in 2025.

Copper exports earned US$28.9 billion in 2025, the central bank reports, nearly a third of all goods Peru sold abroad. The industry’s history and big mines are covered in the Rio Times guide to Peru copper mining.

Silver is the second metal story. MINEM recorded 3,762 tonnes of silver in 2025, and the USGS ranks Peru second in the world, behind Mexico.

The USGS also credits Peru with the world’s largest silver reserves, about 110,000 tonnes. Antamina, Buenaventura and Chinalco Perú were the top three silver producers in 2025.

Zinc output rose 18.6 percent to 1.51 million tonnes in 2025, says MINEM. The USGS ranks Peru second after China, and Antamina alone mined about a third of the national total.

Antamina, in the Áncash highlands, is jointly owned by the global miners BHP and Glencore with two smaller partners. Peru also ranks among the leading producers of tin, molybdenum and lead, by USGS estimates.

Gold, Formal Mines and an Informal Rush

Gold is Peru’s second export after copper. Shipments were worth US$23.3 billion in 2025 and US$21.6 billion in just the first eight months of 2026, central bank data show.

MINEM counted 108.9 tonnes of gold output in 2025, slightly below 2024. Its figure includes estimates for artisanal miners in regions such as Madre de Dios and Puno.

La Libertad, Cajamarca and Arequipa produced almost three quarters of the recorded total. The largest single producer was Yanacocha, in Cajamarca, run by the US company Newmont.

Then there is a gap. By central bank data, Peru exported about 6.7 million troy ounces of gold in 2025, roughly 210 tonnes.

That is nearly twice the output MINEM recorded for the year. The official figures do not show where the difference comes from.

Much small-scale gold mining happens outside the formal system. Two hotspots are Pataz province in La Libertad and the Amazon region of Madre de Dios.

A temporary register, known as Reinfo, lets small miners keep working while they seek formal status. Its renewal has been fought over repeatedly in Congress.

Oil and Gas, From Camisea to the Northern Jungle

Peru’s most valuable energy resource is natural gas from Camisea, a group of fields in the Amazon lowlands of the Cusco region. Pipelines carry the gas over the Andes to Lima and to a liquefaction plant south of the capital.

The gas supplies much of Peru’s electricity and household fuel, and part is shipped abroad as liquefied natural gas. Natural gas exports earned US$1.4 billion in 2025, central bank data show.

Crude oil is a smaller business. Exports of crude and refined products came to 28.5 million barrels in 2025, worth US$1.9 billion.

The main oil fields lie in the northern Amazon region of Loreto and on the north-west coast around Piura and Talara. Perupetro, a state agency, signs the exploration and production contracts with private operators.

Petroperú, the state oil company, runs the Talara refinery and the pipeline that carries Amazon crude to the coast. It has needed repeated financial support from the government in recent years.

Farmland and Fruit Exports

Peru’s Pacific coast is a desert, with almost no rain in most years. Yet river water from the Andes and large irrigation schemes have turned parts of it into export farms.

Projects such as Chavimochic in La Libertad and Olmos in Lambayeque opened new land to private growers. They grow blueberries, grapes, avocados, asparagus and citrus for markets abroad.

Non-traditional farm exports, mostly fresh and processed food, reached US$12.6 billion in 2025, the central bank says. Traditional crops, led by coffee, added US$1.9 billion.

Growth has slowed in 2026. Non-traditional farm exports rose 1.9 percent from January to August, to US$7.2 billion.

In the highlands, most farming is small-scale, with potatoes, maize, quinoa and livestock. Coffee and cacao grow on the eastern Andean slopes that face the Amazon.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Water, Forests and the Anchovy

Water is Peru’s quiet constraint. Most people and most export farms sit on the arid coast, while most rain falls on the Amazon side of the Andes.

Coastal rivers depend on Andean rain and on glaciers that have been shrinking for decades. Mines, farms and towns often compete for the same valley’s water, a frequent source of local disputes.

The Amazon rainforest covers more than half of Peru’s land area. MINAM, the environment ministry, tracks forest loss through its Geobosques satellite monitoring system.

Forest is lost mainly to small-scale farming, coca growing, illegal logging and illegal gold mining. Commercial wood is a minor export, with wood and paper goods worth US$276 million in 2025.

At sea, the cold Humboldt Current supports a huge fishery for the Peruvian anchovy, or anchoveta. Most of the catch is ground into fishmeal and fish oil for fish farms and animal feed.

Fishmeal exports earned US$1.86 billion in 2025 on 1.27 million tonnes shipped, central bank data show. Fish oil added about US$520 million.

The catch swings with ocean temperatures, so quotas change sharply. The Ministry of Production set 1.91 million tonnes for the first 2026 north-central season, against 3 million in 2025.

Traditional fishing exports fell 27 percent from January to August 2026, to US$1.4 billion, central bank data show.

Who Extracts and Who Profits

Under Peru’s constitution, natural resources belong to the nation, and the state grants concessions to companies. Big mining is led by foreign groups, alongside a few Peruvian firms.

Buenaventura, a Peruvian gold and silver miner, trades on the New York Stock Exchange. Compañía Minera Poderosa, a Peruvian gold producer in Pataz, ranked second in gold output in 2025 by MINEM data.

Mining investment reached US$6.23 billion in 2025, up 24.3 percent, MINEM reports. Its official list counts 65 future mines and expansions worth about US$63 billion.

The sector employed 276,765 people directly in December 2025. The annual average, above 264,000 direct jobs, was the highest on record, the ministry says.

The state collects corporate income tax, royalties and other levies. Half of the income tax that miners pay returns to producing regions and towns as the canon minero, a revenue-sharing transfer.

In 2025 mining transfers to regions and towns exceeded S/10 billion (about US$2.9 billion), MINEM reports. Conversions use the rate of 9 October 2026, S/3.44 per US dollar.

The canon accounted for S/6.99 billion (about US$2.0 billion) and royalties for S/2.69 billion (about US$780 million). How well regions spend that money is a long-running debate in Peru.

The bankers, families and companies behind these flows are profiled in the Rio Times guide to who runs Peru’s economy. The outside investors are covered in foreign powers and investors in Peru.

The Environmental and Social Cost

Illegal gold mining causes some of the most visible damage. In Madre de Dios, dredges and pumps have stripped riverbanks and forest, and miners use mercury to bind the gold.

Mercury enters rivers and fish and can harm the people who eat them. Peruvian authorities have run repeated police and military operations against illegal mining camps.

In Pataz, a gold district in La Libertad, illegal mining has been tied to violence. Thirteen kidnapped contract workers from a gold mine there were found murdered in May 2025.

Big formal mines face different conflicts, over water, land, pollution and a share of the profits. The Defensoría del Pueblo, Peru’s ombudsman, lists socio-environmental disputes as the largest category of social conflict.

Las Bambas has faced repeated road blockades by communities along its ore-transport route. Southern Copper’s Tía María project in Arequipa was delayed for years by local opposition.

Oil has its own record of spills. In January 2022 crude spilled into the sea at the La Pampilla refinery near Lima, run by Spain’s Repsol.

Older mines left a legacy too. La Oroya, a smelter town in Junín, became known for heavy lead pollution before its smelter shut in 2009.

A company owned by former workers restarted part of the complex in October 2023, Forbes Perú reported. Its zinc circuit was the first section to resume.

What It Means for US Readers

Several companies that mine in Peru trade on US exchanges, including Southern Copper, Freeport-McMoRan, Newmont and Buenaventura. Peruvian strikes, permits and taxes can therefore move US portfolios.

Peru’s copper feeds the global supply behind power grids, data centres and electric cars. Its fruit fills US supermarket shelves during the northern winter.

The US-Peru Trade Promotion Agreement, in force since 2009, removed most tariffs on trade between the two countries. China is also a major buyer and investor, a rivalry set out in the Rio Times guide to Peru geopolitics.

For travellers, mining conflicts can mean road blockades in the southern Andes, including routes in Cusco and Apurímac. Visitors to Madre de Dios should use licensed tour operators and stay away from mining zones.

Monthly output data, such as the July 2026 copper report, show how quickly the picture changes. Broader news is on the Rio Times Peru page.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how much of Peru’s gold exports come from illegal mines. Official statistics show the gap between recorded output and exports, but not its sources.

Complete official oil output figures for 2026 could not be confirmed. The size of the second 2026 anchovy season was also not confirmed.

It is unclear how long high copper and gold prices will last, and with them the record mining income of 2026. Future rules for small miners remain under debate in Congress.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Peru’s main natural resources?

Copper, gold, silver and zinc lead, followed by natural gas, oil, fishmeal, fruit and Amazon forests. Mining made up about two thirds of goods exports in 2025.

Is Peru the world’s largest copper producer?

No. The USGS ranks Peru third in 2025, behind Chile and the Democratic Republic of Congo, with about 2.7 million tonnes.

Who owns Peru’s biggest mines?

Mostly foreign groups, including Grupo Mexico, Freeport-McMoRan, China’s MMG, Anglo American, BHP, Glencore and Newmont. Peruvian firms such as Buenaventura and Poderosa also play a large role.

How much does Peru earn from mining?

Mining exports reached US$62.7 billion in 2025, by central bank data. Mining transfers to regions and towns exceeded S/10 billion, about US$2.9 billion.

What is the canon minero?

It is the half of mining income tax that the state sends to producing regions and municipalities. It reached S/6.99 billion, about US$2.0 billion, in 2025.

What is the biggest environmental problem linked to Peru’s resources?

Illegal gold mining in the Amazon, which clears forest and releases mercury into rivers, is among the most serious. Water disputes around big mines and oil spills are other recurring problems.

Can US investors gain exposure to Peru’s resources?

Yes, several miners active in Peru are listed in New York, including Southern Copper, Freeport-McMoRan, Newmont and Buenaventura. Prices and Peruvian politics make these holdings volatile, and this is not investment advice.

Sources: Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM), Boletín Estadístico Minero, December 2025; Banco Central de Reserva del Perú, trade statistics 2025–2026; USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026: copper, silver, zinc, gold; INEI 2025 census, via Andina; MINAM Geobosques; Ministry of Production anchovy quota, via Infobae Perú; Defensoría del Pueblo (all accessed 9 October 2026).

World.title: Mexico Security and Crime Explained 2026
World.content:
MEXICO · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country About 131 million people in 32 federal entities (INEGI, 2025).

— What happened Daily homicide victims fell to 40.8 in August 2026, from 86.9.

— The hotspots Colima, Morelos and Sinaloa had the highest 2025 homicide rates.

— US advisory Level 2 overall; six states at Level 4, Do Not Travel.

— Hidden crime 93.4% of 2025 crimes were unreported or never investigated.

— Still open Disappearances and unreported crime may hide part of the decline.

Killings in Mexico have fallen sharply since 2024. But the picture is uneven by state, and much everyday crime never reaches the police.

Mexico security has improved on the main official measure: daily homicide victims fell by 53% between September 2024 and August 2026. Yet violence remains concentrated in a handful of states, and extortion and fraud are more common than ever in surveys.

This guide explains the data, the armed groups, the police and military, and where risk is highest or lowest. Daily coverage sits in the Rio Times Mexico section.

How Mexico Security Has Changed Since 2024

Mexico has two official ways of counting killings, and they measure different things. Both now point in the same direction.

The first is the monthly count of the SESNSP, the National Public Security System secretariat, led by Marcela Figueroa Franco. It tallies victims recorded in investigation files opened by the 32 state prosecutors’ offices.

Yesterday’s subject line: “US charges Maduro and wife with torture of Americans” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

At a government briefing on Tuesday, 8 September 2026, the SESNSP put August 2026 at 40.8 intentional-homicide victims a day. That compares with 86.9 a day in September 2024, the last month before President Claudia Sheinbaum took office.

Omar García Harfuch, the federal Security and Citizen Protection minister, presented the figures as a 53% fall in 23 months. The Mexican daily Crónica reported that the data were consolidated as of 31 August 2026.

The second count comes from INEGI, the national statistics institute, which works from death certificates. On Monday, 3 August 2026, it reported 27,989 presumed homicides in 2025, a preliminary figure.

That equals 21.4 homicides per 100,000 people, down from a definitive 25.8 in 2024. For men the 2025 rate was 38.4 per 100,000; for women it was 4.7.

The two series rarely match exactly, because prosecutors and coroners classify deaths differently. A one-month comparison, like the 53% figure, also exaggerates trends that annual totals smooth out.

The Rio Times examined the limits of the headline number in a separate analysis of the 53% claim. INEGI has not yet published any 2026 death-certificate data.

What Crime Looks Like Beyond Homicide

Most crime in Mexico is not lethal, and most of it is never reported. INEGI’s annual victimisation survey, ENVIPE, is the best guide to that hidden layer.

The 2026 edition, published on Thursday, 10 September 2026, estimates that 23.0 million adults were victims of a crime in 2025. That is 23,473 victims per 100,000 adults, statistically lower than in 2024.

The survey counted 33.8 million crimes, and 28.5% of households had at least one victim. The most common offence was fraud, at 8,290 cases per 100,000 people.

Extortion came second, at 6,831 per 100,000, up from 5,971 the year before. Street or public-transport robbery followed at 5,641.

The key number is what INEGI calls the hidden figure. In 2025, 93.4% of crimes were either not reported or did not lead to a criminal investigation.

The SESNSP reported that recorded extortion fell 2.8% in January to August 2026 from a year earlier. The survey suggests most extortion is never recorded at all.

Perceptions have eased slightly. Between February and April 2026, 74.0% of adults said living in their state was unsafe, statistically lower than in 2025.

INEGI’s quarterly urban survey, ENSU, found that 59.8% of city residents felt unsafe in June 2026, against 63.2% a year earlier. The next reading is due on Friday, 23 October 2026.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The Armed Groups and Who They Are

Organised crime in Mexico is dominated by a few large networks and many local gangs. They earn money from drug trafficking, extortion, fuel theft and migrant smuggling.

On Thursday, 20 February 2025, the US State Department designated six Mexican groups as Foreign Terrorist Organizations:

Sinaloa Cartel : a trafficking network from the north-west, split into rival factions that have fought each other since 2024.

: a trafficking network from the north-west, split into rival factions that have fought each other since 2024. Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) : a group based in western Mexico that expanded nationwide over the past decade.

: a group based in western Mexico that expanded nationwide over the past decade. Gulf Cartel : one of the oldest groups, rooted in Tamaulipas along the Texas border.

: one of the oldest groups, rooted in Tamaulipas along the Texas border. Cartel del Noreste : an offshoot of the former Zetas, active around Nuevo Laredo in Tamaulipas.

: an offshoot of the former Zetas, active around Nuevo Laredo in Tamaulipas. La Nueva Familia Michoacana : a group operating in Michoacán, Guerrero and the State of Mexico.

: a group operating in Michoacán, Guerrero and the State of Mexico. Cárteles Unidos: an alliance of local groups in Michoacán.

On Sunday, 22 February 2026, CJNG leader Nemesio Oseguera, known as El Mencho, died after an army operation in Tapalpa, Jalisco. The Defence Ministry confirmed his death, regional outlets including Zeta Tijuana and La Razón reported.

Arrests of the group’s mid-level figures have continued, including the October 2026 detention of an alleged CJNG fuel-smuggling chief. Removing leaders has historically splintered groups rather than ended violence.

In Sinaloa, the cartel’s internal split coincided with a jump in the homicide rate. It rose from 33 per 100,000 in 2024 to 57 in 2025, INEGI data show.

Police, National Guard and Armed Forces

Mexico’s security forces are layered, and responsibility is often blurred. Understanding who does what helps explain why results differ so much by state.

Security and Citizen Protection Ministry (SSPC) : the federal civilian security ministry, led by Omar García Harfuch, which coordinates intelligence and investigations.

: the federal civilian security ministry, led by Omar García Harfuch, which coordinates intelligence and investigations. National Guard : a national force created in 2019 and placed under the Defence Ministry by a constitutional reform in September 2024.

: a national force created in 2019 and placed under the Defence Ministry by a constitutional reform in September 2024. Defence Ministry (SEDENA) and Navy (SEMAR) : the armed forces, which carry out most high-risk operations against cartels.

: the armed forces, which carry out most high-risk operations against cartels. State and municipal police : local forces that handle most day-to-day policing and vary widely in pay, training and trust.

: local forces that handle most day-to-day policing and vary widely in pay, training and trust. State prosecutors and the federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR): the bodies that open investigations and bring charges.

Mexico City runs its own large force, the Public Security Secretariat (SSC). Its patrols are a common sight in tourist districts.

Security policy is also shaped by relations with Washington, which pressures Mexico on fentanyl, guns and cartel leaders. Recent friction includes a US warning to Mexican governors accused of aiding cartels.

The two governments have also expanded technical cooperation, such as a drone cooperation declaration signed in August 2026. The wider balance of power is explained in the Rio Times guide to who holds power in Mexico.

Hotspots and Safer Areas

Violence in Mexico is highly local. A state can contain both a peaceful tourist city and a rural area controlled by armed groups.

INEGI’s 2025 figures, by state of registration, show the highest homicide rates per 100,000 people in:

Colima : 89, more than four times the national rate of 21.

: 89, more than four times the national rate of 21. Morelos : 58, just south of Mexico City.

: 58, just south of Mexico City. Sinaloa : 57, where cartel factions are at war.

: 57, where cartel factions are at war. Baja California : 55, home to Tijuana.

: 55, home to Tijuana. Sonora, Chihuahua and Guanajuato: 54, 53 and 51 respectively.

The lowest rates were in Yucatán at 2, Coahuila at 3 and Durango at 6. Mexico City recorded 9 per 100,000.

In absolute numbers, seven states accounted for 49.3% of homicides from January to August 2026, according to the SESNSP. They were Guanajuato, Baja California, Chihuahua, Sinaloa, the State of Mexico, Guerrero and Morelos.

Perceptions follow a similar map. In the 2026 ENVIPE, residents of the State of Mexico, Morelos and Tabasco felt least safe, at 90.0%, 88.7% and 87.6%.

Residents of Coahuila, Yucatán and Aguascalientes felt safest, at 27.8%, 35.5% and 41.0%. Some tourist cities changed fast: in Puerto Vallarta, ENSU’s insecurity reading rose from 27.3% in June 2025 to 65.4% in June 2026.

Daily Life for Residents and Visitors

For most residents, the main risks are fraud, extortion, robbery on public transport and threats, not cartel violence. In the 2026 ENVIPE, 60.7% of adults named insecurity as the country’s most serious problem.

Only 43.4% of adults said they felt safe walking alone near their home at night between February and April 2026. Among women the share was 35.4%, against 52.4% among men.

Visitors to major tourist areas generally face petty crime and scams rather than targeted violence. But the State Department warns that violent crime occurs widely, and roadblocks can appear quickly after major security operations.

Practical habits reduce risk: use dispatched taxis or app-based rides, avoid intercity road travel after dark and keep valuables out of sight. Be wary of virtual kidnapping calls, a common extortion scam in which callers fake a relative’s abduction.

What It Means for US Readers

The US State Department rates Mexico overall at Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution, in an advisory updated in May 2026. It cites terrorism, crime and kidnapping, and assigns a level to each state.

Level 4, Do Not Travel : Colima, Guerrero, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Tamaulipas and Zacatecas.

: Colima, Guerrero, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Tamaulipas and Zacatecas. Level 3, Reconsider Travel : Baja California, Chiapas, Chihuahua, Guanajuato, Jalisco, Morelos and Sonora.

: Baja California, Chiapas, Chihuahua, Guanajuato, Jalisco, Morelos and Sonora. Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution : 17 entities, including Mexico City, Quintana Roo, Baja California Sur, Oaxaca and Nuevo León. Coahuila is listed here, though its own entry says Reconsider Travel.

: 17 entities, including Mexico City, Quintana Roo, Baja California Sur, Oaxaca and Nuevo León. Coahuila is listed here, though its own entry says Reconsider Travel. Level 1, Exercise Normal Precautions: Campeche and Yucatán.

Even within Level 3 and 4 states, the advisory lists permitted zones, such as the tourist areas of Mazatlán or central Manzanillo. US government staff may not travel between cities after dark or hail taxis on the street.

The department urges US citizens to follow the same restrictions and to comply at any road checkpoint. It warns that its ability to help is limited in many parts of Mexico.

For businesses, the terrorism designations raise legal stakes: providing material support to a designated group is a federal crime under US law. Companies facing extortion in Mexico should take legal advice.

Security in Mexico also shapes US debates on fentanyl, migration, remittances and cross-border trade. Violence near factories and highways adds cost for US firms operating there.

What Is Not Known

It is not clear how much of the homicide decline reflects real change and how much reflects reclassification. Analysts, including the think tank México Evalúa, have pointed to disappearances and other killings outside the intentional-homicide category.

No reliable total of missing people is given here, because the official register has been under revision and its count is disputed. INEGI’s 2026 death-certificate data will not be available until 2027.

It is also unknown whether the killing of El Mencho will weaken the CJNG or trigger new succession fights. The effect of US pressure, including the terrorism designations, on violence inside Mexico has not been measured.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Mexico safe to visit in 2026?

The State Department rates Mexico overall at Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution, as it does Mexico City and Cancun’s state, Quintana Roo. Risk varies sharply by state, so check the state-level advisory before you travel.

Which Mexican states have a Do Not Travel warning?

In the State Department advisory updated in May 2026, six states are at Level 4. They are Colima, Guerrero, Michoacan, Sinaloa, Tamaulipas and Zacatecas.

Are homicides in Mexico really falling?

Yes, daily homicide victims fell from 86.9 in September 2024 to 40.8 in August 2026, government data show. INEGI put the 2025 rate at 21.4 per 100,000, down from 25.8 in 2024.

What is the most common crime in Mexico?

Fraud, according to INEGI’s 2026 victimisation survey, followed by extortion and street or public-transport robbery. About 93.4% of crimes in 2025 were not reported or did not lead to an investigation.

Which parts of Mexico are safest?

Yucatan had the lowest homicide rate in 2025, at about 2 per 100,000, followed by Coahuila and Durango. Yucatan and Campeche are the only states the State Department places at Level 1, Exercise Normal Precautions.

Who are the main cartels in Mexico?

The largest are the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel. The US designated both, plus four other Mexican groups, as Foreign Terrorist Organizations in February 2025.

World.title: Mexico Natural Resources Explained 2026
World.content:
MEXICO · NATURAL RESOURCES

Key Facts — The country About 131 million people; the world’s largest silver producer in 2025.

— Who owns it The nation owns minerals, oil and water; miners hold 30-year concessions.

— Oil Pemex produced 1.64 million barrels of liquids a day, August 2026.

— What happened Lithium nationalised in 2022; GM corn planting banned by constitution, 2025.

— The US link Mexico bought US$30.3 billion of US farm goods in 2024.

— Still open Rio Grande water Mexico owes the US under a 1944 treaty.

Silver, oil, farmland and forests make Mexico a resource power next door, but the state decides who digs, drills and pumps.

Mexico resources range from the world’s largest silver output to offshore oil, fertile farmland and highland forests. Water is the one resource in short supply.

For Americans, Mexico’s choices shape silver and copper supply, US corn sales, fuel flows and water for Texas farms.

How Mexico Resources Are Owned

Article 27 of the 1917 constitution is the starting point. It says land and water within Mexico’s borders belong originally to the nation, which may grant private use.

Oil and gas in the ground remain national property in every contract, the constitution states. A 2024 amendment, published on 31 October, redefined state energy firms such as Pemex as “state public companies”.

Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Pemex, short for Petróleos Mexicanos, is the state oil company. It can still sign contracts with private partners, and their output counts in its figures.

Metals work through concessions issued by the Economy Ministry. Since a reform of 8 May 2023, a concession lasts 30 years, with one possible 25-year extension.

The same Mining Law bars new concessions in protected natural areas and in zones without available water. Lithium is the exception to the concession system, because it is reserved for the state.

Water rights are handed out by Conagua, the National Water Commission. Article 27 also protects ejidos, the communal landholdings created after the 1910–1920 revolution.

President Claudia Sheinbaum of the left-wing Morena party has governed since 1 October 2024. Daily coverage sits on the Rio Times Mexico news page, and the wider business map is in Who Runs Mexico’s Economy.

Silver, Copper and Gold

Mexico mined about 6,300 tonnes of silver in 2025, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the US government’s minerals statistics agency. That is nearly a quarter of estimated world output of 26,000 tonnes.

Peru came second with 3,600 tonnes and China third with 3,400, by the same estimates. Mexico also holds an estimated 37,000 tonnes of silver reserves.

Copper output was about 690,000 tonnes in 2025, and gold about 140 tonnes. That made Mexico the seventh-largest gold producer, by USGS estimates.

The biggest private player is Grupo México, a mining and rail conglomerate controlled by the Larrea family. It owns 88.9% of Southern Copper, which trades in New York, according to Southern Copper’s latest annual filing.

Grupo México runs the Buenavista del Cobre copper mine at Cananea, in the border state of Sonora. Newmont, the Denver-based gold miner, manages the Peñasquito gold and silver mine in Zacatecas.

Mexican and Canadian companies run many smaller silver and gold mines in the central and northern states. They pay federal mining duties, while landowners and ejidos negotiate access to the land.

The industry lobby, the Mexican Mining Chamber, wants the government to resume granting concessions. Rio Times coverage follows that push to restart concessions and the mining projects left stalled.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Oil and Gas: Pemex Past Its Peak

Pemex produced 1.637 million barrels a day of oil and other liquids from its fields in August 2026. That figure includes private partners, according to Pemex’s monthly statistics report.

Output averaged 1.655 million barrels a day from January to August 2026. That compares with 1.635 million across 2025 and 1.759 million in 2024.

For scale, US oil fields pump several times as much. Mexico’s output still matters because oil duties feed the federal budget.

Pemex reported 4.9 billion cubic feet a day of gas output in the same eight months. About 0.9 billion of that was nitrogen, which is not a fuel.

Crude exports have fallen much faster than output. Pemex shipped 276,000 barrels a day abroad in August 2026, against an average of 806,000 a day in 2024.

Pemex still imported 291,800 barrels a day of gasoline in August 2026. That was more than all the crude oil it exported that month.

Pemex’s debts also weigh on the country. Rio Times coverage of Fitch’s July 2026 review explains how the oil company affects Mexico’s sovereign credit rating.

Lithium: Nationalised Before It Was Mined

A reform published on 20 April 2022 declared lithium a matter of public utility and the heritage of the nation. The Mining Law now bars any concession, licence, contract or permit for it.

Exploration and processing belong to a decentralised state body attached to the Energy Ministry. It was created by decree in August 2022 as Litio para México, known as LitioMx.

The Mexican Geological Survey, a federal agency, must help it locate probable lithium reserves. Any area with lithium deposits counts as a national mining reserve.

The model differs sharply from Chile and Argentina, where private companies produce lithium under state rules. Mexico’s location next to the US car market is why the choice draws attention.

Farmland, Corn and Trade With the US

Mexico is the largest market for US farm exports, according to the US Department of Agriculture (USDA). It bought US$30.32 billion of US agricultural goods in 2024.

Corn led at US$5.62 billion, followed by pork at US$2.58 billion and dairy at US$2.47 billion. Soybeans added US$2.3 billion, by USDA figures.

Corn is also Mexico’s cultural staple, first domesticated there thousands of years ago. In March 2025 the country amended its constitution to protect native varieties.

The amendment says corn grown in Mexico must be free of genetic modification (GM). Any other use of GM corn must be assessed under separate laws for biosafety and health.

The ban applies to cultivation; other uses, including imported grain, fall under the assessment rule. Mexico’s own fields supply avocados, tomatoes, berries and agave for US shelves.

Farming and the US trade link are central to the nearshoring boom and the USMCA review. The USMCA is the trade pact between the US, Mexico and Canada.

Water: The Scarcest Resource

National waters are federal property, and Conagua issues the concessions to use them. Much of the north and centre is dry, while most rain falls in the south.

The 2023 mining reform bars new mining concessions where no water is available. It also requires mines to recycle at least 60% of their treated wastewater.

Shortages hit cities as well as farms. Experts quoted in Rio Times coverage warned that the water crisis could cost up to 5% of GDP.

Under a 1944 treaty, Mexico must deliver at least 1.75 million acre-feet of Rio Grande water to the US every five years. The US, in turn, sends Mexico 1.5 million acre-feet of Colorado River water a year.

An acre-foot covers an acre, roughly a football field, one foot deep. By 12 April 2025, Mexico had delivered only about 0.51 million acre-feet in the cycle ending that October.

That figure comes from the Congressional Research Service, the US Congress’s research agency. It also noted that President Donald Trump raised the prospect of tariffs and sanctions over the deliveries in April 2025.

Forests and Fisheries

Mexico’s forests run from pine, oak and fir in the highlands to tropical forest in Chiapas and the Yucatán Peninsula. Much forest land belongs to ejidos and indigenous communities rather than private owners.

The fir forests of Michoacán and the State of Mexico shelter monarch butterflies that migrate from the US and Canada each winter. Logging, farm expansion and fires all press on these forests.

Mexico has coasts on the Pacific, the Gulf of California, the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean. Its fleets catch shrimp, tuna and sardines, regulated by Conapesca, the national fisheries commission.

In the upper Gulf of California, illegal gillnets set for the totoaba fish have pushed the vaquita porpoise toward extinction. The totoaba is prized for its swim bladder, which is smuggled to Asia.

The Environmental Cost

On 6 August 2014, about 40,000 cubic metres of acidic copper solution spilled from the Buenavista del Cobre mine. That is roughly 16 Olympic swimming pools, and it flowed into the Bacanuchi and Sonora rivers.

Federal authorities trucked drinking water to 12,975 residents of seven municipalities, according to a government white paper. Fishing on the Sonora River was suspended until March 2015.

Profepa, the federal environmental enforcement agency, imposed fines totalling at least MXN 19.5 million (about US$1.1 million). The company also committed up to MXN 2 billion (about US$110 million) to a river trust fund.

Peso conversions use 18.10 pesos per US dollar (open.er-api.com, 9 October 2026), not the rate of the time. The business magazine Expansión reported in December 2015 that the damage repair fell short.

Oil has its own costs, from gas flaring offshore to spills from pipelines and illegal taps. Open-pit mines, like the one pictured above, leave large pits and tailings that need watching for decades.

The 2023 mining reform added water-recycling and other environmental duties. How strictly those rules are enforced is one of the open questions in Mexican resource policy.

What It Means for US Readers

US investors hold Mexican resources through New York-listed shares such as Southern Copper and Newmont. Mining rules in Mexico City can move those stocks.

Mexico supplies nearly a quarter of the world’s mined silver, which is used in solar panels and electronics. Any disruption to Mexican mines can tighten supply for US manufacturers.

US farmers depend on Mexico as their biggest export market, so the corn rules matter in Iowa and Illinois. Fuel flows matter too, because Pemex still imports large volumes of gasoline.

Texas farmers in the Rio Grande Valley depend on treaty water from Mexico. When deliveries fall short, the issue quickly becomes part of US trade and tariff politics.

What Is Not Known

It is not confirmed whether LitioMx has produced any lithium commercially, or when it might. No production figures were found in official sources.

The final shortfall of the treaty cycle that ended in October 2025 is not confirmed here from a primary source. The same applies to the terms and progress of later catch-up arrangements.

It is unclear when, or whether, the federal government will resume granting new mining concessions. Current national figures on forest loss and fish stocks were not available from official sources.

Whether the drop in Pemex output in August 2026 is temporary is also unknown. Monthly figures can swing with maintenance, weather and storms in the Gulf.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Mexico’s most important natural resources?

Silver, copper, gold, oil and gas lead the list, followed by farmland, forests and fisheries. Mexico was the world’s largest silver producer in 2025, by USGS estimates.

Who owns Mexico’s oil and minerals?

The constitution makes the nation the owner of minerals, oil and water. The state runs oil through Pemex and grants private mining concessions of 30 years.

Is Mexico still a big oil exporter?

Less than before. Pemex exported 276,000 barrels a day in August 2026, down from an average of 806,000 in 2024.

Can foreign companies mine lithium in Mexico?

No. Since April 2022 lithium is reserved for the state, and the Mining Law bars any concession or contract for it.

Why does Mexico owe water to the US?

A 1944 treaty requires Mexico to deliver 1.75 million acre-feet of Rio Grande water every five years. The US sends Mexico Colorado River water in return.

Does Mexico allow genetically modified corn?

Not for planting, under a March 2025 constitutional amendment. Other uses of genetically modified corn are assessed under separate laws.

Sources: INEGI, Intercensal Survey 2025; Pemex, Estadísticas Petroleras, August 2026; USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, silver, copper and gold; Constitution of Mexico (Articles 4, 27 and reforms of 2024 and 2025); Ley de Minería (last reform DOF 8 May 2023); Supreme Court DOF summary, 23 August 2022 (LitioMx decree); USDA Foreign Agricultural Service, Mexico; Congressional Research Service, 1944 US-Mexico Water Treaty (April 2025); Government of Mexico, Libro Blanco on the Sonora River spill; Southern Copper Form 10-K (SEC); Newmont operations; Expansión (all accessed 9 October 2026).

World.title: Who Dominates Brazil, Elites and Regions Explained
World.content:
BRAZIL · POWER

Key Facts — The country Brazil has 214.2 million people, the most in Latin America (2026).

— Where wealth sits The Southeast: 42% of people, 53% of output (2022 and 2023 data).

— Inequality Household income Gini index 0.511 in 2025, up from 0.504.

— Congress Farm caucus signatories: 299 of 513 deputies, October 2026.

— What happened Flávio Bolsonaro led Lula 47.03% to 45.16% on 4 October.

— Prediction markets Kalshi: Flávio Bolsonaro 87.0%, Lula 13.0% to win the 25 October runoff (9 October, 5:07 a.m. ET) Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 87% and Kalshi at 87% (Lula: 14% and 13% ), as of 9 October, 2:00 pm ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

Power in Brazil runs through a rich Southeast, a farm lobby in Congress, growing churches and a few political families. Here is who holds it, and who is left out.

Brazil power is concentrated in a few hands and a few places, even in a democracy of 214.2 million people. The Southeast produces over half of national output, and a farm caucus counts 299 of the 513 federal deputies.

For US readers, the presidential runoff on Sunday, 25 October 2026 shows each of these power centres at work. Its result will shape trade, investment and Brazil’s ties with Washington.

How Brazil Power Is Distributed

Brazil is a federal republic of 26 states and a Federal District, with a directly elected president. On paper, power is split between the president, Congress and the courts.

In practice, Brazil power is shared with groups that never appear on a ballot. They include agribusiness, big banks and industry, the churches, the armed forces and a small number of political families.

Yesterday’s subject line: “US charges Maduro and wife with torture of Americans” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

The president needs Congress to pass almost anything, and Congress is fragmented. As of 9 October 2026, 22 parties held seats in the 513-member Chamber of Deputies, its open-data service shows.

That fragmentation gives leverage to the Centrão, or “big centre”, a loose group of centre-right parties. They usually trade their votes for ministries, budget amendments and posts in state companies.

Both houses are led by politicians from the North and Northeast. Hugo Motta of Republicanos, a conservative party, has presided over the Chamber since February 2025 and represents Paraíba.

Davi Alcolumbre of União Brasil, a centre-right party, leads the Senate and represents Amapá, an Amazon state. Each state elects three senators, whatever its size.

So Amapá, with 733,759 people in the 2022 census, has the same Senate weight as São Paulo, with 44.4 million. That rule hands small states outsized power over national laws.

Regions, the Rich Southeast and the Voting Northeast

Brazil’s money and its votes sit in different places. The Southeast, which includes São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais, held 41.8% of the population in 2022.

The same region produced 53.0% of gross domestic product in 2023, IBGE, the national statistics office, reports. São Paulo state alone accounted for 31.5%.

The Northeast tells the opposite story. It is home to 26.9% of Brazilians but generated only 13.8% of output in 2023.

The other three regions, by share of people (2022) and of output (2023):

South: 14.7% of people, 16.8% of output; farming and industry

Centre-West: 8.0% of people, 10.6% of output; the soy and cattle belt, plus Brasília

North: 8.5% of people, 5.8% of output; most of the Amazon rainforest

Output per person in the Northeast is roughly 40% of the Southeast’s, on 2023 output and 2022 census population. That gap drives national politics.

In the first round on Sunday, 4 October 2026, Lula won 63.8% of valid votes in the Northeast. Flávio Bolsonaro took 60.1% in the South, 56.5% in the Centre-West and 51.4% in the Southeast.

These shares are summed from state results of the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), which runs elections. Lula carried all nine Northeastern states plus Amazonas, Amapá and Pará.

Flávio carried the other 14 states and the Federal District. More on who lives where is in the guide to Brazil’s population and ethnic groups.

Race, Class and Who Earns What

Race and class overlap closely in Brazil. In the 2022 census, 45.3% of people described themselves as pardo, or mixed race, and 43.5% as white.

Another 10.2% said they were Black (preta), 0.4% of Asian descent and 0.6% indigenous. Black and pardo Brazilians together make up a majority of 55.5%.

Incomes still follow colour lines. In the second quarter of 2026, white workers earned 4,800 reais a month on average (about US$956), IBGE’s labour survey shows.

Black workers earned 2,754 reais (about US$549) and pardo workers 2,923 reais (about US$582). White workers therefore earned about 74% more than Black workers.

Conversions use 5.02 reais per US dollar, from open.er-api.com on 9 October 2026.

Overall inequality remains high. The Gini index of household income per person, where zero means perfect equality, was 0.511 in 2025.

That was up from 0.504 in 2024, though below the 0.517 recorded in 2023.

Gender gaps show up at the top as well.

Women were 51.5% of the population in the 2022 census. Yet they held only 88 of 513 Chamber seats in October 2026, or 17.2%.

Congress, Parties and the Caucuses That Decide

The largest party in the Chamber is the Liberal Party (PL), the conservative party of the Bolsonaro family, with 98 deputies. Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT), the main left-wing party, has 65.

The next five parties by seats, as of 9 October 2026:

União Brasil (52 seats): centre-right, formed in 2022 from a merger

Social Democratic Party, PSD (48): centre-right, pragmatic, part of the Centrão

Progressistas, PP (46): conservative, a core Centrão party

Republicanos (42): conservative, the party of the Chamber’s president

Brazilian Democratic Movement, MDB (38): centrist, founded in 1966 as the legal opposition under military rule

Party labels often matter less than cross-party caucuses, called frentes parlamentares. The farm lobby’s caucus, the Agricultural Parliamentary Front (FPA), is the clearest example.

As of 9 October 2026, 299 of the 513 sitting deputies had signed up to it, the Chamber’s records show. That is 58% of the house, just short of the 308 votes needed to amend the constitution.

The Evangelical Parliamentary Front counted 212 sitting deputies and the Catholic front 201. The front for indigenous peoples’ rights had 183.

Signatures overlap, and signing does not bind a deputy’s vote. Still, the farm caucus reflects the weight of the Centre-West and South, where Flávio Bolsonaro won most strongly.

For the full list of office-holders, see who holds power in Brazil, from Lula to Congress.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Families, the Military and the Courts

Political families remain a feature of Brazilian power. The 2026 runoff is a family contest: Flávio Bolsonaro, senator for Rio de Janeiro, is Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son.

The former president cannot run. The Supreme Federal Court (STF), Brazil’s top court, sentenced him to 27 years and three months for a coup plot.

His sentence began on 25 November 2025, the court says. After a hospital stay in March 2026 he was moved to house arrest on health grounds, upheld in July.

Another son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, received four years and two months from the STF for trying to interfere in the coup case.

The armed forces ruled Brazil from 1964 to 1985 and kept influence long after. The coup case marked a break, because officers of the highest rank were convicted alongside Bolsonaro.

Admiral Almir Garnier, a former navy commander, received 24 years, the STF says. Retired army generals Walter Braga Netto, Augusto Heleno and Paulo Sérgio Nogueira were also convicted, the same STF ruling shows.

The courts are a power centre in their own right. The STF has 11 justices, and individual justices can issue sweeping orders alone.

Conservative critics call that overreach, while supporters say it protected democracy after the 2022 election. Either way, few big political questions in Brazil end without a court ruling.

Business, Churches and Unions

Big business is concentrated in São Paulo, home to the B3 stock exchange and most large private banks. The state is a business power too, through companies it controls.

The federal government controls Petrobras, the oil company. With the BNDES development bank, it held 35.45% of Petrobras shares in September 2026, while foreign investors held 48.73%.

The biggest companies, banks and business families are covered in who runs Brazil’s economy. Agribusiness adds political muscle through the farm caucus described above.

Religion is shifting power, too. In the 2022 census, 56.7% of Brazilians aged 10 and over were Catholic, down from 65.0% in 2010.

Evangelical Protestants rose from 21.7% to 26.9% over the same period, IBGE says. Afro-Brazilian religions such as Umbanda and Candomblé grew from 0.3% to 1.0%.

That growth gives evangelical churches weight in elections and in Congress. Their caucus is now larger than the Catholic one, 212 deputies against 201.

Organised labour was once a pillar of power, and Lula himself rose as a metalworkers’ union leader near São Paulo. The unions helped found his Workers’ Party in 1980.

A 2017 labour reform, Law 13,467, ended the compulsory union contribution, which had funded unions automatically.

Who Is Left Out

The groups with the least power are the poor, Black and pardo Brazilians, indigenous peoples and residents of urban favelas. Many belong to more than one of these groups.

About 1.2 million people chose “indigenous” as their colour or race in the 2022 census. Their land claims often set them against farm and mining interests with strong friends in Congress.

Millions of Brazilians live in favelas, informal neighbourhoods on hillsides and city edges where public services are weakest.

Women, a majority of the population, hold fewer than one in five Chamber seats. The poorer Northeast, meanwhile, has votes but little economic weight.

Newcomers can find the wider background in Brazil explained for newcomers, and Brazil’s place abroad in Brazil geopolitics explained.

What It Means for US Readers

For US investors, decisions in Brasília shape Petrobras, whose American Depositary Receipts made up 21.59% of its shares in September 2026. They also shape the farm exports that compete with US soy.

The 25 October runoff decides whether the Bolsonaro family returns to the presidency or Lula stays. Polling is tracked in the first Datafolha runoff poll.

For travellers and expats, the regional divide is visible on the ground. São Paulo and the South are wealthier, while the Northeast is poorer and votes differently.

All Brazil coverage is collected on the Rio Times Brazil page.

What Prediction Markets Say

Kalshi, a US exchange regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), prices the runoff as a bet. Its “Brazil Presidential election winner?” market showed Flávio Bolsonaro at 87.0% and Lula at 13.0%.

Those prices were recorded on 9 October at 5:07 a.m. ET. The gap is far wider than the 1.87-point first-round margin, so traders are betting on transfers from eliminated candidates.

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro 87.1% · Lula 13.5% (US$179 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 87% · Lula 13% As of 9 October, 2:00 pm ET (19:00 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

The runoff result is not known, and the new Congress elected on 4 October takes office only in February 2027. Its party balance is not yet in the Chamber’s records.

No primary source reviewed gives the racial make-up of Congress or company boards in 2026. This guide does not estimate it.

Caucus lists show signatures, not voting behaviour.

Whether Jair Bolsonaro stays under house arrest after the election is for the STF to decide. Current favela population figures for 2026 are not available.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who really holds power in Brazil?

Formal power is shared by the president, a fragmented Congress and the Supreme Federal Court. Agribusiness, big business, churches and a few political families add strong informal influence.

Which region of Brazil is the richest?

The Southeast, led by São Paulo state, produced 53.0% of Brazil’s output in 2023. São Paulo state alone produced 31.5%, IBGE data show.

What is the Centrão in Brazilian politics?

It is a loose group of centre-right parties that tends to back whichever government offers ministries and budget funds. Its votes often decide whether bills pass.

Is Jair Bolsonaro in prison?

He is serving a 27-year sentence for a coup plot, under house arrest on health grounds since 2026. His son Flávio is the conservative runoff candidate.

How big is the evangelical vote in Brazil?

Evangelicals were 26.9% of Brazilians aged 10 and over in the 2022 census. In Congress, 212 sitting deputies belong to the evangelical caucus.

When is Brazil’s presidential runoff?

The runoff between Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula is on Sunday, 25 October 2026. The winner takes office in January 2027.

Sources: Superior Electoral Court (TSE), 2026 first-round presidential results by state; IBGE, regional GDP 2023; IBGE, 2022 census by colour or race; IBGE, 2026 population estimate; IBGE, Gini index; IBGE, PNAD Contínua income by colour or race; IBGE, 2022 census religion results; Chamber of Deputies open data, deputies and caucuses; Federal Senate, presiding board; Supreme Federal Court (STF), house arrest ruling; STF, coup case sentences; Petrobras, shareholder composition; O Liberal; exchange rate from open.er-api.com (all accessed 9 October 2026).

World.title: LatAm and Africa Football Odds, Weekend of 10 Oct
World.content:
Prediction Markets: Football

Key Facts —Prediction markets. Kalshi, a US exchange regulated by the CFTC, prices Cruz Azul at 49% to win at Pumas UNAM on Sunday 11 October, 21:00 ET (Pumas 27%, draw 26%). Prices read at 5:34 am ET on Friday 9 October 2026. —Argentina. Lanús is 45% and Vélez Sarsfield 27% on Kalshi for Monday 12 October, 15:00 ET (16:00 in Buenos Aires). No price has been posted for a draw. —Liga MX title. Kalshi gives Toluca 27%, Guadalajara 20%, América 16% and Cruz Azul 11% to win the Apertura, on 805,773 contracts traded. Polymarket has Toluca at 23.5%. —Brazil. Polymarket prices Flamengo at 64% and Palmeiras at 36% to win the Série A, with US$46,864 traded. Flamengo host Fluminense on Sunday 11 October, 16:30 ET. —Libertadores. Flamengo are 43% on Polymarket and 44% on Kalshi to win the Copa Libertadores. The semi-finals start on Wednesday 14 October at 20:30 ET.

Prediction markets make Cruz Azul the favourite, at 49%, to win at Pumas UNAM in Mexico City on Sunday 11 October (21:00 ET). It is a rematch of May’s Clausura final, which Cruz Azul won, and it opens a weekend in which real-money traders also price Brazil’s title race, next week’s Copa Libertadores semi-finals and Africa’s qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations.

For readers in the United States, the prices are a live read on how traders rate Mexican, Brazilian and Argentine clubs. One of the two exchanges, Kalshi, is regulated in the US by the CFTC.

What Prediction Markets Say

A price of 49% means a contract that pays US$1 if Cruz Azul win costs about 49 US cents. Prices are bets by traders, not forecasts by The Rio Times, and they can move quickly.

Kalshi volume is counted in contracts, each worth up to US$1. Polymarket volume is in US dollars, and match prices can add up to slightly more than 100% because each outcome is quoted separately.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Archive photo: Estadio Banorte (formerly Estadio Azteca) in Mexico City. Sunday’s derby is at the university stadium, also in the capital.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

This Weekend’s Matches

Pumas UNAM vs Cruz Azul: Cruz Azul 49%, Pumas 27%, draw 26%

Sunday 11 October, 19:00 in Mexico City (21:00 ET), Estadio Olímpico Universitario, Liga MX Apertura, matchday 11. Kalshi shows 12,765 contracts traded on the game.

Cruz Azul beat Pumas 2–1 on aggregate in the Clausura final in May, after a 0–0 first leg and a 2–1 win at this ground. On 26 September they drew 3–3 with Toluca.

Pumas lost 3–2 at home to Atlético de San Luis on 27 September. The market still gives the hosts a 27% chance, almost level with the 26% it puts on a draw.

Lanús vs Vélez Sarsfield: Lanús 45%, Vélez 27%

Monday 12 October, 16:00 in Buenos Aires (15:00 ET), Estadio Ciudad de Lanús, Argentina’s Liga Profesional, Clausura tournament. Kalshi shows 11,687 contracts traded, but no price has been posted for a draw.

Vélez have 21 points from 11 games and Lanús 17, according to Fox Sports.

The market backs the home side even though Vélez are four points higher. Vélez drew 2–2 at Platense on 5 October.

Our earlier coverage of the league is in Argentine League Final 2026 in La Plata.

Also this weekend: Brazil and Liga MX matchday 11

Brazil’s Série A plays round 30 from 10 to 12 October. Flamengo host Fluminense on Sunday at 17:30 in Rio (16:30 ET), and Palmeiras host Corinthians at the same time in São Paulo.

Liga MX matchday 11 runs from 9 to 11 October, with Tigres vs Toluca on Friday 9 October and América vs Monterrey on Saturday 10 October. None of these games had a match market in our feed of qualifying markets this morning.

Latin America Title Races

Brazil: Flamengo 64%, Palmeiras 36%

Flamengo lead the Série A with 61 points from 29 games after a 2–2 draw with Santos on Thursday, in which Neymar scored twice from penalties for Santos. Palmeiras beat Bahia 1–0 and are one point behind on 60.

Polymarket’s Série A winner market has US$46,864 traded. This is the first edition of this weekly preview, so there is no week-on-week change yet, and from next Friday we will show it.

Copa Libertadores: Flamengo 43% to 44%

Three Brazilian clubs and one Argentine club are left. Fluminense host Palmeiras on Wednesday 14 October at 21:30 in Brasília (20:30 ET), and Estudiantes de La Plata face Flamengo on Thursday 15 October at the same time.

The return legs are on 21 and 22 October, and the final is on 28 November at the Estadio Centenario in Montevideo.

Polymarket puts Flamengo at 43%, Palmeiras at 26.5% and Estudiantes at 12.5%, with US$33,076 traded. Kalshi has Flamengo at 44%, Fluminense at 31%, Estudiantes at 30% and Palmeiras at 20%, on 7,247 contracts.

Mexico: Toluca 27% on Kalshi, 23.5% on Polymarket

Toluca and América both have 20 points after matchday 10, with Toluca ahead on tie-breaks. América still has a postponed game against Tijuana in hand, due in late October.

Kalshi’s Apertura champion market, with 805,773 contracts, shows Toluca at 27%, Guadalajara at 20%, América at 16% and Cruz Azul at 11%. Polymarket, with US$101,358 traded, has Toluca at 23.5%, América and Guadalajara at 16.5% and Cruz Azul at 14.5%.

Polymarket also prices the runner-up spot: América 21.5%, Guadalajara 17.5%, Toluca 16.2% and Cruz Azul 10.5%. Its 2026–27 top-scorer market has Juninho at 12.5%, Paulinho at 11.2% and Juan Brunetta at 10%.

Relegation: Colombia and Peru

In Colombia’s Primera A, Polymarket gives Boyacá Chicó 79.5% and Jaguares 66.5% of going down in 2026, on US$19,567 traded. In Peru’s Liga 1, UTC Cajamarca are 85%, ADT 54.5% and Deportivo Moquegua 52.5%, on US$15,319.

More than one club is relegated in each league, so those prices do not add up to 100%. Both markets are thin, so single trades can move them.

Africa

The Africa Cup of Nations PAMOJA 2027 is co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. The opening match is on Saturday 19 June 2027 and the final on Saturday 17 July 2027, according to the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

No qualifiers are played this weekend. The next window for matchdays three and four runs from 9 to 17 November.

Polymarket’s tournament winner market has US$14,021 traded. Morocco lead at 33.5%, ahead of Senegal at 14.3%, Ivory Coast at 10%, Egypt at 7.4%, South Africa at 7% and Nigeria at 5.9%.

In qualifying Group D, South Africa are 72.5% to finish first and Guinea 25%. South Africa have six points after beating Eritrea 5–0, Guinea have three, and Kenya and Eritrea one each.

In Group F, Burkina Faso are 60% and Benin 34.4%, with Mauritania at 5.2%. Burkina Faso and Benin have four points each and Mauritania three.

Our regular odds pages for both regions are in the Latin America odds hub and the Africa odds hub, and today’s results and fixtures are in the Latin America Sports Daily.

What It Means for US Readers

Kalshi is a US-regulated exchange, so these prices show how American traders value clubs that many US fans follow, especially Mexican ones. The 2026 World Cup was played in the United States, Mexico and Canada, and Liga MX and Major League Soccer clubs also meet every summer in the Leagues Cup.

Treat the numbers as a snapshot. A 49% price for Cruz Azul still means they fail to win more often than not.

What Is Not Known

Line-ups and injury lists for Sunday’s and Monday’s games are not yet public. Weather and late kickoff changes can also move the prices before the whistle.

Kickoff times come from club and press schedules and can change. Some sources list the Lanús game on 11 October, while Promiedos and Kalshi’s own contract date it 12 October.

Many season markets have only a few thousand dollars traded, so their prices are rough guides. We will refresh them next Friday.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who do prediction markets favour in Pumas vs Cruz Azul?

Kalshi prices Cruz Azul at 49%, Pumas UNAM at 27% and a draw at 26% for Sunday 11 October, 21:00 ET. The prices were read at 5:34 am ET on 9 October and can change before kickoff.

Who is favourite to win the Liga MX Apertura?

Toluca, at 27% on Kalshi and 23.5% on Polymarket. Guadalajara is second on Kalshi at 20%, while América and Guadalajara are level at 16.5% on Polymarket.

Who is favourite to win the Brazilian Série A?

Flamengo, at 64% on Polymarket, against 36% for Palmeiras. Flamengo lead the table with 61 points from 29 games, one ahead of Palmeiras.

When are the Copa Libertadores semi-finals?

The first legs are on Wednesday 14 October (Fluminense vs Palmeiras) and Thursday 15 October (Estudiantes vs Flamengo), both at 20:30 ET. The return legs are on 21 and 22 October, and the final is on 28 November in Montevideo.

Are these predictions or bets?

They are prices set by real-money traders on Polymarket and Kalshi, not forecasts by The Rio Times. Kalshi is regulated in the US by the CFTC, and we never link to betting sites or give tips.
