World.title: MELISSA FRAUD SHIELD
World.content:
One of a number of houses in Unions Acres, St James, still waiting for repair to the damage caused by last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

LASCO Financial Services has revealed that it began holding back 30 per cent of donations made through the Government’s Hurricane Melissa relief platform after its system flagged as suspicious, a number of transactions linked to the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM).

LASCO said it remitted 70 per cent of the money received to ODPEM daily while the reserve was being held, with more than 95 per cent of all donated amounts having been paid over to the agency by the end of March, before the 30 per cent withholding was discontinued in June after the risk associated with the account returned to normal.

The disclosure provides a new explanation for the arrangement, which came under scrutiny after the Auditor General’s Department found that 30 per cent of online donations had been retained for up to 45 days by a financial services institution, without a formal written agreement governing the retention.

The audit found that $15.7 million and US$298,429 in donations withheld between October 28 and December 31, 2025 were due to be transferred to ODPEM by February 15, 2026.

However, the financial services institution told auditors on March 9 that none of the withheld funds had yet been transferred.

Four days later, ODPEM provided a transfer receipt showing that $16.1 million and US$305,292 had been sent on March 9, but the auditor general said she could not independently confirm that the money had reached ODPEM’s accounts because the agency had not provided the relevant bank statements.

LASCO Financial, in a July 31 letter to Public Accounts Committee (PAC) Chairman Julian Robinson, said the decision to retain the money followed a review of the risk associated with the account after its payment system detected suspicious activity.

According to the company, the 30 per cent was not treated as money belonging to it, but as a refundable security reserve intended to protect against possible losses arising from disputed or fraudulent card transactions.

The company said a July 8, 2024 agreement with ODPEM expressly provided for a refundable security reserve, but no reserve was instituted at the time, based on the risk assessment then in place.

LASCO Financial said the 45-day period was based on guidance from its banking partners, who advised that this was the period within which a customer could challenge a transaction.

“If a charge-back occurred due to ODPEM transactions, without reserve, LASCO would have to absorb full loss,” the company said, adding that the arrangement was “standard practice by financial institutions in these types of transactions”.

A charge-back occurs when a card transaction is challenged and the money is reversed through the banking system.

LASCO said the reserve was therefore intended to ensure that money would be available if a transaction processed through the donation platform was later disputed and reversed.

The company said the donation button remained active on the Government’s Support Jamaica website and continued to receive contributions, while the withholding arrangement was eventually discontinued in June after the risk associated with the account had returned to normal levels.

The latest explanation comes after the issue was raised during a meeting of the PAC on July 28 at which questions were asked about why a financial institution had been allowed to retain a portion of disaster donations and whether there was a formal agreement authorising the arrangement.

At that meeting, ODPEM Director General Commander Alvin Gayle told the PAC that the funds, which had prompted the auditor general’s concern, had since been received by the agency.

Gayle also acknowledged that there had been no formal arrangement specifically governing the retention of Hurricane Melissa funds, even though there was an existing agreement covering the processing of donations.

In a subsequent August 31 response from the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) to questions from the committee, the Government said the legal teams of ODPEM and LASCO were still discussing the terms of the agreement.

The OPM also told the PAC that ODPEM selected LASCO after assessing the available payment-processing options.

It said LASCO is currently the only financial services provider with which Amber Innovations Inc — the company behind the relevant licensed payment products — has granted a non-exclusive licence for a payment-based solution to merchants.

World.title: ‘I don’t shy away from court’
World.content:
Attorney Hugh Wildman speaking at a news conference on Thursday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Attorney Hugh Wildman on Thursday insisted that he would never deliberately stay way from the fraud trial of his client Fritz Pinnock in the St Andrew Parish Court, but said his involvement in the murder case of six cops in the Home Circuit Court, downtown Kingston, has been creating unavoidable scheduling clashes due to the latter matter being dragged out by the prosecution.

Wildman was defending himself at a news conference he called a day after Justice Sanchia Burrell told Pinnock that he may have to cross-examine a witness himself if no legal representation is present for him when the delay- plagued Ruel Reid and company fraud trial resumes next Monday.

“Today’s press conference is called to respond to the media reports and various comments concerning the Pinnock and Reid matter, where the judge made certain comments in my absence and gave the impression that I deliberately stayed away from the court.

I wish to make it abundantly clear that everybody in Jamaica knows my position; I don’t shy away from court,” Wildman said.

“In fact, I am known to appear in all courts and take a certain stand to defend my clients vigorously,” he said.

“The situation is this: It is a known fact that we are engaged in the trial of the six police in downtown since the 7th of January of this year.

When the case commenced, the trial judge [Sonia Bertram- Linton] made it abundantly clear that she got instructions from the chief justice that that case must be a priority case; that’s what she told us,” Wildman said.

He said that in all his years of practising law he has never seen a situation in which a murder trial is dragged out by the prosecution the way that the policemen’s matter has been.

“The case has been going on unnecessarily long because of the conduct of the prosecutor in recalling and recalling witnesses, evidence to adduce new evidence, and it goes on and on, uncontrolled.

It amounts to an abuse of process.

The case continues and continues, and nobody knows when this case will come to an end,” he said.

“Everybody in the justice system knows about this.

In fact, we have had cases in court where Supreme Court judges have said they know Mr Wildman is engaged in other matters, and they put off the case.

Up to this week…

The point is this, I explained to Ms Burrell the challenge we are having with the downtown case, which is a priority.

It’s a murder case with six policemen.

I’m representing four of the accused persons,” he said, emphasising that, “It is impossible for me to be at two places at the same time.” On Wednesday in the Parish Court, fellow defence attorney Carolyn Chuck told Justice Burrell that Wildman had advised that he would ask another attorney to hold in his stead; but no one turned up.

Chuck went on to share that Wildman had indicated that he could also have challenges with being present next week as he was given time off from the Supreme Court to deal with the arrangements for his mother’s funeral.

Justice Burrell acknowledged the sensitivity of the matter and extended condolence to Wildman’s family.

However, she queried why this had not been communicated before.

“I don’t take lightly that Mr Wildman is making funeral arrangements for his mother, and my condolence goes out to him and his family, but early information- sharing makes a huge difference,” she said.

“I have to be very sensitive because all of us who are here either have a mother or had a mother at some point…

but I am not understanding the lack of communication; the lack of communication is very unhelpful,” the judge said.

Emphasising that the case impacts four other accused, Burrell said Wildman and Pinnock are not entitled to an infinite supply of the court’s resources.

Her comments came on the one-year anniversary of the official start of the trial, which has been plagued with scheduling challenges.

“It cannot be that Mr Wildman avoids appropriate and adequate communication and expects to get what he asks for,” she said.

“How can the rights of four other people be expected to continuously and infinitely, at this point in time, … be expected to yield to Mr Wildman’s failure — I am using the word failure — to organise himself?” Justice Burrell said.

Pinnock, the former Caribbean Maritime University head; former education minister Ruel Reid; his wife Sharen Reid and daughter Sharelle; as well as Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence (Jamaica Labour Party, Brown’s Town Division) are defendants in the high-profile $25-million fraud trial in the parish court.

In the matter being heard in the Home Circuit Court, the six policemen are on trial for murder in relation to the January 12, 2013 shooting deaths of Matthew Lee, Ucliffe Dyer, and Mark Allen on Acadia Drive in St Andrew, during an alleged shoot-out.

On Thursday, Wildman said he was trying to find a solution to his problem, telling the news conference that he has written a letter to Chief Justice Bryan Sykes urging his intervention.

“I was shocked when I heard that the judge was behaving like that, as if I deliberately stayed away from court.

Everybody knows that that is not my style.

I want to be there to defend my client, Mr Pinnock, and defend him vigorously, because we maintain that there is no case against him.

But the point is that I am locked in that trial downtown.

What do I do?” he said.

“Should I have walked away from the criminal case downtown with the six policemen? I don’t know why this is taking so long.

Every day, up to yesterday, I made serious submissions in law based on the constitution, that the trial is an abuse of process with what is going on downtown,” he said.

World.title: Cardi B’s OUT
World.content:
Cardi B

“Mi want back me money.”

That was the blunt response from one disappointed patron on social media Thursday as news spread that international rap superstar Cardi B would no longer headline BZR WKND Jamaica on October 18.

For others, the disappointment quickly turned into questions about their pockets.

“I heard that Cardi cancelled. How do I process my refund?” one patron asked.

“This must be some sick joke cuz me book my flight and buy my concert ticket. Who ago reimburse me?” another wrote.

“Yall need to update us ASAP. This needs to be addressed,” a third demanded.

With Cardi B’s cancellation now confirmed, patrons who had been counting down to what was billed as one of the biggest entertainment weekends on Jamaica’s 2026 calendar are waiting for answers from BZR WKND organisers — particularly on whether the October 18 concert will proceed, whether another headliner will be brought in, and, most urgently, what happens to tickets already purchased.

Cardi B’s representatives confirmed Thursday that the Grammy-winning rapper will not perform at BZR WKND Jamaica, telling Billboard: “Cardi B will not be performing at BZR WKND Jamaica on October 18, 2026.”

The statement added that Cardi B appreciates the “love and support” from her Jamaican fans and hopes to see them in the future, while directing questions about the status of BZR WKND, ticketing, and other event-related matters to the event organisers.

At press time, however, efforts to reach the organisers proved futile, with calls to several key stakeholders going unanswered. Billboard also reported that organisers had not responded to its request for comment.

The silence has left patrons with more questions than answers, particularly those who may have made travel and accommodation arrangements around the highly anticipated event.

And there was plenty to look forward to.

When Cardi B was announced as the headline attraction in August, the booking was positioned as a major moment not only for BZR WKND but for Jamaica’s live entertainment landscape.

The rapper’s October 18 appearance at the National Stadium would have marked her first performance in Jamaica and, more significantly, her first headlining stadium concert in the Caribbean.

For BZR WKND, the stakes were equally high. The festival was being positioned as a four-day celebration of music, culture, food, tourism, fashion, and entertainment, with Cardi B’s stadium show serving as its marquee attraction.

Organisers had envisioned the event as more than a concert, with the weekend expected to attract music lovers and visitors from Jamaica and overseas while contributing to the country’s tourism and entertainment sectors.

At the time of the announcement, organisers Ryan Burke and Roy “Gramps” Morgan described Cardi’s booking as a defining moment for both BZR WKND and Jamaica’s live entertainment industry.

The anticipation was palpable.

BZR WKND had already established itself as a major player on the local concert calendar with its 2023 staging, which featured Chris Brown & Friends at the National Stadium. For 2026, the ambition was to go bigger, with international media attention, overseas visitors, and thousands of patrons expected to converge on Kingston.

The momentum appeared to be building as early bird tickets were reported as sold out, while the official ticketing platform later described the event as having generated “overwhelming demand” and said purchasers had been placed in an e-mail queue for ticket confirmation.

Even Cardi B herself appeared to be embracing the occasion. During a social media live approximately a month before the scheduled performance, the WAP artiste spoke about preparing for her Jamaican showcase and acknowledged the reputation of the local audience as one that would not be easily impressed. She reassured fans that she was taking the performance seriously and was preparing to step up her training and rehearsals ahead of the show.

That preparation, coupled with the scale of the booking, only heightened expectations for what would have been Cardi B’s Jamaican début.

The October 18 concert was also shaping up as a major international showcase, with Grammy-nominated R&B star Keyshia Cole joining Cardi B as a co-headliner and Queen of Dancehall Spice announced as host.

Dancehall acts Malie Donn, Ding Dong, Stalk Ashley, and Shaneil Muir have also been announced among the performers.

Cardi B’s representatives have not stated why she will no longer perform, and no information has been released indicating the status of the October 18 showcase and whether it will proceed with a revised line-up.

More importantly for patrons, no refund arrangement had been announced by the organisers up to press time.

Although there is no indication that the current cancellation is connected to a previous legal dispute involving the brand’s inaugural staging, the development puts BZR WKND under renewed scrutiny.

Following the success of Chris Brown & Friends in 2023, Solid View Limited — the company responsible for the execution of the stage layout — became embroiled in a legal dispute with H&L over outstanding payments for materials supplied for the concert.

H&L sought recovery of approximately $5.6 million, with recovery and administrative costs bringing the dispute closer to $7 million. The company contended that materials and supplies had been urgently requested and delivered for the August 2023 Chris Brown and Friends concert, but that only approximately $1.22 million of a bill totalling more than $6.9 million had been paid.

The case represents a legal hangover from BZR’s 2023 launch, although the management structure for the 2026 staging has evolved and there is no evidence linking that dispute to Cardi B’s withdrawal.

For now, however, it is the patrons — rather than the history of the brand — who are demanding attention. After weeks of promotion, anticipation, and investment, those who bought into the promise of seeing one of the world’s biggest female rap stars make her Caribbean stadium debut are now waiting for the organisers to explain what happens next.

World.title: PATCHING UP
World.content:
Kingston Mayor Andrew Swaby watches as workers carry out repairs on Seaview Avenue in St Andrew on Thursday, with a line of motorists passing through the work area.

WITH potholes causing almost daily logjams in the Corporate Area, the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) has started a major road patching project across the city.

Kingston Mayor Andrew Swaby says patching has started on badly damaged sections of 20 to 25 roads, including some which he said are under the control of the National Works Agency (NWA).

Swaby said the municipal corporation is targeting some of the worst-affected areas in downtown Kingston, and New Kingston, with surrounding communities also included in the programme.

“They are not only community roads but actually we are fixing some main roads, and…

it’s important for us to fix those main roads because clearly, where you have these big craters across the road it impedes traffic.

It appears you have to slow down and it builds up that traffic,” Swaby said after touring some of the road work on Thursday.

According to Swaby, the KSAMC was helping to repair some roads which are the responsibility of the NWA because of the effect their condition was having on traffic.

The decision comes against the background of a monthslong dispute between the leadership of some municipal corporations and minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan over the condition of roads and the amount of money available to repair them.

Morgan has repeatedly argued that municipal corporations must do more to maintain roads under their control.

In September, Swaby told the Jamaica Observer that most of the roads repaired by the NWA in Kingston and St Andrew were KSAMC roads and argued that the Parochial Revenue Fund — which supports road work and other municipal works — had increased significantly without a similar increase in road repairs.

Swaby has repeatedly argued that the corporation’s resources are stretched thin because the same funds used for road repairs must also support other municipal responsibilities.

On Thursday, Swaby doubled down on his position as he pointed to the funding pressure and said the KSAMC would be better able to meet its mandate if it had more money.

“Obviously, if we had more funds, we would be in a better position to respond to the people of Kingston and St Andrew, and we are trying our best to see how we can garner the funds from what is owed to us, along with what the Government gives us, to fix these roads,” he said.

“Let me remind people that the Parochial Revenue Fund not only fixes roads, but it is the same fund that is required to do other things.

So we don’t have a dedicated resource, a fund to say every month we are in a position to spend ‘x’ on roads.

There are times… we have to divert those funds in cleaning drains.

So we continue to face the challenges, and we are looking at ways of how best we can fix these roads,” Swaby said.

The mayor’s explanation came months after the KSAMC announced a $220-million road rehabilitation programme covering all 40 divisions of the municipality.

By March, the corporation said 33 roads had been repaired at a cost of $90 million, with the remaining programme intended to cover additional roads.

In June, the KSAMC also increased allocations under its Divisional Allocation Fund from $10 million to $13 million for each urban division and $13.5 million for rural divisions.

The fund covers road repairs as well as other activities, including drain cleaning, emergency work, and community programmes.

World.title: Arrested German spy chief lashed out at his old agency over allegations he spied for Russia
World.content:
Jäger did not respond to the letter at the time, according to Hanning, who spoke to WELT before his arrest.

Hanning’s subsequent arrest, including on suspicion of attempted treason, has caused considerable concern abroad. Grzegorz Malecki, the former head of Poland’s foreign intelligence service, told WELT that the case was “extremely concerning” and could deepen allies’ distrust of the BND. He warned this had the potential to undermine intelligence-sharing with Germany.

The BND has also raised eyebrows within Germany’s intelligence community over allegations that it allowed Hanning’s former chief of staff, who is also in custody, to work for Hanning outside his official duties.

While civil servants are generally permitted to take on outside employment, any approval allowing a member of the BND to work for Hanning would have had to be decided at the senior management level, said Günter Heiss, a former intelligence coordinator under former Chancellor Angela Merkel. “Without knowing the details, I would never have approved anything like this had I been in a position of responsibility at the BND.”

Bernd Schmidbauer, a former minister of state and intelligence coordinator under Chancellor Helmut Kohl, told WELT that Hanning had made major contributions to Germany’s national security. The affair was therefore “not only a tragedy for the German intelligence services, but also for the former senior official himself,” Schmidbauer said.

Hanning was among Schmidbauer’s closest aides during the 1990s and went on to lead the BND from 1998 to 2005.

Dirk Banse is an investigative reporter at WELT. Philipp Fritz is WELT’s Eastern Europe correspondent. Uwe Müller is a freelance reporter based in Berlin.

The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, The Telegraph, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

World.title: Dutch PM slams ‘absurd’ US decision to livestream execution
World.content:
“As far as I’m concerned, it is really up to the social media platforms in Europe to prevent this from being circulated and broadcast on their channels. But I fear it will be impossible to prevent,” he said.

Jetten added that if the execution does appear on European social media, there will be “a great number of reports filed,” as violent content must be moderated by social media platforms under European law.

“Video-sharing platforms that allow video content displaying scenes of gratuitous violence must use effective age assurance so that children cannot normally see this content,” a spokesperson for the Irish Media Commission told POLITICO. This means platforms can show violent content as long as they ensure it doesn’t reach minors.

The media regulator is currently investigating X over possible breaches in online safety rules for failing to carry out proper age checks.

The UN has said livestreaming an execution would amount to torture. “The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture,” the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights told AFP.

The body said its statement is in line with previous ones it has released about public executions in Afghanistan and Iran.

The European Commission did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.

This is a developing story.

World.title: France, Germany try to save face on joint tank project
World.content:
France’s chief of defense staff, Gen. Fabien Mandon, told lawmakers Thursday that Germany had pulled out of the project. His comments landed especially awkwardly as German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is currently on a state visit to France.

Later in the evening, Mandon tried to backpedal in a written statement, arguing the project was only delayed to the late 2040s.

In recent years, Franco-German defense industrial projects have repeatedly failed. MGCS — which involves KNDS France, KNDS Germany, Rheinmetall and Thales — has been bogged down by years of delays, industrial disputes and political tensions. POLITICO reported in June that France and Germany would most likely build separate tanks.

Now, Pistorius has said the two countries will still work together on “unmanned systems and automated processing.”

The German minister pledged that the project wouldn’t meet the same fate as the Future Combat Air System, the joint next-generation fighter jet program that collapsed before the summer. “The crucial point is that we learn from our mistakes. That is why MGCS is in no way at risk and remains an important future project for our two nations and our two armed forces,” he said.

But the imbroglio highlights strains in the defense relationship between Paris and Berlin, and an increasing number of French lawmakers are now calling for Paris to look for other partners.

“Defense cooperation with Germany is at an all-time low, since Germany is going it alone,” a French lawmaker working on defense policy told POLITICO on condition of anonymity.

Rixa Fürsen contributed to this article from Bordeaux, France.

World.title: China und die EU haben nach Angaben Pekings eine Einigung zu Hybrid-Autos erzielt
World.content:
Handelskommissar Maroš Šefčovič bemüht sich um eine Zusage aus Peking, den boomenden Export chinesischer Plug-in-Hybrid-Elektrofahrzeuge nach Europa einzudämmen.

PEKING – China und die EU haben nach Darstellung des chinesischen Handelsministeriums eine Einigung über den Export von Hybrid-Elektrofahrzeugen erzielt.

Die Ankündigung am Freitag erfolgte, nach dem Abschluss zweitägiger Gespräche zwischen Handelskommissar Maroš Šefčovič und chinesischen Regierungsmitgliedern in Peking. Sie waren Teil der Bemühungen der EU, ihr Handelsdefizit mit China in Höhe von 1 Milliarde Euro pro Tag zu verringern und Druck von der europäischen Industrie zu nehmen.

„Nach intensiven Beratungen haben beide Seiten eine Einigung über den Handel mit Hybridfahrzeugen erzielt, die mit den Regeln der Welthandelsorganisation im Einklang steht“, hieß es in der chinesischen Erklärung.

World.title: EU and China clinch deal to curb hybrid car exports
World.content:
Speaking in Beijing, the commissioner said the two sides had reached an agreement that would help to shield European automakers from low-price Chinese competition. He declined to enter into specifics before EU leaders officially mandate the EU executive to move forward.

“We have reached a shared understanding to moderate China’s export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the European Union. This opens the prospect of cutting China’s exports by more than a half,” Šefčovič told reporters.

The estimate was based on projections of how Chinese exports would grow over the next four years without the agreement. In practical terms, it would mean that “several millions of car exports from China to the European Union” would be prevented, he explained.

China’s Commerce Ministry highlighted the understanding on hybrids in a parallel 16-point statement, but offered no details on how exports would be restrained. It said the two sides “will continue to strengthen communication and cooperation under the trade monitoring mechanism and further leverage dialogue mechanisms to enhance mutual understanding.”

Šefčovič declined to elaborate when asked whether the deal would allow the EU to impose safeguards — a mixture of import quotas and tariffs — a step that Brussels has been considering. He said the arrangement would comply with the rules of the World Trade Organization.

First step

Šefčovič said that Beijing had also agreed to lower duties on European goods worth €4 billion, ranging from olive oil to footwear, a move that would save exporters €225 million.

World.title: Andy Burnham vows to ease non-compete clauses
World.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers a speech during the The Innovation Nation Summit at Bruntwood SciTech on October 09, 2026 in Manchester, England. | Christopher Furlong/Getty Images

Drive — first reported by POLITICO Thursday — comes after intense lobbying from the startups sector.

LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed Friday he will legislate to ease restrictive non-compete clause rules for workers — but stopped short of committing to a ban.

​Burnham said in a speech in Manchester that he wants to "make sure that non-compete clauses will no longer be a barrier to hiring for our most promising start-ups and scaling firms" — but did has yet to set out the extent of the crackdown.

​The scope of the new rules will come later, ahead of legislation. POLITICO first reported the planned crackdown Thursday.

World.title: Finance ministers strike market supercop deal despite Brussels’ objections
World.content:
“We deeply regret that the compromise now on the table falls significantly short of the level of ambition needed,” Finance Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque told ministers during Friday’s public Ecofin debate in Luxembourg. “We need [the European Securities and Markets Authority] to become an effective supervisor. The current compromise text would not allow for that.”

France spearheaded a last-minute push over dinner Thursday to strengthen the watchdog’s executive powers. Paris took issue with a rule that would allow nine national supervisors to force the watchdog’s executive board to submit draft decisions for further scrutiny before they’re adopted. The Irish EU presidency tweaked the rule overnight to limit national supervisors’ ability to delay decisions and preserve the watchdog’s power to act in emergencies, according to a compromise document obtained by POLITICO.

That was enough for France and most other countries. But not for the Commission, nor European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, who was equally critical of the Council compromise. Beyond the governance concerns, Albuquerque took aim at supervisory carve-outs that the Irish introduced to accommodate Germany’s push to exclude its stock exchange, Deutsche Börse, from EU oversight.

The carve-out club

The carve-out shields stock exchanges from direct EU supervision unless they meet certain thresholds for trading activity and cross-border reach. Spain’s stock exchange, Bolsas y Mercados Españoles, would also benefit from the carve-outs, triggering criticism from smaller EU countries that accused the waiver of granting the bloc’s largest nations preferential treatment.

Belgium was particularly critical because its Brussels-based securities depository Euroclear is expected to come under direct EU oversight and face supervisory fees, while some major stock exchanges could remain under national oversight. Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever will take the issue to EU leaders at the end of next week.

“We cannot support the carve-outs. The package includes as many ins as there are outs,” Belgian Finance Minister Jan Jambon said during Friday’s public debate. “I think Germany has won in certain cases.”

World.title: Hitler Mussolini wins local election
World.content:
Aerial view of the Plaza de Armas with the government palace on the left and the cathedral on the right in Lima's downtown on January 4, 2026. | Connie France/ AFP via Getty Images

Peruvian voters pick their new mayor, despite his unusual name.

Voters in the Peruvian town of Queropalca have chosen their new mayor: Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores.

The unusually named candidate for the center-left Ahora Nación party won 34% of the vote. According to local media, the top three candidates were separated by just 42 votes.

Simeon’s candidate application form gives few details (and none about his name), apart from the fact that he manages the Simeon Sac Investment Group.

World.title: Rare waterspouts slam western Sicily, wrecking homes and a school
World.content:
One of the worst-hit buildings was the Terrenove campus of Alcide De Gasperi school in Marsala, which its headteacher described as destroyed. All 273 children inside were moved to safety by staff, and no serious injuries were reported among pupils or employees. In Petrosino, a car was swept into a ravine, injuring both occupants.

 

Early reports said nine people, including four children, had been treated for minor injuries at Marsala hospital. Later accounts put the total at 11, including two people taken to hospital in nearby Mazara del Vallo.

Emergency teams remained at work as authorities assessed the damage to buildings, vehicles and farmland. The full extent of the destruction was still being established.

World.title: Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi foils Russia’s plan to encircle the Donbas, ISW analysis shows
World.content:
Ukrainian forces have derailed Russia’s plan to encircle and occupy the remaining Ukrainian-controlled territory of the Donetsk region this year, the Washington-based think tank Institute for the Study of War (ISW) concluded in an assessment based primarily on open-source intelligence.

 

The Russian campaign centred on a deep pincer movement targeting what the report calls the “fortress belt” — a defensive and logistical network protecting the Ukrainian-held portion of the Donbas — advancing from Lyman in the north and Dobropillia in the south-west, with both arms intended to link up near Barvinkove in the Kharkiv region.

Completing such an encirclement would have gone a long way towards Moscow’s longstanding objective of occupying all of Donetsk region and would have given the Kremlin something to show Russian society for the costs of the war.

Ukraine foils Russian offensive in Donetsk ISW

Ukraine’s counter-offensive on the Lyman axis, dubbed Operation Vivaldi, dismantled the northern arm of that pincer.

Ukrainian forces advanced along the Ridkodub–Nove–Novomykhailivka line in the north and the Yarova–Drobysheve–Stavky line in the south, collapsing the salient Russia had built to threaten Sloviansk from the north-east and forcing Russian units onto the defensive.

Commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps Andrii Biletskyi said the first three phases of the operation in mid- to late September liberated 176 square kilometres of territory.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy put the figure at between 125 and 140 square kilometres as of 3 October, adding that Russian losses had risen sharply over the preceding two to three months.

Ukrainian servicemen run along a street in Druzhkivka; photo provided by the press service of Ukraine's 93rd Separate Mechanised Brigade Iryna Rybakova/Ukrainian 93rd Mechanized brigade

ISW suggested the operation may have been more successful than Kyiv’s official figures reflect.

The defeat of the northern pincer forced Russia to abandon its plans to advance on Sloviansk from the north-east and deprived it of positions intended to threaten northern approaches to the fortress belt.

Ukrainian servicemen watch a first-person-view (FPV) drone in Druzhkivka on 12 September 2026. Iryna Rybakova/Ukrainian 93rd Mechanized brigade

Ukraine’s retained control over the Lyman area also preserved key supply routes. Russian units on other parts of the front may have been redeployed to reinforce the northern sector.

Russia’s south-western advance from the Pokrovsk–Dobropillia area — the surviving arm of the original encirclement — now faces far more ambitious objectives on its own.

ISW regards the collapse of the northern pincer as an operational failure, as Russia has not just lost ground around Lyman but also a key component of the campaign plan for the fortress belt.

Russian forces retain limited gains around Kostyantynivka and east of Sloviansk but have struggled to sustain the pace of advance in both areas.

Settlements liberated in Operation ISW

ISW argued that their reliance on infantry infiltration, drones and bombardment can produce gradual attrition but cannot generate the fast mechanised manoeuvres required to collapse Ukraine’s defences at the scale Moscow needs.

The situation remains fluid, the institute added, and Russian forces will probably adapt over time, but for now, Ukraine appears to have halted the advance.

A further Russian mobilisation and technological adaptation could alter the balance, although neither would necessarily enable a breakthrough.

Putin’s September figures challenged

ISW also challenged claims, widely circulated in pro-government Russian media, that Russian forces occupied further 1,301 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory in September alone, roughly two and a half times the figure reported in previous months.

Based on geolocated photo and video footage, satellite imagery and visually confirmed data, the institute calculated that Russian assault units had in reality been pushed out of at least 80 square kilometres in September.

Ukrainian servicemen in front-line Druzhkivka; photo provided by the press service of Ukraine's 93rd Separate Mechanised Brigade Iryna Rybakova/Ukrainian 93rd Mechanized brigade

Russia's net retreat in September rose to 175.18 square kilometres, including areas it temporarily penetrated but did not hold.

Putin told the Valdai Club last week that Russia now occupies 89% of Donetsk region. ISW puts the figure of Russian-occupied territory in the Ukrainian region at no more than 81%.

A local resident pushes her belongings in a cart along the streets of Druzhkivka in Ukraine's Donetsk region on 12 September 2026. Iryna Rybakova/Ukrainian 93rd Mechanized brigade

The institute assessed that Putin’s claims of Russian breakthroughs in September were “so far removed from reality that they resemble hallucinations.”

It could not determine whether Putin knows the figures he cites are false or has come to believe the fabricated frontline data he receives, a product of what ISW describes as a deeply embedded culture of dishonesty in the Russian military command.

World.title: Latvia’s border guard seeks greater powers amid increasingly violent border crossings
World.content:
On 5 October, a group used makeshift stairs to enter Latvia. While the Baltic country of two million has faced irregular migration from Belarus since 2021, the latest incident was particularly aggressive.

 

The group of 20 migrants was led by “armed, masked escorts openly threatening Latvian soldiers,” Latvia’s Interior Minister, Jānis Dombrava, told Euronews. In the following hours, border surveillance equipment was damaged, reducing Latvia’s “ability to detect and respond to further incursions.”

“The combination of armed intimidation and targeted sabotage raises the risk of a violent confrontation and tests both our defences and our willingness to respond,” Dombrava said, adding that it’s “a security threat, not simply a migration-management problem.”

Latvia completed the fencing of its 173-kilometre border with Belarus this year and installed advanced surveillance systems, making crossings harder. The obstacles are making facilitators increasingly aggressive, according to Guntis Pujāts, head of Latvia’s State Border Guard.

“That’s why they are trying to be more aggressive and so to throw stones as well, to show what looks like a weapon and so on,” Pujāts told Euronews, adding that the incident “shows that the situation is not going to decrease but in the opposite way”.

More powers to Border Guard

The State Border Guard is now seeking greater powers to protect its personnel and secure the country’s border, as Latvia enters its fifth year of dealing with irregular migration from Belarus. The interior minister supports the move.

Currently, border guards already have the right to use firearms in circumstances prescribed by law, including when responding to serious threats and attempted acts of sabotage.

Pujāts wants to broaden their powers, as well as those of police and military personnel supporting border operations, to enable them to “protect the security of Latvia”.

On Thursday, the Border Guard submitted a proposal to the Interior Ministry seeking changes to the rules.

Under the proposed changes, border guards would no longer have to issue a warning before using force in certain circumstances, Pujāts said. They would also be able to use the tools at their disposal to stop and “neutralise” people damaging border infrastructure.

“We will not be obliged to warn before, and we will be allowed all tools that we have to stop and so to neutralise persons who are damaging our border infrastructure,” he said.

The interior minister confirmed to Euronews that he will propose amendments “to give those protecting our country clearer powers and greater discretion when facing threats of this kind.”

“Those who protect Latvia's state border – border guards, soldiers and other officials – must be confident that they will not be unjustifiably subjected to criminal prosecution for the lawful use of firearms or special means,” he said.

Pujāts said he did not know how long it would take for the proposal to become law. Asked when he would like the changes to take effect, he replied: “Yesterday, or the day before yesterday.”

World.title: EU calls US sanctions on International Criminal Court 'regrettable'
World.content:
The European Union on Friday described US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) as "deeply regrettable" and said it was "ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work".

 

"The EU will work closely with the ICC to ensure it continues to operate effectively," the European Commission said, adding it hoped that the six-month delay before the sanctions applied meant "there is room for dialogue"

One possible EU response would be to activate a legal instrument known as the "blocking mechanism", which prohibits European firms from obeying the US sanctions "actively or by deliberate omission", giving the European Union a potential means of cushioning some of the impact.

Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen described the mechanism as the "nuclear option", but said the Netherlands had nevertheless asked Brussels to prepare it.

US sanctions on the ICC: What happened?

The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the ICC, accusing the tribunal of political bias and unfairly targeting Americans and Israelis over alleged war crimes.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the measures on Friday, shortly after South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. However, the decision to impose sanctions had been made well before the Nobel announcement.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us,” Rubio said in a video address posted to social media. “The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”

The sanctions freeze any ICC assets held in the United States and give US companies and individuals six months to end their business dealings with the court.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday welcomed US sanctions against the ICC, which has issued an arrest warrant for him over alleged crimes committed in Gaza.

"The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," Netanyahu's office posted on X.

How has the ICC reacted to the US sanctions?

The ICC condemned the sanctions, describing them as an attack on the rule of law and the international legal order.

“It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do," the court said in a statement. "It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.”

ICC President Tomoko Akane said the court would “continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes.”

World.title: Former Prince Andrew receives £302,000 for surrendering royal lease
World.content:
Britain's former Prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has received £302,000 (around €347,000) in compensation after being forced to give up the lease on his longtime home amid controversy over his links to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

 

The Crown Estate confirmed on Friday that Mountbatten-Windsor was entitled to compensation because he left Royal Lodge less than 25 years into his 75-year lease.

The amount was deducted from the £1.8 million (around €2.07 million) he owed for repairs to the property, leaving him with a bill of around £1.5 million (€1.73 million).

“The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return,” the Crown Estate said in a statement.

Police searched Royal Lodge for six days in February as part of an investigation into allegations of misconduct in public office linked to his relationship with Epstein. Mountbatten-Windsor has denied any wrongdoing.

On Thursday, he won a legal challenge after police acknowledged that the search warrants they had obtained were "unlawful".

King Charles III stripped his younger brother of his princely title and ordered him to leave Royal Lodge last year amid growing scrutiny of his relationship with Epstein.

Millions of pages of documents released by the US Justice Department have revealed further details about their ties.

Andrew's continued residence at Royal Lodge had also drawn criticism because he paid only a nominal rent for the property.

He signed the 75-year lease in 2003, agreeing to spend £7.5 million (around €8.63 million) on renovations and make an initial payment of £1 million (around €1.15 million).

World.title: Which European countries are winning the tech funding race?
World.content:
European tech funding surged to €15.8 billion across 300 funding deals in September, bringing the total for 2026 to almost €60 billion, according to the latest figures from online publication tech.eu, although half was made up by UK investments.

 

The spike in activity represents a quarter of the year’s investment so far, a strong rebound on August’s activity which saw just €3.2 billion raised across 165 deals.

The activity also shows that European companies are attracting significant investment in technology, raising the prospect that they could one day scale up and help ease the continent’s reliance on US Big Tech.

However, investment still falls way behind the US, which attracted $50 billion in the same period and $800 billion in annual cloud/AI infrastructure.

Source: tech.eu Cleared

Of September’s 300 deals, 25 companies raised more than €100 million each, including three rounds exceeding €1 billion secured by AI platform company Mistral and AI infrastructure firm Nscale. 34 deals were made with undisclosed values.

September’s largest deal came from French AI company Mistral, raising €3 billion in a series D round at a post-money valuation of more than €21 billion.

Cloud computing and artificial intelligence secured the most investment by sector, with €5.541 billion invested in cloud across 44 deals and €4.194 billion in AI.

Fintech (€847.7 million), health tech (€826.3 million), space (€725.8 million), robotics (€508.3 million), software (€421.1 million), security (€319.8 million), telecoms (€315 million) and deep tech (€274.5 million) made up the rest of the top 10 invested tech industries.

The UK remains Europe’s top fundraising market in September, securing €7.3 billion, half of the month’s total, in over 65 transactions.

Trailing the UK are France (€3.478 billion), Germany (€1.155 billion), the Netherlands (€1.119 billion), Spain (€615.8 million), Portugal (€524.1 million), Sweden (€399.9 million), Italy (€373.1 million), Bulgaria (€177.7 million) and Finland (€175.8 million).

Source: tech.eu Cleared

September’s investments were made by more than 11,700 investors, with French public sector investment bank BPI France taking part in the most deals (8).

German public-private venture capital firm High-Tech Gründerfonds came in second with 7, followed by Italian venture capital firm Vento with 6, the UK’s national innovation agency Innovate UK with 6, UK venture capital firm Balderton Capital with 5, and the European Investment Bank with 5.

The EU has a number of funding instruments targeting tech, as the bloc aims to not only end its reliance on America’s Big Tech but also secure its own technology sovereignty.

In July, the European Commission launched a €10 billion public-private initiative to support the building of seven AI gigafactories across Europe. It also aims to unlock €20 billion in private funding to power trillion-parameter models to rival leaders such as Claude and ChatGPT.

The European Investment Bank also runs the TechEU Programme, which pools €70 billion in debt and equity to mobilise €250 billion by 2027 to take European startups from seed to IPO.

The European Commission has also made available €8.1 billion worth of funding through its Digital Europe Programme to support supercomputing, cybersecurity, advanced digital skills and semiconductors via the Chips Act.

And finally, there’s the Scaleup Europe Fund, a €5 billion initiative managed by Swedish private equity firm EQT to invest in AI, quantum computing, clean tech and biotech.

World.title: Iran's IRGC strikes tanker and threatens to target vessels beyond Hormuz
World.content:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed responsibility on Friday for setting an oil tanker ablaze in the Strait of Hormuz and threatened to pursue vessels it deems in violation beyond the strait and across the wider region, as maritime security agencies reported two further strikes on commercial ships in the Persian Gulf.

 

The IRGC Navy said it targeted the engine room and propulsion system of the MV Sun Shine, a tanker belonging to the company Natwit, after the vessel attempted to use what it described as an unauthorised route through the strait's southern section. The attack caused a fire on board.

In a statement, the IRGC warned that action against "violating" vessels would no longer be confined to the Strait of Hormuz and that any ship using what it deems unauthorised routes would be pursued and "punished" anywhere in the region.

Companies it accuses of co-operating with the US would be sanctioned and all their vessels targeted, it added.

The IRGC laid blame for the incidents in the strait on the US military, accusing Washington of interfering in the decisions of shipping and insurance companies and paying "large bribes" to induce compliance.

"Direct responsibility for these incidents and the escalation of tensions in maritime transport in the region lies with the aggressive US army," the statement said.

Tehran's Friday prayer leader separately told his weekly sermon that the strait would remain closed until Iran's conditions were fully met.

Hojjatoleslam Mohammad Javad Ali-Akbari said Iran had set out "seven conditions" and would decide its next steps once they were met, adding that military readiness had improved, weak points had been addressed, and Iran's strategy had shifted from defence to offence.

Iran has said it controls the Strait of Hormuz and will not permit military forces from hostile countries in the area, vowing to respond "decisively" to any attempt to disrupt its management of the strait.

Lanes clear, CENTCOM says

US Central Command said on Friday it had cleared the strait's main shipping lanes, removed naval mines from principal transit routes, and declared them open to all vessels not in violation of US maritime sanctions against Iran.

Thousands of commercial ships had passed through safely as a result, CENTCOM said.

The competing claims came as the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reported that an LPG carrier was struck by unknown projectiles on Friday morning, 13 nautical miles west of Al-Jazira in the United Arab Emirates, causing a major fire that was later brought under control.

UKMTO had reported the previous day that an oil tanker north of Qatari waters was struck by several projectiles resulting in casualties, in the first such attack in six months.

In a separate incident on Thursday, the maritime intelligence company Vanguard reported that a tanker had caught fire roughly 40 kilometres off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, identifying the vessel as probably the Dalkut, sailing under the Marshall Islands flag.

At least 12 attacks, attempted attacks or harassment incidents targeting oil tankers and gas carriers were recorded in the strait between 28 September and 5 October, the highest weekly figure since the war began on 28 February, according to media reports.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments normally pass, has been effectively closed since the outbreak of the war, following Iranian missile and drone strikes on commercial vessels and a US Navy blockade of Iranian ports.

The latest data indicate that oil exports from other countries in the region, excluding Iran, have returned to pre-war levels in recent days.

World.title: UN voices 'concern' over violence as French students plan more protests
World.content:
The United Nations (UN) said on Friday it was monitoring protests by high school students across France "with concern", as nationwide demonstrations entered their fifth consecutive day.

 

"We are following with concern incidents related to the student protests and high school blockades in France, some of which have turned violent," said Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the UN human rights agency.

Nearly 7,000 people, of whom 86 percent are minors, have been taken into police custody since mid-September, according to France's Justice Ministry.

The students, mostly aged between 15 and 18, are protesting against teacher shortages, overcrowded timetables, deteriorating school facilities and buildings ill-equipped to cope with rising temperatures.

While the demonstrations have been largely peaceful, some protesters have set fires and vandalised bus shelters.

Police have responded with tear gas, batons and blast balls, prompting accusations of excessive force from human rights groups and student protesters.

Authorities have launched 18 internal investigations into allegations of police misconduct.

Students protest against under-resourced schools in Paris, Thursday, 8 Oct., 2026. (AP Photo/Aurelien Morissard)

Government pledges action to address student demands

In an effort to ease tensions, Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced late Thursday that around 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to cover staff shortages at the 114 high schools most affected by the protests.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has also pledged to introduce a plan to address the crisis by the end of October.

Meanwhile, Economy Minister Roland Lescure said the government could accommodate demands for additional school funding despite tight constraints on the 2027 budget.

Under the current draft budget, education is set to receive the second-largest funding increase after defence, with spending rising by 1.4% to €90.9 billion.

Student union representative Marius Mesnil said "we're being offered a few crumbs", while calling for another wave of demonstrations Tuesday.

World.title: Podcast: AI in France, translators fight back, musicians' mentor
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is everywhere in France but who's using it, and how? We also look at its impact on translators and how they're striving to keep humans at the helm. And Nadia Boulanger – the pioneering French composer and conductor who taught generations of musical greats.

Advertising

AI is widely used in France, despite many peoples' misgivings. Tech consultant Frederic Cavazza says adoption is being driven by individuals, rather than a coherent or systemic approach. That results in a paradox: the technology is everywhere, but guidance and confidence in it is lacking. (Listen @2'40'')

One field that is heavily impacted by generative AI in France – and the non-English-language world – is translation. Low-cost translation agencies are increasingly using machines to deliver first drafts and relying on humans for ungratifying, poorly paid "post-editing". But translators are fighting back. The En chair et en os collective and the recently-launched STEF union for translators in publishing marked last week's World Translation Day with symbolic strike action. They gathered to find collective ways of keeping humans at the heart of the translation process, including an initiative to "sabotage" the post-editing system. (Listen @17'50'')

The story of French musician Nadia Boulanger, a talented composer and the first woman to conduct some of the world's top orchestras. Today she is best remembered for teaching an extraordinary number of the 20th century's most famous musicians, from Aaron Copland to Philip Glass, Burt Bacharach and Quincy Jones. (Listen @10'30'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: UAE: Omani Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack
World.content:
A Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight into the terminal at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport, according to a UAE official.

The Omani co-pilot who attacked the captain of the Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport in a suicide attack, according to the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor.

The statement released on Friday by Attorney General Hamad Saif al Shamsi and published by the state media did not appear to implicate Flydubai in any wrongdoing.

What has the investigation revealed so far?

According to the statement, UAE public prosecutors believe that the co-pilot's plan was inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US and aimed at "causing the greatest possible loss of life."

The investigation found that the suspect had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the flight route and airport. He had worked for several airlines in different countries, including Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, before joining Flydubai in January 2026.

The prosecutor's findings also showed that he met the professional and security requirements for employment.

These requirements included holding a pilot's license, providing a certificate of good conduct, and completing the necessary background checks.

"None of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot," according to the statement.

Flydubai passengers recount terror after hijacking attempt To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What happened on Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv?

On September 30, the Indian captain of a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was injured when the co-pilot attacked him with an axe.

The captain opened the cockpit door, enabling passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and force an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Passengers described rushing the cockpit and fighting for control after the plane suddenly descended around 5,000 meters (17,000 feet).

Most of the passengers on board were Israeli. They have been hailed as heroes in Israel.

World.title: China, EU reach deal to 'moderate' China's car exports to EU
World.content:
An agreement between the EU and China would reduce exports of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid cars to the 27-member European bloc by up to 50%, according to the EU trade envoy.

European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic announced on Friday that China and the European Union had reached a deal that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the EU by more than half.

This announcement followed two-day talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU's growing trade deficit with China.

Earlier, Sefcovic said this week's talks were the culmination of three months of intensive work.

What do we know about the EV deal?

According to Sefcovic, the deal would "moderate China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU."

He added that this opens the prospect of cutting China's exports by more than half, based on projections over a four-year period.

"By this step, we're actually preventing several millions of cars exports from China to the European Union," Sefcovic said.

Although he did not offer details on how the agreement will be implemented, Sefcovic said he believed the two sides had achieved a very good result.

Sefcovic said he believes the EU and China have achieved a very good result in trade talks Image: Johannes Neudecker/dpa/picture alliance

What else was decided?

Sevcovic added the two sides also reached an agreement to reduce Chinese import duties on €4 billion ($4.5 billion) worth of EU exports, including car parts, olive oil and footwear.

They also agreed to simplify China's process for granting export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets.

The agreement will require approval from the leaders of all 27 EU nations, who will discuss the outcome at the start of their summit in Brussels on Thursday.

How China is upping pressure on German businesses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rebalancing EU-China trade

According to UN Comtrade data, Chinese exports to the EU totaled $560 billion (€500 billion) last year, up from $517 billion in 2023. Exports to major economies, including Germany, Italy, Spain, and Poland, each rose approximately 10% from a year earlier. Shipments to Hungary increased by 43%.

Meanwhile, China imported $268.3 billion (€240 billion) worth of European goods last year, down from $269.4 billion the previous year. Purchases from Denmark, Ireland, and France led the way.

Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned lawmakers at the European Parliament that the trade gap had reached a tipping point. She said the EU would use all available tools to rebalance the relationship.

World.title: Brussels: Rioters clash with police at anti-austerity rally
World.content:
Violent rioters, many of whom were masked, confronted police at the edge of an anti-austerity march in Brussels. Police responded with water cannons and tear gas.

Hundreds of protesters clashed with police in the Belgian capital on Friday during an anti-austerity march organized by trade unions.

Masked protesters dressed in black threw rocks and other projectiles at police in Brussels. Anti-police slogans echoed through the streets, and similar graffiti covered nearby walls.

An AFP reporter witnessed two buses being attacked after the passengers were evacuated. The rioters smashed the windows and ripped out the seats. Meanwhile, youths set fire to trash cans, rental bikes, and scooters.

According to Reuters, firefighters extinguished several fires, including those on buses.

The police responded to the violence by using water cannons and tear gas Image: Yves Herman/REUTERS

How did police respond to protests in Brussels?

The police said officers used water cannons and tear gas after young people on the outskirts of the protest targeted them with sticks and bottles.

"Several hundred youths gathered along with the demonstrators," police said in a statement. "The atmosphere gradually became more tense and there were serious disturbances to public order."

In a preliminary update, the police said they had arrested approximately 20 people, mostly minors.

Police also said the main trade union march had gone ahead peacefully. Before the rally, union head Bert Engelaar called on rioters to stay away from the protest.

"Those individuals have nothing to do with the message with which thousands of others come out on the streets," Engelaar wrote on Facebook.

Despite organizers urging rioters to stay away from the protests, violent youths confronted police and vandalized property Image: Yves Herman/REUTERS

What are the government's goals?

Chaotic scenes of violence occurred during a demonstration in which between 30,000 and 50,000 people participated. It was one of many nationwide union protests against planned austerity measures.

Belgium is burdened by substantial public debt and a persistent budget deficit. Led by Prime Minister Bart De Wever, the center-right government aims to find €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in savings by the end of its term in 2029.

Rather than imposing cuts in areas like health and hiking VAT, trade unions are pushing for the government to increase taxes on the highest earners.

The clashes in Brussels came after a week of tension in Liege, where authorities banned public gatherings after students clashed with police and vandalized shops. Over 200 people were arrested in Liege, and dozens of police officers were injured.
