World.title: Eritrean troops in Ethiopia raise fears of a regional war
World.content:
Ethiopia and Eritrea are trading blame for confrontations in Tigray amid international calls for restraint. Their respective allies have the potential to catapult the conflict into a regional war.

Various sources have confirmed the presence of Eritrean armed forces in Ethiopia. An AFP report quoted a foreign security source, speaking on condition of anonymity, as estimating that 5,000 to 8,000 Eritrean soldiers were present in the northenmost state of Ethiopia, Tigray.

Meanwhile, Ethiopia and Eritrea have ramped up their war talk.

According to Reuters, the government of Ethiopia has written to the UN Security Council, calling for the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean troops from its territory.

In the letter, dated ‌Oct. 8, Ethiopian ‌Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia left "no option but to defend itself against Eritrea,"

in a post on X on October 7, Eritrean Minister of Information Yemane Meskel had accused Ethiopia of "incessantly beating the drums of war."

Two days later, he wrote in Tigrinya, a working language of Eritrea and the main language of Tigray, that "the sovereign state of Eritrea is bound by blood and law." adding "woe to those who touch it."

This comes as the regional conflict in Tigray has deteriorated rapidly in recent weeks.

Some experts have suggested that Ethiopia may have intentionally triggered the escalation. Just last week, it expelled diplomats from Egypt and Eritrea, causing the latter to sever diplomatic ties altogether.

On Monday, when Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for another five years as Ethiopian prime minister, he stated that access to the sea was a priority. The statement fueled fresh speculation that he intends to take Eritrea's strategic port of Assab by force and prompted fierce reactions from the Eritrean side.

Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Abiy's internal opposition: Tsimdo and the Alliance for Survival

While the Ethiopian National Defence Forces (ENDF), aided by the Tigray Peace Force milita, have made significant advances and notably recaptured the Tigray federal state capital of Mekelle, opposition to Ethiopia has found new formats for collaboration.

One is the Tsimdo movement, named after a Tigrinya term that loosely translates as "engagement."

"The Tsimdo concept initially surfaced through cross-border peace initiatives involving activists, religious figures, and local communities in the Tigray and Eritrea border villages in 2025," Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, senior East Africa analyst with the US-based conflict monitor ACLED, told DW.

It has since undergone several reconfigurations and now encompasses diverse groups within Ethiopia, mostly defined along ethnic lines and with long-standing grievances against the federal government.

The Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, or simply Alliance for Survival, that was proclaimed in September, stems from this movement. According to Jalale, the alliance aims at removing the current government and initiating a constitutional dialogue.

The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The new alliance says a lot about the long history of unresolved conflict in Ethiopia, said Abdurahman Sayed, an analyst at the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration.

"The fighting inside Ethiopia has never stopped," Sayed told DW.

"With the Oromo Liberation Army, it's been going on for decades, with the Amhara, it's been going on for the last three years, at least. With the Tigrayans, the Pretoria agreement about three years ago was just a cessation of hostility that would have led to some kind of sustainable peace by addressing the root causes of the conflict — but it failed to do that, so they're back to the conflict situation now."

However, of the seven groups in the alliance, ACLED data shows that only three were involved in recent fighting: The Tigrayan Defence Forces (TDF), the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), and a fairly recently formed ethnic Afar group called Ugugumo.

Amhara Fano fighters (pictured here in 2021) who fought in the two-year Tigray War are part of the new Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival Image: Solan Kolli/AFP

Joint declaration by Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia

The success of the Alliance for Survival would depend in large part on the support they get through external actors, according to ACLED. Those could include neighboring Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia.

"All these four countries have grievances against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government," Sayed said.

"The Egyptians have issues with the Nile River and how it should be administered, including the dams that are already there and those planned to be built around the Nile River. The Sudanese also have their own concerns that Ethiopians are supporting the [Rapid Support Forces] militia, which is fighting the Sudanese army."

In the case of Somalia, the issue of sea access has sparked tensions. Landlocked Ethiopia has negotiated access to the port of Berbera in Somaliland . In 2024, it signed a memorandum of understanding with the breakaway region, causing uproar in Somalia, which considers the deal a violation of its national sovereignty. Turkish mediation was needed to calm things down.

Somaliland: Somalia's breakaway 'nation' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"So all those neighboring countries have their own concerns and they feel this threat that is coming from Ethiopia needs to be tackled collectively."

On October 4, the leaders of the four countries issued a joint declaration that didn't mention Ethiopia but seemed to send a strong signal. The leaders stressed the importance of international law, "particularly respect for the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of the states of the region."

And they maintained that "the governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of the littoral states."

Although the leaders of Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia vowed to promote "peaceful solutions to conflicts," the reality on the ground may prove otherwise.

Edited by: Benita van Eyssen

World.title: Macron and Steinmeier struggle to revive Franco-German ties
World.content:
Presidents Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Emmanuel Macron are about to step down from their offices. Their meeting in France made it clear how urgently the Franco-German partnership needs new momentum.

The German delegation passed through Paris without being hindered by the student strikes taking place on the streets of Paris. The motorcades moved through the French capital without disruption. Around the Arc de Triomphe and the Champs-Elysees, however, traffic was at a standstill for hours. Due to the high-profile visit, the streets were cordoned off over a wide area.

Emmanuel Macron had decided on a special gesture to send off Frank-Walter Steinmeier, his German guest: The military honors took place under the Arc de Triomphe. And so, early in the morning, the German national anthem rang out in the heart of Paris — amid sunshine and bitter cold.

It was a generous gesture of friendship and symbolism, yet it seemed to be from a bygone era. In both countries, populists on the political fringes are gaining support. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) ranks first in nationwide polls. In France, Emmanuel Macron could soon be succeeded by either Jean-Luc Melenchon of the far left or Marine Le Pen of the far right.

Added to this is an economic crisis that threatens prosperity. Unresolved issues of social justice are driving younger generations into the streets. At the same time, social media is increasingly becoming a tool of disinformation and "accelerating doubts about democracy," Macron said in Paris.

While the AfD may soon form its first state government in Saxony-Anhalt, President Steinmeier remained confident. He insisted that Germany would continue to "play a leading role in Europe" in the future and that Germans would remain good Europeans. But he did not say where he drew this certainty from. Questions from journalists were not permitted at the joint press conference at the Elysee Palace.

A future, but no plan

Political scientist Jacob Ross isn't surprised by this. Both Macron and Steinmeier lack a "genuine agenda for Germany, France, and Europe." Both represent political systems that "seek to respond to 21st-century crises with 20th-century solutions," said the expert on German-French relations at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP).

Even though Steinmeier and Macron have different political styles, Ross sees parallels — especially where their policies have failed. One example of this is strategic foreign policy issues, such as dealing with Russia. "For a long time, they pursued a policy based on integrating Russia into Europe, and then both were overwhelmed by the events of 2022 and had to adjust their course," said Ross. Since then, both have merely reacted to current affairs, according to the political scientist.

Little support for Macron's ideas

Emmanuel Macron has made some bold moves for Europe, but without support from Berlin, says Ross. Germany's political leadership has long reacted with caution to proposals from Paris.

A joint initiative that both countries recently promoted to the European Commission is aimed at combating unfair competition. Countries that gain an advantage through unfair practices should face strict European measures.

Macron joined German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in speaking out in favor of this. Although China was not explicitly named, the initiative is seen to be primarily aimed at that country. Beijing uses enormous subsidies to support its companies, whose products flood the European market, while European firms continue to face barriers when trying to access the Chinese market.

How Europe's defense sector is trying to gear up To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany and France have also long sought greater cooperation in the defense sector. Yet major joint defense projects are making little progress. When the planned joint fighter jet, the FCAS, fell through in June, officials emphasized ongoing cooperation on the future MGCS main battle tank. And yet differences on this became apparent during the state visit.

As German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius arrived in Paris, French Chief of the General Staff Fabien Mandon stated during a hearing in the French National Assembly that Germany had decided to withdraw from the tank project. A day later, Mandon clarified that he had expressed himself ambiguously. But some observers believe that such misunderstandings are a sign of dissatisfaction on both sides — below the political level — regarding cooperation with the other partner.

It is this political level that often ends up having to set the record straight in such cases. This time was no exception: Pistorius firmly refuted the claim that the project was on the verge of being scrapped. "The MGCS project is not over; it is not dead; it has not been terminated by anyone — quite the contrary. It is a core project of Franco-German cooperation on land systems," said the German defense minister.

The focus is primarily on digital information processing in combat, as well as unmanned and automated systems. Germany and France would continue their cooperation, Pistorius insisted, and MGCS is an important future project for both countries and their armed forces.

The French and German Presidents took part in a ceremony in the heart of Paris Image: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS/dpa/picture alliance

The future of defense and space

On Friday, the presidents of France and Germany visited several facilities near Bordeaux that are closely linked to space exploration and nuclear deterrence. These include ArianeGroup, a Franco-German company that, among other things, manufactures the nuclear-capable M51 missiles for French nuclear submarines. The itinerary also included visits to startups that are looking far into the future.

It was unofficially reported during the visit that this focus of the trip was a personal priority for Macron. The French president has long spoken of a European dimension to France's nuclear deterrent. Considering announcements from the US saying it would reduce its commitment to Europe, his views are gaining increasing traction.

As early as 2020, Macron proposed a strategic dialogue on the role of French nuclear weapons in European security. Several countries, including Germany, have since expressed interest. Now, further steps are being considered. The focus is on what Macron once called "forward deterrence," such as joint military exercises and visits to strategically important locations. A permanent deployment of French nuclear weapons in other countries remains off the table. Furthermore, according to French nuclear doctrine, France always retains sole decision-making authority over the use of its nuclear weapons.

Steinmeier's two-day state visit to France ended on Friday afternoon. So far, there has been little sign of new momentum in Franco-German relations. This makes it all the more urgent for the successors to the two presidents to develop a shared vision for the future of the relationship between the two countries starting next year.

Macron and Steinmeier will step down from their posts almost simultaneously in 2027 after ten years in office. The state visit to France thus also served as a final joint meeting, marked by some ceremonial farewells.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis
World.content:
AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal has raised questions about machine-generated texts.

It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence (AI) transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated?

Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might appear rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of tech giants and the future of creativity. Many agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough.

This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and if so, can this be proven?

These are some of the questions raised by the current scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien and his debut novel, "C'etait ca ou mourir," (This title means "It Was Either That or Die" in English but an English translation has not yet been published), which was published in Canada in the spring.

The controversy around Thelyson Orelien's book has sparked a larger debate on AI and authorship Image: Joel Saget/AFP/dpa/picture alliance

The book about global migration was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. Soon after the book was published in France, it was longlisted for the prestigious Prix Goncourt.

But then, all of a sudden, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orelien, a rising literary star, found himself branded a fraud despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Goncourt was withdrawn.

So, who should we believe? An author or an AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing?

When the origins of texts become uncertain

"We will have to learn to live with doubt," says Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.

Hannes Bajohr, professor for German Studies at the University of California, Berkeley Image: Jen Siska

He has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process.

Nina George, a best-selling author and the honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this.

At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues such as AI and copyright reform.

Nina George is a leading advocate for European authors' rights and copyright reform Image: Sabine Kieselbach/DW

George has addressed the European Parliament and the German Bundestag, speaking and writing tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she says, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is the creation of a human. The focus of her campaigns are the tech corporations' self-serving mentality and copyright protection.

Can anyone become an author with AI?

But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy but as a tool that makes writing easier?

US author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars and Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so.

"I'm dyslexic," he said in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further."

Luke Stoffel talks openly about his use of AI when writing Image: Privat

It was only with the help of AI, he said, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked.

In May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association (IBPA) for the book.

For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, each year she releases more than 200 different novels, spanning the genres of romance, thriller and mystery.

She sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable, she says, and each book reaches more than 5,000 people according to her.

Many publishers already working with AI

Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical and points out that many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal."

It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thelyson Orelien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure.

For now, the battle against the tech giants continues, some of which are themselves increasingly concerned about losing control.

At the very start of the Frankfurt fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, which they said is more urgent than ever. More than 140 publishers have signed it.

But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debates in the future.

World.title: US imposes sanctions aiming to 'dismantle' International Criminal Court
World.content:
The US has announced new sanctions on the International Criminal Court. It's the latest in a series of steps by the Donald Trump administration as it seeks to "dismantle" the intergovernmental organization.

US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize.

This comes as the US has in recent months made no bones about pursuing what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court."

The United States and Israel had both strongly opposed the court's arrest warrants for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Since 2020 and the back end of Trump's first term, the US had also opposed investigations into military actions in Afghanistan that "deprioritize" alleged US wrongdoings, focusing on the Taliban, but can nevertheless include them.

ICC judges living under US sanctions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did the State Department say about the ICC sanctions?

"President Trump will never allow the International Court to prosecute Americans," Rubio said in a statement .

"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," he said.

Rubio said that both US political parties had long agreed that the ICC should not have jurisdiction over US citizens, but said "only President Trump" resolved to take action.

"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court," Rubio said. "If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer."

ICC President Tomoko Akane was sanctioned by the US in August Image: Eva Plevier/ANP/AFP

How did the ICC respond?

The ICC said the US sanctions aimed to obstruct an independent international court supported by more than half of the UN's members.

"The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes," said ICC President Tomoko Akane, who already faces US sanctions.

The ICC called the Rome Statute, which underpins membership of the court, a "collective promise" that the most serious international crimes must not go unpunished.

"That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it," the court said. It appealed to members to take "concrete actions" to ensure the court would still have the necessary means to continue its work.

"No one should be punished for serving the cause of justice," it said. "History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an insitution created to protect them came under attack."

The US announcement came just hours after Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge, was given this year's Nobel Peace Prize Image: Daniel Karmann/dpa/picture alliance

What did other countries say about the US sanctions?

A collection of US allies that are full members of the ICC including Germany issued a joint statement reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC."

"As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States," the governments of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the UK said .

They said that, despite the ICC's best efforts to prepare and mitigate their effect, the sanctions "will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked the US government for its "leadership" in issuing the sanctions.

"The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," he said.

Sanctions announced shortly after former ICC judge's Nobel Peace Prize

The State Department released the announcement a few hours after the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, who was an ICC judge from 2003 to 2012.

Last year Trump repeatedly complained that he should have won the accolade for promoting world peace, prompting Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado to present him with her trophy as a gift.

Without naming names, the Nobel Committee clearly referenced US sanctions against the ICC when announcing Pillay as this year's laureate.

"The Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law national and international — underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently," the Committee wrote.

It said judges like Pillay "guard the thin red line between order and chaos," but lamented that "today ... these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked."

What is the ICC?

The International Criminal Court is an intergovernmental organization and international tribunal based in the Dutch city of The Hague.

It's the only permanent international court with the theoretical jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for international crimes like genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and illegal aggression.

The ICC was established in 2002 and is governed by the Rome Statute.

More than half the countries in the world, 125 in total, are full parties to the Rome Statute, having signed and ratified it.

Several of the world's most significant powers, including China, India, Israel, Russia and the United States, do not recognize the court's jurisdiction and are not parties to the statute.

A grey area, however, remains since the court accepts challenges from ratified members against individuals from countries that do not recognize it.

That is why high-profile arrest warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, and Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have been issued in recent years — following respective complaints from Ukrainians and Palestinians.

What were the prior signs of Trump administration pressure on the ICC?

The US has been increasingly critical of the ICC during Trump's second term.

Rubio has often led the charge. In July, he wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal saying, "America never agreed to a world tribunal that can override our own courts and the Constitution."

He argued it was possible for US "soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders" to be "dragged before an international court" and tried by judges "from random countries across the globe."

Just over a week later, on July 25, Venezuela's new administration — transformed after the US abduction of Nicolas Maduro in January — announced that it planned to withdraw from the Rome Statute and the ICC.

A few days later, the military junta in Chad announced that it was withdrawing from the ICC following a US request.

The recent sexual misconduct scandal surrounding the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan, who was dismissed in July, provided more ammunition the US could aim at the court.

In August, the US imposed sanctions on the ICC's president, Japanese judge Tomoko Akane, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the court.

Speaking at the UN General Assembly last month, Donald Trump branded the ICC 'evil,' but stopped short of announcing sanctions even as reports of the plan circulated Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance

World.title: Saudi coalition vows 'firm' response after airport attack kills 3
World.content:
Saudi Arabia and its allied forces in Yemen vowed a "firm response" to Houthi attacks that target civilians. The kingdom's authorities said three Saudi nationals were killed in Thursday's attack on Riyadh airport.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen launched strikes that destroyed targets used by the Houthis, a coalition spokesperson said Friday.

Major General Turki al-Maliki said three rocket launch platforms were destroyed, adding that Houthi attacks on civilians would be met with a "firm response."

The Saudi-Houthi conflict has intensified in recent weeks, with Saudi Arabian authorities having said Friday that Houthi attacks on Riyadh's main international airport on Thursday killed three Saudi citizens and injured several people of "different nationalities."

The King Khalid International Airport was targeted twice on Thursday, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said. The first attack aimed at airport facilities and the second targeted an aircraft that belonged to the Saudia airline.

Houthi attacks on Riyadh raise the stakes of reignited conflict

Hundreds of flights were canceled because of Thursday's attacks, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.

The Indian Embassy later said Air India had suspended operations through to Saturday, while the Lufthansa Group said its airlines would suspend flights to Riyadh through to October 16.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) on Friday recommended airlines not to operate in additional portions of Saudi Airspace in an updated bulletin.

The EASA said recent attacks had demonstrated the ability and the intent of the Houthis to strike targets deeper inside Saudi territory, including the capital.

On Thursday, the Iran-backed Houthis warned employees at Saudi oil facilities that oil installations remain a target.

Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Saudi-Houthi conflict: What to know

The Houthis have fought a Saudi-led coalition since 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war to reinstate the internationally backed government in Sanaa. Houthi rebels took control of the capital in 2014.

But ever since, the Saudi-led coalition has found it hard to turn the tide of the war that quieted under a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

In the last weeks, the Houthis stormed down Yemen's coast, capturing a wide swath of territory that has given them greater control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

A Saudi-led coalition has pressed a counteroffensive against the Houthis fighters and recaptured several areas along the strait, Yemeni officials have said. But the fighting appears to be far from over.

World.title: Hemos instalado placas solares para abastecer las zonas comunes del edificio. ¿Tenemos los vecinos derecho a bonificación en el IBI?
World.content:
Pregunta. ¿La instalación de placas solares en una comunidad puede reducir el IBI de los vecinos que las han financiado?. Las placas solamente dan energía a elementos comunes y no a las viviendas. M. Muñoz

Respuesta. El artículo 74.5 del Real Decreto Legislativo 2/2004, por el que se aprueba el texto refundido de la Ley Reguladora de las Haciendas Locales, contempla una bonificación potestativa de hasta el 50% de la cuota íntegra del IBI para aquellos inmuebles en los que se hayan instalado sistemas de aprovechamiento térmico o eléctrico de la energía solar o de la energía ambiente. La aplicación de esta bonificación queda condicionada a que las instalaciones cuenten con la correspondiente homologación administrativa y a que los requisitos concretos estén desarrollados en la ordenanza fiscal de cada municipio.

En consecuencia, los propietarios no pueden beneficiarse de una reducción del IBI de sus viviendas particulares cuando las placas solares instaladas por la comunidad únicamente suministran energía a los elementos comunes del edificio. La norma vincula la bonificación a los inmuebles en los que se encuentra instalado y se aprovecha directamente el sistema energético. Por ello, cuando la energía generada se destina exclusivamente a servicios o instalaciones comunes, y no al consumo de las viviendas o locales individualmente considerados, no se cumple el requisito exigido para acceder a la bonificación respecto de cada inmueble.

Así lo recogen, con carácter general, numerosas ordenanzas municipales. En el caso de viviendas y locales integrados en edificios sometidos al régimen de propiedad horizontal, suelen limitar la bonificación a aquellos supuestos en los que la instalación solar compartida suministra energía de forma efectiva a todos o a parte de los inmuebles privativos que componen la comunidad, y no únicamente a los elementos comunes del edificio.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: En la isla de Rügen, un patrimonio entre lo mitológico y lo real
World.content:
Bañada por el mar Báltico, la isla más grande de Alemania tiene el aura de las islas griegas del Egeo. Sus templos son los acantilados, los balnearios y un delirio de hormigón del tamaño de un gigante levantado por los nazis

A la isla de Rügen, a la que Caspar David Friedrich fue en varias ocasiones para dibujar y después pintar en su estudio de Dresde Acantilados blancos en Rügen (1818), se llega desde España haciendo escala en Hamburgo o en Berlín. En la ciudad hanseática de Hamburgo está el Kunsthalle, museo que no alberga el mencionado cuadro pero sí su famoso El caminante sobre el mar de nubes. Rügen es una isla alemana, aunque le quedan mucho más cerca Polonia, Dinamarca y Suecia que Baviera, Estado federado alemán del que durante un tiempo estuvo también alejada ideológicamente. A pesar de su condición insular se puede llegar en coche y en tren; hay un puente que la une al continente, a la altura de la localidad germana de Stralsund.

Hitler y el Ejército soviético, antes de que Rügen se convirtiera en un destino vacacional báltico, dejaron su sello en sus playas de arena fina blanca, en sus bosques oscuros que casi llegan a la orilla del mar y en sus acantilados color tiza. Viajar a esta isla oriental es hacerlo al pasado. Estar en ella es como asistir a una clase de geopolítica.

Más información Por la cuenca del Ruhr, en El Dorado del sueño alemán que vive una segunda vida

Esta parte del este de Alemania siempre ha sido codiciada por daneses, suecos y soviéticos, a estos últimos les interesaba la industria de procesado de pescado de Stralsund. Una ciudad con un nombre que suena más a escandinavo que a germano, en la que, junto a la protestante iglesia de Santa María, gótica, austera e imponente, hay un monumento y un pequeño cementerio de soldados soviéticos. Un espacio que a algunos guías turísticos locales se les hace bola contar. Fuera de su centro histórico se encuentra la estación en la que se puede coger un tren con destino a Bergen auf Rügen, la capital de la isla de Rügen. El recorrido, que no llega a media hora, atraviesa la pequeña isla de Dänholm, cruza el mar Báltico y llega hasta el centro de Rügen.

Este es un destino vacacional muy popular del Estado de Mecklenburgo-Pomerania Occidental, en el que se alternan playas, pueblos pesqueros y mansiones nobiliarias y en el que a Thomas Mann no se le pasaron por alto los balnearios de Binz y Sellin. Localidades termales y costeras del este de la isla más grande del país que, como Baabe y Göhren, son paradas de la línea Putbus-Göhren que cubre el Rügensche BäderBahn - Rasender Roland, un ferrocarril a vapor de vía estrecha con más de cien años de antigüedad. Con el desarrollo del turismo de masas en la década de los años cincuenta, este ferrocarril se convirtió en el principal medio de transporte para ir a los balnearios isleños. Hoy es un guiño a un mundo evaporado.

Parada del ferrocarril a vapor en Sellin. Wilfried Wirth (Alamy / cordon press)

Lo que permanece en Rügen es aquello a lo que el ser humano no ha podido meter mano tanto como le hubiera gustado. Sus acantilados de caliza, sus hayedos, sus lagos y sus playas. Un entorno natural que Caspar David Friedrich pintó a partir de los bocetos que dibujó durante sus varias visitas a la isla en diferentes momentos de su vida. Casi siempre estuvo en la zona norte, en lo que hoy es el parque nacional de Jasmund, donde se encuentran los acantilados Wissower. Una zona costera en la que, además de los acantilados, hay formaciones geológicas de roca caliza, muy blanda y porosa. No existe el punto desde el que Friedrich pintó los acantilados de la península de Jasmund porque esa pintura es fruto de una composición de varias imágenes desde diferentes lugares. Sus pinturas son invenciones, pero con el paso del tiempo sus cuadros se han convertido en la campaña de promoción turística de un destino mitológico.

El parque nacional de Jasmund. Joko (Alamy / cordon press)

En el centro de visitantes Königsstuhl se encuentra el gran reclamo del parque nacional de Jasmund: una pasarela doble que se asoma a los acantilados de la península homónima. El otro gancho del sitio son sus visitas guiadas y teatralizadas. Las guías, mientras se adentran en el bosque, recrean lo que podía ser un día de Friedrich en este lugar con potencial esotérico, y emulan a Christiane Caroline, su mujer, paseando mientras cuenta cómo era el pintor. El artista era tan enigmático como los bosques oscuros y abruptos de Rügen en los que también hay ruinas funerarias. “Las tumbas son testigos mudos de un pasado remoto y parecen susurrarle secretos a David Friedrich”, se lee en el libro La magia del silencio, de Florian Illies. El pintor romántico plasmó en un cuadro el dolmen de Dwasieden, Tumba megalítica en la nieve.

Acantilados en el parque nacional de Jasmund, en la isla de Rügen. Manfred Gottschalk (Getty images)

La mejor panorámica de los acantilados es la que se tiene a bordo de las embarcaciones y los ferris que parten del vecino pueblo de Sassnitz. Los hay que hacen travesías de recreo, otros van rumbo a Escandinavia. Su puerto llegó a albergar casi 200 barcos pesqueros que partían a faenar al mar Báltico, al mar del Norte y al océano Atlántico. Hoy aquel ambiente es más turístico que portuario. Algunos barcos son puestos de comida y en el pueblo se suceden residencias particulares, villas de la época dorada de los balnearios de la zona y casas de huéspedes. Construcciones encantadoras que no tienen nada que ver con la mole de hormigón abandonada y oculta por la vegetación que hay en Prora construida por el régimen nazi, al sur, muy cerca de Sassnitz, en una bahía que mira al este.

El Coloso de Prora

El empeño de Adolf Hitler de ligar a Caspar David Friedrich con el régimen nazi retardó su reconocimiento internacional. Uno y otro compartieron, con diferente suerte, afición por la pintura y a los dos les llamó la atención la isla de Rügen. Friedrich la pintó y el dictador que fracasó en su carrera artística mandó construir en ella, entre 1936 y 1939, un complejo vacacional. Una estructura con dimensiones colosales, la más grande que puso en pie el Tercer Reich, junto con el recinto de los congresos del Partido Nazi en Núremberg.

El llamado Coloso de Prora son varios edificios de seis alturas comunicados entre sí por larguísimos pasillos que hacen que el conjunto mida casi cinco kilómetros de largo. Una hora lleva recorrerlo de una punta a otra. No hay objetivo angular capaz de fotografiarlo, salvo desde el aire. En su interior se habilitaron 11.000 habitaciones para que 20.000 personas, familias obreras colectivizadas y sin derechos, pasaran sus vacaciones estipuladas. Todo esto era parte de la política laboral y social del nacionalsocialismo. Antes de que los trabajadores pudieran disfrutar del complejo como turistas, Hitler invadió Polonia y los planes cambiaron. Los suyos y los del resto del mundo. Los únicos civiles que se alojaron en aquel coloso de hormigón fueron las familias que sufrieron los bombardeos que destruyeron Hamburgo.

Vista área del comprejo de Prora, en Rügen. Moritz Kertzscher (Getty images)

Con el final de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, la isla de Rügen se quedó en el lado oriental y Prora se convirtió en una base militar soviética invisible en los mapas y desde el mar. Con la caída del Muro de Berlín, los soldados abandonaron la base militar y el complejo de Prora se quedó ahí, incomodando a unos y a otros. Hoy es una atracción turística más. Se mantiene en pie, pero el bosque denso que lo rodea lo ha engullido y, a pesar, de sus dimensiones, no se ve hasta que uno lo tiene delante de sus propios ojos. Parece un camaleón enorme al que le cuesta respirar.

Diferentes fundaciones, asociaciones y sociedades han trabajado para preservar su condición como monumento histórico protegido. La fundación NEUE KULTUR inauguró el centro de documentación en el año 2000. En 2012, la asociación Centro de Documentación de Prora asumió la gestión del centro. En la actualidad alberga diversas exposiciones sobre la historia y el contexto de este complejo, entre una permanente y otras temporales, además de una cafetería. Lo que no está expuesto en este lugar es el cuadro Acantilados blancos en Rügen. Para ver esos acantilados, que primero imaginó y después pintó Caspar David Friedrich, hay que ir a la Fundación Oskar Reinhart de Winterthur (Suiza).

World.title: Trump administration sanctions International Criminal Court
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The United States has announced sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), escalating Trump’s war on the international tribunal.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” US secretary of state Marco Rubio said in an announcement.

The Trump administration has previously pledged to dismantle the court “brick by brick” and has sanctioned 13 current and former staff members, but this is the first time it has levied sanctions against the institution itself.

Ahead of the announcement, prime minister Rob Jetten said the Netherlands will protect the ICC “stone by stone”.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said the country would stand behind the court. “The announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court are an undesirable new escalation,” Berendsen said in a statement. “I deeply regret this new step.”

The sanctions will cut the court off from any US company or organisation, including providers of financial and technology services.

The announcement came hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the ICC and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

Trump has long coveted the prize, telling reporters earlier this week that he deserved the award for what he said was ending eight wars.

World.title: Russia wants NL to hand over ICC judges
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Russia has asked the Netherlands to hand over nine International Criminal Court (ICC) officials who were convicted in absentia last year.

The prosecutor’s office in Moscow requested the extradition of the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and other staff members for their involvement in the arrest warrant of Russian president Vladimir Putin.

The ICC issued the warrant for Putin’s alleged involvement in “the war crime of unlawful deportation of children” from occupied Ukraine.

The ICC has also issued an arrest warrant against Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights.

In December, a court in Moscow convicted Akane and others in absentia, sentencing them to prison terms ranging from 3.5 to 15 years.

Japan, Akane’s home country, said the request was regrettable. “Measures targeting individuals connected to the ICC are unjust and unacceptable,” Masanao Ozaki, the country’s deputy chief cabinet secretary, said.

The United States has also sanctioned 13 staff members, including Akane, over the investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

World.title: Unions call regional transport strike, threaten weekly walkout
World.content:
Regional bus services across the Netherlands will be heavily disrupted on Wednesday, after the FNV and CNV unions called a nationwide 24-hour strike in a dispute over a new pay and conditions deal.

If Wednesday’s strike does not shift the employers, the unions say they will hold an action day every week, and will only announce the dates shortly beforehand. Earlier this month they said they were considering weekly strikes in the run-up to Christmas.

Some 13,000 workers, mainly bus drivers, are covered by the public transport collective agreement, which expired on July 1. Staff at Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Keolis, Transdev and RET’s regional services are involved. City transport in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague is not affected.

Talks broke down after eight rounds of negotiations. This week an ultimatum to the employers’ organisation VWOV expired without a response.

“Employers are holding on to drastic cuts in working conditions,” FNV negotiator Marijn van der Gaag said in a statement. “In doing so, they are forcing their staff to take action.”

The unions say employers want to reduce sick pay, add more unpaid breaks to shifts and give staff less say over their rosters. Rosters are currently fixed about eight days in advance, and employers want to cut that to four days or less, Van der Gaag said.

The FNV wants a 6% pay rise. The CNV is calling for 9.5% over two years, as well as better arrangements for older workers and faster access to permanent contracts.

“We will not let employers sabotage the action by drawing up emergency rosters at the last minute,” CNV negotiator Niels Rook said, explaining why dates will not be announced in advance.

World.title: Former ICC judge Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

Most recently, the 85-year-old chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel had committed genocide.

Announcing the prize in Oslo, Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said it was going to someone who “held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict”.

Reacting to the news in Nuremberg, Pillay said “if you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”

The award comes as the system of international justice is under attack. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has threatened to dismantle the International Criminal Court “brick by brick, if necessary”, and the US has sanctioned several of its staff.

Pillay played a significant role in the anti-apartheid movement in her homeland as a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela and other activists. She went on to serve as a judge on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, spending the last four of her eight years there as its president.

She was one of the ICC’s first judges, sitting in the appeals chamber from 2003 until 2008, when she stepped down to become UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

In 2019, she was appointed as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice by the Gambia, which had filed genocide proceedings against Myanmar over its treatment of the Rohingya minority.

Last year, as chair of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, she said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

In a post on social media, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Pillay. “Few have devoted their lives to justice, peace and human dignity like she did,” she said.

The prize is administered by the Nobel Foundation and comes with 12 million Swedish kronor (around €1.07 million).

World.title: Museums, festivals and clubs in Groningen ban smart glasses
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

In a joint statement on Friday some 30 cultural organisations in Groningen announced they were banning the use of smart glasses from their buildings and events.

The devices, the most popular version is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.

“This technology compromises the privacy and safety of visitors, staff, and artists, and undermines trust in an open, respectful environment,” the statement says.

Backers including the Groninger Archieven, the Groninger Museum, Noorderlicht, Stichting Kunst & Cultuur and the Grand Theatre Groningen.

Last week, eyewear chain Hans Anders announced it would stop selling Meta camera glasses following demands from privacy advocates concerned about the so-called “pervert glasses”.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP has warned that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR laws unless permission is given by everyone in the images.

The consumer watchdog Consumentenbond has also issued a warning about the glasses, noting that it was possible to manipulate or cover the indicator light to make it even harder to tell images were being captured.

MPs have called for a full ban on the glasses but the cabinet is opposed to a blanket measure and wants to see other restrictions put into place.

Utrecht music venue Tivoli Vredenburg banned smart glasses at its events in 2025 and has since refused entry to one man who would not take them off.

World.title: NL’s only legal medicinal cannabis grower goes bust
World.content:
Patients who use medicinal cannabis face having to switch to imported products after the only licensed grower in the Netherlands was declared bankrupt on Thursday.

A court in Groningen declared Veendam-based Bedrocan bankrupt two weeks after the company had applied for protection from its creditors. The firm, whose main growing site is in Emmeloord, employs around 70 people.

Bedrocan ran into trouble after the health ministry ended its contract at the start of this year. All medicinal cannabis sold in Dutch pharmacies is bought and distributed by the state-run Bureau for Medicinal Cannabis (BMC).

The ministry ended the deal in anticipation of a change in the law that will let growers sell directly to pharmacies. But health minister Sophie Hermans (VVD) told MPs in July that the change is not expected to take effect until July 1, 2028.

That left Bedrocan unable to supply the BMC and not allowed to sell to pharmacies itself, the Volkskrant reported. The state was by far its largest customer.

Limited stockpile

The BMC built up a stockpile of Bedrocan cannabis before the contract ended, but the minister said it was limited and had a finite shelf life. The BMC will switch to imported cannabis during 2027, with products matching current THC and CBD levels as closely as possible.

Around 7,000 people in the Netherlands are prescribed medicinal cannabis, according to the Volkskrant. They include people with multiple sclerosis (MS), severe pain, certain forms of epilepsy, and patients in palliative care.

Patients fear a different variety will not work as well for them. Cannabis contains many compounds that together determine its effect, and the mix depends on the plant and how it is grown.

The MS association has written to Hermans warning that some long-term patients depend on a specific variety.

Bedrocan also supplied patients in other European countries through the BMC. The BMC is due to stop exporting at the end of 2026. In September, Bedrocan told foreign pharmacies and wholesalers to order from it directly.

World.title: MPs vote to fly rainbow flag at parliament for first time
World.content:
The rainbow flag will fly at the Dutch parliament building on Sunday, Coming Out Day, after MPs overturned a decision by managers of parliament to drop the plan.

MPs backed the move by 90 votes to 36 in a vote late on Thursday night, public broadcaster NOS reported.

Parliament’s presidium, which runs its day-to-day affairs, initially agreed to the plan but changed its mind after Christian parties were told about the plan, RTL Nieuws reported on Thursday.

The orthodox Protestant SGP led the objections. “The rainbow flag is not a national flag but a flag of interest groups, which has grown into a symbol of activism,” SGP MP Diederik van Dijk told NOS.

Roll-call vote

Kati Piri, MP for opposition party Pro, then tabled a motion saying parliament should “stand up for the rights of the global LGBTI movement” and ensure “an inclusive working environment” for its staff.

Van Dijk responded by demanding a roll-call vote, in which each MP votes individually rather than by party. That meant MPs who had already gone home on Thursday had to return to The Hague.

Most MPs from D66, the VVD, CDA, PRO, PvdD, SP, ChristenUnie, 50PLUS and Volt voted in favour. The anti-immigration PVV, far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD), Denk and the SGP voted against, while MPs from JA21 and the Markuszower group were absent.

Purple Friday

The vote came on the eve of Purple Friday (Paarse Vrijdag), when schools mark LGBTI acceptance. This year it is being held in October for the first time, having been moved from December at the request of schools.

A record 3,130 schools have signed up, including 2,130 primary schools, compared with 2,890 last year, LGBTI rights organisation COC told news agency ANP.

The COC linked the rise to a survey published last month that found acceptance of homosexuality has slumped among teenagers. Only 22% of secondary school boys and 51% of girls now have a positive view, down from 40% and 78% in 2021.

Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar. They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time. 🔴Ubili kozę na zapleczu. Wkrótce decyzja sądu, zastanawia ruch prokuratury Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026 The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar. After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time. The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”. However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.” Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska. The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Not all cases involving illegal animal slaughter have been treated as causing low social harm. Last month, a court in the town of Limanowa convicted three men for carrying out illegal halal ritual slaughter and selling unapproved meat. The main suspect, a Polish man, was found guilty of overseeing the operation, while two Azerbaijani nationals were convicted of helping distribute the illegal meat. The verdicts can still be appealed. Although it has relatively small Muslim and Jewish populations, Poland is one of Europe’s biggest producers and exporters of kosher and halal meat. Almost a third of Poland's meat exports are halal and kosher, making it one of Europe's leading producers. Having fought off attempts by the ruling party to ban ritual slaughter, the industry is now hoping to expand further to cater to a growing market https://t.co/duOJTfHoLT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2022 However, the country has itself been experiencing growing levels of migration in recent years. Most of the new arrivals are from neighbouring Ukraine and Belarus, but there are also growing numbers from outside Europe, too. Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients. Poland’s current government has blamed some immigrant groups for a rise in crime and has stepped up deportations of those found to have broken the law. However, data show that, overall, immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than Poles themselves. World.title: Polish police detain more teens following school knife attacks amid fears of further incidents
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Following this week’s two knife attacks on schools in Poland, police have today carried out security checks on over 10,000 schools and detained at least 10 more people, many of them teenagers found to have made online threats or been in possession of weapons. Meanwhile, many parents decided not to send their children to school today, as rumours swirled online that this week’s attacks were somehow coordinated and that further incidents were planned on Friday. The issue has also sparked a political dispute, with the government criticising opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for previously vetoing laws intended to improve children’s safety. The opposition in turn accuses the government of failing to protect schools properly. 🚨 Ponad 10 tysięcy skontrolowanych placówek i 10 osób zatrzymanych w całym kraju. Bezpieczeństwo w szkołach priorytetem Policji ⬇️ Tragiczne zdarzenia, do których doszło w ciągu ostatnich dni na Mazowszu, wywołały w przestrzeni medialnej falę nieprawdziwych informacji,… pic.twitter.com/WVkYUdVO9C — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) October 9, 2026 On Thursday, a 39-year-old school caretaker was killed in an attack by a 15-year-old former pupil on a primary school. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that the assailant had been wearing a head-mounted camera intended to broadcast the attack. That came a day after a 19-year-old student carried out a knife attack on another school, leaving eight people injured. Two other teens were also detained on suspicion of planning attacks in other locations. In response, Tusk announced on Thursday that police would carry out regular checks on schools. However, on Friday, many parents in the Masovia province around Warsaw, where both of this week’s attacks took place, decided to keep their children at home. Some districts closed schools entirely. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school by a 15-year-old former pupil. Yesterday, a knife attack by a 19-year-old at another school left eight people injured. The assailant also had a homemade explosive that failed to detonate https://t.co/xJAzhT6u3U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 Concern was stoked by claims circulating on social media that this week’s school attacks were part of a coordinated action by a group of teenagers, who were planning further incidents on what they were calling “Bloody Friday”. Two schools in the town of Legionowo, just north of Warsaw, were closed on Friday after local authorities said they received “unconfirmed information that they were on a list” relating to the alleged group. Poland’s national police headquarters issued a statement on Friday morning saying that they were aware of the rumours but that “so far nothing indicates such an event is actually happening”. They urged people to remain calm, not share unverified information, and rely only on credible sources. At the same time, police and local authorities stepped up security in schools. At 9 a.m. on Friday, the national police headquarters announced that checks had been conducted at over 10,000 schools around the country and that ten people had been detained. Among those to be arrested was a 17-year-old in the town of Ełk, who had reportedly made online threats to attack other students, and a 13-year-old in Sochaczew who wrote in a chat that he would bring a machete to school. The boy later said it was a “silly joke”. In Bartoszyce, a school principal saw that an 11-year-old student had posted a photo of a knife alongside a statement indicating a threat. Police detained the boy and found an “imitation knife” in his backpack. In Ostrów Mazowiecka, police announced they had arrested a 15-year-old boy who had sent out images of himself in a Guy Fawkes-style mask, saying that he planned to take people’s lives. In Warsaw, police detained a 14-year-old who was found to be in possession of a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers. 🚨 Policjanci z Mokotowa niezwłocznie po otrzymaniu informacji o zagrożeniu bezpieczeństwa zatrzymali na terenie szkoły 14-latka, który posiadał nóż z ukrytym ostrzem. Nastolatek miał przy sobie także 11 petard hukowych. W sprawie prowadzone są dalsze czynności. Dokumenty… pic.twitter.com/lbQrqe2pgl — Policja Warszawa (@Policja_KSP) October 9, 2026 The situation has also taken on a political dimension. On Thursday, Tusk criticised Nawrocki for earlier this year vetoing a government bill intended to improve online safety by blocking harmful content. The president had argued that the measures were an “Orwellian” threat to free speech. In a hastily called vote in the lower-house Sejm on Thursday evening, Tusk’s ruling coalition passed a new version of the bill that will now be sent to the upper-house Senate. Once it receives final parliamentary approval, the legislation will return to Nawrocki for his signature or veto. Meanwhile, education minister Barbara Nowacka also noted that Nawrocki had vetoed a bill introducing new rights and responsibilities for school pupils, including greater powers to confiscate dangerous items. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Mieliśmy jedną z najmocniejszych propozycji zmiany prawa w Europie, która miała chronić w internecie przede wszystkim dzieci i młodzież. pic.twitter.com/dyxY6prGzB — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 8, 2026 In response, presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz criticised those who were “exploiting this issue for political purposes”, saying that “a political argument is the last thing we need right now”. Meanwhile, Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of focusing on “political warfare” instead of ensuring security in schools. “There is no coordination or top-down directives on what to do, where it is safe, and where there is risk or threat,” he wrote on social media, calling the situation “chaos”. World.title: Polish parliament approves ban on nighttime alcohol sales in shops
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours. The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved. #PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6 — tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026 The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package. The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently. Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales. In the first six months following the implementation of its restrictions in 2023, Kraków saw a nearly 50% decrease in nighttime police interventions, with other cities reporting similar improvements. The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400). Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage. The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 zloty for stronger drinks. Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops. The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026 In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show. The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005. They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 1, 2026 In June, an IBRiS poll for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 55% of Poles support some form of ban on nighttime alcohol sales while 43% are opposed. A survey by IBP for Super Express published today showed even stronger support, with 67% in favour of a ban and only 26% opposed. Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. World.title: Polish man suspected of helping Russian plot to assassinate Zelensky sentenced to 5.5 years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding. The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024. Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers. Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine. “These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year. Poland and Ukraine have revealed further details of a foiled plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa at Poland's Rzeszów airport. A Polish man was last month indicted in relation to the incident, which he is accused of seeking to carry out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/Lrp99vH4s2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2025 Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim. However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities. Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet. In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison. However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP. “Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz. Poland has charged three of its own citizens with working on behalf of Russian intelligence. They are accused of spreading disinformation, conducting reconnaissance of NATO troops, and undergoing firearms training in preparation for acts of sabotage https://t.co/maYd0kb9HW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 20, 2026 Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia. In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers. The AWB last year launched 48 investigations related to espionage, more than twice as many as in 2024. Over those two years, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 In January, Polish prosecutors indicted five people – four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian – accused of carrying out a plot on behalf of Russia to plant explosives in packages that were then dispatched by courier services across Europe. In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops. In July this year, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb. World.title: Beavers destroy sign warning about beavers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it. The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack. “We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters. “So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.” Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000. Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP. However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.
