World.title: One person killed in second school knife attack in Poland in two days
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school carried out today by a 15-year-old former pupil. It comes just a day after another knife attack by a 19-year-old on a different school in Poland, which left eight people injured. The assailant was also carrying a homemade explosive device that failed to detonate. Meanwhile, police also announced today the arrest of a 17-year-old who had reportedly threatened to attack a school and was found to be in possession of knives. The developments have caused shock in Poland, a country where such violent incidents are normally rare. “We are seeing a radicalisation of young people,” warns the education minister, who has called for tougher controls on online content. W rękach Policji jest już 15-latek, który około godziny 9 wszedł do szkoły w miejscowości Leszczydół-Nowiny, w powiecie wyszkowskim i ostrym narzędziem ranił 3 pracowników placówki. Wśród rannych jest dyrektor, który ujął 15-latka. Policja była na miejscu już po kilku minutach od… pic.twitter.com/EV1RPP7LA5 — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026 The latest attack took place in a primary school in the village of Leszczydół-Nowiny, around 60 km (37 miles) northeast of Warsaw, on Thursday morning. A 15-year-old former pupil of the school entered the facility and stabbed three members of staff, including the principal, who managed to subdue him. One of the victims, a 37-year-old female caretaker, died from her injuries. The other victim, a teacher, was hospitalised. The attacker was detained and will appear before a family court, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The incident comes just a day after another similar tragedy only 50 km away, in the town of Ostrołęka. On Wednesday morning, a 19-year-old attacked a vocational high school, leaving four students, two teachers and two bystanders injured before being captured. The assailant, who has been named only as Jakub Z. under Polish privacy law, is a student at the school. On Wednesday evening, national prosecutor Dariusz Korneluk told broadcaster TVN that the attacker had a homemade explosive in his backpack “that almost detonated”. “The backpack was already in the computer room and, only due to the responsible actions of the teacher and the students, was it thrown out of the window” after smoke had begun to billow out of it, he said. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek pledged that “prosecutors will ensure that the perpetrator answers for every blow inflicted and faces the legal consequences…There is no tolerance for violence in Polish schools”. Policjanci z Ostrołęki w pobliżu plaży miejskiej zatrzymali 19-letniego mężczyznę podejrzewanego o zaatakowanie ostrym narzędziem osób w pobliżu i na terenie szkoły w Ostrołęce. Ze wstępnych informacji wynika, że mogło dojść do zranienia 7 osób. Policjanci na miejscu wykonują… pic.twitter.com/cRzqMs36rD — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 7, 2026 On Thursday morning, around the same time as the attack in Leszczydół-Nowiny was unfolding, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński announced that a 17-year-old boy had been detained by police after threatening to attack another school. The suspect, who resides in the same Masovia province where Wednesday and Thursday’s attacks took place, “was found with two knives”, said Kierwiński, quoted by news website Interia. His internet history also showed that “he was looking for information on how to carry out this type of bloody act”, added the minister. The potential incident was prevented after fellow pupils reported to teachers that the suspect announced he wanted to “do something bad at school”. Last week, a 13-year-old was detained by police after telling a fellow online gamer that he was planning an attack on his school in the village of Książki, north-central Poland. He reportedly confessed to having killed cats and said that he wanted to attack random people with a cleaver in the school halls. Dzięki przytomnej reakcji uczniów, nauczyciela oraz błyskawicznej akcji policjantów z Sierpca powstrzymano 17-latka, który zapowiadał, że „zrobi coś złego w szkole”. Policjanci zatrzymali nastolatka i zabezpieczyli należące do niego noże, a w jego telefonie natrafiono na historię… pic.twitter.com/oUkwKbHmNr — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026 The Polish authorities have recently warned of growing concern over radical ideas spreading among young people. Last month, the security services detained three teenagers accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One was charged with planning an attack on a school and a mosque. Last year, a 19-year-old student was detained after it was determined he was planning an Islamic State-inspired attack on a Christmas market. In August, he was indicted to stand trial. In February, an 18-year-old was indicted over claims he planned to attack a school, also inspired by the Islamic State. Speaking on Wednesday, after the Ostrołęka incident but before today’s events, education minister Barbara Nowak warned that “we are seeing a radicalisation of young people”, reports the Onet news website. She called for “much greater control over what happens on the internet”. Earlier this year, Poland introduced a new law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour. The government is also working on measures to block children from social media and has banned the use of smartphones in schools. Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) has announced the launch of the country’s first fund to support companies developing space technologies. Vinci Space Tech Fund will be worth 500 million zloty (€114 million), investing up to 100 million zloty each in 15-20 firms in the sector. The brainchild of finance minister Andrzej Domański, the fund aims to foster the growth of Polish space technologies and bolster the country’s technological independence. Kosmos to nie tylko gospodarka i innowacje. Kosmos to także bezpieczeństwo Polski. 🇵🇱 Dziś w Krakowie uruchamiamy pierwszy w Polsce fundusz dla sektora kosmicznego – Vinci Space Tech Fund. 500 mln zł na rozwój sektora @BGK_pl Vinci. Mamy ambitne spółki, znakomitych naukowców i… pic.twitter.com/NQBy8HYOcY — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 6, 2026 According to the growth and technology ministry, one of the fund’s strategic partners, BGK will invest between 10 and 100 million zloty in companies with a potential for rapid growth and expansion into international markets through its Vinci investment vehicle. The fund’s other partners are the Polish Space Agency and Kraków Technology Park (KTP), where the launch took place, along with ICEYE, a world-leading Finnish microsatellite manufacturer and operator co-founded by Pole Rafał Modrzewski. Announcing the fund, Domański highlighted the space sector’s role in responding to threats, protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening energy security and monitoring Poland and its surroundings. “The money from the Vinci fund is an investment in Poland’s capacity to build its own strong companies and develop competences that will be strategically significant for our economy and security,” he said. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Mirosław Czekaj, president of the BGK management board, also noted that the development of the space industry would help “to build Poland’s technological sovereignty”, as one of the projects that are “vital to the Polish economy”. The fund is expected to invest in 15 to 20 companies, mainly Polish, although companies from elsewhere in Europe may also qualify if they have their main business operations in Poland, the ministry said. Its key investment areas include satellites, optics and Earth observation, satellite communications, electronics and photonics, rockets and propulsion systems, and artificial intelligence. In addition to funding, companies will benefit from advice and support from the fund’s partners. KPT, the city of Kraków and the Faculty of Space Technologies at AGH University are expected to provide much of the initiative’s academic, research and technical expertise. ICEYE, meanwhile, will share its experience of growing a space company and expanding into global markets. Last month, the company opened a satellite technology centre in Warsaw, and it plans to invest more than 120 million zloty in Poland by 2028, reports industry website Space News. Modrzewski said that raising capital in Poland was difficult when the company was founded 12 years ago, but that it has become easier as space has emerged as one of the country’s “strategic domains”. “The availability of capital in Poland will allow our companies to build their position on the global market without needing to leave the country at an early stage,” Modrzewski said, quoted by financial news site Bankier.pl. Vinci has previously invested in ICEYE as part of its private equity fund. Astronaut @astro_slawosz's recent trip to the International Space Station highlighted the Polish space industry's growing importance. Once limited to making components for others, Poland is now building its own spacecraft and participating in missions https://t.co/TmQiD91IzZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2025 Poland’s space sector has expanded rapidly since the country joined the European Space Agency in 2012, moving from supplying components for foreign missions to developing its own satellites and space systems. A key milestone came in 2024 with the launch of EagleEye, Poland’s largest satellite, which was designed and built by a consortium of Polish companies and research institutions. In 2025, a Pole went to space for the second time in history, 50 years after the first Polish astronaut’s flight. The sector is now taking on larger international projects, while Russia’s war in Ukraine has highlighted the importance of domestic space capabilities for national security. In July this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency centre focusing on civil security and resilience. World.title: Warsaw records EU’s highest employment rate
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data. The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013. Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%. The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030. At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%). After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU. In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%). And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%). Poland's unemployment rate of 2.6% in January is the lowest ever recorded in the country by @EU_Eurostat and was the joint-lowest that month among all EU member states For more, read our full report here: https://t.co/eP5A9JT4eg pic.twitter.com/A9oHu2zLZ6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%. The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation. At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts. World.title: Prague Outperforms Vienna and Berlin in Visitor Ratings
World.content:
Prague has received higher visitor satisfaction ratings than Vienna and Berlin, according to the latest Global Tourist Perception Index by Data Appeal Mabrian Intelligence.

The Czech capital scored 92.7 out of 100, compared with 85.6 for Vienna and 78.4 for Berlin, Prague City Tourism (PCT) announced on Thursday.

The results reflect six years of efforts to improve tourism services, visitor experiences and the city’s destination branding, the organization said during International Customer Service Week, held from October 5 to 9.

The Global Tourist Perception Index assesses several aspects of the visitor experience, including hotel satisfaction, safety and tourism products. Prague scored highest among the three capitals, according to PCT.



Visitor spending rises as tourism shifts upmarket

Data from Mastercard transactions indicate that spending by visitors from key foreign markets increased by 18% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while the number of visitors rose by approximately 1%.

Social media analysis also points to Prague’s growing association with culture. More than a third of social media posts shared by visitors about the city focused on art and culture, an increase of around five percentage points year-on-year. Nightlife accounted for just 4.5% of reported reasons for visiting, according to PCT.

The Data Appeal Mabrian Intelligence Platform also gave Prague a score of 80 out of 100 for hotel service satisfaction, ahead of Vienna at 75.8 and Berlin at 71.8.

Figures from hotel data provider STR point to further growth in the market. Between January and August 2026, hotel occupancy in Prague increased by 4.9% year-on-year, while the average room rate rose by 5.1%.

Occupancy reached 84.7% in August. According to a recent overview of Prague’s tourism sector by the Czech Institute of Tourism, the average room rate was approximately €123, rising to €170 in the city center and €241 in the luxury segment.

Prague attracts hotel investors

The city is also gaining ground among hotel investors. According to the Cushman & Wakefield Hotel Investor Compass 2026, published in March, Prague ranks among the 15 most attractive European cities for hotel investment, ahead of Vienna, Zurich and Budapest.

Investor interest in Prague’s hotel market has increased for two consecutive years. In the previous edition of the study, the city recorded the largest year-on-year increase in investor interest among the markets surveyed, at 14%. The latest edition showed a further increase of 7%.

World.title: Prague 7 Turns Streets Into Outdoor Art With Designs by Local Children
World.content:
Prague 7 has transformed several streets around local schools with large-scale colorful paintings created with the help of local schoolchildren.

The new artwork can be seen on Rajská, Plynární, Jablonského and Antonínská streets, as well as part of Bubenská Street. The municipality placed the designs mainly near schools and along busy pedestrian routes.



On Antonínská Street, students from grades five through eight at Strossmayerovo Square Elementary School helped create the artwork. They produced the original drawings, which artist Jakub Karlík then combined into the final design.

Several other educational institutions are located close to the painted streets, including Bratrská Elementary School, the Holešovice Business Academy, the Higher Vocational School of Fashion Design and the Secondary Industrial School of Fashion Design.

The new designs have received mostly positive reactions from local residents. Comments on Prague 7’s Facebook page described the streets as more cheerful and said the artwork had made the area more interesting.

There has also been criticism, particularly over the cost and the practical impact of painting the asphalt. Some residents questioned whether the project was necessary and raised concerns about the roughness of the surface, pedestrian movement and whether the paint could become slippery.

Prague 7 said anti-slip paint was used, similar to materials applied to cycle paths and sports surfaces.

The project cost 755,000 CZK, covering the designs, preparation, materials and application. According to Prague 7 spokesperson Martin Vokuš, each of the two phases took around 20 days.

The municipality awarded the contract directly to Karlík. Before selecting his proposal for the Antonínská and Bubenská sections, Prague 7 compared three offers and chose his as the most advantageous.

World.title: Beer Consumption in Czech Republic Falls to Lowest Level on Record
World.content:
Czech beer consumption fell to its lowest level on record in 2025, with the average resident drinking 121 liters during the year, according to data from the Czech Association of Breweries and Malt Houses (ČSPS).

Total domestic consumption reached 14.86 million hectoliters, down 3.2% from 2024. The figure is the lowest recorded since nationwide beer consumption statistics began.

Overall beer production in the Czech Republic also declined last year. Breweries produced 19.96 million hectoliters of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer, 4.3% less than in 2024.



The decline affected nearly every category, with non-alcoholic beer the main exception. Production of non-alcoholic and flavored non-alcoholic beer increased by 4% to 1.68 million hectoliters.

Demand for non-alcoholic beer has been rising steadily for more than a decade. Between 2019 and 2024 alone, production increased by around 50%.

Pubs lose ground as more Czechs drink at home

The shift in drinking habits is particularly visible in restaurants and pubs. Draft beer accounted for 28% of beer sold on the Czech market in 2025, down one percentage point from the previous year.

The longer-term decline is more significant. Draft beer represented 35% of sales in 2019 and 51% in 2008.

The ČSPS said the figures reflect changes in consumer behavior, including greater interest in moderation and healthier lifestyles. When Czechs do go out for beer, they are increasingly looking for quality and variety rather than simply drinking larger quantities.

Czech beer exports also decline

Exports followed the domestic market downward. Czech breweries exported 5.48 million hectoliters of beer in 2025, an 8.2% decrease compared with the previous year.

European Union countries accounted for around 90% of Czech beer exports, with Germany and Slovakia among the largest buyers.

Imports also declined, falling by 18.3% year on year. Foreign beer accounted for only 2.5% of total beer consumption in the Czech Republic, down 0.5 percentage points from 2024.

World.title: Nearly Half of Czechs Spend More Than 30% of Their Income on Housing
World.content:
Nearly half of people in the Czech Republic spend more than 30% of their net income on housing, while around one in 10 spends more than half.

Housing is generally considered financially burdensome when rent, utilities and other related costs exceed 30–40% of household income. The EU average is around 24%.



The findings come from a survey by Česká spořitelna and Evropa v datech, conducted with Ipsos among 1,000 respondents in February.

Housing affordability remains particularly difficult for young Czechs. Among people aged 18 to 29, 58% live with their parents at least part of the time, while 29% live with friends or a partner.

The survey found that 60% of people under 30 who are dissatisfied with their housing situation have postponed a major life decision because of it. For around one-third, this has happened repeatedly. Starting a family is among the decisions affected by housing conditions.

Homeowners were considerably more likely to be very satisfied than renters, with 41% of owners describing themselves as very satisfied compared with 18% of renters.

Czechia still has the least affordable housing in the EU

The Czech Republic improved by six places in this year’s housing conditions ranking, reaching 17th among the 27 EU member states. The improvement was linked to increased investment in residential construction, fewer households facing excessive housing costs or difficulties paying for heating, and relatively favorable rental conditions.

Buying a home, however, remains more difficult than elsewhere in the EU.

An average-sized Czech apartment costs 13.3 average annual gross salaries, compared with 13.6 a year earlier. The figure has improved only slightly, while other countries have made faster progress. In Hungary, the ratio fell from 13.6 to 11.9 annual salaries, while Slovakia improved from 13.2 to 11.7 and Slovenia from 13.4 to 11.4.

Ireland has the most affordable housing by this measure, with an average home costing 6.2 annual salaries, followed by Belgium and Finland.

An average apartment in Czechia costs roughly the equivalent of 29 years of average rent. In city centers, the figure is close to 31 years, compared with less than 13 years in Ireland.

High housing costs are changing household decisions

Housing expenses are also forcing some households to reduce other spending. Last year, 40% cut their budgets because of housing costs. Nearly one-quarter reduced spending on holidays, hobbies and entertainment, while 16% cut spending on essentials such as food, clothing and personal-care products.

Around 38% of Czechs see living with parents as an economic necessity caused by high property prices. Another 26% consider it a reasonable temporary solution, while 9.4% see multigenerational living as a viable long-term model.

At the same time, 46% of young people expect to inherit property from their families.

World.title: Famous Dancing House Photo Spot in Prague Is Set for a Major Makeover
World.content:
Jiráskovo Square in Prague is set for a major redesign that will change one of the city’s best-known photo spots near the Dancing House.

The project, estimated to cost around CZK 35 million, will replace part of the damaged lawn with paving, restore a historic fountain and move the monument to writer Alois Jirásek.



The Prague 2 district plans to carry out the transformation over the next two years. The redesign is based on a 2022 study prepared by archiF studio.

The square’s lawn has long been a problem. Its location directly opposite the Dancing House makes it a popular stopping point for tourists, many of whom step onto the grass to take photographs with the distinctive building in the background.

One of the most common poses involves visitors appearing to support the Dancing House with their foot or kick it. The repeated foot traffic has left the grass heavily damaged, despite attempts to restore it.

Under the new plans, part of the lawn will be replaced with a paved surface. This will create a more durable area for visitors to take photographs while reducing pressure on the remaining greenery.

Historic fountain to return to operation

The redesign will also restore the Cubist fountain created by architect Vlastislav Hofman. The area around the fountain will be repaved, while the fountain itself will be returned to its original appearance and function.

Water is expected to flow through the fountain again after decades.

Architect Soňa Formanová, one of the project’s authors, said the team was able to locate Hofman’s original documentation, including plans covering the fountain and the approaches to the nearby bridge.

The project will also introduce a raised edge around the lawn that can be used for seating. New flowerbeds and trees are planned for the northern part of the square, while existing shrubs considered unsuitable for the area will be removed.

The monument to Alois Jirásek, the Czech writer after whom the square is named, will be relocated to the center of the small park.

World.title: Queer Arts Festival PINKBUS Returns With New Performances and International Guests
World.content:
The PINKBUS Festival will return to Prague on November 3-14 with several days of theatre, dance, drag, music, visual art and performance.

This year’s edition, titled Forward March!, will focus on the need to keep moving forward amid an uncertain social and political climate.

Organised by the PINKBUS queer arts platform, the festival aims to create a space for artists and audiences to meet, experiment and share experiences. The programme combines established artists with new projects and will also mark the beginning of a new season for the platform.



One of the highlights of this year’s festival will be the premiere of two original works developed through the PINKBUS open call First Ride.

Richard Eliáš, an Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague (AVU) student, will present the interdisciplinary drag fantasy I Guess It’s Kind of My Fault, or What?. The second project, by the performative art collective Izbová teplota & Alejandra, is Štúrovci Went to Devín and Had Some Fun, offering a new and unconventional take on the group of Slovak national revival figures known as the Štúrovci.

The festival will also feature international guests. French artists Nicolas Poggi and Giselle Hauscarriaga will present SUDOR (Sweat), a Czech premiere performed with a local cast. The post-performative work explores physical exhaustion, sweat and the limits of the body.

Another premiere, Lipsync Her Name… Because It’s Precious, is being created in collaboration with the Italian festival RAINBOW.IT and Slovak organisation DRAMA QUEER. The performance focuses on three figures from European LGBTQIA+ history: Lucy Salani, Romina Cecconi and Ota Tasinata.

Directed by Tomáš “Grófka” Procházka, the production combines three monodramatic sketches exploring identity and the determination to remain true to oneself. The cast includes Italian actor Antonello Foddis and his drag alter ego La Trave Nell’Okkio, as well as Czech performer Venice, also known as Martin Talaga.

The programme will also include the PINKPANEL discussion series. This year’s edition, titled (The Tinsmith’s) Hammer Against Queerness, will examine the potential impact of current cultural policy on LGBTQIA+ artistic production and discuss possible forms of resistance.

The festival will conclude with a special BEST OF edition of the PINKBUS variety show, featuring Venice, Just Karen, La Cuntessa, Tonic Garbáge, Helena Araujo and other performers, alongside special guests.

World.title: Roger Waters Brings New Pink Floyd Show to Prague in June 2027
World.content:
Roger Waters will bring a new Pink Floyd concert production to Prague next year, with LEGACY – A Pink Floyd Show scheduled for June 8, 2027, at O2 universum.

The new production has been created under Waters’ direction and will feature a ten-piece band led by his son, Harry Waters. The Prague show will focus on music from what is widely regarded as Pink Floyd’s most influential period, spanning 1971 to 1979.



The setlist will draw from four of the band’s best-known albums: The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

The music will be accompanied by a new visual production featuring high-resolution LED screens and imagery inspired by Pink Floyd’s original artwork and stage concepts.

Harry Waters will serve as the show’s musical director, performing on Hammond B3 organ and piano while also contributing vocals. He has a long history with the band’s music and spent more than 15 years performing alongside his father on major tours, including The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall.

His connection to Pink Floyd goes back even further. As a child, Harry’s voice appeared on “Goodbye Blue Sky” from The Wall. He also saw the original The Wall concert production at a young age.

The band includes drummer Graham Broad, guitarist Edo Scordo, bassist and backing vocalist Dahniel Knight, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Ryan Saranich, keyboardist Matt Riddle, lead vocalist Clifton David Broadbridge and backing vocalists Eva Avila and Genevieve Little.

Roger Waters co-founded Pink Floyd in 1965 and became the band’s principal lyricist and conceptual leader following Syd Barrett’s departure. He played a central role in the creation of albums including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

Ticket prices start at 1,600 CZK

Live Nation Club and O2 presale starts October 8, 2026, at 10:00 AM

Tickets on sale via Ticketmaster and Ticketportal starting October 9, 2026, at 10:00 AM

World.title: GALLERY: Vltava Philharmonic Reveals Its Interiors for the First Time
World.content:
Prague’s planned Vltava Philharmonic has offered the first detailed look inside the building, releasing visualizations of its main foyer and the spaces serving its three principal concert halls.

The interior design will combine wood, glass and stone, with flowing shapes inspired by the Vltava River and the building’s distinctive sloping roof. The plans also emphasize open public spaces designed to connect the concert halls with the rest of the building.



The main foyer will be dominated by a large glass wall extending across several floors. Its curved geometry is intended to echo the movement of the Vltava and will separate the open foyer from other areas of the building.

Light-colored solid wood panels will cover the ceilings, following the contours of the roof above. Stone elements will be used in areas connecting the public foyer with the foyer of the main concert hall, including spaces designed for both seating and standing around bar counters.

´

The project has become significantly more expensive

The cost of the Vltava Philharmonic has increased sharply since the project was first estimated.

In 2021, the projected construction cost was CZK 6.1 billion. After the Danish architecture studio Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) won the international competition in 2022, the estimate rose to CZK 9.4 billion.

A more detailed architectural study completed in 2024 put the figure at CZK 11.65 billion. The latest estimate is CZK 11.98 billion for the building itself.

Once improvements to the surrounding area are included, the overall project is expected to cost almost CZK 17 billion.

Construction could begin in 2028

The city expects to obtain the permit in the first quarter of 2027. A general contractor would then be selected, with construction currently scheduled to start in the first quarter of 2028.

Trial operations are planned to begin in 2033.

The Vltava Philharmonic will occupy three underground and six above-ground floors. In addition to five concert halls, the complex will include facilities for the Czech Philharmonic and the Prague Symphony Orchestra (FOK), a music department operated by the Municipal Library of Prague, a creative hub, a restaurant and publicly accessible terraces.

The building is being designed by Bjarke Ingels Group, whose proposal was selected in the international architectural competition in 2022.

World.title: Viktor Orbán defends Ukrainian gold convoy operation as lawyer says motion filed to name him as suspect
World.content:
Hungary’s former prime minister Viktor Orbán insists authorities acted without government instructions in the controversial Ukrainian gold convoy case. However, a lawyer representing a senior prosecutor says a motion has been filed to question Orbán as a suspect, as investigators examine alleged misconduct surrounding the operation.

Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has defended the authorities’ actions in the Ukrainian gold convoy case, saying they acted independently and successfully, and that he would have issued instructions had they been necessary.

His statement, sent to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI), came as the lawyer representing a senior prosecutor involved in the wider affair claimed that a motion had been filed to name Orbán as a suspect. According to the lawyer, the prosecution service has yet to respond to the request.

Orbán has not been formally named as a suspect in the case, according to the report.

The Fidesz party leader described the affair as “Europe’s biggest corruption scandal” and referred to the “financial operations of the Ukrainian mafia”, claiming that these had been stopped and dismantled in Hungary. Those characterisations are Orbán’s own claims; an earlier money-laundering investigation into the shipment was closed without finding a criminal offence.

Orbán and János Hajdu, former head of TEK. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Lawyer says Orbán’s potential criminal liability should be investigated

Speaking on ATV’s Egyenes Beszéd programme, lawyer Lóránt Horváth confirmed that the proceedings now have five suspects. He represents Pál Fürcht, a senior prosecutor, and said the investigation should examine whether people at higher political levels were involved.

Horváth said a motion had already been submitted seeking to have former prime minister Orbán questioned as a suspect, but that the prosecution service had not yet provided an answer.

According to the lawyer, Orbán could potentially face allegations of abuse of office as a principal offender and of incitement in connection with other suspected offences. These are allegations and legal assessments made by Horváth, not established findings by investigators or a court.

The lawyer also said information had emerged during the investigation that could raise questions about the possible involvement of certain employees of the Office of the Prosecutor General. He claimed that Fürcht had raised concerns with the prosecution service’s leadership as early as May, but that the matter ultimately led to disciplinary proceedings.

Horváth described the transfer of the investigation from the Budapest Regional Investigative Prosecutor’s Office to the Central Investigative Chief Prosecutor’s Office as unusual. In his view, investigators had already interviewed numerous witnesses and gathered substantial evidence.

He suggested that the transfer could either mean the number of suspects would remain at five or that the investigation would expand to include more senior figures. He said he believed the latter course was warranted.

Defence minister demands answers from Orbán

Orbán’s statement also followed a public challenge from Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi on Thursday. The minister called on the former prime minister to clarify whether he had ordered the operation to stop the Ukrainian cash shipment.

Orbán responded that the authorities had acted within their own powers and without government instructions.

“The authorities performed exemplary and successful work, carrying out their duties within their own powers and doing an excellent job without government instructions,” he said, adding that he would have issued the appropriate instructions if necessary.

He also argued that the officials involved deserved recognition and rewards, accusing the current government of putting employees who had served the country’s interests through an ordeal for carrying out their duties.

His statement does not establish who initiated the operation or clarify whether political figures were involved in the decisions surrounding it.

What happened in the Ukrainian gold convoy case?

On 5 March, officers from Hungary’s National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) and the Counter Terrorism Centre (TEK) seized two vehicles on the M0 motorway near Budapest on suspicion of money laundering.

The vehicles belonged to Ukraine’s state-owned Oschadbank and were transporting cash and gold from Austria’s Raiffeisen Bank to Ukraine. The shipment contained USD 40 million, EUR 35 million and nine kilograms of gold.

Seven Ukrainian nationals travelling with the shipment were questioned and subsequently expelled from Hungary the following day. The crew, reportedly unarmed, later complained of inhumane treatment and violations of their rights.

The operation prompted questions about the role of Hungary’s security services and the legal basis for the seizure. It later emerged that the Constitution Protection Office had filed the report that triggered the authorities’ action, drawing on information gathered from another intelligence agency, the Information Office.

If you missed it: New document links Viktor Orbán to decision behind Ukrainian gold convoy case

Money-laundering investigation closed without finding a crime

A key development in the case is that NAV suspended its money-laundering investigation in June before terminating it in August, citing the absence of a criminal offence.

That decision contrasts with Orbán’s description of the affair as a major corruption scandal involving the Ukrainian mafia. However, the closure of the original investigation does not resolve separate questions about how the operation was conducted or whether officials acted lawfully.

On 2 October, the Central Investigative Chief Prosecutor’s Office took over the investigation into the conduct of officials involved in the case.

The five suspects include János Hajdu, the former head of TEK, István Szatmári, a former senior official at the Constitution Protection Office, and three police officers. According to Horváth, Hajdu is suspected of unlawful detention, Szatmári of incitement to commit document forgery, and the three police officers of document forgery in an official capacity. The lawyer clarified that the police officers had already been named as suspects in July.

World.title: 114-year-old Hungarian swimming baths shut down with immediate effect
World.content:
Esztergom’s historic Szent István Swimming Baths have been ordered to close after inspectors raised concerns over chlorine levels and the lack of an approved water-treatment policy. The mayor plans to challenge the decision as the city scrambles to find alternative swimming facilities for local athletes.

One of Esztergom’s best-known swimming facilities has been forced to close with immediate effect following a decision by the Komárom-Esztergom County Government Office over alleged breaches of public swimming pool regulations.

The Szent István Swimming Baths, which are 114 years old, were ordered to suspend operations after a public health inspection found high chlorine levels in the pool water and established that the facility did not have a valid policy governing chemical water treatment.

Esztergom Mayor Ádám Hernádi announced the decision in a video posted on Facebook on Friday, saying the official order had arrived shortly after lunch. The municipality had asked for permission to continue operating the facility’s outdoor pool under its usual inflatable winter dome, but this request was not granted.

Why has the historic swimming pool been closed?

The government office’s public health department launched proceedings against the baths in September after identifying concerns about the water’s chlorine content and the absence of an approved water-treatment policy.

According to documents reported by Telex, the authorities found that disinfectants had been added to the pool without the necessary authorisation or an approved Public Baths Health and Technical Operating Policy (KTSZ).

The closure will remain in force until the municipality obtains approval for a policy that meets the relevant technical requirements and demonstrates that the pool’s water-treatment arrangements are suitable. Failure to comply could result in a fine of up to HUF 5 million (approximately EUR 12,000).

The legal background dates back to a 2023 government decree that changed the health and technical requirements for public baths. Under the rules, every facility must have a valid KTSZ by 31 December 2026.

The government office had reportedly already warned Esztergom in March that its pool’s traditional operating method posed a problem under the new regulations. However, the immediate closure followed the conclusion of the separate proceedings launched in September over the use of disinfectants.

Hernádi has disputed the authorities’ position on the water quality.

“There is no more chlorine in it, and no more chemicals than there were a hundred years ago, or even in the 1990s, when I learnt to swim here myself,” the mayor said.

His comments reflect the municipality’s position, while the closure order is based on the authorities’ findings concerning water treatment and regulatory compliance.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Where will local swimmers go now?

The sudden closure has left the municipality searching for alternative facilities, particularly for local athletes and swimming clubs that rely on the pool for training. According to the mayor, Esztergom is negotiating with neighbouring Dorog and Štúrovo (Párkány), across the Danube in Slovakia, to arrange access to their swimming pools. A pool at Esztergom’s Aquasziget leisure complex is also expected to provide an alternative for swimmers.

The closure also threatens the usual winter swimming season at the historic baths. During the colder months, an inflatable dome is placed over the 50-metre outdoor pool, allowing it to be used in more comfortable conditions.

The city spent HUF 200 million on a replacement dome a few years ago. With the baths now closed, it is unlikely to be installed for the coming season. Hernádi said the municipality was examining its legal options to challenge the government office’s decision, arguing that Esztergom should not be left without its historic swimming facility.

A major renovation could cost HUF 6 billion

The dispute comes as the city considers a substantial overhaul of the ageing baths. The facility currently operates using a traditional fill-and-drain system rather than recirculating its pool water. Water enters the pool from a natural spring and is subsequently discharged into the Danube.

The 2023 regulations mean that a water-recirculation system would need to be installed, requiring significant investment and wider renovation work.

According to a statement issued by the mayor earlier this week, a complete renovation could cost close to HUF 6 billion (approximately EUR 16.4 million). The municipality does not currently have the necessary funding available.

The original plan was to keep the baths open throughout the winter season, remove the inflatable dome in spring and then begin a more extensive renovation in April. The latest decision means the facility has been shut several months earlier than anticipated.

Hernádi also pointed to the city’s financial constraints. He said the withdrawal of around HUF 56 billion in state funding in 2023 had affected several local projects, including the swimming baths.

Esztergom must also pay more than HUF 2.66 billion in solidarity contributions to the state in 2026, according to the mayor. He argued that two years’ worth of these payments would be enough to cover a project on the scale of the baths’ complete renovation.

The municipality intends to include the renovation in its next annual budget. According to the mayor’s earlier statement, work could begin in spring once the necessary permits have been obtained and the public procurement process has been completed.

World.title: Severe turbulence forces flight to divert, 8 passengers rushed to hospital
World.content:
Eight people were hospitalised in Miami on Friday morning after a flight bound for New York City was diverted to Miami International Airport following reports of severe turbulence, authorities said.

According to officials, Avianca Flight 42 was travelling from Medellin, Colombia, to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport.

Avianca flight got into serious turbulence

Miami International Airport officials said that Avianca Flight 42 was travelling from Medellin, Colombia, to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport when it encountered severe turbulence. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said the aircraft landed safely at Miami International Airport at about 3.30 AM local time (0730GMT).

The department said that eight people were injured, including one who required transportation to a trauma centre, Anadolu Agency writes.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

However, airline officials told CBS News Miami that nine people were injured in the incident, including three crew members and six passengers. A passenger who was at Miami International Airport as the Avianca flight arrived said she noticed several ambulances waiting to assist those injured.

“When we arrived, when we landed, we saw that very close to where we were going to disembark, there were more than five or six ambulances. Seven of them with their lights on as if they were waiting for something,” passenger Maria Paula Jimenez said. “When we arrived, well, you know, it wasn’t normal.”

Avianca officials said the airline’s airport team was assisting the remaining passengers with arrangements to continue their journey to New York City.

World.title: Romanian man beat and forced Hungarian man to work for food in Hungary
World.content:
A Romanian national is facing charges of human trafficking and forced labour after allegedly assaulting, threatening and exploiting a vulnerable Hungarian man, including forcing him to work for little or no pay in Hungary and abroad.

Romanian man abused his victim in Hungary

As MTI stated, a Romanian man has been charged with aggravated human trafficking and forced labour for allegedly coercing a Hungarian man into working through violence and threats, the Pest County Prosecutor’s Office announced on Thursday. According to prosecutors, the defendant reached an agreement with the victim in 2022.

The Hungarian man, who lived in poverty in Nagykőrös, central Hungary, was promised work as a driver in exchange for accommodation, food and a small salary. However, from the spring of 2023, the defendant allegedly began assaulting and threatening the man, forcing him to carry out agricultural and construction work instead. In return, the victim reportedly received only minimal amounts of food and occasional payments of HUF 1,000.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Victim allegedly taken abroad and deprived of documents

In 2025, the defendant allegedly took the man abroad for work, confiscated his documents and kept him in inhumane conditions. Authorities in the unnamed foreign country discovered the alleged abuse during an inspection and initiated proceedings against the defendant over suspected unlawful detention and forced labour. With the help of the foreign authorities, the victim was able to return to Hungary in September 2025.

The ordeal allegedly continued the following month, when the defendant appeared at the victim’s home in Nagykőrös. Prosecutors say he assaulted the man and forced him to work for him again, this time without paying him at all. The police eventually located the victim following a missing-person report and subsequently arrested the defendant, who was taken into custody.

Prosecutors seek prison sentence and deportation

The Pest County Prosecutor’s Office is seeking an enforceable prison sentence, a fine and the defendant’s expulsion from Hungary. The charges concern aggravated human trafficking and forced labour. The case will be heard by the Budapest Environs Regional Court, which will determine the Romanian man’s guilt. The allegations have not yet been proven in court, and the defendant is presumed innocent unless found guilty.

Read also: 15-year-old boy beaten with branches in Hungary after refusing to give up his property

World.title: Hungary to terminate Southern Railway Ring contract with Mészáros firm to avoid risking billions in EU funding
World.content:
The government will terminate the contract for Budapest’s Southern Railway Ring and order Lőrinc Mészáros’s V-Híd to leave the construction site, citing suspected collusion in the tender process that could put HUF 320 billion (EUR 0.88 billion) in EU funding at risk.

Hungary’s government has announced plans to terminate the construction contract for Budapest’s Southern Railway Ring following alleged irregularities in the public procurement process. Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced the decision at a joint press conference with Prime Minister Péter Magyar on Friday.

The government also intends to exclude companies owned by Hungarian businessman Lőrinc Mészáros from state railway construction tenders over alleged conflicts of interest.

Photo: MTI

The Southern Railway Ring project aims to expand the railway line between Kelenföld and Ferencváros from two tracks to three or four, improving capacity and introducing new stops. The route is particularly important for domestic rail traffic and European transport corridors.

Mészáros’s company V-Híd won the largest construction package in 2021 with a bid worth HUF 337 billion. The wider project has received substantial EU funding, but the European Court of Auditors reportedly identified suspected collusion in the procurement process, threatening the availability of up to HUF 320 billion in support.

Photo: MTI

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Government orders construction work to stop

According to Vitézy, the concerns centre on the Kontúr Group, a company involved in preparing the project’s estimated costs, and its alleged links to V-Híd. The minister said similarities between the cost calculations and the winning bid, alongside other connections between the companies, raised serious questions about whether the tender was conducted fairly.

These allegations have not, in the information provided, been established as criminal wrongdoing by a court.

Vitézy said the project is approximately 42 per cent complete. The state has reportedly paid V-Híd around HUF 100 billion in advances, while work worth HUF 44 billion has been completed. Terminating the contract could allow the state to seek repayment of more than HUF 50 billion, although recovering the money may prove difficult.

The government plans to assess the completed structures, materials and outstanding work before deciding how to proceed. If necessary, it will launch a new public procurement procedure in an effort to preserve the EU funding.

Photo: MTI

Delays could last for years

The decision could significantly disrupt construction. Vitézy warned that the railway project could be delayed by months or even years while the government takes over the site and arranges a new contract.

The authorities say they will seek to maintain existing rail services and protect completed structures during the interruption. The project must also meet the relevant EU funding deadline, with completion required by the end of 2030.

The government has also announced plans to report suspected budgetary fraud to Hungary’s National Tax and Customs Administration. The next steps will depend on the assessment of the construction site and whether the project can be restarted under a new, compliant tender.

World.title: National Assembly speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer meets US delegation in Budapest
World.content:
Ágnes Forsthoffer welcomed a delegation led by Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx to Hungary’s Parliament, where discussions focused on strengthening bilateral parliamentary ties and addressing the country’s key challenges.

Hungarian National Assembly Speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer met an American delegation led by Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx at the Hungarian Parliament building on Thursday, calling for closer cooperation between the two countries’ legislatures.

In a Facebook post published on Friday, Forsthoffer said the US delegation had praised the results of Hungary’s spring election and asked about the most pressing challenges facing the country.

Trust, the budget and energy diversification

Forsthoffer said she had highlighted several priorities during the meeting, including restoring public trust both domestically and internationally, stabilising the difficult budgetary situation inherited by the new government, and diversifying the country’s energy sources.

She also stressed the importance of ensuring that the state operates transparently and economically. According to the Speaker, the American delegation offered cooperation and support in parliamentary affairs, an offer she said she welcomed and was keen to build upon.

The meeting comes as Hungary seeks to strengthen its international relationships and address economic and energy-related challenges. However, Forsthoffer’s statement did not provide further details about specific agreements or initiatives discussed during the talks.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

New Hungarian-American parliamentary friendship group planned

Forsthoffer also announced that a Hungarian-American parliamentary friendship group would soon be established. According to her post, 34 MPs have already indicated their intention to join, making it potentially the largest such group. The initiative is intended to help develop relations between the two countries, with the Speaker highlighting potential opportunities in areas including the economy and innovation.

“We trust in the further development of Hungarian-American relations, which will open doors between the two countries, including in the fields of the economy and innovation,” Forsthoffer wrote. She thanked the visiting delegation for its visit and what she described as its supportive trust.

While the meeting signalled an interest in closer parliamentary cooperation, Forsthoffer’s public account focused on the broad direction of future relations rather than outlining concrete policy commitments. The planned friendship group could provide a parliamentary framework for maintaining dialogue and exploring areas of shared interest between Hungarian and American lawmakers.

Read also: Ukraine thanks Hungary for ‘green light’ on key EU accession talks

World.title: Hungary considers ‘exit tax’ on wealthy citizens moving their money abroad
World.content:
Hungary’s government is considering a 15 per cent tax on unrealised gains for wealthy Hungarians who change their tax residency and move abroad. The proposed measure would apply to assets worth more than HUF 500 million, although the details have yet to be finalised.

Taxing the rich for moving money abroad?

Hungary’s government is considering introducing an ‘exit tax’ targeting wealthy citizens who move abroad and take their assets with them, according to reports on the government’s proposed tax reforms. The measure would apply to Hungarian citizens who change their tax residency and have wealth or savings exceeding HUF 500 million (approximately EUR 1.37 million).

Under the proposal, they would face a 15 per cent personal income tax on gains accumulated since acquiring their assets, even if those gains had not yet been realised through a sale. The tax would effectively treat the assets as if they had been sold at the time of departure, triggering a tax liability on the increase in their value, writes Népszabadság.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Different deadlines for moving within and outside the EU

The proposed rules would distinguish between those relocating within the European Union and those moving to countries outside the bloc. Hungarians moving to another EU member state would reportedly receive a ten-year deferral before having to pay the tax. Those relocating outside the EU, however, would be required to settle their tax bill in the year they leave, provided their assets exceed the HUF 500 million threshold.

The proposal is not yet final, and its details could still change. The government is expected to complete its tax package within the next week or two if it intends the new rules to take effect in January. The proposed exit tax would be separate from the government’s planned wealth tax, which is also open to public consultation.

More on the economy: An exact date of Hungary adopting the euro emerged with new roadmap proposed

Hungary’s wealth tax aims to raise HUF 200 billion

Finance Minister András Kármán has argued that Hungary’s tax system places a disproportionate burden on lower-income households because consumption is taxed heavily, while wealth is taxed relatively lightly. According to the minister, wealth inequality has increased in recent years, making a wealth tax necessary to create a fairer distribution of the tax burden.

Under the current proposal, individuals with assets worth more than HUF 1 billion (around EUR 2.74 million) would pay an annual wealth tax of one per cent. A higher rate of 1.5 per cent would apply to fortunes exceeding HUF 100 billion (close to EUR 274 million), with the first payments scheduled for 2027. The government expects the wealth tax to generate HUF 200 billion (around EUR 548 million) in annual revenue, describing this as a conservative estimate.

Kármán has said the wealth tax was designed to make transferring assets abroad unnecessary, arguing that wealthy individuals could face higher corporate and income taxes in other countries. Nevertheless, officials have reportedly begun developing the separate exit-tax proposal as a safeguard against the transfer of wealth overseas. The plans remain subject to change, and it is not yet clear what the final legislation will look like.

Read also: Hungary scraps EUR 73 billion motorway deal linked to Orbán-era allies, launches criminal complaints

World.title: 18-year-old Budapest student missing for three days as police appeal for information
World.content:
An 18-year-old secondary school student has been missing from Budapest for three days, with police appealing to the public for information about his whereabouts.

Bauer Dénes left his home in the Hungarian capital’s Zugló district at around 6 PM on 6 October and has not been located since, according to the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK).

The 14th District Police Department has issued a missing person notice and is continuing to search for the teenager. Police are asking anyone who may have seen the young man or has information about his disappearance to come forward.

What does the missing student look like?

According to the police description, Bauer is approximately 182 centimetres tall, with short brown hair and green eyes. When he left his home, he was reportedly wearing a blue hooded sweatshirt, greyish jeans and dark blue trainers with white soles.

Authorities have not provided further details about the circumstances of his disappearance in the available reports.

Dénes Bauer. Have you seen him? Photo: police.hu

Police appeal for public assistance

The Budapest police are urging anyone with information about Bauer’s current whereabouts or the circumstances surrounding his disappearance to contact the authorities.

Information can be provided anonymously through Hungary’s free, round-the-clock Witness Hotline on +36-80-555-111. Anyone with information can also call the national emergency number, 112.

Police have stressed that even seemingly minor information could help establish where the missing teenager may be.

Anyone who recognises Bauer from the description or may have encountered him since he left home on 6 October is encouraged to contact the authorities as soon as possible. The search remains ongoing.

World.title: Week in Review: Realities Old and New
World.content:
A new election in Bosnia and Herzegovina came with new technologies intended to increase the integrity of the voting process, sparking speculation ahead of the vote about how this might affect the results. Ultimately, the new technologies proved to be about the only novel thing in the elections.

Contrary to the expectations of many, voters reaffirmed support for entrenched nationalist parties even more strongly than they did four years ago. Nominally civic, leftist or pro-Bosnian parties were big losers. Our two analyses take a look at who the winners and losers of the elections were, as well as the prospects for government formation at state and entity levels.

World.title: For the Trump Administration, Kosovo is Now Just a Bargaining Chip
World.content:
Kosovo has finally broken its political deadlock, with parliament electing a new President after 20 months of wrangling that produced two early elections and brought the country to the brink of a third.

But the political turmoil is far from over. Demonstrations have erupted over the indictment of four former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders and the country remains deeply divided over its political future.

For a young country still struggling to find its political footing, one thing has been conspicuously missing: the United States. Washington once played a parental role for Kosovo, stepping in to broker deals and settle disputes, as US Ambassador Christopher Dell famously did in 2011, when he helped propose a presidential candidate after Kosovo’s political leaders could not agree on one. Today, Washington appears reluctant to play that role.

Since the end of the Kosovo war, Washington has envisioned its role as having a defined endpoint: the US would win the war, and Europe would take responsibility for maintaining the peace. Kosovo, and more broadly the Balkans, would eventually become a European responsibility.

World.title: Montenegro Detains Co-Founders of Pro-Russian Telegram Channel
World.content:
Montenegrin police on Friday arrested the two co-founders of the pro-Kremlin Telegram channel Rybar, Mikhail and Valeria Zvinchuk, along with three associates, accusing them of malicious political meddling in the Balkan state.

Founded in 2018, Rybar is a prominent Russian digital propaganda and geopolitical analysis network centred around a channel on Telegram, which is reported to have more than 1.3 million followers.

The Telegram channel administrators confirmed that the Zvinchuks had been detained along with other Russian citizens. They insisted that all of them were in Montenegro legally.

“Specifically, their plans included filming the Cetinje Monastery, for which a completely official request had previously been submitted. At present, the project team is in contact with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Russia, which is working to resolve the situation,” the channel administrators wrote on Telegram.

“Since there were no violations of local legislation, we are awaiting the release of all those detained,” they added.

Mikhail Zvinchuk is a prominent Russian military blogger who has been under EU sanctions since 2023 for allegedly spreading “disinformation and pro-Russian propaganda”.

He was a member of a working group set up by Russian President Vladimir Putin in December 2022 to coordinate Russia’s mobilisation efforts in support of the war in Ukraine.

Mikhail and Valeria Zvinchuk are officially designated on the British sanctions list.

In October 2024, the US State Department offered a $10-million reward for intelligence on Rybar over allegations that it was involved in interference in the American presidential elections intended to “sow discord, promote social division, stoke partisan and racial discord, and encourage hate and violence”.

The State Department accused Rybar of “bolstering Russia’s military capabilities and advancing pro-Russian and anti-Western narratives”. Zvinchuk was one of nine named people about whom the US was seeking information.

In June 2024, Bosnian Serb authorities announced a collaboration with Zvinchuk during his visit to Bosnia’s Serb-majority Republika Srpska entity, where he met Drazen Visnjic, director of the entity’s Agency for Information and Communication Technologies.

The Agency at the time said Zvinchuk and Visnjic had agreed to cooperate on establishing a media school, as well as other projects.

World.title: Albania Parliament Approves Municipal Reform Plan Amid Protests
World.content:
The Albanian parliament in session. Photo: Photo: Malton Dibra/LSA.



After a tense session lasting more than 12 hours, Albania’s parliament voted in the early hours of Friday morning for territorial reform legislation, as people protested against the outside the building and clashed with police.

Police said eight protesters were arrested during the clashes.

Opposition Democratic Party MPs opposed the reform. One MP, Gazment Bardhi, threw bottles of water at Prime Minister Edi Rama during the vote.

The government argues that the current map of 61 municipalities no longer reflects Albania’s demographic and economic reality.

Critics, however, say the only result will be greater centralisation and the further isolation of rural communities from public services, spurring even greater depopulation.

There was some criticism of the reform within Rama’s ruling Socialist Party, too, with MP Erion Brace expressing opposition but finally voting in favour. Asked why by journalists, he said: “I am still against the reform … I will tell you tomorrow about the motives for my vote.”

The law needed 84 votes to pass. The Socialists have 83 seats. According to media, Rama ordered Socialist MPs to “either vote in favour or leave the party”. With votes from the Social Democratic Party MPs, the law passed with 85 votes in favour.

Rama later on Friday said that the vote in parliament “gave Albania another modernising push”.

Albania’s municipalities have responsibility for waste management, drinking water, urban planning, public transport, social services, environmental protection, energy efficiency, climate adaptation, civil protection and local public procurement.

The reform comes 12 years after the last shake-up in which the number of municipalities was slashed from 400 to 61.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Reports of Trump’s Attempt to Reshape Poland’s Govt Spark Political Row
World.content:
Hungary tables wealth tax; Budapest mulls bid to host 2036 Olympics

Fulfilling a campaign promise, PM Peter Magyar announced this week his government would introduce a special wealth tax on individuals whose assets exceed 1 billion forints (2.7 million euros). The draft legislation – which is still subject to debate – uses a broad interpretation of private wealth, including real estate, assets in companies, shares, and savings held in both domestic and foreign banks. Those affected would have to pay an additional 1 per cent tax, effective from August 2027, over the 1-billion-forint threshold. For wealth exceeding 100 billion forints (272.5 million euros), the tax rate would be 1.5 per cent. The government expects the wealth tax to affect around 15,000 people in Hungary and generate an additional 800 billion forints (2.2 billion euros) in revenue over the next four years. According to Forbes magazine, the number of ultra-wealthy individuals who would come under the 1.5 per cent threshold is only around 35 or 36. As the wealth tax would be imposed on individuals, many families can breathe a sigh of relief, as their wealth would be assessed on an individual basis. Critics, however, warn that wealth taxes imposed on billionaires have not necessarily been successful internationally and could trigger an exodus of some individuals. To prevent people from circumventing the system, the Hungarian government would introduce a ten-year period during which those whose wealth was accumulated in Hungary would remain liable for the tax, regardless of their country of residence.

Hungary has expressed interested in hosting the 2036 Olympic Games, as was revealed by the International Olympic Committee this week. Under the previous government of Viktor Orban, which was keen to use international sporting events to burnish Hungary’s reputation, the country considered bidding to host the 2024 Olympics, but was forced to withdraw its application in 2017 after the newly established Momentum party collected more than 260,000 signatures in support of a referendum against the plan. Experts say that most of the sports infrastructure needed to host the Olympics has already been built over the past decade, largely due to Orban’s strong interest in sports. Budapest – and Hungary more generally – would now be well suited to hosting the Games, they say. The capital has already hosted the World Athletics Championship in 2023, while its swimming facilities are due to host the 2027 World Aquatics Championships, meaning that organising the Olympics would not require massive additional investment in sports infrastructure. A so-called Budapest Olympics Masterplan was already submitted in March by the previous government. The plan envisages a “regional Games”, with some basketball and golf events staged in Austria and Slovakia hosting equestrian events. Surfing would be held in Ericeira, Portugal. Gergely Karacsony, the mayor of Budapest, has cautiously floated the plans several times throughout the year, while PM Magyar also expressed support for hosting the Olympics in earlier interviews. “As the sports infrastructure required to host the Olympic Games has already been built in Hungary in recent years, an Olympic bid that involves no stadium construction and requires no significant investment in sports infrastructure is both feasible and realistic,” hvg.hu quoted the mayor’s office as saying. The costs are estimated at 5.5 billion euros, with 90 per cent expected to come from the private sector, while the projected economic benefits are estimated at 4.7 billion euros. According to a recent Median poll, 64 per cent of Hungarians would support hosting the Olympics. This is a considerable increase from the 50 per cent polled only two years ago. The list of countries competing with Hungary for the 2036 Games currently includes Germany, Turkey, South Africa, South Korea and Qatar.

World.title: Kosovo President’s Election Kindles Hope of Return to Stability
World.content:
Justina Shiroka Pula was inaugurated as Kosovo’s President on Wednesday after two days of unrest, three weeks of peaceful protests, and almost two years of political crisis.

The day before, Pristina woke up to the lingering smell of tear gas, which the Kosovo police had used to disperse a protest that turned violent on Monday night.

The protesters were demanding legal changes to curb the jurisdiction of the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers, after it convicted four former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders of war crimes.

On Tuesday, Kosovo also braced for the announcement of a new snap parliamentary election, as October 6 was the deadline for MPs to elect a new head of state. If the deadline expired, new polls would have been obligatory under the constitution.

World.title: ‘ChatGPT Diagnosed Me’: Patients’ Faith in AI Leaves Albania’s Doctors Feeling Frustrated
World.content:
After three intensive sessions and a series of specialised tests, Albanian psychologist Sonila Jaupbashi realised that the patient sitting across from her was not suffering from obsessive-compulsive disorder, or OCD.

The young woman, a third-year medical student in Germany, insisted she had been suffering from OCD for years.

“I had spent time and three difficult sessions, using specialised tests and questionnaires that are used to establish this diagnosis, and she had spent quite a lot of money,” Jaupbashi recalled to BIRN.

“Later, she admitted that she had been diagnosed by ChatGPT.”

World.title: EU Seeks Strict Classification of Toxic Compound Found in Croatian Subjects
World.content:
October the 9th, 2026 – The EU is seeking much stricter classification of the toxic compound discovered in the blood of Croatian subjects.

The European Chemicals Agency has announced that its Committee for Risk Assessment recommends that trifluoroacetic acid, known as TFA, and its inorganic salts be classified as substances toxic to reproduction. Index reports that this is one of the concerning PFAS compounds that was recently found in the blood of all 110 participants in a study conducted by the Greens/EFA group in the European Parliament. Among the test subjects were ten people from Croatia, from Gospić, Knin and Pula.

It is important to emphasise that ECHA has not yet adopted a final, legally binding ban or classification. The Committee for Risk Assessment (RAC) adopted an expert opinion and sent it to the European Commission, which still has to decide whether to introduce such a classification into European legislation.

what is being sought?

RAC recommends that TFA and its inorganic salts be classified in category 1B for adverse effects on development and in category 2 for adverse effects on sexual function and fertility. Their classification as persistent, mobile and toxic substances (PMT) and as very persistent and very mobile substances (vPvM) has also been recommended. This means that they are difficult to break down, move easily through soil and water, and can pollute water resources over a long period. Such a classification does not mean that every measured amount of TFA will automatically cause a health problem in humans. It indicates the hazardous properties of the substance itself, while the actual health risk also depends on the level and duration of exposure.

tfa was discovered in the blood of all 100 subjects

The Greens/EFA study covered 110 volunteers from nine European countries. TFA was detected in the blood of all participants. The authors of the study emphasise that this is an exploratory study that is not representative of the population of individual countries and that the results should be interpreted with caution. There is currently also no appropriate health reference value for the concentration of TFA in blood serum on the basis of which it could be concluded from the finding alone that an individual is health-endangered. In the Croatian part of the testing, ten people from Gospić, Knin and Pula participated, who travelled to Brussels for testing organised by Možemo! MEP Gordan Bosanac.

should the ec react more quickly?

After ECHA’s announcement, Bosanac called on the European Commission to speed up the procedure. “I welcome this decision of the European Chemicals Agency, which comes a few days after our study showed that TFA is present in the blood of European Union citizens,” he said. He announced that together with Greens/EFA MEPs he will demand that the Commission react within the next three to six months, instead of the procedure, as he claims, being stretched out until the end of the decade. Bosanac had earlier also requested a broader restriction of PFAS compounds, the gradual phase-out of their production and use, and European funds for more extensive population testing.

ECHA’s expert opinion is now with the European Commission. If the Commission, after consultations with Member States and other interested parties, accepts the recommendation, TFA and its salts would receive a harmonised and legally binding classification at EU level. Such a decision could then trigger additional restrictions under European chemicals regulations and other sectoral laws.

World.title: Friends of Animals Demand a Ban on Loud Pyrotechnics in Croatia
World.content:
October the 9th, 2026 – The Friends of Animals (Prijatelji životinja) Association is seeking a ban on all loud pyrotechnics in Croatia after the Netherlands set the ball rolling.

Friends of Animals have called on the Croatian Government to further restrict the use of loud pyrotechnics, after the Netherlands banned citizens from buying, possessing and using category F2 and F3 pyrotechnic products from the 1st of August this year. Index reports that in Croatia, firecrackers and string firecrackers from those categories have been banned for personal use since 2021, but other F2 and F3 products are still permitted under prescribed conditions. The association is demanding that the ban be extended to all category F2 and F3 pyrotechnics whose main effect is a strong explosion and noise.

“It isn’t logical to ban one product because of the noise and allow others that produce an equally strong or even stronger bang, just because they are not called a firecracker but, for example, an aerial bomb,” said Snježana Klopotan Kačavenda from Friends of Animals.

According to the association, the Dutch ban covers entire categories F2 and F3 for private users, while citizens still have access to category F1 pyrotechnics, which pose a very low risk and produce negligible noise. Professional fireworks remain possible under special conditions, and exceptions can be approved for some organised New Year’s celebrations. Friends of Animals believe that such a model would reduce the number of injuries, fires, material damage, noise and stress for people and animals.

The association has already proposed amendments to the Act on Explosive Substances and the Production and Trade of Weapons to the Ministry of the Interior. In addition to the ban on loud category F2 and F3 pyrotechnics, they are demanding that the use of the remaining permitted pyrotechnics for citizens be limited to only two hours around midnight on New Year’s Eve. They also propose that sales be allowed only on the 29th, 30th and 31st of December, that advertising of pyrotechnics and their sale in mixed-goods stores be banned, and that places of use and the number of public fireworks displays be further restricted.

Friends of Animals state that their petition for a ban on loud pyrotechnics has so far been supported by more than 40,000 citizens. “Croatia already has experience with the ban on firecrackers, a concrete proposal for amendments to the law and more than 40,000 citizens’ signatures for a ban on loud pyrotechnics,” the association concluded.
