This well-loved place understands the city like no other. It’s a café by day, then come evening, its not-so-secret bar opens. After more than a decade in the Legazpi Village neighborhood, it remains the kind of place both locals and visitors make a point of visiting.

A MODERN CLASSIC. After more than a decade, The Curator still sets the standard for handcrafted drinks.

Makati before the aesthetic

Chino Roces area (Little Tokyo, Makati Cinema Square)

Long before Japanese food went ubiquitous, locals flocked to Chino Roces for reliable favorites at Little Tokyo, while nearby Makati Cinema Square (officially Makati Central Square) retains its unpretentious charm — a retro hub where you can find old-school eateries, bowling alleys, art galleries, and eccentric bars. The ukay-ukay stalls here also draw a younger generation of thrift shoppers.

THE ORIGINAL JAPAN TOWN. Little Tokyo has remained a favorite for Japanese food and a taste of old Makati.

STILL STANDING STRONG. Makati Cinema Square has outlasted trends by remaining stubbornly itself — eccentric and unapologetically old-school.

To see Makati as a local is to know the city in all its contradictions. It is glass towers and narrow side streets, MICHELIN-recognized restaurants and Jolly Jeep meals, and so much more.

People may come for the version of Makati they have seen online, but when you’ve lived here most of your life, you come to recognize it in all its versions. Still, Makati has never belonged only to those who live here.

Every day, it welcomes people who come to work, eat, explore, or simply find their place in the city. And maybe this is why “Makati-maxxing” has captured the attention of many. The city leaves enough room for everyone to make some part of it their own. – Rappler.com

World.title: Pope Leo approves Tagle as first Asian dean of Catholic cardinals
World.content:
IN ATTENDANCE. Cardinal Luis Tagle attends Pope Leo XIV's inaugural Mass in Saint Peter’s Square, at the Vatican, on May 18, 2025.

The dean of the college of cardinals is considered the 'first among equals' among the Church's highest-ranking clerics and is responsible for taking charge of the secretive conclave process

VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo XIV approved Filipino Cardinal Luis Tagle‘s election as the dean of the Catholic Church’s college of cardinals, the Vatican said on Friday, October 9, in the first selection of an Asian cleric to lead the elite group that one day will choose Leo’s successor.

A former archbishop of Manila, Tagle has served as a senior Vatican official since 2020. He was widely seen as a likely papal candidate in the May 2025 conclave that elected Leo to lead the Church after the death of the late pope Francis.

Tagle, 69, replaces Italian Cardinal Giovanni Battista Re, who is 92 and retiring from the role.

Leo, 71, is relatively young for a pope, plays sports, and is in good health.

The dean of the college of cardinals is considered the “first among equals” among the Church’s highest-ranking clerics and is responsible for taking charge of the secretive conclave process, held in the Sistine Chapel, once a pope dies or resigns.

The dean, elected by his peers and approved by the pope, serves a five-year term that can be renewed once, according to Church law. The role has mostly been filled by Europeans, but was held by the late Beninese Cardinal Bernardin Gantin from 1993-2002.

Tagle was seen as a close ally of Pope Francis and is known for an infectious smile and is sometimes called by his diminutive nickname “Chito.” He leads the Vatican’s Dicastery for Evangelization, effectively the Church’s missionary arm. – Rappler.com

World.title: Over Two-Thirds of Myanmar’s Population Poor or at Risk of Poverty: UN
World.content:
More than 37 million people—over two-thirds of Myanmar’s population of more than 54 million—are experiencing or at risk of “multidimensional poverty,” according to the latest report from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) released on Thursday.

Drawing data from a nationwide household survey of nearly 7,500 people in 2025, the UNDP’s latest analysis examines what it calls multidimensional poverty, which looks beyond income and also covers non-financial deprivation, including access to education and healthcare, and other basic needs, amid economic and political crisis and natural hazards.

It said nearly 18 million people (32.6 percent) in Myanmar are multidimensionally poor, while more than 19 million (35.5 percent) others are vulnerable. That brings the total figure to more than 37 million people (68 percent) who either face poverty or are at risk of falling into it.

“Myanmar may no longer dominate international headlines, but the hardships facing millions of people continue to deepen,” said Kanni Wignaraja, UN assistant secretary-general and UNDP regional director for Asia and the Pacific. “We are seeing a depth of poverty in Myanmar that is eroding human development itself. This is a no-win war. Everyone is losing. The core muscle of the country is being systematically eroded.”

The survey found that people in rural areas are poorer than those in urban areas.

In terms of both severity and scale, the UNDP report highlights Rakhine State as the worst-affected area, with approximately 1.66 million residents enduring the most intense multidimensional poverty. Sagaing Region followed with a larger total of approximately 2.38 million people experiencing less severe poverty. Ayeyarwady Region ranked third.

The UNDP’s analysis indicated that poverty is driven by a combination of long-standing household vulnerabilities, including low education levels, insecure jobs and limited income, and wider pressures such as rising prices, natural hazards and armed conflict.

In war-torn Rakhine and Karenni (Kayah) states, poverty has been compounded by conflict, displacement and restrictions on movement.

To address poverty effectively, the report concluded that aid must provide intensive support to hard-hit conflict zones while reaching larger numbers of poor residents elsewhere, with assistance tailored to local needs.

World.title: Regime Shuts Down Myanmar’s Surging Online Gold Market
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has moved to ban online sales of gold and jewelry, citing the risk of flawed products and market destabilization.

On Wednesday, the Commerce Ministry announced it has suspended issuance of licenses for selling gold, raw gold, jewelry, art objects, and household items via online platforms. It threatened unlicensed traders with prosecution under the 2013 Essential Commodities and Services Law, which carries six months to three years in prison and fines up to 500,000 kyats (roughly US$ 240).

Under existing rules, online sellers must obtain a Commerce Ministry license, while those dealing in gold and gemstones must also secure a permit from the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Conservation.

Industry insiders told The Irrawaddy that more than 700 businesses have applied for licenses to sell gold and jewelry online in recent years. However, the ministry has now refused to extend expired permits, with inspections and enforcement expected to begin at the end of this month.

Online gold and jewelry shopping has become popular in Myanmar over the past few years, with internet outlets hiring actors and celebrities to promote their livestream sales.

Traders say the clampdown follows growing complaints from buyers that jewelry purchased via livestream “flash sales” was later rejected by pawnshops or gold shops.

“Online customers have no way of verifying the weight, quality, or reference price of their purchases. That leads to disputes and losses,” one Yangon jeweler explained.

Last month, Mandalay police announced the arrest of 11 foreign nationals and 17 Myanmar citizens accused of running online gemstone scams. Authorities said the suspects were using fake jade to defraud buyers in livestream sales.

Online gemstone sales remain permitted provided merchants hold a license from the Myanma Gems Enterprise and refrain from selling gold.

While the Yangon Region Gold Entrepreneurs Association has set the domestic reference price for 24K gold at 7.1 million kyats per tical, the market price exceeds 10 million kyats — a gap of 3 million kyats. Before the 2021 coup, a tical sold for under 1.4 million kyats.

Business owners warn that banning online sales will hurt digital commerce and marketing, which had surged during the pandemic. “Shops that relied on livestream promotions will struggle. Now we can only depend on walk-in customers,” one trader said.

World.title: China Takes Top Investor Crown in Myanmar, and More
World.content:
China now Myanmar’s top investor, trade partner

China is now officially the top foreign investor and trading partner in Myanmar, consolidating its economic grip as others retreat, according to a report by Japan External Trade Organization.

In fiscal year 2025 ending this March, Myanmar approved US$472.6 million in foreign direct investment, down another one-third or 31.5 percent from a year earlier. But inflow from China rose 2.1‑fold to $201.1 million, meaning it now accounts for 42.6 percent of the total.

The previous leader due to long-standing commitments, Singapore, dropped to second place with $155 million, while Hong Kong contributed $54.9 million, the report said citing data from Directorate of Investment and Company Administration.

Much of the Chinese and Hong Kong capital is in light industry, particularly garment and shoe factories.

Myanmar’s exports to China also climbed 24.7 percent to $4.312 billion over the period, while imports surged 42.6 percent to $5.952 billion. That means China now accounts for over one-third of of Myanmar’s total trade or 35 percent, up from 27.8 percent the previous year.

With the border disruptions, trade has shifted to alternative routes, says the report. The figures did not count China’s trade with territories controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance in northern Shan State bordering Yunnan.

Chinese documentary maps scam empires in lesser-known Shan hubs

A docuseries aired this week by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV has shed light on scam syndicates that thrived in four areas along Myanmar’s northern border. While Kokang’s scam empires have long made international headlines, the documentary focuses on three lesser‑known hubs—Wa, Mongla and Muse—as it boasts of Beijing’s “achievements” in cracking down on them.

The show identifies quasi-autonomous Wa territory as the incubator of regional scam economy. At the height of the boom, Mong Pawk alone hosted 265 scam centers involving nearly 60,000 people. But unlike the Kokang clans, who resisted Beijing’s demand to halt operations, the long- ruling United Wa State Army (UWSA) cooperated after one leader was arrested in Kunming and warrants were issued for others.

In October 2023, Wa authorities launched large‑scale sweeps of scam compounds, the documentary reveals. Since then, the UWSA has reported regular transfers of Chinese suspects and illegal immigrants, introducing procedures for voluntary return. More than 1,400 Chinese nationals have been reportedly handed back this year.

But it was in Mongla, controlled by the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA), where Beijing started its crackdown in September 2023, and the group cooperated with Chinese authorities. A second strike in July 2024 led to a border law enforcement cooperation agreement between Yunnan police and Mongla authorities, establishing monitoring and repatriation mechanisms.

The crackdown proved most difficult in Muse, where Beijing identified 33 distinct local armed groups and militias, each with over 100 members, alongside Myanmar military‑aligned forces. Unlike the fortified scam parks in Kokang, Muse syndicates operated out of ordinary hotels, apartments, and villas. Despite joint raids in April 2024, scam sites keep popping up like a game of Whac-a-Mole, with arrests continuing this year.

Scam arrests in junta-aligned territory

This week Naypyitaw reported the arrest of 87 scammers—75 Chinese nationals and 12 Myanmar—in the remote valley of Hopong in the Pa-O Self-Administered Zone in southern Shan. They were reportedly operating in makeshift huts, with dozens of computers, more than 500 phones and Star Link satellite dishes.

The self-administered zone, which also includes Hsihseng and Pinlaung townships, is controlled by the Pa-O National Army that is allied to the Myanmar military. Its leaders including Aung Kham Hti have close ties to regime chief Min Aung Hlaing.

The Chinese docuseries admitted that scam centers once entrenched in northern Shan State near the China–Myanmar border have relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy on Thai border since the crackdown in late 2023 but did not say where else they have scattered. The Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar has been identified scam operations in at least 17 townships in Shan including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse.

Taiwan warns against travel to Myanmar

Taiwan issued a fresh warning against travel to Myanmar this week, citing risks related to online scam centers, escalating conflict, and limited options for citizens’ rescue. The Taiwanese Foreign Ministry singled out the regime’s aerial massacre in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State in late September which killed at least 50 and injured 58, as evidence of insecurity.

At a press conference in Taipei, Michael Lin of the ministry’s Department of East Asian and Pacific Affairs said fighting between ethnic groups and the military regime make emergency rescues “extremely difficult.” He also warned of risks from scam centers, which are known to abduct unwary travelers, noting that its overseas missions have “almost no options” to assist citizens who get into trouble.

“If you know relatives or friends who insist on visiting these areas, make every effort to dissuade them, to avoid unnecessary trouble for themselves and their families,” Lin added.

The warning comes as the military regime intensifies its efforts to woo Chinese tourists from mainland China. Myanmar drew barely over 250,000 Chinese visitors in 2025, a sharp decline from the pre-coup boom.

Chinese explosives depot in KIA territory blows up

A blast at a Chinese road-building firm’s explosives warehouse in the village of Lagwi in Kachin State’s Chipwi Township killed seven and injured 11 on Oct. 2. The area is under the control of the Kachin Independence Army (KIA), which seized it in 2024 to secure its major export to China—rare earths.

The blast was so powerful it destroyed nearby homes and school buildings and was the third deadly incident at explosives depots in ethnic armed group territories this year. On May 31, a warehouse controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army in Namhkam Township blew up, killing more than 50 and injuring over 70. And on Sept. 8, a site under the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) in Hseni exploded, leaving at least 15 dead. Chinese companies are involved in mining in both areas.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Leader Says Will Take Back Migrants From Malaysia ‘as Soon as Possible’
World.content:
PUTRAJAYA, Malaysia—Myanmar will accept more returning migrants currently held in Malaysia “as soon as possible,” the war-torn nation’s leader said Thursday despite human rights concerns over the opaque repatriation scheme.

Min Aung Hlaing made the pledge on a visit to his counterpart in Malaysia, as he works to bring his country back into the international fold after staging a 2021 coup.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim invited Min Aung Hlaing, now installed as civilian president, for a two-day visit to discuss the return of thousands of migrants to his country.

Malaysia has historically offered safe haven to those exiled from Myanmar, hosting 190,000 refugees or asylum seekers from the nation—mostly Rohingya—according to the UN.

But Anwar is making a repatriation push amidst an uptick of anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia, defying concerns from the UN that his scheme cannot guarantee their safe return.

The country has been wracked by war since Min Aung Hlaing’s putsch, and there are fears the persecuted Rohingya may return to a country where they suffer violent persecution many deem genocide.

“We will take those verified nationals back as soon as possible,” Min Aung Hlaing said at a joint news conference with Anwar, in Putrajaya, the administrative capital.

‘Enhance collaboration’

Min Aung Hlaing has been a pariah in many capitals abroad since his putsch unleashed a civil war, but Anwar invited him for talks about returning Myanmar migrants.

Nearly 1,500 migrants arrived in back in Myanmar on Sunday after a five-day navy vessel voyage from Malaysia, where they were being held in detention centers before being shipped out.

Anwar in July announced that Myanmar agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya members, but the Malaysian government later said those sent back would be of “various ethnicities,” not only Rohingya.

Myanmar last month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the UN and rights groups.

Min Aung Hlaing’s two-day trip also comes as he makes a push for diplomatic recognition after being installed in April as civilian president, following elections branded a charade by democracy watchdogs.

Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) said in July they were seeking “gradual” engagement with Myanmar.

The 11-nation organization has frozen Myanmar out of high-level summits since the coup, presenting a united front to pressure its leaders into engaging in its conflict resolution plan.

But analysts say the consensus is now fraying.

Malaysia is the fifth ASEAN nation to host Min Aung Hlaing since he transitioned to ruling the country as nominally civilian president.

A five-point peace plan adopted by ASEAN’s leaders in April 2021, which among other things call for an immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar, has shown very little signs of progress.

This was highlighted by a Myanmar military airstrike late last month on a market in western Myanmar killing some 50 people—one of the deadliest recent bombings of the civil war.

Said Anwar on Thursday: “Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration.”

The aim ultimately was to “take Myanmar as part of our community of nations without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN.”

World.title: From Refuge to Repatriations: Malaysia’s Myanmar U-Turn
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia—Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim once urged his Muslim-majority nation to show solidarity with the persecuted Rohingya who fled Myanmar en masse, but this week rolled out the red carpet for the man accused of orchestrating their genocide.

Min Aung Hlaing touched down on Wednesday, invited for a two-day visit to discuss thousands of Myanmar migrants being sent back under a repatriation scheme touted by Anwar.

Malaysia has historically offered safe haven to those exiled from Myanmar by persecution or conflict.

The nation hosts 190,000 Myanmar refugees or asylum seekers, according to the UN, two-thirds of them from the Muslim Rohingya ethnic group.

But experts say fears that they burden Malaysia have been amplified by a cocktail of misinformation and an embattled Anwar, who hopes to capitalize on anti-Rohingya sentiment ahead of upcoming elections.

To carry out the repatriation plan, he has welcomed Min Aung Hlaing—previously shunned and credited with ordering the 2017 crackdown that sent legions of Rohingya fleeing to Malaysia in the first place.

Domestic hostility

Myanmar says it has repatriated around 8,000 citizens by air and 1,500 by sea so far this year, while Malaysia announced it is preparing 3,500 more to go back.

Kuala Lumpur has declined to say what proportion of returnees are Rohingya.

But experts say Malaysian attitudes towards migrants, particularly the Rohingya, soured during the COVID-19 pandemic when they became targets of misinformation about the disease.

“That hostility did not simply disappear afterwards,” Khoo Ying Hooi, an associate professor at Universiti Malaya, told AFP.

“This year there was another very visible surge in anti-Rohingya rhetoric online, alongside harassment.”

Newer resentments include claims that Malaysians are losing jobs to migrants, as well as the narrative that they are straining public resources or involved in crime.

“The early sympathy was very strong because Malaysians largely encountered the Rohingya through the language of persecution,” said Khoo.

“They were Muslims fleeing horrific violence in Myanmar, so religious solidarity and humanitarian sympathy came together quite naturally.”

But James Chin, a Malaysia expert at the University of Tasmania in Australia, said the nation was now dealing with a popular backlash against “allowing too many Rohingya to come”.

“This is ironic, because the only reason they were allowed to come in the first place is due to Islamic solidarity,” he told AFP.

“It has now changed completely the other way around.”

‘Election ploy’

In the past, Anwar appealed to Malaysians for solidarity towards migrants who fled upheaval in Myanmar credited to Min Aung Hlaing.

Min Aung Hlaing was the leader of the military when it began a 2017 crackdown evicting Rohingya in droves from their homes in western Myanmar.

The campaign is currently being weighed as a potential genocide by the International Court of Justice, but many rights monitors and some nations already deem it one.

Anwar’s about-face, which has seen him welcome Min Aung Hlaing and send back migrants, is partially due to a shift in domestic politics, experts say.

His Pakatan Harapan coalition has suffered setbacks in recent state elections in the runup to regional and national polls, which must be held by February 2028.

Among their defeats were losses to a coalition fronted by the United Malays National Organization, a formerly dominant party that draws much support from the Malay majority.

Yap Lay Sheng, a senior human rights specialist with NGO Fortify Rights, said Anwar’s repatriation push was an “election ploy” to court the vote of ethnic Malays.

“Anwar is being outflanked from the right in Malaysia. The conservatives and the nationalists have fashioned themselves as champions of the Malay majority interests.”

Targeting immigrants allows him “to be seen as a defender of the collective interest against outsiders,” said Yap, a powerful message for political campaigning.

‘Greater scrutiny’

Malaysia says all returned migrants have been sent from detention centers where they made voluntary decisions to go home.

But the UN has panned the scheme for being opaque and failing to provide guarantees of safety on return, as required by international law.

Min Aung Hlaing staged a 2021 coup that plunged the country into a grinding civil war, causing a fresh wave of upheaval sending yet more citizens fleeing abroad.

He is now making a push to normalize diplomatic ties after being installed as civilian president in April, following elections staged by his military junta and derided by democracy watchdogs.

Deals to return migrants may improve Anwar’s electoral prospects at home, but experts say it could tank Malaysia’s credibility abroad.

The repatriation came days after Malaysia’s foreign minister spoke at the UN General Assembly, advocating for international law to come to the aid of Palestinians.

“Malaysia speaks so strongly about the protection of civilians, humanitarian principles and the consistent application of international law in Palestine,” said Khoo of Universiti Malaya.

“There will inevitably be greater scrutiny of how those same principles are applied closer to home.”

World.title: Malaysian Firms Linked to Myanmar Military Aviation Supply Chain: JFM
World.content:
Several Malaysian companies, including some with direct financial ties to the state, are actively supplying or seeking to supply aircraft parts and maintenance services to the Myanmar military, which has been widely condemned for bombing its own civilian population, an investigation by Justice For Myanmar (JFM) revealed Wednesday.

JFM’s findings, based on leaked documents and commercial trade records, were announced during Myanmar coup president Min Aung Hlaing’s controversial official visit to Malaysia on October 7-8 at the invitation of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

The rights group said three Malaysia-based aerospace procurement and services companies—FJ Global Aeroparts (M) Sdn Bhd, Asia AeroTechnic Sdn Bhd (AAT), and Skyways Technics Asia Sdn Bhd—supplied or sought to supply parts to the regime military and its brokers, or in one case was approached to perform repairs, between 2023 and this year.

FJ Global sought to supply the regime with spare parts and critical components including weapons system parts for Russian- and Chinese-made aircraft used by the regime in its aerial campaigns, JFM said, adding that the company has sent multiple requests for quotations to international suppliers for spare parts for the regime’s warplanes and drones.

In February, FJ Global secured financing from state-backed Perbadanan Usahawan Nasional Berhad (PUNB), a company under the Prime Minister’s Department that is wholly owned by Yayasan Pelaburan Bumiputra, which is chaired by Anwar.

AAT is wholly owned by MARA Corporation, which is owned by MARA, an agency of Malaysia’s Ministry of Rural and Regional Development. According to JFM’s sources, regime military engineers visited the company in February 2026 regarding repairs to an Airbus A-319 owned by the Myanmar military.

JFM also claimed that Skyways Technics Asia, the Malaysian subsidiary of Denmark-based Skyways Technics A/S, has made numerous shipments of aircraft parts to arms brokers Light Head Group of Companies, KLS Aviation, United Five and Lucky High, which are registered suppliers to the Myanmar army’s Directorate of Procurement. JFM assessed that the Air Force was the likely end user.

Regime-controlled Myanmar National Airlines and Mingalar Aviation Airline (formerly Air KBZ), owned by the 24Hour Group founded by tycoon Aung Zaw Zaw, a crony with close ties to the junta boss, have also sought export approval to send aircraft parts to Skyways Technics in Malaysia for repair or exchange, the rights group said.

It noted that by knowingly providing support to the Myanmar military, which is widely accused of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity, Malaysian businesses could be aiding and abetting the regime’s crimes.

JFM also highlighted Malaysia’s ongoing facilitation of the regime’s participation in regional defense and security programs. Kuala Lumpur has invited a police official of the regime’s notorious Special Branch to attend the 29th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Intelligence Community Conference (AICC) in Kuala Lumpur in November.

Regime military officials were also allowed to participate in the 14th ASEAN Defense Minister’s Meeting (ADMM)-plus Experts Working Group on Counter-terrorism, which was jointly chaired by Malaysia and India in 2025.

The rights group said Malaysia’s support for the regime exposes the hypocrisy of its stated commitment to ending violence in Myanmar.

“It is deplorable that Malaysia is awarding false legitimacy to the war criminal Min Aung Hlaing and handing people back to his criminal junta while doing nothing to stop its companies from supplying a military that is committing mass atrocities,” said JFM spokesperson Yadanar Maung.

The rights group added that “Instead of taking steps to cut off the resources needed for the junta to continue its violence, Malaysia has turned a blind eye to business complicity, while providing false legitimacy to the junta and handing Myanmar people to a murderous military that threatens their lives.”

“Malaysia’s stance on the Five-Point Consensus [ASEAN’s peace plan for Myanmar] and its calls for peace in Myanmar ring hollow while it fails to stop its companies from providing the military equipment and services that support its campaign of terror against the people,” Yadanar Maung said.

On September 28, regime airstrikes on a busy market and surrounding areas in Arakan Army-administered Kyauktaw town, Rakhine State, killed 50 civilians and injured nearly 60. The deadliest-ever aerial attack on civilians in the state drew global condemnation. However, the regime has continued its deadly aerial campaign of bombing civilian targets in resistance-controlled areas across the country.

Malaysia has faced widespread criticism from international rights groups and politicians for rolling out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing, who faces an arrest warrant issued by an Argentine court over the military’s persecution of the Rohingya. The International Criminal Court’s prosecutor has also sought a warrant for his arrest over alleged crimes against humanity.

Malaysia recently defended its invitation as a necessary gesture to the coup leader for agreeing to receive deported Myanmar nationals.

World.title: Chinese Docuseries Hails Scam Victory as Myanmar Fraud Empire Rebuilds
World.content:
A Beijing-sanctioned docuseries on Myanmar’s scam industry has hailed the extradition of fugitive tycoon She Zhijiang as the crowning achievement of China’s crackdown. Yet the telecom fraud empire he built in the border town of Myawaddy continues to thrive despite international pressure.

Once a bustling trade hub, Myawaddy is now among the most complicated combat landscapes in Myanmar, fought over by resistance forces, splinter factions, and regime‑aligned militias each tied to cross‑border commerce and illicit economies.

The fraud industry’s origins trace back to 2016–2017, when She Zhijiang’s Yatai International Holdings struck a deal with warlord Saw Chit Thu, commander of the military-aligned Karen Border Guard Force (BGF). Marketed as a U$ 15‑billion “New City” project, Shwe Kokko was pitched as a blockchain hub but quickly morphed into casinos, call centers, and cyber‑fraud parks.

Belt and Road Beginnings

Yatai stated the project was part of the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s flagship international infrastructure development scheme. Thousands of Chinese nationals poured in. But by 2020, civil society groups were sounding alarms about criminal activities under militia protection, prompting the Chinese Embassy in Yangon to declare that the project had nothing to do with the BRI.

Aung San Suu Kyi’s NLD government ordered a suspension, but admitted it was difficult to enforce given the involvement of armed groups. After the 2021 coup, civil war engulfed the country and the scam industry boomed.

Today, Myawaddy’s scam compounds are hosted by the BGF (now rebranded as the Karen National Army—KNA) and the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), both allied with the regime. The documentary aired this week by China’s state-run CCTV made no mention of either militia.

At its peak, more than 40 heavily guarded scam compounds operated in Myawaddy, according to a Chinese police source quoted in the docuseries.

She Zhijiang was arrested in Bangkok in August 2022 and later extradited to China, but his legacy lives on in Myanmar’s borderlands.

Crackdown ‘Backfired’

The arrest of She Zhijiang had limited impact on the Myawaddy scam economy because he was just one of many investors, said one local China analyst.

“There are other criminal syndicates with longer tentacles than She Zhijiang. Since his arrest, nearly five dozen scam sites have sprung up across Karen and Shan states,” he said, adding that Beijing’s crackdown may have worsened the problem by forcing the syndicates to relocate deeper into Myanmar.

Beijing itself admits that syndicates uprooted from northern Shan State in late 2023 regrouped in Myawaddy, swelling the scam economy there.

China finally intervened in early 2025, forced into action by public anger over the trafficking of Shanghai soap actor Wang Xing into a scam compound. Wang was lured by a fake casting offer in Bangkok, whisked across the Moei River, and resold three times in four days by Myawaddy scam compounds before being rescued.

In March 2025, Beijing established a trilateral ministerial mechanism with Bangkok and Naypyitaw to combat scam syndicates operating along the Thai-Myanmar border, pinpointing Myawaddy as a key target.

Later that year, under mounting international pressure, Myanmar’s military demolished scam compounds in Shwe Kokko and KK Park during high-profile raids. However, locals reported that syndicates simply relocated to less conspicuous sites in Myawaddy and neighboring townships, under DKBA and KNA protection.

Regime-Aligned Scam Militias Untouched

“We have a zero‑tolerance policy for crimes like online fraud and gambling,” regime boss Min Aung Hlaing declared on Police Force Day earlier this month. Yet his BGF/KNA allies—Saw Chit Thu, Saw Mote Thone, Tin Win and others—remain untouched along with scam compounds they protect that have defrauded billions of dollars from American citizens, according to US authorities.

The CCTV documentary also celebrates the extradition of Chen Zhi, accused of running a multibillion‑dollar cyberscam network from Cambodia.

Meanwhile, China’s Public Security Ministry claims telecom fraud cases have declined since October 2025, following the crackdown in northern Myanmar. Not so, states the International Organization for Migration (IOM), which reports a sharp rise in trafficking to scam centers across Asia, with victims from more than 80 countries coerced into the trade. The UN estimates compounds in Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos still employ around 300,000 people.

Last month, Beijing unveiled the International Alliance Combating Telecom and Cyber Fraud with much fanfare, listing 46 founding countries including Myanmar. Officials hailed it as a landmark in global cooperation. Yet on the ground in Myawaddy, the scam industry remains a lucrative lifeline for militias and regime allies—a shadow economy still flourishing despite raids, indictments, and international pressure.

World.title: Myanmar Regime’s New Labor Minister Outlines Mission: Milking Migrants
World.content:
Less than 48 hours after taking charge of the Labor Ministry, Maung Myint’s first public statement ignored protections for Myanmar workers and instead focused on squeezing them for revenue.

On Monday, the newly appointed minister declared that income tax for migrant workers was too low, while vowing to tighten the regime’s remittance rules. Posting on TikTok, he said overseas workers “represent the nation” and should therefore contribute more to the country.

Economic collapse driven by regime mismanagement, withdrawal of foreign investment, sanctions, and civil war following the 2021 coup has triggered a mass exodus of workers. As a result, remittances soared to US$ 5.6 billion in 2025 according to Bloomberg—nearly 7 percent of GDP and double the 2019 figure. While remittances have become a crucial lifeline for millions of struggling families, the cash-strapped regime has targeted them as lucrative source of foreign revenue.

Maung Myint served as labor minister under Thein Sein in 2012-13, returning this April as hotels and tourism minister for the rebranded regime before being shunted the Labor Ministry on October 3.

Two days later, he warned that overseas workers are required to remit 25 percent of their wages through regime-controlled banks. “But some fail to do so, meaning the state sees no returns from workers it has sent abroad. We need to correct this and ensure the regime benefits,” he said.

Emphasizing management of overseas workers as a “key duty” of his ministry, he added that remittances from Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, China, Cambodia, Laos, the Middle East, the US and Europe were “too small” and must be increased.

Thailand hosts the largest number of Myanmar migrants, estimated at 4-5 million, followed by Malaysia (300,000–350,000). Myanmar is now the second‑largest labor exporter in Asia after the Philippines.

Labor rights activists point to the regime’s remittance policy as textbook exploitation.

“It imposes rigid rules to grab as much tax as possible from migrant workers. Cash-strapped and incapable of running an economy, it can only think of targeting citizens abroad who face deepening hardship as a result,” said Aung Kyaw, a labor activist in Thailand.

Myanmar migrant workers traditionally rely on the informal hundi system to transfer money back home. However, under the regime’s remittance rule introduced in September 2023, workers must remit at least a quarter of their foreign currency earnings through official channels. Workers have denounced the rule as brazen exploitation due to the exchange rate gap.

“If they want us to remit 25 percent through legal channels, they should use the market exchange rate. Currently, the market rate is 130 kyats per baht, but the regime offers just 63 kyats. If I remit 5,000 baht via a regime bank, I lose over 300,000 kyat instantly,” one worker in Thailand told The Irrawaddy.

The Central Bank’s official rate is 2,100 kyat per US dollar though since December authorized banks have offered 3,600 kyats. However, the market rate is around 4,300 kyats.

In August, the regime instructed Yangon employment agencies to enforce a Family Remittance Management System to ensure workers comply with the rule. Over 100 licensed labor agencies were recently fined and suspended for failing to provide remittance records.

The ministry is now collecting lists of workers who ignore the remittance rule, threatening them with non-renewal of passports and Overseas Worker Identification Cards.

Adding to the burden, the junta imposed a 2 percent income tax on overseas workers starting October 1, 2023. Only those who can show tax receipts are allowed to renew passports or obtain new ID certificates.

Thein Sein’s government abolished the traditional taxation of overseas workers under military rule. Desperate for hard currency, the current regime has not only revived the practice but doubled down on milking the very diaspora it forced into exile.

World.title: Caspian Sea’s Shrinking Shoreline Puts Regional Economies at Risk, Tokayev Says
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for coordinated regional action to address the Caspian Sea’s shrinking water levels, proposing a shared digital monitoring platform and an international biodiversity fund. The environmental crisis also poses growing risks to regional economies and communities, he said, speaking at the Caspian Ecological Summit on Oct. 9 in Avaza.

According to him, the sea’s surface area had decreased by more than 16,000 square kilometers between 2000 and 2025, while the Caspian seal population had fallen from around one million to 270,000 over the past century.

“The Caspian is a unique natural treasure, a source of well-being for millions of people, and a key transport and energy hub for the entire Eurasian continent. Therefore, preserving the Caspian Sea’s ecosystem requires special attention, primarily from our states,” Tokayev said.

“If urgent and decisive measures are not taken now, the environmental situation will deteriorate rapidly, causing irreparable damage not only to the peoples of the Caspian countries but also to the entire international community,” he added.

Shared monitoring and scientific cooperation

To address the ecological crisis, Tokayev proposed leveraging the Caspian Sea Research Institute, established in Kazakhstan in 2024, and partnering with research centers across the Caspian region to conduct comprehensive studies and develop joint strategies for adapting to environmental changes.

He also proposed creating a shared digital platform to collect and analyze information on water resources, shoreline changes, biodiversity, pollution and river flows.

“Satellite technologies, artificial intelligence and modern forecasting systems will make it possible to conduct real-time monitoring and identify and eliminate environmental risks in a timely manner,” Tokayev said.

Climate risks threaten regional economies

Tokayev said the Caspian’s decline must be considered in the context of wider climate change across the region. According to projections he cited, temperatures in some parts of the region could rise by 5 degrees Celsius by the end of the century, intensifying glacier melt, water shortages, droughts and land degradation.

He also referred to World Bank estimates that nearly 2.5 million people in the region could face the risk of internal displacement due to climate factors by 2050.

“The shrinking of the sea creates threats to shipping and port infrastructure, fisheries, energy, industry and the sustainable development of coastal communities. These are complex challenges that could lead to a large-scale environmental catastrophe,” Tokayev said.

He cited the Aral Sea disaster as a warning of the consequences of unsustainable resource management.

“We must under no circumstances allow such a situation to happen again. Saving the Caspian, which was once rightly called ‘great’ and ‘wise,’ is not simply our responsibility but a matter of honor for the statesmen of our time,” he said.

Kazakhstan highlights restoration efforts

Tokayev pointed to Kazakhstan’s environmental restoration efforts as examples of what sustained action can achieve. He said the area of the North Aral Sea had increased by 36%, accompanied by improved water quality, recovering fish stocks and a gradual revival of economic activity in surrounding areas.

He highlighted that some of the lessons from the North Aral restoration could be applied to the Caspian, particularly by combining engineering measures with scientific and nature-based approaches.

Tokayev highlighted the Caspian seal, whose population has declined substantially, as a particular concern. He also urged countries to intensify efforts against illegal fishing, poaching and the illicit trade in biological resources through information-sharing among law enforcement and environmental agencies, joint operations and digital monitoring.

Tokayev also announced the creation of an International Biodiversity Fund intended to bring together global efforts to protect shared natural heritage. Protecting rare species and the Caspian’s unique ecosystems will be among its priorities, according to Tokayev.

Joint projects and international coordination

Tokayev called on Caspian countries to develop a consolidated portfolio of promising projects covering both the sea itself and the river basins that feed it.

“We must restore water flows, river deltas and wetlands, and bring hydraulic structures into proper condition. Grants, concessional lending and other channels of climate financing can and should support this work,” he said.

Tokayev welcomed Azerbaijan’s proposal to establish an intergovernmental commission on the Caspian’s shrinking water levels at the level of deputy prime ministers. He also noted that Caspian states had approved Kazakhstan’s proposal to develop an interstate program for conserving the sea’s water resources.

“The Caspian is a single ecosystem that does not recognize state borders, so shared success is impossible without coordinated action in international organizations and financial markets,” he said.

Tokayev concluded by calling on regional governments and international partners to use existing political dialogue, legal frameworks, institutions and scientific expertise to preserve the Caspian as a source of life and prosperity for future generations.

World.title: News Digest: Kazakhstan’s Royal Visit, UNESCO Heritage Sites, Caspian Sea and More
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest covers the upcoming Belgian royal visit, Kazakhstan’s newly recognized UNESCO heritage sites, Japan-funded Caspian Sea monitoring and more.

King Philippe’s state visit to Kazakhstan to open new chapter in bilateral ties

King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium will pay a state visit to Kazakhstan on Oct. 12-14, marking the first state visit by a European monarch to a Central Asian country and a historic milestone in 35 years of diplomatic relations, reported Paris Match on Oct. 6.

The royal visit will bring a delegation of around 110 people, including four ministers, 25 business leaders and seven university rectors. The program will cover Astana and Almaty, with discussions focused on critical raw materials, transport connectivity, investment, energy, innovation, artificial intelligence and academic cooperation.

The visit is expected to give new momentum to bilateral ties as Belgium seeks to diversify its international partnerships and strengthen engagement with Central Asia.

Belgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot described Kazakhstan as a strategically important country located at the crossroads of major geopolitical and economic routes.

“Central Asia is a strategically important region and opens real opportunities for Belgium,” Prévot said, highlighting Kazakhstan’s critical raw materials and its role in regional energy and transport networks.

He also announced plans to open Belgium’s embassy in Uzbekistan next year and tour all Central Asian countries in 2027.

The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or the Middle Corridor, is expected to be an important element of bilateral cooperation. The route connects Asia and Europe through Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Türkiye.

According to the information provided ahead of the visit, freight volumes along the corridor have increased fivefold over six years, from 0.8 million tons to 4.1 million tons annually, with a target of 10 million tons.

Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Belgium Roman Vassilenko described Belgium as an important partner in the European Union, while noting the potential for cooperation in logistics, port infrastructure, agriculture, pharmaceuticals, science and green technologies.

King Philippe previously visited Kazakhstan three times as Crown Prince, including trips to Baikonur in 2002 and 2009 and an economic mission in 2010.

The upcoming visit, however, will be the first state visit by a Belgian monarch to Kazakhstan. It is also the first state visit by a European monarch to the country, underscoring the growing strategic importance of Kazakhstan-Belgium relations.

Inside Kazakhstan’s historic rock-hewn mosques now recognized by UNESCO

Five rock-hewn mosques and associated sacred sites dating from the 12th to the 18th centuries make up Kazakhstan’s newest UNESCO World Heritage property. The complexes preserve centuries of Sufi tradition alongside much older beliefs, Euronews reported on Oct. 7.

The World Heritage Committee adopted the decision at its 48th session on July 25 in Busan, South Korea. This follows President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s 2024 instructions to pursue the inscription of these rock-hewn mosques on the World Heritage List.

Set amid the otherworldly landscapes of Mangystau, the newly recognized mosques and their associated sites are named after revered Sufi masters: Beket-Ata, Shopan-Ata, Karaman-Ata, Shakpak-Ata and Sultan-Epe.

Japan funds $3 million Caspian Sea monitoring Project in Kazakhstan

Japan is funding a $3 million project to improve monitoring of the shrinking Caspian Sea, focusing particularly on Kazakhstan’s shallow northern basin. The project, implemented by the United Nations Development Program in Kazakhstan, was officially launched in Aktau on Oct. 5. Experts from across the Caspian region are expected to take part in joint research and a regional scientific platform partnership designed to improve the exchange of data and expertise, reported The Times of Central Asia on Oct. 6.

For Kazakhstan, the most immediate problem lies in the northern Caspian. The water there is extremely shallow, meaning that even relatively small declines in sea level can push the shoreline back considerable distances. Habitats used by Caspian seals and sturgeon are already changing, while ports and shipping face growing difficulties.

Scientists link the decline to changes in the Caspian Sea’s water balance. The sea has no connection to the world’s oceans and depends on river inflow, precipitation, and evaporation. The Volga supplies most of its river water, while rising temperatures are increasing evaporation.

Kazakh-British Business Council plans next meeting in London in 2027

The next meeting of the Kazakh-British Business Council is planned for London in 2027, Trend reported citing Samruk Kazyna.

The statement follows the fifth meeting of the Kazakh-British Business Council, which was held in Astana with the participation of more than 100 representatives of the business communities and government agencies of Kazakhstan and the UK.

Central Asia in search of its identity

The article explores how Central Asian countries are strengthening regional cooperation, economic integration and a shared identity without the need for supranational institutions, reported Asia News on Oct. 9.

“The main question is no longer which centre of power Central Asia will align itself with, but to what extent it will succeed in moving from the multifaceted nature of its states towards autonomy and regional action, whilst continuing to integrate with the outside world, yet becoming a region strong and connected enough to open up to it on favourable and equitable terms,” the article reads.

World.title: Tokayev Urges CIS to Rethink Cooperation as Global Trade Ties Shift
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed a new development strategy for the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) through 2035, calling for closer industrial and technological cooperation as traditional trade relationships come under strain.

Tokayev suggested creating a portfolio of joint industrial and technological projects until 2030 during his remarks to the Oct. 9 meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State in Avaza.

He also proposed holding a CIS-sponsored artificial intelligence forum in Astana next year and establishing a mechanism to exchange experience in AI strategies, legislation and government support.

He said a new architecture of international relations is taking shape, the system of global economic ties is breaking down, technological competition is intensifying, and uncertainty and unpredictability are increasing.

“Against this backdrop, direct and trusting dialogue, which makes it possible to find coordinated solutions that take into account the interests of every state, is becoming critically important,” Tokayev said.

CIS development strategy through 2035

The CIS, a regional grouping established in 1991 following the collapse of the Soviet Union, had played an important role in maintaining stability and preserving ties among its members, according to Tokayev.

“The creation of the CIS made it possible to avoid a total conflict in the so-called post-Soviet space. It would not be an exaggeration to say that the consolidating mission of the CIS was particularly evident during the period when our countries gained independence,” he said, highlighting that the countries preserved historical ties and built a fundamentally new format of interstate cooperation.

Tokayev called on member states to define the organization’s long-term priorities and its place in Eurasia’s changing geopolitical landscape.

“We, the CIS member states, must answer the question of what we want the Commonwealth to look like in the long term and what place it should occupy in the rapidly changing geopolitical architecture of Eurasia,” Tokayev said.

He noted that CIS markets remained important for Kazakhstan, accounting for more than a quarter of the country’s foreign trade turnover. Bilateral and regional trade with CIS partners reached nearly $40 billion last year and increased 10% in the first seven months of 2026.

Joint industrial projects and trade barriers

Tokayev proposed creating a portfolio of flagship CIS industrial and technological projects with a focus on products with higher added value.

He said modern infrastructure for business cooperation and new production facilities was emerging across much of the organization, but countries needed to make fuller use of this potential.

Tokayev also highlighted Kazakhstan’s efforts to establish a network of cross-border industrial and trade centers along its borders with Russia, Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic. The proposed joint project portfolio would complement these initiatives by encouraging industrial cooperation and investment across the region.

Russian language and cultural cooperation

Tokayev also urged CIS leaders to support the International Organization for the Russian Language, emphasizing the language’s role in education, science and cultural exchanges across the region.

“This organization has favorable prospects. I am confident of this, given that around 300 million people around the world have varying degrees of proficiency in the language,” he said.

He also stressed the importance of preserving and respecting the linguistic and cultural diversity of member states.

“Meanwhile, it is extremely important to maintain a careful attitude toward the linguistic and cultural diversity of CIS states, show due respect for the history, traditions and culture of all peoples, and seek more effective forms of cooperation in the humanitarian sphere to bring our peoples closer together,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev invited scholars, legal experts and historians from CIS countries to participate in an international conference in Almaty in November marking the 35th anniversary of the historical document establishing the organization. The conference will be organized by the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies.

Tokayev also welcomed Uzbekistan’s upcoming chairmanship of the CIS in 2027.

World.title: From Theater to Dance: Weekend Picks to Explore
World.content:
ASTANA – Step into the city’s cultural scene through theatre, performances and music. The Astana Times editorial team has curated a special list of events perfect for enjoying with friends and family.

Astana

“Ana Zholy” (A Mother’s Journey) musical performance, Oct. 11

The performance is a story about mothers, women and their lives. It explores the bond between mother and daughter, difficult choices and dreams that are sometimes left behind. It also touches on the words and feelings that are often left unspoken.

Venue: Musical Theater of Young Spectators; 47B Zhakyp Omarov Street. Tickets are available here.

Symphony Music Concert, Oct. 10

The evening will bring together the sound of traditional folk instruments and a symphony orchestra. The programme offers a chance to hear familiar musical traditions in a larger orchestral setting, combining the distinctive sound of national instruments with symphonic arrangements.

Venue: 8/1 Kuanyshbaev Street. Tickets are available here.

Non-Stop Opera, Oct. 10

Step into the world of opera and classical music with a programme featuring opera singers from Astana, Almaty and Tashkent. The evening will include excerpts from works by Rossini, Verdi, Offenbach and Bernstein.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konayev Street. Tickets are available here.

Folk Show, Oct. 11

Traditional Kazakh music meets contemporary sounds in a programme that combines folk works with world-famous hits and film soundtracks. The concert includes pieces such as “Adai” and “Makhambet” alongside music from Pirates of the Caribbean, Gladiator, Troy and other well-known works.

Venue: Qazaqconcert; 10/1 Mangilik Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

“The Bat” operetta, Oct. 10

Johann Strauss II’s beloved operetta brings together comedy, mistaken identities and lively music. The classic story follows characters caught up in a series of romantic and humorous complications, making it a light choice for a theatrical evening.

Venue: Abay Opera Theater; 110 Kabanbay Batyr Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Mundial Dance Cup, Oct. 10-11

Dance takes centre stage at this international competition, bringing together participants from Kazakhstan and several other countries. The programme includes Pro-Am competitions, solo performances, American Smooth and showcase performances.

Venue: Koktobe Hall; 35 A Omarov Street. Tickets are available here.

Hockey Match, Oct. 11

Sports fans can head to the arena for a hockey matchup between HK Almaty and HK Gornyak. The game offers a chance to enjoy a live sporting atmosphere and follow the teams as they compete on the ice.

Venue: Olympic Arena; 44/3 Abay Street. Tickets are available here.

World.title: Avaza and Kazakhstan’s Eurasian Framework of Access. How Astana Uses Multilateral Formats to Manage Connectivity
World.content:
Over two days in Turkmenistan’s Avaza resort area, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev took part in high-level meetings. On Oct. 8, the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia convened for the first time with Azerbaijan as a full participant. On Oct. 9, the CIS Council of Heads of State and the first Caspian Environmental Summit followed, part of a diplomatic week that Ashgabat presented as a showcase of its chairmanship.

Such trips are usually described through the lens of balanced diplomacy, with Astana balancing its neighbors, Moscow and Tehran. That framing holds, yet it explains little about why Kazakhstan needs so many platforms with overlapping membership, and why a president who regularly criticizes multilateral institutions for weak results keeps investing political capital in them.

The answer becomes clearer through the logic of Geo-Connectivity. In this framework, the resilience of a country’s external economic ties rests on four elements, namely goods, demand, infrastructure and the ability to secure access to that infrastructure. The first three create an economic link. The fourth determines the degree of dependence. For Kazakhstan, multilateral formats serve primarily as a tool for working on that fourth element. Through them, Astana shapes transit rules, route security and the availability of alternatives where its own leverage falls short.

Three platforms, three systems of dependence

Each meeting in Avaza corresponds to a distinct geographic system through which Kazakhstan connects to world markets.

The Consultative Meeting with Azerbaijan covers the western direction and the intraregional system. It includes the critical nodes of the Middle Corridor, the ports of Aktau and Kuryk on the Kazakh shore and Baku on the opposite one.

Tokayev proposed discussing, at expert level, the integration of the Middle Corridor with the TRIPP route through Armenia, and he cited a World Bank estimate that cargo flows across the Caspian could quadruple by 2040. He also listed the domestic projects meant to feed this route with cargo.

The Moiynty-Kyzylzhar and Darbaza-Maktaaral lines are nearing completion, the Bakhty-Ayagoz section is scheduled to open in 2027, and work has started on the Aral-Caspian mainline. Regional observers described his speech as a combination of infrastructure planning and candid criticism of regional governance.

The CIS meeting serves the northern system. Most of Kazakhstan’s oil exports pass through Russian territory and ports. In 2025, 64.8 million of Kazakhstan’s 78.7 million tons of oil exports moved through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, and disruptions in 2026 forced a downward revision of the production plan.

Good relations with Moscow do not fully insure this node, yet without a regular channel of dialogue Astana cannot manage the risks attached to it. Tokayev therefore used the same Avaza speech to reaffirm the importance of the North-South corridor. The CIS session brought together nine leaders of the Commonwealth and, for the first time in the organization’s history, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was invited to its expanded session. The leaders planned to adopt a statement on the 35th anniversary of the CIS and documents on law enforcement, cultural and information cooperation and foreign policy coordination.

The Caspian Environmental Summit addresses a node shared by the western and northern systems. The sea’s level has been falling since the mid-1990s and in 2025 it reached a historic low below minus 29 meters on the Baltic datum.

Shallowing limits vessel draft in ports and threatens the capacity of the Middle Corridor. Tokayev warned at the 2025 SCO summit that the situation was approaching an ecological disaster and later called for an interstate program to preserve the sea.

The summit, held at the initiative of President Serdar Berdimuhamedov, gathered the leaders of all 5 littoral states, who were expected to adopt a declaration on the sea’s environmental problems.

It follows 20 years of the Tehran Convention, the region’s framework for protecting the marine environment. Russia, according to presidential aide Yuri Ushakov, attributes fluctuations in the sea level mainly to climate. For Kazakhstan, this is one of the risks it cannot reduce alone and can only share with partners.

Dovetailing as insurance for access

Researchers Aliya Tskhay and Filippo Costa Buranelli describe the behavior of Central Asian states in multilateral structures as “balancing regionalism” operating through bridging, dovetailing and branding.

Dovetailing borrows its name from a carpentry joint whose interlocking pins hold two parts together. States bring the same issues to different platforms, and separate formats lock into a sturdier structure.

In the logic of Geo-Connectivity, this mechanism has a practical purpose. When a critical dependency is anchored in several formats at once, access to it no longer hinges on the position of a single partner.

The Middle Corridor appears on Kazakhstan’s agenda in the Organization of Turkic States, in dialogues with the EU and China, in the SCO and now in the format with Azerbaijan.

The idea of an International Water Organization, which Kazakhstan advanced under the UN umbrella, in Avaza became part of a common Central Asian position alongside the Framework Convention on Water Use. Astana is assembling a Eurasian framework from multilateral platforms that holds its links to markets in place when individual routes fail.

Criticism as a demand for results

Tokayev has been consistent in his criticism of multilateral institutions. At the 80th session of the UN General Assembly in September 2025, he spoke of a real crisis of trust in multilateral institutions, proposed discussing a revision of the UN Charter and argued that responsible middle powers deserve a stronger voice in the Security Council.

During its SCO chairmanship, Kazakhstan advocated a stronger role for the organization’s Secretariat and Secretary-General, and it thanked SCO partners for supporting the transformation of CICA into a full-fledged international organization.

In Avaza, the same logic was applied to Kazakhstan’s own region. Tokayev stated that of more than 200 initiatives put forward since 2018, only a small share had been implemented, and he proposed that foreign ministries take inventory of them.

At the same time, he insisted on preserving the meetings as a platform for direct dialogue among leaders, free from excessive formalization.

This criticism fits the arm’s reach principle, under which a state concentrates resources where it can genuinely strengthen critical links.

The Consultative Meetings belong to this category. Kazakhstan’s weight there is at its highest, major external powers are absent, and the rules of transit between neighbors depend largely on the participants themselves.

This is why Astana demands an audit in this particular format while defending its informal character.

The fate of a 2023 agreement shows how difficult the task is. At the Fifth Consultative Meeting in Dushanbe, transport ministers signed the Agreement on Strengthening Land Transport Connectivity in Central Asia, which provides for a joint commission to monitor implementation and is listed among the summit’s 3 main documents. Uzbekistan approved it in October 2024, and Kyrgyzstan decided to accede in February 2026. An institution designed to secure access to regional infrastructure spent nearly 2.5 years in domestic procedures.

From a list of initiatives to a map of dependencies

The audit proposed in Avaza could become Kazakhstan’s first step toward a tool its foreign policy still lacks, namely a map of critical dependencies in which each initiative is assessed by the route, commodity or node it protects.

The plan to raise intraregional trade from about $13 billion to at least $20 billion, the linking of border logistics hubs with industrial cooperation centers and the new railway lines gain priority once it is clear which supply chain they make more resilient. The same test applies to newer proposals such as the regional AI partnership program and the declaration on responsible use of artificial intelligence, which still lack timelines and budgets.

The second task concerns early warning. Caspian shallowing, pipeline disruptions, instability in transit states and changes in access rules at foreign ports are discussed in different formats. Bringing these signals into a single monitoring system would allow Kazakhstan to use multilateral platforms proactively.

The author is Allen Alekeyev, the deputy head of research at Nightingale Int. analytical center.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: How Export Growth Helped Kazakhstan Return to Current Account Surplus
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan recorded a $2.4 billion current account surplus in the first half of 2026, equivalent to 1.6% of gross domestic product (GDP), reversing a $3.6 billion deficit in the same period last year, as export growth outpaced imports, according to the National Bank.

The improvement follows a $13.1 billion current account deficit in 2025. The current account had been in deficit in nine of the 10 years from 2016 to 2025, averaging around 2.7% of GDP annually. The balance improved by nearly $6 billion year on year, with the strongest contribution coming in the second quarter, when the surplus reached $3.2 billion.

What the surplus means for Kazakhstan

The current account records a country’s transactions with the rest of the world, including trade in goods and services, investment income and current transfers. A surplus means that receipts from these transactions exceed payments abroad. For Kazakhstan, the shift into surplus reduces the economy’s reliance on external financing to cover current international payments. Stronger export receipts can also support the supply of foreign currency and create conditions for accumulating external assets.

Historically, Kazakhstan’s goods trade has generated a surplus, but payments of income to foreign investors have often offset a significant share of it. The current account last recorded a substantial surplus in 2022, reaching $6.4 billion, before returning to deficit in subsequent years.

Export growth drives external balance

A key factor behind the improvement was the expansion of Kazakhstan’s trade surplus. In the first half of 2026, the surplus in goods trade more than doubled, from $7.7 billion to $16.2 billion.

Exports of goods, measured using the National Bank’s balance-of-payments methodology, rose 27.1% to $48.5 billion. Growth was recorded across more than 80% of commodity categories.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, exports of copper and copper cathodes increased 58%, copper ores and concentrates rose 42.9%, uranium grew 15.1% and wheat increased 28.2%. Sulfur exports nearly tripled, while silver exports more than doubled.

The positive trend continued over the first seven months of the year. Goods exports increased 15.8% to $50.9 billion, while the foreign trade surplus reached $14 billion, up $5.4 billion from the same period in 2025.

Non-commodity exports also expanded amid growth in manufacturing output. They rose 19.5% to $18.6 billion, while manufacturing production increased 9% over the period.

Agricultural exports grew 34.8%, from $3.7 billion to $5 billion. Key contributors included wheat, up 25.5%, sunflower oil, up 49.1%, animal feed, up 68.2%, flax seeds, which more than doubled, and flour, up 37.1%. These products accounted for nearly 60% of agricultural exports.

Imports shift toward production and investment

Imports also increased, but at a considerably slower pace than exports. Under the National Bank’s balance-of-payments methodology, goods imports rose 6.2% to $32.3 billion in the first half of 2026.

The composition of imports changed, with higher purchases of production inputs and equipment alongside a decline in consumer goods. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, imports increased 5.5% to $31.5 billion. Intermediate goods accounted for 47.6% of the total, with imports in this category rising 14% to $15 billion.

Imports of investment goods increased 10.6% to $8.1 billion. Purchases of electricity-generating units rose 83%, machinery for lifting and handling goods increased 70.1%, and equipment for sorting and crushing soil more than doubled.

Intermediate goods imports also grew, including natural gas, up 96.3%, turbojet engines and gas turbines, up 2.7 times; petroleum products, up 41.6%, uranium, up 2.6 times, and gold, up sixfold.

The increase in equipment purchases coincided with higher investment in fixed capital, which grew 9.6% in real terms to 9.5 trillion tenge (US$21.2 billion). Investment in manufacturing rose 33.3% to 1.43 trillion tenge (US$3.2 billion), accounting for 15% of total fixed-capital investment.

Manufacturing output increased 9.8%, while machinery production grew 23.1% and chemical industry output rose 20.7%.

The figures suggest that part of the import growth is linked to the construction of new facilities, the expansion of existing production and technological upgrades. The economic returns from these investments will depend on the capacity being brought into operation and its contribution to domestic production.

Consumer imports decline

In contrast to purchases of equipment and production inputs, imports of consumer goods declined. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, consumer goods imports fell 10.5% to $8.3 billion in the first half of 2026. Imports of passenger cars decreased 21.9%, pharmaceuticals fell 18.7%, suitcases and bags dropped 49.4%, women’s textile clothing declined 38.9%, and air conditioners fell 34.3%.

The National Bank reported that imports of non-food consumer goods had been declining for 11 consecutive quarters, beginning in the fourth quarter of 2023.

The decline in passenger car imports coincided with an increase in domestic production. From January to June, Kazakhstan produced 88,886 passenger cars, up 37.2% year on year, while sales in the official dealership segment remained stable. This points to partial import substitution through domestic vehicle assembly.

World.title: Rybakina Confirms Participation in 2026 WTA Finals in Indian Wells
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina has confirmed her participation in the 2026 WTA Finals, which will take place in Indian Wells, California, from Nov. 8 to 15.

In a video message published on the Women’s Tennis Association’s (WTA) official social media accounts, the world No. 1 expressed her excitement about qualifying for the season-ending tournament.

“I’m very happy to qualify for the WTA Finals. Come and watch us play in Indian Wells,” Rybakina said.

Rybakina secured her place in the tournament ahead of schedule, becoming the first player to qualify for this year’s edition. She will return to defend her title after winning the WTA Finals last season. The Kazakh player has enjoyed an outstanding season, winning the Australian Open and the US Open before reaching the top of the world rankings for the first time in her career.

Aryna Sabalenka and Mirra Andreeva have also secured places in the singles competition. The remaining five spots will be determined over the coming weeks.

Rybakina’s participation comes after concerns over a back injury forced her to withdraw from a recent tournament in Wuhan, China. She took time off to recover following a demanding North American swing.

The WTA Finals bring together the leading players of the season. This year’s tournament is scheduled to run from Nov. 8 to 15 at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden.

World.title: Kazakhstan Bridges Distances With Major Transport Upgrades
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan built, reconstructed and repaired more than 19,000 kilometers of roads between 2023 and 2025, while expanding railway infrastructure and domestic flight connections to improve regional connectivity and strengthen its transit capacity.

The modernization program includes major infrastructure projects and digital technologies aimed at reducing travel times, improving passenger mobility and accelerating freight transportation along international corridors, according to the Kazakh government’s press office.

Road upgrades improve regional access

Road construction, reconstruction and repairs covered 5,656 kilometers in 2023, increasing to 7,306 kilometers in 2024 before reaching 6,178 kilometers in 2025.

In 2026, work is underway on more than 11,000 kilometers of roads, including 3,400 kilometers of national highway construction and reconstruction, 5,000 kilometers of major and medium-scale repairs on national roads and 2,400 kilometers of local road repairs.

The upgrades come amid growing demand for road transport. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, the number of passengers transported by road rose from 1.5 billion in 2023 to 1.7 billion in 2024 and 1.9 billion in 2025. In the first eight months of 2026, the figure reached 1.3 billion, up 3.9% from the same period in 2025.

Efforts to improve rural accessibility have also advanced. Between 2023 and 2025, work was completed on 10,200 kilometers of local roads, including 556 kilometers of newly built roads, providing year-round connections to district and regional centers.

The government expects 95% of national highways and 92% of local roads to meet technical standards by the end of 2026, up from 92% and 86%, respectively, in 2023. The targets for 2029 are 97% and 94%.

Major highway projects are expected to further reduce travel times and expand interregional and transit connections. Among them is the 896-kilometer Center-West route, which will connect Astana with western Kazakhstan through Arkalyk and Yrgyz.

Railway expansion strengthens passenger and freight transport

Kazakhstan has laid 911 kilometers of new railway tracks over the past five years, with another 800 kilometers under construction and approximately 2,600 kilometers of existing tracks undergoing modernization.

Railways carried a combined 60.2 million passengers between 2023 and 2025. Since the beginning of 2026, Passenger Transportation, a national passenger rail operator, has served 7.5 million passengers, with the highest passenger volumes recorded in Almaty, Astana, Shymkent and the Abai, Aktobe, Karagandy, Kyzylorda and Zhambyl Regions.

Passenger services have also become more accessible. Women-only carriages now operate on 13 routes and have carried 946,000 passengers since their introduction. Passengers with disabilities and their companions are eligible for a 50% fare discount on socially significant routes, while 396,000 tickets for designated accessible spaces were issued in the first seven months of 2026.

Digitalization is also accelerating international freight transportation. The Digital Trade Corridor platform integrates railway systems in Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Georgia along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, through a single-window system.

Its Tez (fast in Kazakh) Customs module enables paperless customs transit procedures, reducing clearance times from eight hours to 30 minutes. Combined with other infrastructure and operational improvements, cargo delivery times along the corridor have fallen from 38 days to 13-17 days, according to the government. The next target is to achieve consistent delivery times of 10-12 days for shipments from China to ports in Georgia and Türkiye.

Domestic aviation network expands to 890 weekly flights

Kazakhstan’s domestic aviation network has grown steadily, with airlines operating 630 weekly flights across 51 routes in 2023. This increased to 669 flights across 57 routes in 2024 and 821 flights across 60 routes in 2025. As of September 2026, approximately 890 weekly flights operated across 60 domestic routes.

The expansion has been accompanied by the restoration of regional airports. On Aug. 22, subsidized flights began operating between Arkalyk and Astana, Almaty and Kostanai following the reopening of Arkalyk Airport. Each route operates twice a week, with flights between Arkalyk and Astana taking approximately 40 minutes.

Airport modernization is continuing elsewhere in the country. The runway at Pavlodar Airport was upgraded in 2026, while construction of new airports in Zaisan, Katon-Karagai and the Kenderli resort area is scheduled for completion by the end of the year.

Further runway construction and reconstruction projects are planned through 2029 in Astana, Almaty, Shymkent, Taraz, Aktobe, Oral and Zhezkazgan, alongside terminal upgrades at major airports.

To support air cargo transportation, the government has introduced a 12-year duty-free regime for cargo aircraft and simplified export procedures for selected goods, including aviation-related products, to countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

World.title: Armenian AI factory rejects Russian allegations of intelligence gathering
World.content:
Firebird AI rejects Russian espionage allegations

“Claims circulating about Firebird AI’s activities are untrue and have no factual basis,” the Armenia-based company Firebird AI said in response to remarks by Alexei Shevtsov, deputy secretary of Russia’s Security Council.

On 8 August 2026, Firebird AI opened the first AI factory in the city of Hrazdan. It is the largest data centre in the region and plans to expand its operations further. The facility already uses more than 6,000 NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 graphics processing units (GPUs). By the end of 2027, the company plans to deploy more than 70,000 NVIDIA Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips. The project has received around $500 million in initial investment. Total investment could reach $4 billion or more.

The Russian official claimed that this powerful data centre could be used for espionage: “Such centres could support analytical and intelligence operations on behalf of Western intelligence agencies, including against Iran, Russia and countries in the South Caucasus and Central Asia.”

This is not the first time Alexei Shevtsov has criticised projects under way in Armenia. Around the same time, he also expressed concern about the Armenian-American TRIPP initiative, known as the “Trump Route”, which aims to unblock regional transport links. According to Shevtsov, the project could lead to the deployment of US private military companies and intelligence infrastructure in Armenia.

“The computing capacity is used exclusively for civilian purposes”

Firebird AI said its AI factory is a technology company that develops and operates high-performance computing infrastructure.
