“The US export licence issued to the company restricts the use of the relevant computing capacity exclusively to civilian purposes.”

Firebird AI’s management said the Russian Security Council deputy secretary’s claims showed a lack of understanding of how AI computing infrastructure operates.

“The geographical location of these services does not, in itself, determine the nature or purpose of their use.”

What concerns Russia

Alexei Shevtsov said that Firebird AI’s US jurisdiction could allow US intelligence agencies to access all the data stored on its servers.

“This means that data belonging to Armenian government agencies, companies and citizens could become accessible to the United States without the consent of the Armenian authorities.”

However, the main concern centres on the possibility that the data centre could gather intelligence. This could allegedly affect not only Russia’s interests but also those of Iran, for example.

The Russian Security Council representative then turned to Armenia’s energy capacity.

“According to announced plans, Firebird intends to increase the capacity of its Hrazdan complex to 300 MW by the end of 2027. This represents almost a quarter of Armenia’s winter peak electricity demand of 1.3 GW. The announced plans will require additional generating capacity to keep the centre running.”

This issue concerns Russia because Armenia plans to build a new nuclear power plant, and Russia hopes to secure the contract. Russia built the existing Metsamor nuclear power plant. Against this backdrop, Shevtsov questioned the need to diversify Armenia’s partnerships in the nuclear energy sector.

Armenia may instead opt for the small modular reactors that the United States has offered, as previously discussed. In that case, Shevtsov said:

“I would like to emphasise that the United States has not built and is not building any small modular reactors abroad. Meanwhile, Rosatom is currently building 30 power units abroad, including small modular reactors. The choice, as they say, is obvious.”

World.title: ‘Civil society has the right to participate safely’: OSCE chair responds to Georgian authorities
World.content:
At the OSCE Human Dimension Conference in Warsaw, a representative of Switzerland, the organisation’s chair for 2026, said that the Chairpersonship was concerned about remarks made by the authorities in Georgia regarding the participation of Georgian civil society representatives in the conference, as well as information received from human rights defenders.

The Swiss representative’s statement followed comments by Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili about NGO representatives attending the conference in Warsaw. On 7 October, Papuashvili said he did not understand how they had paid for the trip or who was funding them:

“How do they pay for these trips, and who funds them? These organisations are not registered in the transparency register. If they do not disclose [the source of their income] to the state, it means they are funded by ‘black money’. This is further evidence that organisations in Georgia receive ‘black money’, including from various European institutions,” the speaker said.

What did the Swiss representative say?

“Providing a platform where civil society representatives can participate and engage with OSCE participating States and executive structures is one of the OSCE’s core values. They must be able to do so without facing any negative consequences.

This is essential for the OSCE’s mechanisms to function. We are concerned about comments made in connection with the participation of Georgian civil society representatives in this conference, as well as reports received from various human rights defenders attending the OSCE Human Dimension Conference in Warsaw. We reiterate the importance of ensuring safe participation in OSCE events, without any reprisals.”

Incident at the conference

The conference in Warsaw is attended by Baia Pataraia, head of the Georgian NGO Sapari, and Tamar Oniani, head of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association.

On 5 October, during a speech by a representative of the Georgian delegation, Pataraia held up a banner reading: “Free all Georgian political prisoners.”

Pataraia says her protest was peaceful and silent, and that she had arranged it in advance in accordance with OSCE rules.

“Wherever I find myself alongside the [Georgian] government, I will remind them that prisons are full of political prisoners and that the Georgian people will never accept this,” she says.

Pataraia adds that Germany, Slovenia and other countries have urged Georgia to implement the recommendations of the Moscow Mechanism and stop persecuting media representatives, politicians and civil society members.

In this context, she also criticised the Georgian authorities’ bid to make Georgia the OSCE chair in 2027.

“They want benefits, money, prestige and power from everyone, but they themselves fulfil none of their obligations,” Pataraia said indignantly.

The ruling Georgian Dream party is seeking to secure the OSCE chairpersonship for 2027. Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili says the country has already submitted its application to the OSCE and hopes to win the support of participating States. However, according to the publication Rapporteur, EU member states do not support Georgia’s bid.



OSCE conference in Warsaw

World.title: Abkhazia plans pension reform, new law to take work history into account
World.content:
The government of Abkhazia has drafted a pension reform bill aimed at streamlining pension legislation, taking employment history into account when calculating pension payments and introducing specific support measures for socially vulnerable groups.

The draft pension law was prepared by the Ministry of Social Welfare and Demographic Policy. According to Minister Kama Adzynba, the bill aims to streamline regulations governing employment-related, insurance-based and funded pensions, as well as payments for special services to the country.

One of the key principles of the proposed reform is to take individuals’ employment history into account when determining pension payments. Currently, pensions in Abkhazia stand at 6,000 roubles [approximately $70], a standard amount paid to everyone, regardless of whether they have worked for many years or have never been formally employed.

Pensioners who hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship and also receive a Russian pension have their Abkhaz pension reduced to a largely symbolic 500 roubles [around $6].

The new system is intended to address this “injustice”. It also provides for survivor’s pensions and other social benefits, which are expected to exceed the basic social pension.

The bill also introduces special pensions for distinguished service to the country. Recipients of state orders and veterans of the 1992-93 Georgian-Abkhaz war are among those proposed for inclusion in this category.

The draft law will be submitted to parliament for consideration.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s $90bn reserves draw criticism from former opposition leader
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s foreign currency reserves

Ilgar Mammadov, former chairman of Azerbaijan’s Republican Alternative (ReAl) party, has criticised the country’s accumulation of $90bn in foreign currency reserves. In a Facebook post, he argued that there was little reason to take pride in such substantial reserves when some elderly citizens were forced to survive on modest social benefits.

Mammadov proposed using part of the reserves to improve living standards while expanding economic freedoms.

“There are no reasonable grounds for a country like Azerbaijan to hold $90bn in foreign currency reserves,” the politician wrote.

What makes up Azerbaijan’s $90bn in foreign currency reserves?

Azerbaijan’s strategic foreign currency reserves comprise the Central Bank’s foreign exchange reserves and the assets of the State Oil Fund (SOFAZ). According to figures published by the State Statistical Committee, their combined value stood at $90.77bn as of 1 September 2026. This represents the total value of funds held in various financial assets.

The two institutions’ reserves serve different purposes. The Central Bank’s reserves are used to maintain stability in the foreign exchange market and mitigate risks associated with external payments.

The State Oil Fund accumulates revenues from oil and gas production, invests them, makes transfers to the state budget and builds up savings for future generations. Its assets are invested in bonds, equities, gold and property.

The authorities regard the substantial reserves as an indicator of the country’s financial resilience. Speaking at the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in September, President Ilham Aliyev stressed that the reserves were approximately 20 times greater than the country’s external public debt.

According to Aliyev, this demonstrates the strength of Azerbaijan’s financial system and the stability of its national currency.

‘These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace’

Mammadov also approaches the issue from the perspective of public welfare. He argues that elderly citizens have contributed to the creation of national wealth not only through formal employment but also through domestic and agricultural work.

“Only the government of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) can proudly boast of having $90bn in foreign currency reserves in a country where 180,000 elderly citizens receive no retirement pension and are forced to make do with an old-age allowance of $130. This is simply shameful.

“People over the age of 65 have contributed to society throughout their lives through their labour and their role as consumers in the economy, helping to create the conditions for accumulating $90bn in foreign currency reserves.

“Whether it was a housewife who spent years supporting her husband as he worked as a labourer or engineer, or a man who worked in the fields for a pittance, supplying city residents with fresh fruit and vegetables, they all contributed to building up these reserves.

“This is a hardworking generation that the YAP authorities have left with virtually no means of subsistence in old age, while continuing to boast about the country’s foreign currency reserves.”

Mammadov argues that taking pride in growing reserves while this generation faces financial hardship is also morally unacceptable.

“Viewed from this perspective, even the question of economic efficiency becomes secondary. These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace.”

Assets held abroad and dependence on oil

Mammadov also argues that holding substantial foreign currency reserves abroad carries political risks. He cites Iraq and Libya as examples, pointing to the depletion of their financial resources during wars and the freezing of their assets. He links these events to the interests of external powers and suggests that Azerbaijan could face similar risks.

“By maintaining foreign currency reserves on this scale, Azerbaijan is merely provoking major players in the current world order, who are accustomed to playing by their own rules. It is like putting on our most expensive jacket, stuffing its pockets with bundles of cash and going for a walk at night down the most crime-ridden street in the city.

“There are plenty of historical examples. In 1980, Iraq’s foreign currency reserves stood at 36bn–40bn. In today’s money, that is just over $90bn. And what happened? A war with Iran was soon orchestrated, partly for the sake of that money, though not exclusively. As a result, all the money was spent on purchasing weapons from abroad, and the reserves were exhausted. Who benefited? The arms dealers.

“In 2011, Libya’s foreign currency reserves had barely reached $150bn when the country was plunged into turmoil. Some of the money was spent on arming the sides in the civil war, while around a third of the assets were frozen in foreign financial institutions (and someone is still profiting from them). The rest has never been traced.

“In today’s world, where the law of the jungle prevails, there is no point in keeping such substantial foreign currency reserves abroad. One day, a provocation could be staged against us too, and the money could be seized,” he wrote.

Mammadov also sees a potential collapse in financial markets as a serious threat. He believes securities are significantly overvalued and that a sharp fall in their prices could result in substantial losses for Azerbaijan.

Another of his arguments concerns the economy’s dependence on oil. Recalling the currency devaluations of 2015, he notes that the country’s foreign currency reserves failed to prevent the sharp depreciation of the manat.

“The reason reserves are rapidly depleted during a crisis and cannot serve as a financial safety net lies in the unhealthy state of our economy and its dependence on oil.”

According to Mammadov, if oil prices remain low for a prolonged period, substantial foreign currency reserves alone cannot guarantee economic security.

What does Mammadov propose?

Mammadov is not calling for Azerbaijan to spend all its foreign currency reserves. He believes some funds should be retained to deal with economic crises and natural disasters, although he does not specify how much should be set aside.

“There is an urgent need to improve people’s living standards, particularly those of the elderly. At the same time, economic freedoms must be expanded without delay so that citizens can realise their creative and entrepreneurial potential and generate new wealth,” the politician wrote.

Mammadov sees the rule of law as a fundamental prerequisite for these reforms. He concluded his post by urging voters to support the Republican Alternative (ReAl) party.

World.title: Pashinyan on extradition of Azerbaijani soldier, meeting Aliyev and Medvedev’s statement
World.content:
Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

The extradition of Azerbaijani serviceman Nasimi Musayev is not under discussion, and Baku has not made such a request. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists this during his traditional hour-long briefing.

“What extradition are you talking about? There is no such issue, and we are not discussing it. Azerbaijan has made no request,” he said.

At the same time, he stressed that Armenia would have returned Musayev on the same day if he had not committed a crime.

Pashinyan described the Azerbaijani serviceman, who illegally crossed into Armenia and shot a resident of the village of Shaki, as having committed an “ordinary crime”. The prime minister drew parallels with other forms of cross-border crime:

“We also have other cases of cross-border crime. Drugs are constantly exported to Armenia and transported through Armenia in transit. There is no need to turn this into an apocalypse.”

The prime minister does not believe the incident in Shaki could threaten the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

He considers the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established an achievement that requires protection. He warns that they could destroy it in a day, while reaching the current state of relations could take another 30 years. For this reason, he does not consider it appropriate to make statements that could threaten the peace process.

On 1 October 2026, Nasimi Musayev illegally entered the village of Shaki in Armenia’s Syunik Province. Local residents found him inside a house, where he opened fire with an assault rifle and wounded a 39-year-old woman. Her three children witnessed the incident. Her two sons also suffered injuries, while her daughter has yet to recover psychologically.

Musayev fled after the shooting, but authorities detained him shortly afterwards in another house. The Armenian Prosecutor’s Office brought criminal charges under five articles of the Criminal Code. The charges include illegally crossing the border, causing serious bodily harm to a local resident and violating the inviolability of a home. A court ordered his detention for two months.

During the briefing, the prime minister also addressed Dmitry Medvedev’s controversial statement about turning Armenia into a “new Ukraine”, a possible meeting with Aliyev at the CIS summit and the issue of missing persons.

“No official meetings are planned”: on contacts with Putin and Aliyev

On 8-9 October, Pashinyan will attend the CIS summit in Turkmenistan. Asked about possible meetings with the presidents of Russia and Azerbaijan, he recalled that his latest meetings with Putin and Aliyev took place in Bishkek last month. He also spoke to the Russian president by phone the day before.

“The format is such that contacts with the president of Russia and the president of Azerbaijan will certainly take place. We will be in the same place today and tomorrow. No official meeting is planned. If it turns out that such a meeting is necessary, it may take place,” he said.

“Armenia has already faced such a threat”: response to Medvedev

People in Armenia continue to discuss Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev’s statement. He said that Armenia’s leadership had decided to change the country’s course and that this would not lead to anything good.

“The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” Medvedev said.

Journalists asked Pashinyan whether Armenia could face such a threat. He replied:

“Armenia has already faced a similar danger and situation. In September 2022, [during the Azerbaijani armed forces’ invasion of Armenia’s sovereign territory], the CSTO failed to fulfil its obligations.”

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation is a military alliance led by Russia. Armenia is a member of the CSTO. Under the organisation’s charter, its allies had to provide military assistance to a member state, but that did not happen.

The Armenian prime minister could not explain why Medvedev was making such statements and threats:

“Following the same logic, someone else could say: ‘We do not want Armenia to turn into a “new Russia”, given that explosions can be heard in various parts of Russia.’ This is an unfortunate genre.”

He assured that Armenia would not turn into anything else and would instead become an even more independent state.

“Some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes”: on missing persons

Azerbaijan periodically demands that Armenia provide information about the fate of missing Azerbaijanis and the locations of their graves. President Ilham Aliyev repeated the demand at an international conference on missing persons in Baku.

According to Armenia’s prime minister, both sides should make joint efforts to establish the fate of missing people:

“We have stated that we are ready to cooperate. The problem is that some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes, including to generate hostile rhetoric and pursue other aims.”

According to figures Pashinyan presented, the whereabouts of around 1,000 people who went missing during wars since the 1990s remain unknown in Armenia.

He says the wording itself — “their whereabouts are unknown” — shows how little information the authorities have about these people:

“Some circles in Azerbaijan sometimes try to create the impression that we know where these people are and refuse to share the information. But that is not the case.”

Pashinyan believes the two sides should resolve the issue through cooperation and close this chapter. He said that in Bishkek, he and the Azerbaijani president also discussed stepping up joint efforts by the relevant commissions of the two countries.

World.title: ‘Light rosè’, or why claim that Abkhazia has no good wine is outdated. VIDEO
World.content:
Wine in Abkhazia

For a long time, Abkhazia was known mainly for its basic range of wines. The region’s unpredictable climate, with annual rainfall of up to 2,000 mm, was seen as a challenge, as was the popularity of mass-produced semi-sweet wines.

However, modern winemaking practices have challenged this perception. Today, Abkhaz wine producers are shifting their focus towards premium wines.

The Association of Winemakers is actively reviving local indigenous grape varieties. It says fermentation control and modern scientific methods now make it possible to produce delicate, dry and fresh rosé wines.

World.title: European Parliament resolution on banning opposition parties in Georgia: what it says
World.content:
On 8 October, the European Parliament adopted its latest — and seventh — critical resolution on Georgia. This time, it focuses on the ruling Georgian Dream party’s attempts to ban five opposition parties and political groups.

In the resolution, the European Parliament strongly condemns the attempts to outlaw these opposition parties and calls for the immediate withdrawal of the constitutional lawsuit against them.

The draft resolution also once again calls for the release of political prisoners and sanctions against those responsible for Georgia’s democratic backsliding. It specifically names Georgian Dream founder and honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, party secretary-general Kakha Kaladze, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili.

The document says that the actions of Georgian Dream have caused the situation in Georgia to deteriorate further. Democracy and media freedom have declined, while human rights and the rule of law face growing violations. The document says this increasingly conflicts with Georgia’s international obligations and responsibilities, including the Copenhagen criteria.

The draft resolution also notes that two German foundations — the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation — had to close their offices in Tbilisi after the authorities rejected their funding applications under the grants law.

The draft resolution also again refers to the persecution of journalists in Georgia who covered the authorities’ repression of the opposition and civil society.

According to the draft resolution, the European Parliament:

Strongly condemns the attempt to outlaw Georgia’s opposition parties and calls for the immediate withdrawal of the constitutional lawsuit against them. It stresses that a functioning political opposition is an indispensable pillar of democracy and that using judicial mechanisms to eliminate legitimate political opposition is incompatible with democracy. It notes that banning the only opposition party represented in the Georgian parliament undermines the government’s previous narrative that it targeted only parties “under boycott”;

Since October 2024, the European Parliament has adopted six critical resolutions concerning the Georgian government. In these documents, MEPs have criticised Georgian Dream’s policies on democracy, the rule of law, human rights and the country’s European integration.

World.title: UN Human Rights Council adopts resolution on Georgia’s occupied territories
World.content:
UNHRC resolution on Georgia’s occupied territories

On 7 October, the UN Human Rights Council adopted a resolution in Geneva concerning Georgia‘s occupied regions.

According to Georgia’s Foreign Ministry, the resolution, entitled “Cooperation with Georgia”, addresses the human rights situation in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia).

The UN Human Rights Council calls for unhindered access to the occupied territories for the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as international and regional human rights mechanisms.

The resolution also condemns Russia’s actions aimed at annexing Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, and reaffirms support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

It expresses concern over discrimination and human rights violations against ethnic Georgians in the Russian-occupied regions.

The document also highlights the importance of the Geneva International Discussions, established under the ceasefire agreement of 12 August 2008.

The resolution, submitted by Georgia, was adopted by consensus, as it was last year.

World.title: Azerbaijan Airlines сancels four flights due to Russian airspace restrictions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Azerbaijan Airlines (AZAL) has canceled four flights scheduled for today due to restrictions imposed in Russian airspace.

The airline's press service said that changes had affected flights J2-185/J2-186 on the Baku-Moscow (Domodedovo)-Baku route and J2-805/J2-806 on the Baku-Moscow (Vnukovo)-Baku route, scheduled for October 9.

The morning J2-185 flight from Baku to Moscow was forced to land in St. Petersburg. Further airspace restrictions made it impossible for the aircraft to return to Baku. Meanwhile, the morning J2-805 flight from Baku to Moscow returned to Heydar Aliyev International Airport.

The restrictions also affected the aircraft's ability to reach their destination airports on schedule and operate subsequent flights. As a result, the evening return flights J2-186 and J2-806 on the respective routes were also postponed.

AZAL is closely monitoring the situation and taking measures to provide passengers with the necessary assistance. Passengers will be informed of changes to the flight schedule through the airline's official information channels.

“Passenger and flight safety remain the top priority for Azerbaijan Airlines. All operational decisions are made in consideration of the prevailing circumstances and safety requirements,” the statement said.

World.title: Tokayev backs Azerbaijan’s Caspian Sea commission proposal
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Kazakhstan supports Azerbaijan’s proposal to establish an intergovernmental commission on Caspian Sea shallowing at the level of deputy prime ministers, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said.

This was reflected in a press release issued today by the press office of the Kazakh president.

Speaking at the first Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan, Tokayev said that although an international legal and institutional framework for Caspian cooperation was already in place, existing measures were insufficient to address the sea’s declining water levels.

He noted the importance of the Tehran Convention, which marks the 20th anniversary of its entry into force this year, and highlighted the contribution of the United Nations Environment Programme to environmental protection efforts.

Tokayev also said that the Caspian littoral states had approved Kazakhstan’s proposal to develop an interstate program for preserving the Caspian Sea’s water resources.

“It is time to move toward coordinated action to mitigate the effects of the Caspian Sea’s shallowing and help our economies and ecosystems adapt to the ongoing changes,” Tokayev said.

He also cited Kazakhstan’s environmental restoration efforts as examples that could be applied to the Caspian Sea. According to him, the area of the North Aral Sea has increased by 36%, improving water quality, restoring fish stocks and gradually reviving economic activity in surrounding areas.

Tokayev added that Kazakhstan had restored saiga populations, supported snow leopard populations and was returning rare animal species to their natural habitats.

He also noted that Kazakhstan was implementing a special program to restore the Turan tiger, thanking Russia and President Vladimir Putin for providing several Amur tigers that are now adapting to conditions in Kazakhstan.

World.title: Judith Lucy's cancer journey will reveal resilience she didn't know she had
World.content:
Welcome, Judith Lucy, to the After Cancer Diagnosis Club.

It's a club no-one wants to join. There are a host of peculiar requirements. And the club remains a mystery to anyone who is not already a member.

Based on her post on Tuesday, Judith has already enjoyed the induction. The shock of diagnosis is all the more shocking because no-one can tell you precisely what the diagnosis is. Surprise!

For many, an initial finding turns out to be the tip of the cancer iceberg, with each step potentially cascading into more possibilities and medical pathways.

Judith Lucy in her natural environment, generating laughs on stage. (Supplied: Nick Robertson/Just For Laughs)

As a lovely breast care nurse explained to me down the phone as I waited for the biopsy result that ensured my entry to the After Cancer Diagnosis Club, you never really get one diagnosis.

But the upside is, that means even the worst news can change!

Judith spoke highly of her delightfully named surgeon, Dr Fun. You will rely on them like no-one you've ever relied on before to meticulously work their way through microscopic layers of skin and tissue and extract the stuff that will kill you.

All journeys are different

There are so many decisions to make in those first few days and there is so much information. Who knew there were so many types of cancer? What's the difference between a stage and a grade?

The medical professionals who work in this field are brilliant and in Australia we have remarkable survival rates.

But it's an extraordinary journey, and it's different for everyone.

Loading...

A few years back, my mammogram and my dental check-up were both due in the same week, but I only had time for one: I picked the scan foolishly thinking it would be the least problematic!

Good choice. That led to a repeat mammogram, which led to a guided biopsy, which led to a complete mastectomy, resulting in an even worse diagnosis.

At that point my oncologist arrived and explained that in a year it would most likely be largely behind me. A year!

She was right, of course. A year of chemo, radiation and then mostly it was done. But, of course, it wasn't really done.

Just because you're not hooked up to an infusion every week doesn't really signal "the end" of cancer treatment.

Stretching out for years ahead – for me at least – is the Tamoxifen treatment, daily oral hormone therapy medication that rattles your bones. Then I opted for the reconstruction and a second mastectomy. Judith plans the same. No regrets here, but these are exhausting procedures.

And after the treatment there is the constant vigilance. Too many headaches? Scan for brain metastases! Strange rash that won't quit? Biopsy for a recurrence!

Finding a path

My gorgeous kids were my anchor. The sound of my eldest tapping away at her homework next to my hospital bed made me feel safe enough to sleep, but it's a cruel thing asking to borrow your children's strength.

And you'll do most of this alone, sorry to say. Even the most willing families and friends will struggle to understand the fear, the aches, the change.

As one of my friends once described it, "done or dead" is what most people can deal with. Best to project positivity at all times. Emphasising the bright side and gags about a free boob job is the safe way to go. But it can make the experience all the lonelier.

Loading...

"I'm fine" is so much easier an answer for others to hear than "I hurt all the time" or "God, the tiredness!".

Bits of my body will never feel the same. You know how amputees talk about phantom pains? I have a phantom itch where my breast tissue used to be, but no amount of scratching can get to it because there is no sensation in the skin.

It's constant reminder of what was there. As if you needed one.

Listen to Judith and get your boobs checked.

And Judith, you're about to be amazed by the people you meet and what you're capable of.

Annie White is an ABC journalist.

World.title: Family turns bare island into reef oasis after guano mining destroys it
World.content:
Lady Elliot island has been rehabilitated by hand, with more than 20,000 plants. ( )

For thousands of years the tiny island at the southernmost tip of the Great Barrier Reef was alive with cacophonous birdsong.

Lady Elliot Island, pictured in 1973, was left bare for a century after guano mining. ( )

But within a decade of guano miners arriving in force with their picks and shovels in the 1860s, Lady Elliot Island was silent, denuded of all foliage and bereft of the seabirds that once lived there.

It remained a barren wasteland for more than 100 years before one family decided to revive it and started planting trees.

The cotton-wool clouds separate to reveal the first glimpse of Lady Elliot Island.

A ring of waves crashes on the outer edge of the reef, and the island's airstrip is a prominent ribbon of jade encased in forest green.

From the sky, the coral cay 80 kilometres off the coast of Bundaberg is a picture of pristine natural beauty.

On land, birdcalls fill the air.

Humans now have a permanent presence here, but for millennia, this island belonged solely to seabirds.

That's what made it such a prize to guano miners in the mid 19th century.

"The thing that seabirds do really well is poo," says Christine Dudgeon, who manages the island's research and rehabilitation program, Leaf to Reef.

" It was covered in about two metres of guano, and this was a really valuable substance at the time for fertilisers. "

An illustration of birdlife on Lady Elliot Island, circa 1843. ( )

Guano, the accumulated waste from birds or bats, is rich in nitrogen, phosphate and potassium.

This nutrient powerhouse fuelled the new world of modern, input-intensive farming that emerged in the early 1800s.

After German explorer Alexander von Humboldt took samples of guano back to Europe, farmers' demands for the fertiliser soared.

Commercial guano mining started in Peru in 1840, but the profitable global trade quickly expanded to hundreds of Pacific and Caribbean islands that were uninhabited by humans.

Seabird colonies along Australia's east and west coasts were displaced as miners moved in, destroying entire island ecosystems to meet agriculture's insatiable demand for fertiliser.

These s and trading cards from the mid 1800s show how popular guano fertiliser was across the world. ( )

With hundreds of thousands of seabirds nesting, feeding and pooing on the 45-hectare Lady Elliot Island, settlers quickly identified the coral cay as a guano goldmine.

At the time, it was a valuable commodity, fetching more than £5 per tonne.

However, initial attempts to remove guano from Lady Elliot Island in the early 1850s were thwarted when two ships, the Bolton Abbey and The Countess of Minto, came to grief — one was wrecked on the reef encircling the island and the other was driven out to sea.

Ten years later, in 1863, the Queensland government granted Jack Askunas the first official mining lease for the island for £300 per year.

He cleared trees, shrubs and grasses to reach the guano, destroying habitat that had supported birdlife for thousands of years.

An estimated 20,000 tonnes of guano, with a raw market value equating to about $30 million today, was removed from the island over the next decade.

Islands on both sides of Australia were targeted by guano miners in the mid 1800s. ( )

In his wake, Askunas left a demolition site, uninhabitable even by the seabirds that used to nest there.

"This became like a moonscape, absolutely barren," Dr Dudgeon says.

"Then after that, they [the miners] put some goats onto it just in case there were shipwrecks, so that there was some food [for survivors]."

Any plants that sprouted were eaten by the goats.

Then came the lighthouse keepers — who arrived with very pretty, but very invasive plants, which the island's environmental staff are still trying to eradicate.

It took the bird's eye view of an entrepreneurial aviator to change the island's fortunes.

Before: The island was stripped of all foliage. . . After: Houses are now surrounded by shrubs, trees and grass. . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE The island was stripped of all foliage. / Houses are now surrounded by shrubs, trees and grass.

A man with a plan, a woman with a green thumb

Aviator Don Adams saw the potential for tourism opportunities when he flew over Lady Elliot Island in the 1960s and was immediately attracted to its coral reef.

But with almost no vegetation, he knew substantial rehabilitation of the island would be essential.

All that remained were eight Pisonia trees that the miners had left behind. Those trees still stand today, making them at least 160 years old.

Don and Moya Adams began the painstaking work of rehabilitating Lady Elliot Island when Don saw its tourism potential. ( )

Don Adams with his plane on Lady Elliot Island in the 1960s. ( )

Mr Adams and his wife Moya reached an arrangement with the Commonwealth Department of Transport to build an airstrip on the island, in return for a lease on a portion of land for recreational purposes.

Their son, Peter Adams, remembers many weekends and holidays sharing the island with daytrippers who his father would take snorkelling and scuba diving on the reef.

At that time, it was far from a luxurious resort.

"The accommodation was pretty basic. We had an A-frame house, we had kerosene fridges and gas lights. We only had tank water," Mr Adams recalls now.

Peter Adams spent much of his childhood on Lady Elliot Island. ( )

"Before the airstrip, the lighthouse keepers used to refer to it as the Alcatraz of the Barrier Reef because … you got sent there and that was it.

"But [with] the aeroplanes, you could be in Bundaberg within half an hour."

Mr Adams spent the last half of his childhood, from ages nine to 18, on the island and recalls flying model aeroplanes, go-karting and riding motorbikes around its two-kilometre circumference.

The island was so bare that Peter Adams and his friends were able to drive go-karts all over it in the 1960s and 70s. ( )

The island was a great place to fly model planes because they couldn't get stuck in trees. ( )

In the 1970s, Peter Adams and the lighthouse keeper's children loved to explore the island's coral reef. ( )

He distinctly remembers that the vegetation was so sparse at the time that you could see from one side of the island to the other.

Wanting to rehabilitate the coral cay correctly, Don and Moya started by surveying native species growing on similar islands in the Great Barrier Reef.

Coconuts collected from Dunk Island were used to grow coconut palms on Lady Elliot that are still standing.

The first house built by the Adams family on the island. ( )

It wasn't long before Moya Adams had a thriving garden around the family's initial house. ( )

But the real engine room of the revegetation project was a nursery created in the backyard of the Adams family home in Hervey Bay, where Moya propagated casuarina, pandanus and umbrella trees.

The family flew hundreds of saplings to the island.

Then the hardest part started — hand-planting and hand-watering.

"I distinctly remember digging holes in the coral with a crowbar," Mr Adams says.

"I remember … walking around with a bucket of water trying to keep these things alive for a long time."

He says "it was a start" to the rehabilitation program that won Don and Moya a conservation award from the Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland in 1974.

"I remember somebody saying, 'Why did you cut down the trees to make the airstrip?' And, well, the airstrip was there before the trees grew," Mr Adams says.

Aviator Don Adams was determined to rehabilitate Lady Elliot Island after seeing it from the air in the 1960s. ( )

The island became Don's happy place.

"It was a bit of a sanctuary for Dad out there," he says.

"Out of all the things Dad did in his life, I remember him once saying his small involvement with Lady Elliot was the thing he was most proud of."

'They will be seen, they will be heard'

Now known as the Home of the Manta Ray, Lady Elliot Island's menagerie of marine creatures and its spectacular coral reefs, are marketed as its main tourism drawcards.

But it is the ubiquitous birdlife, which has triumphantly reclaimed this island in recent decades, that provides the holiday soundtrack for visitors to its eco-resort.

Seabirds return to roost and nest at sunset. ( )

The view of the sun setting over the horizon is crisscrossed by thousands of dark streaks as white-capped black noddies return to nest after a day of fishing, swooping between guests on their way to dinner.

They are among a diverse range of seabirds now nesting and roosting on the coral cay once again.

A white-capped black noddy. ( )

Brown boobies are among the seabirds that nest on Lady Elliot Island. ( )

A wedge-tailed shearwater soars over the ocean. ( )

Greater frigatebirds roost and feed on the island, but don't nest there. ( )

Crested terns breed in a maintained paddock on Lady Elliot Island. ( )

Roseate terns live on the island. ( )

A sooty tern soars over the ocean. ( )

Bridled terns live on the island. ( )

A pair of white-breasted sea eagles are the only raptors on the coral cay. ( )

By day, wedge-tailed shearwaters, or muttonbirds, along with brown boobies and crested terns soar over the breaking waves, looking for their next meal.

On land, red-tailed tropicbirds can be found hunkering under shrubbery as they keep their newly hatched chicks warm.

Bartailed godwits are often seen walking in the grass on the island, but don't nest there. ( )

Whimbrels wander around grassy patches on the island, but don't nest there. ( )

Pacific golden plovers congregate around the airstrip and resort, but don't nest on the island. ( )

An Eastern reef egret. ( )

Flocks of ruddy turnstones can be seen along the shoreline. ( )

Seagulls are a familiar sight. ( )

Sooty oyster catchers have distinctive eyes and beaks. ( )

It is perhaps not so surprising then to find that earplugs are supplied in the resort's rooms to help guests block out the birds' night-time calls.

It's a professional hazard that brings much joy to University of the Sunshine Coast seabird researcher Zerra Egerton.

"We are in their territory. I always think of us as guests here," she says.

"So when I hear the babies crying all night long, I am just stoked. They can wake me up as much as they like.

Zerra Egerton often finds red-tailed tropicbirds nesting on the ground beneath shrubs. ( )

Red-tailed tropicbirds lay their eggs in divots scraped out of dirt, leaf litter or coral rubble. ( )

Red-tailed tropicbird chicks are often found in nests protected by shrubs. ( )

"It's true that maybe not a lot of people necessarily come here to experience the bird life. But once they're here, and especially in summer, you cannot avoid the birds.

"They will be seen. They will be heard. They will be felt, occasionally."

The birds have an intricate and symbiotic relationship with the island's vegetation.

A Pacific reef heron shelters under branches. ( )

Common noddies are abundant on the island. ( )

House sparrows make large, untidy nests. ( )

Only a small family of brown quails lives on the island at this stage. ( )

Buffbanded rails nest on the island. ( )

Capricorn silvereyes mate for life on Lady Elliot Island. ( )

The trees and foliage once again provide protection and nesting materials, while the birds bring nutrients from the sea to the land, which supports vegetation growth.

"There was no-one here [in the 1800s] except the birds," Ms Egerton said.

"To [the miners], it just looked like a resource that they could take without any moral implications … it was just an opportunity.

"But now we see that system so differently."

Clumps of guano, the accumulated droppings of seabirds, are found all over the island. ( )

Solar panels fuel 'beating heart' nursery

The care and preservation baton has been passed on to the Gash family.

Husband and wife duo, Peter and Julie, first visited the island in the 1980s and became involved in its tourism activities in 1997, when their company, Seair Pacific, began flights to and from the island.

Once their daughters, Amy and Chloe, arrived, the family's attachment to Lady Elliot's unique beauty deepened, and the Gashes became the island's custodians (leaseholders) in 2005.

Peter, Julie, Amy and Chloe Gash say taking care of the island is their priority. ( )

Amy Gash says using solar power helps protect the island's environment. ( )

Determined to continue the rehabilitation work started by the Adams family, and maintained by the intervening leaseholders, the Gashes investigated ways to create an even more eco-friendly resort.

Two decades on, 33-year-old Amy Gash is now the resort's executive general manager, and often scoots around the island on a battery-powered buggy.

"We believe it's our responsibility to keep this place as pristine and as beautiful as it is for today, and also [for] the future," she says.

"We really wanted to … minimise our footprint and basically transition from that traditional reliance on fossil fuels."

In 2008, the family built a "first-of-its-kind hybrid solar power station", and has installed more than 1,000 solar panels and 250 batteries on the island.

"We can almost confidently run 100 per cent of the time on solar power," Ms Gash says.

Solar panels provide most of the energy on Lady Elliot Island. ( )

The eco resort is powered by a massive battery bank. ( )

Amy Gash with the island's power source, 1,000 solar panels. ( )

Over the past two decades, more than 20,000 trees have been planted on the island.

"We carry on that program that was started in the 70s by Don Adams," Ms Gash says.

"We're really proud to have partnered with the Great Barrier Reef Foundation in about 2017, which really helped us accelerate the planting of trees here at Lady Elliot.

" Everything you see … has been planted by hand on Lady Elliot Island, or it's been introduced by a bird species bringing out its seeds along the way. "

Liam Turner, the ecosystem manager of the revegetation program, said that in the 10 years since the island's nursery was established, staff had propagated 22 species of native trees, shrubs and grasses.

Liam Turner runs the island's propagation and planting program. ( )

Native species found on other reef islands have been selected for the revegetation project. ( )

More than 20,000 native trees, shrubs and ground-covers have been planted on the island. ( )

The plants are all potted in fertilised soil from the island to guard against invasive diseases. ( )

"The nursery is the beating heart of the whole program," he says, adding that revegetation has been completed across about 70 per cent of the island.

However, taking care of the environment is a never-ending job, as 120 species of introduced weeds compete with native grasses and ground covers.

"You can't just remove weeds and expect everything to return to some sort of semblance of what it was prior to guano mining," Mr Turner says.

"In place of those weeds, we've got to put in all the native [plants] … And on top of that, we've got to continue doing maintenance in those areas to keep the weeds away and allow that native vegetation to establish.

"They do suppress and naturally compete with the weeds once they start getting established, but you've got to get them to that point."

This is where the eco-resort plays a role, with all food scraps providing an essential ingredient for the nursery's potting mix.

Liam Turner says keeping weeds at bay long enough for the native plants to thrive is an ongoing challenge. ( )

The nursery uses locally made potting mix to limit the chance of disease and invasive insects reaching the island. ( )

The nursery uses potting mix created on the island over a two-year process. ( )

Seedlings growing in the island's nursery. ( )

"It gets mixed in with cardboard and woodchips, goes through a big auger and then that gets turned into a pretty nasty putrefied substance [that comes] out … after about two weeks," Mr Turner explains.

The substance is then mixed with green waste and isolated for two years.

"We get this beautiful black soil at the other side of it, which we use for all our potting mixes that we have in the nursery," he says.

"It's good that we can produce it here so we're not importing soil to the island and … [potentially] introducing all sorts of pests and diseases.

"My big dream is that eventually we'll get to a point where none of that's necessary and the ecosystem's kind of self-sustaining and can sort itself out, which we are seeing signs of, which is fantastic."

'We never want it to go quiet again'

The thriving seabird population on Lady Elliot Island is testament to the success of Don Adams' vision to rehabilitate the barren wasteland left by guano miners in the mid 1800s.

Dr Dudgeon says the birdlife has made "an extraordinary recovery".

An estimated 100,000 black noddies now nest in the trees of Lady Elliot Island each year. ( )

The primary species responsible for the nutrient flow is the black noddy, about 100,000 of which nest on the island each year, up from just a few thousand in the 1960s.

Another of the island's notable species is the red-tailed tropicbird, which is only found in two locations in Queensland.

"Tropicbirds started nesting here in the 1980s and it certainly seems that their nests are increasing over time, which is parallel with increasing vegetation that's available for them," Dr Dudgeon says.

Christine Dudgeon says once the island was found to be covered in guano, its fate was sealed in the mid 1800s. ( )

Pandanus trees, with their distinctive roots, can be found around the island. ( )

She says seeing the changes to the island's ecosystem is encouraging.

"A lot of us work in places where you're seeing the more negative impacts all the time," she says.

" It's a great privilege to get to work out here and see … what a healthy environment is, what a biodiverse environment is. It's a very inspirational place. "

Like Dr Dudgeon, Ms Egerton is astounded by the transformation from desolate island to subtropical paradise.

"It was quite bleak, just a bare white rock and quite a gruelling place to exist on for months on end," she says.

"It's incredible what's been achieved in such a short period of time in terms of the seabirds returning and the vegetation."

While the birdlife can be noisy, sleep-disruptive and a tad smelly, Ms Egerton wouldn't have it any other way.

Zerra Egerton says the birdlife recovery on the island has been remarkable over the past few decades. ( )

The environmental rehabilitation of Lady Elliot Island is now 70 per cent completed. ( )

"It's very, very special to have seabirds that breed [here] because that means that this island is literally sustaining their populations," she says.

" We love this island and we love the animals here, and we don't ever want it to go quiet again. "

Credits:

World.title: Two men met on a Port Adelaide ship — a Nobel and Apocalypse Now ensued
World.content:
The oceans of the world do not allow us to retrace our steps, for the simple reason that the nature of waves is not conducive to the creation of footprints.

But that doesn't mean treasure can't be pursued on the high seas of history.

Indeed, it's on those waters that the scholarly wayfarer encounters strange flotsam, sometimes in the form of other human beings.

When a young English law graduate met a Polish sailor aboard the clipper ship "Torrens" at Port Adelaide in 1893, neither could have realised they were participating in a moment that would fascinate future generations.

But the lawyer was nevertheless prompted to write of the sailor:

" He is a man of travel and experience in many parts of the world, and has a fund of yarns on which I draw freely. He has been right up the Congo and all around Malacca and Borneo and other out of the way parts. "

The most arresting clue in that description is the word "Congo".

The portrait is of Józef Korzeniowski, better known to subsequent generations of readers as Joseph Conrad.

The novelist's name is now associated with a series of masterpieces, including Heart of Darkness.

A contested work, it has long since occupied an exalted place in the post-colonial canon as an indictment of European brutality in Africa, and was the inspiration for the film Apocalypse Now.

Heart of Darkness was the inspiration for Apocalypse Now. (AFP/Zoetrope Films)

Conrad's portraitist and fellow seafarer was John Galsworthy — a man who would attain an equal literary eminence.

In 1932, he was honoured with the Nobel Prize, which was awarded to him largely in recognition of his social saga about a typically myopic upper-middle-class Edwardian family (the wryly named Forsytes) whose members are riven by conflicting senses of duty.

The meeting of the two budding authors on the Torrens was purely serendipitous, but its ripples spread across the lives and works of both men, and continue to reach us today.

Much has changed since the Torrens docked in 1893, but the maritime atmosphere remains. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Paths to, and from, a meeting

In 1893, neither Conrad nor Galsworthy was a published novelist, let alone a public figure, and the paths by which they converged on Port Adelaide were as dissimilar as they were remarkable.

Conrad was the more worldly man. Born in 1857 into minor nobility in what is now Ukraine, he was the son of an insurgent opposed to Russian rule over Poland.

A newspaper article from 1941 on the friendship between John Galsworthy and Joseph Conrad. (Trove: The Advertiser)

After resolving while still a child to become a sailor, Conrad voyaged the world and made several journeys to Australia, collecting material for stories along the way.

The Oxford-educated Galsworthy, on the other hand, was sent to sea by his father in order to hone skills in maritime law.

He also hoped to cross paths with Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson, who had settled in Samoa.

Instead, he found Conrad.

"In that meeting commenced one of the most loyal of personal and literary friendships, which grew deeper and stronger throughout all the subsequent years," The Age newspaper later reported.

The clipper ship "Torrens" docked at Port Adelaide. (State Library of South Australia B 11871)

The pair spent weeks aboard the Torrens before Galsworthy disembarked in South Africa.

Conrad, who was already at work on his first novel, was perhaps less liable to literary influence than was the impressionable Galsworthy.

In a late essay that was also an obituary to his old friend, the Englishman reflected on the times he stayed with Conrad and his wife Jessie, and on the impact Conrad had on his own career.

"[Conrad] was indefatigably good to me while my own puppy's eyes were opening to literature, and I was still in the early stages of that struggle with his craft which a writer worth his salt never quite abandons," Galsworthy wrote.

A portrait of John Galsworthy from 1909. (National Portrait Gallery/Creative Commons)

Further light is shed by Elsie Belle Champion, a Melbourne booklover who both visited and corresponded with Galsworthy.

Newspaper reports from the 1930s attribute to her the following remarks:

"Galsworthy told me that he first thought about writing after having met Joseph Conrad in Adelaide. They had many talks on literature on the ship's bridge at night."

Ashes to ashes, waves to waves

Neither Galsworthy nor Conrad reached especially old age — Galsworthy died aged 65 and Conrad at 66 — but each, in a sense, achieved a tragic longevity.

Loading...

Both came from backgrounds that suited them for leisure and comfort, but both lived into a time in which it was increasingly impossible to ignore the plain fact of human misery, or to insulate oneself from the impulse to do something about it.

They were not temperamentally suited to what is today called "activism" — which, in any case, is the wrong word for the way in which both responded to the iniquities of the time.

European civilisation had produced things (art, culture and modes of living and thinking) they could not help but value, and its greatest gift to them was a kind of urbane conscience.

But it was that exact same conscience that compelled these two men to attack at the base some of the unconscionable foundations upon which their own privilege rested.

A memorial service was held for Galsworthy at Westminster Abbey, following his death in 1933. (Reuters: Clodagh Kilcoyne)

They would perhaps not have wished it thus, but they are best remembered by us as pallbearers of empire.

"We had been celebrating not only the departure of a noble character and a great writer, but the obituary of an age," journalist Henry Nevinson wrote after the public memorial service for Galsworthy, at Westminster Abbey in 1933.

It was an age, Nevinson added, that "was crumbling into the ashes".

Galsworthy had sung the swan song of a social class that prided itself on rectitude but that achieved decorum through a great deceit.

It was Conrad who traced this deceit to its source. In Heart of Darkness, he savaged the savagery then being inflicted on those deemed "savages".

After his death in 1924, Conrad was laid to rest in the cathedral city of Canterbury.

A ferry sails across the English Channel towards Dover on the Kent coast, not far from Conrad's resting place in Canterbury. (Reuters:Toby Melville)

Scottish author Robert Cunninghame Graham accompanied him on his final voyage, from church to burial ground, and penned a poignant reminiscence of the moments that followed the sinking of Conrad's coffin into the soil.

"And so we left him with his sails all duly furled … and with the anchor holding truly in the kind Kentish earth," Graham wrote.
