World.title: Live: Matildas take on world number three Germany in friendly
World.content:
Firstly, yes, it's called a 'friendly' but that doesn't mean these upcoming matches against Germany today and Haiti on Wednesday should be treated lightly.

These clashes are extremely important preparation for the 2027 Women's World Cup. Both teams have already qualified for the tournament, meaning all focus is on getting ready for it.

For the Matildas, a lot of attention is on younger talent. Hoping to debut in these matches is uncapped trio Tori Tumeth, Courtney Newbon and Hana Lowry - all called up for the first time to the squad.

Tori Tumeth for Vancouver Rise FC. (Getty)

Meanwhile, in-form Charli Grant, Alexia Apostolakis and Daniela Galic will be hoping to get some more national minutes under their belts.

Alanna Kennedy and Charlize Rule are unavailable due to injury, while Kyra Cooney-Cross and Mary Fowler are also out.

Germany will be without captain Giulia Gwinn and key player Vivien Endemann, who have been replaced by Sarai Linder and Nicole Anyomi.

World.title: How Firmus, the biggest IPO in three decades, fell over
World.content:
It was supposed to be the second biggest stock float in Australian history.

Sydney-based AI startup Firmus Technologies was close to listing on the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) at a $43.7 billion market capitalisation.

It would have been the biggest IPO since Telstra listed in 1997.

The company, founded in 2019 by Oliver Curtis, Tim Rosenfield and Jonathan Levee, had planned to raise about $7 billion by going public.

The intention was to list and then borrow more to build data centres across Australia, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.

Investors grow anxious

By Wednesday night the IPO plans began to unravel and reports emerged that bankers were considering lowering the share price and valuation towards $30 billion.

On Thursday morning, as Firmus scrambled to try and save the IPO from failing, it withdrew from appearing at a federal parliamentary inquiry into AI.

By Friday the founder's grand plans had fallen apart and the float was pulled.

Tim Rosenfield, Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff (centre) and Oliver Curtis (right) at the Firmus Technologies site in Launceston. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Despite being backed by global AI giant Nvidia, investors had grown anxious.

Firmus had previously said it secured $US2 billion in commitments from investors, including Nvidia and Blackstone.

Other potential investors felt the company's share price offer was overpriced, some felt there was not enough detailed information in the IPO prospectus, and many were spooked that the rapid growth of AI and data centres would soon stop.

The founders are now hoping to pursue further private funding and Firmus will attempt to list on the Nasdaq next year.

What caused the Firmus float to fail?

A mixture of factors led to the float's demise, including the high per-share price offer, which by Thursday had reportedly fallen from $11 to $8.25.

The company was being given a similar valuation to Woolworths, according to Morningstar senior market strategist Lochlan Holloway.

"The economics look good now and the growth is very fast now, but what that looks like again in five or 10 years is the big question mark," he said.

Lochlan Halloway says the company was being given a similar valuation to Woolworths, while making the revenue of a start-up. (ABC News)

The timing of the IPO was also wrong.

Commentators say fears of an AI bubble, set against a backdrop of mounting concerns from politicians and the community about the rapid rise of data centres, also played a part.

"Firmus ran into a wall of AI anxiety right at the time that they had planned to list," Philip Wohl from Reliance Investment Research said.

And then there was some angst over Mr Curtis's colourful past. He served a year in jail in 2016-17 for insider trading before co-founding Firmus as a bitcoin mining company in 2019.

Mr Wohl said Firmus's assertion that it was market volatility that prevented it listing at its desired price was "a euphemistic way of describing exactly what happened".

"The market is more uncertain now when it comes to AI hardware and, given the perhaps aggressive pricing that they were targeting, they really didn't see the demand," he said.

'They do have to come back to the market'

Ten Cap Investment co-founder and lead portfolio manager Jun Bei Liu said the IPO was overpriced, but thought a second attempt was on the cards.

Firmus pulls blockbuster float Firmus searches for private funding as it withdraws its application to list on the ASX just a day after closing its books to investors.

"The valuation for the company was way too high to start with," she said.

"It is almost three times what the valuation was when they raised money just a few months ago.

"At some stage they do have to come back to the market simply, because it's a very capital intensive business. It requires listed shares."

Floodline Research founder Anna Wu said the founders should have tried to list in the United States in the first place because the Nasdaq was a bigger and more accepting market than the ASX for emerging tech.

"The downside is much tougher competition and as an Australian company Firmus may struggle to attract the same attention and valuation as its US peers," she said.

The Nasdaq has recently hit record highs and is up 43 per cent in the past year, but Australia's tech sector has faltered by comparison.

The ASX All Technology Index, which tracks the share prices of 42 tech-linked stocks on the ASX, has dropped almost 18 per cent this year, including 9 per cent in September alone.

In part that is because Australian technology listings are more heavily skewed towards software companies, which have been sold off in the so-called SaaSpocalypse as investors worry that AI will undercut their business models.

Anna Wu says the timing for the Firmus IPO was bad. (Supplied)

Investors were also questioning whether Australia had the energy infrastructure energy to support data centres.

"We're in a slightly different regime now for AI in terms of its life cycle," Ms Wu said.

"It's no longer 2023, where everything's about big ideas and anything with AI in the name would go past any valuation test."

She said the lack of details on the Firmus IPO and concerns about Mr Curtis's criminal past also weighed on some investors.

"That creates more ambiguity," she said.

"So when the market gets hit by oil anxiety every second day, and when investors are facing a much higher capital cost, that would actually drive the question on the valuation.

"It probably sends the sentiment signal to the broader community that right now — an IPO is not a free lunch anymore."

Nvidia's play in an Aussie startup

Nvidia was contacted for comment about its position on Firmus after the IPO flop.

Ms Wu said Firmus was likely tap the AI giant for a greater investment.

Nvidia already has a 7.2 per cent stake in Firmus and has reportedly been providing funding as well as selling Firmus its chips.

"Nvidia … is going around the world buying anything that it thinks is going to take over in the local market," Ms Wu said.

Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara, California. (Getty Images: Justin Sullivan)

Mr Holloway said the investment made sense as Firmus data centres got "their chips out there."

For customers such as Meta and OpenAi, partnering with companies like Firmus can be the only option to access these chips.

"There is a very, very short supply of Nvidia's high-quality chips and a lot of demand for AI model training," Mr Holloway said.

" If you had access to those chips, which Firmus did with its partnership with Nvidia, you can basically name your price. "

Ms Wu said the backing of Nvidia was still on the cards.

"Nvidia's long-term partnership with Firmus is an endorsement … but also, it's a move towards expanding in the Australia-Pacific region and trying to integrate with the local infrastructure provider."

'Too many unknowns' about IPO

Mr Curtis and his publicist wife Roxy Jacenko opened up a Singapore office two years ago, sparking intrigue from the Australian expat population.

Oliver Curtis and Roxy Jacenko, seen here in August 2024. (Instagram: Roxyjacenko)

But IPOs in Australia are notoriously challenging to get right.

Mr Holloway said the IPO uncertainty had led more companies in Australia to put off listing.

"We've seen the number of IPOs on the ASX fall considerably in the last few years," he said.

Rather than "floating in public markets, remaining in private hands is becoming much easier" because a surplus of private cash.

But analysts say IPOs being delayed or pulled is likely to become more common.

Firmus's website said it had two sites operational in Australia and Singapore, and that five were "under development".

"There were just too many unknowns here and it required too much optimism for investors to take that leap of faith with Firmus," Mr Wohl said.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon's messages about Jesse Baird before alleged murders
World.content:
Ten months before he was allegedly killed, Jesse Baird said he was not in a relationship with Beau Lamarre-Condon.

"Beau and I see each other from time to time however we aren't 'seeing' each other or in a relationship," Mr Baird wrote in an Instagram message in April 2023.

Mr Lamarre-Condon, accused of his murder, had taken a photo of the exchange after going "through [Mr Baird's] phone" while staying over.

He forwarded the image to his colleague and friend, Senior Constable Nicole Harvell.

A photo taken of an exchange between Mr Baird and another man in April 2023. ( )

Beau Lamarre-Condon: Argh idk if I'm being stupid or not or I'm wasting my time

Ms Harvell replied to him in the morning.

Nicole Harvell: … he told him he's not seeing you. Well of course he's seeing you. That was a massive lie

Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder, accused of shooting Mr Baird and his new boyfriend, Luke Davies, using a police pistol in February 2024.

The former police officer's lawyers have indicated an argument of self-defence, telling jurors that separate struggles inside Mr Baird's Paddington home in Sydney resulted in two tragic deaths.

The Crown said Mr Lamarre-Condon developed an "obsessive and jealous infatuation" with Mr Baird after the end of a somewhat casual romance, and had allegedly stalked him in the months prior.

Mr Lamarre-Condon's lawyer said it was not disputed his client "did some stupid things, such as looking through the phone of Jesse Baird, deleting contacts of other men, and deleting text messages".

Former TV presenter Jesse Baird. ( )

Flight attendant Luke Davies. ( )

Family and domestic violence support services: NSW Domestic Violence Line on 1800 656 463

Lifeline on 131 114

Men's Referral Service on 1300 766 491

Mensline on 1300 789 978

Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578

Emergency services on Triple Zero (000) if you need immediate care

Ms Harvell is the latest of a number of witnesses whose communications with the defendant have been tendered as evidence.

They are being asked in court what he told them of his connection with Mr Baird at various points.

Mr Lamarre-Condon confided in Ms Harvell from March 2023 about what she dubbed the "Jesse saga".

His messages with her paint a picture of how the accused perceived the on-again-off-again relationship, his insecurities about Mr Baird seeing other people, and his online surveillance in the lead-up to the alleged double murder.

A 'semi white lie'

The jury has heard Mr Lamarre-Condon met Mr Baird in 2022, but there was a "disconnect" between what each saw as the nature of the relationship and where it was going.

Mr Baird regarded it as "somewhat casual", while the defendant was "infatuated", the prosecutor has said.

In March 2023, Ms Harvell and Mr Lamarre-Condon discussed how Mr Baird seeing another man left him feeling "triggered", and he was checking Mr Baird's Instagram followers.

In the weeks that followed, he described the pair going on dates, a getaway with a dog, and spending Easter together.

Loading...

There were two apparent break-ups between the pair, according to the evidence so far; first in April 2023 and another later that year in November.

On April 17, Mr Lamarre-Condon addressed what he had recently seen on Mr Baird's phone.

Beau Lamarre-Condon: Ending it with him this arvo

Nicole Harvell: … Are you going to tell him about the messages you saw?

Beau Lamarre-Condon: … Yeah I'll tell him about the messages but I might tell a semi white lie and not say I went through his phone 😅

Ms Harvell told the court Mr Lamarre-Condon knew Mr Baird's phone passcode.

She said at that point, Mr Lamarre-Condon had spoken to her about it not being an exclusive relationship, and said he "came across to me as paranoid" about Mr Baird's interest in him.

Ms Harvell recalled being told it was the accused who ended the "so-called relationship", partially because he had seen an unfamiliar pair of underwear in Mr Baird's room.

She told the court he was initially "satisfied" with his decision, but later became "quite fixated".

Via text, Mr Lamarre-Condon questioned if Mr Baird had muted his Instagram stories to "get over me" and checked what he was listening to on Spotify in May.

From planned trip to 'over'

In October, Mr Lamarre-Condon announced Mr Baird would accompany him on a holiday.

Beau Lamarre-Condon: Ummm sooooo

Jesse is coming to Bali with me for NYE

Nicole Harvell: … But still not in a relationship?

Beau Lamarre-Condon: Well no, but I'm actually really happy with it rn.

Come November, a month out from the flight, Mr Lamarre-Condon said they were no longer seeing each other.

Nicole Harvell: Heard from Jease? …

Jesse*

Beau Lamarre-Condon: Yeah it's over

Nicole Harvell: … What!?

This second apparent break-up was attributed in court to the defendant's targeted use of Instagram stories to discourage romantic rivals, and his alleged interference with Mr Baird's phone by blocking contacts.

Ms Harvell said in an attempt to get other men to "back off", Mr Lamarre-Condon uploaded a generic photo of flowers, making it visible only to certain accounts through the app's 'close friends' function.

Mr Baird was not able to view that post, but someone who did sent him a screenshot.

He confronted the accused, asking via text: "What's this about?"

Ms Harvell said Mr Lamarre-Condon, in "damage control", paid $160 for a florist to replicate the bouquet and asked his mother, Coleen Lamarre, to pose for the photo and write a note herself.

Flowers posted to Beau Lamarre-Condon's 'close friends' Instagram story. ( )

Mr Baird asked the accused about the story, which had been sent to him. ( )

Coleen Lamarre posed with another bouquet. ( )

A note on the flowers addressed to Ms Lamarre. ( )

The 888-word message

Mr Lamarre-Condon sent Mr Baird a series of messages asking him to call or "chat in person", saying he was "confused" and he did not "understand why this [the flowers] is an issue", a screenshot sent to Ms Harvell showed.

He then shared an 888-word draft to her of a message he wanted to send to Mr Baird on November 16.

Beau Lamarre-Condon: … You feel as if I possibly blocked someone on your Instagram, as I was with you this morning, which would be a massive betrayal of your trust …

… When I re-entered this situation with you, I even said to you I want to live in the moment with you and I don't want to know about anything or anybody else …

Mr Lamarre-Condon said Mr Baird had mentioned a "few examples" of concern brought to his attention, including the "flower situation".

Beau Lamarre-Condon: … Where I honestly didn't do that, you not believing my word after never giving you a reason not too …

I'm sure you would feel gutted/hurt not knowing how to prove your innocence …

'Come clean'

The next day, Ms Harvell told the accused she was "torn" whether it would be worth him telling Mr Baird about blocking a man he had been casually seeing.

Nicole Harvell: One part of me would say come clean but the other part says no after that long message

Mr Lamarre-Condon then sent Ms Harvell a screenshot of a follow-up message to Mr Baird saying "after sleeping on it I really want to take ownership of something".

About six hours later, the accused said Mr Baird had blocked him on social media.

On the morning of November 18, Ms Harvell touched base with Mr Lamarre-Condon.

Beau Lamarre-Condon: I'm so in the wrong though and it sucks!

Nicole Harvell: … He caused you to do this. Honestly. He was the biggest mind f**k

About 11:35am, he sent a text to Ms Harvell, sharing another message intended for Mr Baird.

Beau Lamarre-Condon: After seeing you today in paddington, it just reaffirms everything my gut was telling me, along with you just blocking me on Instagram — you're a manipulative player

… You lead me on to believe from the very start that this could be a possible relationship

… Then when I finally walked away from this … you send me a lovely text message saying you're so sorry for all the hurt you've caused, wished you were ready for a relationship because I'm everything you want on paper …

Mr Lamarre-Condon said the "cherry on top" was making "one mistake" about the blocking.

Beau Lamarre-Condon: Yes I didn't initially own it but at the end of the day I said I need to do what's right and apologise to you and be honest …

… The difference between you and I is I never did anything intentionally to hurt you …

… I walk away with my head held high …

Nicole Harvell: … That message was the most satisfying thing I've ever read

'Let it go'

On November 19, one day later, Mr Lamarre-Condon sent Ms Harvell photos of Mr Baird in the Blue Mountains taken from a website used to anonymously watch Instagram stories.

He said to Ms Harvell:

Beau Lamarre-Condon: Appreciate you seriously though! Xx

Nicole Harvell: You too ❤️. I feel like I've been there from the start of this Jesse saga as understand it all xx

After discussing photos of Mr Baird with Ms Harvell, the accused said:

Beau Lamarre-Condon: I need to let it go and keep reminding myself it was for the best x

Among the final messages between the workmates, Mr Lamarre-Condon wished her a safe flight on February 18, 2024.

The next day, he is alleged to have murdered Mr Baird and Mr Davies, before taking part in what the Crown has described as a calculated cover-up over several days.

His friend saw media articles about the couple's disappearance, which named the accused.

Nicole Harvell: F**k Beau are you okay?

There was no reply from Mr Lamarre-Condon, who the Crown says handed himself into a police station the following day.

Credits

Reporting: Millie Roberts and Jamie McKinnell

Production: Millie Roberts

World.title: 'Cutthroat' hawker culture fights for survival in Singapore
World.content:
Debbie Yam stands over a raging gas burner, tossing wave after wave of oil and smoking rice in a scorching hot wok.

Ten years as a hawker, she no longer singes her eyebrows or hair.

Working 70 sweaty hours every week is a far cry from the corporate career she expected to have.

After graduating with a business degree, she took over her great-grandfather's hawker stall which was short-staffed.

"I like to eat the food here … and where else am I going to find these flavours if the shop is going to be closed down?"

Singapore hawker food is famed for being delectable and affordable. (Supplied: Martin Ng)

But she is unsure whether her great-grandfather's fish-head noodle and stir-fry stall can keep weathering the "cutthroat" industry.

"If the money doesn't make sense anymore, then there is no amount of passion that can make me drive the project even for another 10 years," she said.

Singapore's hawker centres — where individual stallholders sell cheap, freshly-made dishes in government-owned 'community dining rooms' — are an iconic part of the city state's heritage.

Hawker centres are government-owned public spaces where neighbours and friends can socialise outside their small apartments. (ABC News: Lachlan Bennett)

Its value to social cohesion was why UNESCO inscribed Singapore's hawker culture on its Intangible Cultural Heritage List in 2020.

But a price ceiling combined with rising inflation, costs of imported ingredients, and labour shortages leave little incentive to stay.

Invisible price ceilings

To rebuild the nation after World War II, Singapore introduced feeding schemes to sustain time-poor labourers needing a filling and cheap meal.

According to the Singapore government's National Environment Agency (NEA), more than 6,000 food stallholders operated across 120 state-owned hawker centres.

Jenny Dorsey, a chef and food studies researcher, said government policies designed to keep meals cheap, fixed consumer expectations creating an "invisible price ceiling" for hawkers.

Singapore's hawkers used to sell food on the street before the government moved them into permanent centres to regulate pricing and safety in the 1970s. ("Singapore-Food stall-1973-74-WUS08225" by Rainer Halama is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Over time the NEA wanted hawkers to operate with less state support.

While it did not mandate meal prices, stalls at "socially conscious" hawker centres are required to offer a "value" meal which is benchmarked about $S3.50 ($3.93).

But the NEA outsourced management of these hawker centres to private companies, which charged higher fees.

This downward pressure on price expectations is at odds with rising wages and inflation, risking the "extinction" of the trade, Ms Dorsey said.

Roasted meat at a chicken rice stall in Singapore ("Roast meats at a chicken rice stall" by PipeDr3am2000 is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0)

No cap on costs

Ms Yam's great-grandfather started as a street vendor in 1946.

He became a "pioneer" stallholder in 1978 when the government moved food peddlers into permanent state-owned centres to improve sanitation and regulate food standards and pricing.

Still leasing that same stall, Ms Yam pays a "legacy" monthly rent of about $S400 ($446).

Debbie's great grandfather was part of the 'pioneer' generation of hawkers who moved from the street into a government-owned centre. (Supplied: Debbie Yam)

About one-third of stallholders still pay subsidised rates as low at $S192 ($215), while new stallholders bid for leases at market rates.

"There will be people bidding for the store at $S4,000 [per month]. This is 10 times the difference, so how can they price their food so low?" Ms Yam said.

The NEA estimated ingredients to account for just over half of hawkers' operating costs.

Hawker cuisine reflects the evolution of cuisines that early migrants from China, Malaysia, and India brought and sold to make a living. ("Singapore 1973-74-WUS08144" by Rainer Halama, is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.)

While discounted ingredients can be ordered through a government network of bulk suppliers, most hawkers still get cheaper produce through their own suppliers.

Ms Yam said many younger hawkers enter the trade because of the low barrier to entry, but few stay.

The NEA introduced a Hawker Incubation Scheme in 2018 offering temporary subsidised rent and equipment fit-outs.

As of June 2026, it said about half of the 109 aspiring hawkers on the program achieved viability.

Debbie Yam has learnt about 150 recipes to operate her great-grandfather's stir fry and fish noodle soup stall. (Supplied: Debbie Yam)

A competitive edge

Stallholder Kenny Ngoo, 32, has found "fulfilment" serving Korean-inspired fried chicken and rice bowls for between $S8 ($9) and $S11 ($12.30) for a decade.

His price list reflects his higher rental of$S3,000 ($3,363), but he believes subsidised rents do not harm hawker culture.

Instead of competing with cheap meals, new stalls need to get "creative" and offer a gourmet version of a traditional dish, or experiment with fusion cuisine.

"I think it's a win-win for both," he said.

To remain competitive against cheaper-priced stalls, Kenny Ngoo sells a fusion of Korean-inspired chicken with rice or pasta. (Supplied: Kenny Ngoo)

But Mr Ngoo is worried about the loss of diversity in hawker food with the rise in stall chains and commercial franchises that benefit from economies of scale.

Part of the appeal is stalls having different recipes of the same dishes, he said.

Kenny Ngoo says hawker food could become more standardised as more multi-stall chains that use the same recipes open up. (Supplied: Kenny Ngoo)

Next door to Ms Yam's 50-year-old hawker centre is a privately owned food court that is newer, cleaner, and air-conditioned.

Ms Yam said while the prices might be similar, the commercial centres lacked heritage and specialised skills, something consumers might not appreciate.

The government has promised to invest up to $S1 billion over the next 20 to 30 years to upgrade accessibility and climate resilience at existing hawker centres.

Replenishing a workforce

James Sai, now retired, ran his father's coffee stall and worked 12 hours every day, resting only during the Lunar New Year week.

"In my time, the hawker trade was considered an uneducated, unskilled job without a future," he said.

While that stigma is fading, it is still not an aspirational career choice for young people (or their parents), said Mr Sai's daughter Faye, who with her siblings has expanded the business across three stalls.

The Sai family served coffee out of a shophouse (right) before moving into a hawker centre under a 1978 government initiative. (Supplied: Faye Sai)

According to Singapore's government, the median age of hawkers is 60 years old.

A government-funded scheme to match retiring veterans with aspiring hawkers to pass on their signature recipes and skills has only seen only a handful of successful handovers.

Besides the gruelling conditions, job insecurity, and lack of employer benefits, not everyone can work in government-owned stalls.

Stallholders must spend a minimum number of hours on the premises on days they are open, disadvantaging elderly hawkers and those who cannot work long hours.

After university Faye (right) and her siblings (pictured) returned to become the third generation running her grandfather's coffee stall. (Supplied: Faye Sai)

Additionally, only Singaporean citizens and permanent residents can rent a stall, and only they and long-term visitor pass (LTVP) holders can work in it.

Ms Sai said allowing more foreigners to work could relieve labour shortages for some stalls.

But the government is reluctant.

Few young people are continuing in the hawker industry where the median age is 60 years old. ("ChinatownDimsumHawker 08.jpg" by Phoebe is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0)

An NEA spokesperson told the ABC allowing LTVP holders to be employed struck a "careful balance" between managing workforce challenges and "preserving the 'local' identity" of hawker culture and heritage.

A culinary tapestry worth preserving?

Ms Dorsey remembers a hawker selling his grandfather's pig organ soup.

She said the family-run stall is the last to serve what used to be a common side dish: sticky rice and chestnuts steamed in pig intestine.

Researcher Jenny Dorsey says even as wages rise, consumers remain unwilling to pay more for hawker food creating a price ceiling. (Supplied: Jenny Dorsey)

It is a recipe only the stallholder's mother knows, but one that will not be passed down because its preparation was too laborious to be financially viable, Ms Dorsey said.

" That's a little piece of history that [will be] gone, and this has happened to a lot of different hawker foods across time. "

Ms Yam says the hawker centre is also where community bonds were forged and fellow hawkers became extended family.

"It's about visiting the same coffee uncle every single day [who] knows your order just by looking at you."

Even her fish supplier — the same one her great-grandfather used — is considering shutting up shop.

With the convenience of online shopping and supermarkets, this tapestry of heritage and community was not valued in today's economy, she said.

She said society needed to figure out what they valued about hawker culture.

"Does it mean affordability of food to the masses, or does it mean there is some sort of skills that you are trying to preserve?"

Hawker centres are where communities can forge bonds over shared meals, says Debbie Yam. (Reuters: Edgar Siu)

Ms Dorsey said the government needed to define what its objectives are.

"We're kind of in this weird policy tension point that nobody has really resolved," she said.

An NEA spokesperson said its policies struck a "careful balance" between keeping hawker food affordable, supporting hawkers, and safeguarding the long-term sustainability" of the trade, and the agency would continue reviewing them.

World.title: ‘Too busy yelling and screaming’: How a musical enigma learnt to let go of drama
World.content:
CultureMusicTake 7 ‘Too busy yelling and screaming’: How a musical enigma learnt to let go of drama In our weekly series asking the big questions of high-profile people, iOTA reveals his solution to procrastination, his greatest fear – and his desire to know whether dinosaurs had feathers. Michael Dwyer October 10, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

He’s played Hedwig, Dr Frank-N-Furter and that Doof Warrior dude with the flame-throwing guitar in Mad Max: Fury Road, so iOTA’s Kiss T-shirt makes perfect sense as interview apparel. To this day, the Pinjarra-raised singer-songwriter and actor scours eBay for vintage posters and merch for his inner child’s favourite band. He’s no Peter Pan, though. His first album in 10 years finds him in much more contemplative acoustic territory, his flamboyant theatrical creations packed away as he considers the existential implications of its title, Hours Disappear. Singer-songwriter iOTA returns with Hours Disappear, his long-awaited seventh album. Maja Baska The album re-thinks several songs from iOTA’s 1999 debut, The Hip Bone Connection, alongside new material: a neat way of addressing how much life has happened while reminding him to get cracking on what’s left. “In the next 20 years,” he promises, “there’s going to be a lot of music.”



Worst habit? Procrastination through fear. Fear of the unknown and just never really knowing what the right decision is. I’m getting better, but it has been something that’s perhaps slowed me down. I’m always trying to second-guess everything, worried about not taking the right step and what that might mean. You can overthink it so much that you don’t end up doing anything. All you have to do is make a decision. Flip a coin and away you go. You’ll be OK. iOTA in 2007. Domino Postiglione Greatest fear? A loss of freedom. Not being free to do whatever I want to do, not being free to think the way I want to think. If you spend any time on social media, you can see those walls close in. If you spend enough time looking at one subject, it keeps feeding you more of that sort of stuff. And I definitely go, “I see what you’re doing here…” but it just makes you think, “What else is influencing me?”



The line that stayed with you? “Your life is your life. Know it while you have it. You are marvellous, and the gods wait to delight in you.” [The Laughing Heart by Charles Bukowski]. It’s a beautiful poem, but I think that’s the nice part of it; the best part of it. I only found it about two years ago. I was doing a cabaret show based on light and darkness [iOTA in the Dark], and I was looking for ideas and that one really stuck with me. It’s just beautiful. And he’s such a great character. Biggest regret? Not being present. Not always staying in the moment. I suppose you get better at doing that, like you get better at everything as you get older. When some big drama is happening, when it’s over, you come out of that drama and you go, “Where was I then?” I don’t even know. I was just too busy yelling and screaming or jumping up and down. You kind of lose yourself in all of that and I regret that. Also, just being so far away from my family [in WA]; not being present enough with my parents as they get older.



Tell us about your turning point... When I turned 50 [in 2018], I had this profound realisation that there was less time in front of me than behind me, and it really was a visceral recognition that I had. I mean, we all know it’s not forever, but just make those calculations. Twenty years doesn’t seem that long ago, but think 20 years ahead and oh my god, I’m going to be 70-something! It’s kind of scary, but it also brings this urgency to your life and to the work that you do. It really made a difference, and I like the change that it’s made in me. It’s brought more of an urgency to my life. It’s made life feel more profound and important, and it’s given me a way forward. The artwork or song you wish was yours? Related Article Take 7 After a one-night stand, this comedian was told he’d be a dad. But not all was as it seemed I don’t want anybody else’s song to be mine, or wish that I’d written it. I love so many people’s music and art … but when I think of David Sylvian’s album, Secrets of the Beehive, and also Jane’s Addiction’s Ritual de lo Habitual album, or anything by Kate Bush … I’d love to be able to find the spirit of those albums and make that mine. They’re edgy and they’re not too commercial, but they’re just in this nice sweet spot of cool and interesting and strange and magical. I’d like to find something like that for myself, to make an album that felt like those albums.

World.title: Lisa says her husband is ‘trolling’, but he denies it. Who’s right?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsWordPlay Lisa says her husband is ‘trolling’, but he denies it. Who’s right? David Astle October 10, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Every week, you may find Lisa Quinn’s husband puttering in the Hawkesbury River in his tinnie. Lover of the elements, the mangrove quiet, Terry spends hours trying to outsmart mulloway. Yet, his biggest challenge is a verb. According to Lisa at least, who dropped a line – a query, I mean. Her email set the scene: early morning, the Evinrude purring, Terry slides upstream or down, testing his luck with a spinner. He calls it trawling, while Lisa (at home) thinks trolling fits the bill. Who’s right? Terry says he’s trawling on the Hawkesbury, while his wife Lisa believes he’s trolling. Who’s correct? Getty Images Unqualified as a marriage counsellor, I’m calling it evens. Though if push comes to shove, Lisa has the edge. Both actions stem from tragelen in Dutch, meaning to drag, linking to Latin’s trahere, to pull. A fertile root, this gives us tract (a stretch of land) and contract (to draw in), distract and extract and all those other kinetic verbs. In Terry’s case, he’s dragging a lure, seeking to attract a fish. Trawling fits the bill, as does trolling, its poetic cousin, springing from troller in Old French, meaning to wander. You may troll the hills of Tyrol, say, following a trail, which also shares the French source. As does trolley, wandering the aisle.



Stroll, however, is more family friend than relative. The verb hails from Strolch in German, a vagabond, potentially tied to astrologo in Italian, as many mediaeval drifters often turned a penny with fortune-telling. Or that’s one theory. But let’s return to Terry and that mulloway dilemma. Are trawl and troll synonyms? Yes and no say most dictionaries. In the Macquarie, say, trawl’s fifth definition is troll, a straight swap. The snag lies in Definitions 1-4, which all involve a net. While Meaning 3 gets messier, bringing the bottom into the picture: “to fish with a net whose edge is dragged along the sea bottom to catch the fish living there”. Terry doesn’t do that. Related Article WordPlay Flong time no see: My adventures with a daily dictionary dip He uses a single line, mid-depth. One rod, one spinner, one tinnie. The nuance is spelt out by the Alaska Gold Seafood Company of all websites, saying, “Trolling and trawling sound alike, but differ in how they work and their effects on the ocean. A troller is a vessel operated by a single fisherman or two to three people (not infrequently family members) that pull hooks through the water typically targeting a single species such as wild king salmon.” Trawling by contrast is omnivorous, the net swallowing any nonchalant ling lingering, plus random “bycatch” minding its own business. Look up troll and the commercial vibe is lost. The net vanishes, the factory ship sinks. Trolling is “to fish with a moving line”, be that lured or baited. Said aloud, there’s a melodic charm about troll, echoing Definition 5 (obsolete) – “to sing or utter in a full rolling voice”. Terry, I’d say, has his recreational verb in troll, so long as we ignore the gremlin in the room.

World.title: What it will cost to score public access to the ‘invitation only’ Birdcage marquees
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life What it will cost to score public access to the ‘invitation only’ Birdcage marquees Stephen Brook and Cara Waters October 10, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The VIP marquees at the races during Melbourne Cup week were once the height of exclusivity – no invite, no entry. Now some – including Crown and Asahi – are selling tickets allowing the public to gain entry to parts of the exclusive marquees. Revellers on the dance floor in the Mumm marquee at the Birdcage on Oaks Day at Flemington last year. Penny Stephens Preparations are in full swing at Flemington for later this month when Crown will move its Marmont restaurant into its marquee, selling $2195 tickets for the ground floor and first floor on Cup Day and $895 on Stakes Day with a vibe of “where California cool meets Melbourne swagger”. The invite-only tradition will be kept alive on the top floor.



“We’re still preserving the exclusive Crown experience across our VIP floor for talent, media, members and VIP guests,” a Crown spokeswoman said. Last year Marmont was ticketed, but was in a separate marquee at the rear of the Birdcage and the luxurious three-storey Crown marquee on the front row remained invitation only. Related Article Exclusive

City life ‘We’re not going to hold back’: Chris Lucas’ restaurants racing to Flemington for Cup carnival The Asahi Birdcage marquee will split in two, with a walk-in bar downstairs where Birdcage attendees can pay for drinks. Upstairs will be the traditional invite only space on Derby Day and Melbourne Cup Day, but on Oaks and Stakes days will become Club Asahi with the VRC selling tickets for $1595 each. “The Asahi Super Dry Beer Garden will take inspiration from the hospitality and architecture of modern Japan,” said Lauren Fildes, Asahi Beverages Marketing general manager.



“We’ll host key customers, suppliers and others, with a focus on ensuring guests enjoy the races while experiencing a touch of contemporary Tokyo in the Birdcage,” she said. The Crown and Asahi packages both include free-flowing drinks, food and entertainment. The Birdcage shake-up comes as the VRC looks to shore up its corporate partnerships after posting a $7.2 million loss last year, its fifth consecutive multimillion-dollar loss since 2021. Inside the lower ground floor of the Crown marquee last year with DJ Grant Smillie and chef Guillaume Brahimi, this year it will house paying punters. Eddie Jim Charging attendees for entry is one way brands can offset some of the huge cost of securing a spot in the Birdcage and represents a move away from the previous strategy of spending millions on a marquee as a marketing gesture alone.



Even luxury brands are keeping a sharp eye on their return on investment for this Melbourne Cup Carnival. Birdcage stalwarts including Emirates, Myer, Lavazza and Penfolds as well as luxury jeweller Kennedy and streaming service Paramount + (Channel Ten) have all pulled the pin on their Birdcage involvement in recent years. Crown has cut back its involvement with the Victoria Racing Club handing over the catering contracts at the racetrack in April to international hospitality giant Delaware North. The gambling giant finally returned to profit last year – its first in five years – after cutting costs. Lexus will again have the premium location at the top of the racetrack straight with a luxury three-storey marquee offering perfect views.



Guests will be chauffeured in a fleet of Lexus cars to the track and can book in for a sit-down lunch at the ground floor of the marquee. The marquee is invitation only, except for members of Lexus’ Encore loyalty program who have the option to buy a ticket. Sailor Jessica Watson unveils Mumm’s 2025 marquee. Eddie Jim Even with Birdcage entry now more widely available than ever, Mumm and Nine will continue to allow entry only to invited guests. Mumm’s marquee will have a vintage train theme and has been dubbed the “The G.H. Mumm 1827 Express”.



Kevin Mapson, managing director for Pernod Ricard Pacific, said it will “hark back to the golden age of luxury train travel”. Related Article Updated

Victorian racing The club that runs the Melbourne Cup just posted a $7.2 million loss. This is why it says that’s a good thing Staff will be dressed in train uniforms with food by Chris Lucas’ Maison Batard restaurant, including scallop tartare with champagne jelly. Mapson said Mumm is not selling any tickets to its marquee, keeping it strictly invitation only. “The biggest challenge for us is we have a limit on how many people we can get into the marquee because we are the marquee that people want to go to,” he said. “We really struggle with managing the numbers, so that’s why we’re invite only.”



Alcohol giant Diageo operated a tiny speakeasy bar last year, but has expanded to a two-storey marquee on the front row showcasing its Don Julio tequila brand. The ground floor of the Mexican themed marquee will be invitation only but upstairs the “Hacienda Social Club” is open to all Birdcage guests. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mountains of Trouble:  Bumpy road for Rinehart’s offshore mining push
World.content:
Lucia Chicaiza watched a caravan of headlights inch towards her northern Ecuadorian township. When the trucks and armoured vehicles stopped, they disgorged hundreds of men carrying guns and anti-riot shields.

They were met by a crowd of farmers, women and elderly people gathered on the main street of the La Merced de Buenos Aires township – little more than a collection of wooden homes in windswept Andean moorland foothills.

Soon, all that stood between the crowd and more than 500 heavily armed police and soldiers was a green hand-painted banner declaring the township’s right to “peaceful resistance”.

“They were armed as if they were going to war,” remembers Chicaiza, the parish’s president, of that night in August 2021. “We will never forget it.”

The troops were there to protect the interests of Australia’s richest person – billionaire mining magnate Gina Rinehart.

For more than 100 days, local villagers like Chicaiza had blocked Rinehart’s subsidiary company Hanrine Ecuadorian Exploration and Mining from accessing its sprawling exploration concessions in the gold and copper-rich ridges ringing the town.

Villagers claimed the concessions were awarded in a dubious process marred by irregularities, without consultation, and potentially in breach of Ecuadorian law.

Parish president Lucia Chicaiza in La Merced de Buenos Aires. James Ross

That cold morning in 2021, Chicaiza watched police use their shields to charge against elderly women to break the human chain of protesters blocking the road. She remembers officers stepping on the women and dragging them by the legs as they teargassed their way into the township.

Locals futilely fought back for hours before troops cleared the way for Hanrine’s buses and trucks. Chicaiza says workers inside clapped and laughed as they went past.

The incident is just one of many controversies surrounding Hanrine’s operations in Ecuador that have received little scrutiny in Australia.

This masthead spent a month in Ecuador investigating the activities of the company wholly owned by Rinehart’s Hancock Prospecting, and its alleged role in major security and environmental concerns. Over the course of several months, it examined hundreds of pages of government documents, company records, court files and research papers.

It interviewed dozens of villagers, environmental activists, experts and former Hanrine employees. They detailed allegations of human rights breaches; a culture of intimidation and fear; violence; enablement of illegal mining; and irregularities in the granting of the company’s concessions.

The claims raise questions about the conduct of one of Australia’s largest companies in a nation wracked by corruption and unrest at a time when spiking copper and gold prices mean its significant reserves of both are attracting international interest. Hanrine has also entered a partnership with another Australian miner to develop a project in southern Ecuador.

There is no suggestion Rinehart authorised or condoned Hanrine’s alleged conduct, or was aware of the allegations against her company.

The accusations against Hanrine also expose what governance groups say is a lack of scrutiny subsidiaries face when they operate overseas, especially where they benefit from murky legal and regulatory frameworks and weak institutional oversight.

“The case of Hanrine is a case of extreme violence at a Latin American level,” says Yuly Tenorio, an Ecuadorian lawyer who has represented La Merced de Buenos Aires locals in court, pointing to incidents beyond the 2021 police and army operation.

“We feel there’s a systemic violation of rights, and that’s unforgivable.”

The villagers have since had wins against Hanrine – the company effectively abandoned its worker camps after claims over water rights halted its exploration.

It’s a fragile status quo. Hanrine retains its rights over the concessions, and locals fear the company could return.

Its exit also created a vacuum that hundreds of illegal gold miners have filled. Backed by violent armed groups, they’ve taken over parts of Hanrine’s concessions, unleashing a major security crisis in the once-sleepy farming town.

The illegal mines have been declared a military target and come under heavy artillery fire by the armed forces, turning Rinehart’s Ecuadorian possessions into a literal battlefield.

Villagers and environmental groups believe Hanrine has an ethical and legal responsibility to prevent illegal mining and the environmental degradation it causes even if the company cannot, for now, mine the area itself.

Anti-corruption and human rights groups, including Transparency International Australia and Global Witness, say Hanrine also has human rights and transparency obligations.

“This includes ensuring proper consultation, free, prior and informed consent with local communities on whose land mining is being proposed,” says Transparency International Australia chief executive Clancy Moore.

Legal experts say Ecuador’s dated mining laws operate in a grey area, responsibility is determined ad hoc, guidelines around environmental liability are murky, and enforcement is close to non-existent. Laying blame for the disastrous chain of events in La Merced de Buenos Aires is complicated.

Stressing it has never progressed beyond exploration activity, Hanrine categorically denies any wrongdoing and claims criticisms are “unsubstantiated allegations supplied by anti-prosperity environmental activists and individuals aligned with, and profiting from, illegal mining and associated criminal activity, as they provide support and supplies for a profit to illegal miners operating there”.

Hanrine chief executive Carlos de Miguel said in a statement in response to extensive questions by this masthead that the company complied with relevant laws and regulations.

“To suggest otherwise is false and blatantly defamatory,” he said.

THE GOLD RUSH

Hanrine had just won the rights to thousands of hectares of land in La Merced de Buenos Aires when illegal mining arrived in the parish in late 2017.

Traces of gold were discovered around the community of El Triunfo, a collection of farms on the town’s outskirts, attracting illegal miners from across Ecuador and neighbouring countries.

Versions of how the precious metal came to be found vary. Some claim granting Hanrine concessions tipped the illegal miners off about potentially lucrative mineral deposits.

Others say a worker digging up a local road accidentally discovered gold. The labourer, this version of events goes, was from Zaruma, a gold mining town in Ecuador’s south and itself home to a booming illegal mining industry. He had recognised the find immediately, tipping off other miners.

“No one believed it,” says Sulema Armas, a dairy farmer and mining opponent from La Merced de Buenos Aires. “We said: ‘These people are crazy. Why are they going up there and filling bags with rocks?’ We were so naive.”

Mining was so foreign to locals that at one point police officers helped illegal miners load bags of rock into vehicles, unaware they were being mined for gold.

Before long, 10,000 illegal miners flooded La Merced de Buenos Aires, quickly outnumbering its 2000 inhabitants. Organised crime groups followed, seizing control of the territory and taking a cut of miners’ profits in exchange for protection, a tactic known in Ecuador as a “vaccine”.

La Merced de Buenos Aires became a lawless town where prostitution, gambling, drug trafficking and violence ran rampant. Shootings between members of rival groups vying for control of the mines became commonplace.

So did kidnappings, extortions, executions and mutilations. Workers were punished if they were suspected of working with rivals. Others simply disappeared.

“They would take the dead bodies out in pick-up trucks,” Lucia Chicaiza says. “People were getting shot, stabbed. A couple of times, people even saw [the miners] taking bodies out with their throats cut and arms cut off.”

Locals felt they had been abandoned by authorities, until a deadly gunfight between armed groups in 2019 thrust La Merced de Buenos Aires into the national agenda. Scores died in the fighting, their bodies dumped in ravines and unmarked graves.

“They’re going to dig for gold and they are going to find corpses,” says a local source familiar with the mining conflict who did not want to be identified for fear of reprisals.

The then Ecuadorian president, Lenin Moreno, declared a state of emergency over “the grave internal commotion”, allowing the government to deploy thousands of police and military personnel to clear out the illegal miners.

A fleeting peace returned. Soon, though, rumours circulated that the land the illegal miners had taken over belonged to a company.

“It was then that we found out it was Hanrine,” says Chicaiza.

HANRINE WHO?

Hanrine had obtained its concessions, more than 20,000 hectares of land known as the IMBA project, in late 2017, but illegal mining prevented exploration.

After the government’s 2019 intervention, Hanrine could finally attempt to move in. But locals like Chicaiza, who had spent years fighting for authorities to intervene in the illegal mines, felt blindsided.

Ecuadorian authorities had granted Hanrine the concessions without consulting villagers in La Merced de Buenos Aires or the Awa Indigenous community, whose ancestral lands encroach into part of the tenement. That is despite two separate provisions in the country’s Constitution recognising the rights of locals and Indigenous groups to be consulted on environment-altering projects.

Community consultation failures have previously led to other companies losing their tenements. In 2018 an Ecuadorian court ruled 52 concessions in and around the A’i Cofan Sinangoe Indigenous community’s territory in the Amazon be revoked on the basis they had been granted without consultation.

A human rights committee of non-government MPs in Ecuador’s national assembly would later describe the lack of consultation as a “clear violation of the rights of Indigenous communities and the general population of the parish”. It called for a thorough investigation into the concession process, which was also plagued by irregularities.

An earlier report by a government watchdog found the awarding of the concessions lacked necessary geological and technical information, mining areas were reserved for longer than allowed, mining titles were registered after the required deadline, and the administrative protection granted to Hanrine over illegal mining in the area had been based on the wrong technical report.

In Ecuador, consultation is a constitutional responsibility of the state. Mining companies may also sign up to voluntary codes, such as that of the International Council of Mining and Metals or the Initiative for Responsible Mining Assurance, which recognise the need to engage, consult and build trust with local communities, particularly Indigenous groups.



Neither Hanrine nor Hancock Prospecting is publicly listed as a signatory to either framework.

Still, Global Witness head of policy and advocacy Emily Iona Stewart says there is “no scenario where a mining company as large as this is not aware of the duty of care that they have”.

“The less you do as a company upfront in terms of working with the community, in terms of raising your standards, the more violence that there is further down the line, which is exactly what this company is experiencing,” Stewart says.

Shortly after Chicaiza found out about Hanrine, she says, buses filled with its staff started arriving at La Merced de Buenos Aires.

Locals, scarred by their experience with illegal mining groups, blocked them from entering the township and declared they were exercising a right to peaceful resistance against mining in the territory, legal or otherwise.

As blue-overalled workers filed out of the vehicles, Chicaiza immediately felt some faces looked familiar.

“We recognised many of them as those working in the illegal mines,” she remembers.

“Those people who had been controlling everything with machetes, revolvers and threats, arrived dressed in company uniforms.”

This masthead has identified one man involved in the early illegal gold rush in La Merced de Buenos Aires who was later in charge of a community engagement program supported by Hanrine.

Luis Valencia was part of a bizarre illegal-miner push in 2019 to convince the Ecuadorian government to allow them to mine part of Hanrine’s concessions to rein in the violence. Valencia, a former conservationist who fought palm oil plantations and loggers in the late ’90s, told the media at the time: “We are all armed over there because everyone has to look out for their own interests.”

In a local TV interview, he claimed he had negotiated a deal with Hanrine to utilise 300 hectares for “artisanal mining”, a controversial term often used to disguise large-scale illegal mining linked to organised crime networks.

“Now we are illegals, we are delinquents, because we are in a territory that is already under someone else’s name, that was handed out,” Valencia said at the time.

He died in a hail of bullets during an ambush in his home town of San Lorenzo in 2024.

In response to questions by this masthead, Hanrine confirmed it had supported a program run by Valencia but said the company “never allowed any other party to explore or conduct any mining activity on our tenements”.

But the damage to the town from years of illegal mining and subsequent violence was done.

“We opened our eyes and said no more. Since then, we have been resisting,” Chicaiza says.

Some locals, including members of the Awa Indigenous community, took up jobs with Hanrine as it began setting up, lured by steady income, improved housing and associated benefits.

A member of the Awa Indigenous community wears a Hanrine T-shirt during a communal labour meet-up known as a “minga” in Palmira de Toctemí, a community in the Awa’s ancestral land in La Merced de Buenos Aires parish. Photo: James Ross.

For others, the company represented an extension of the illegal mining threat to the environment, and they were hell-bent on fighting it.

Yuly Tenorio, the Ecuadorian lawyer who has represented La Merced de Buenos Aires locals, says Hanrine should have, at several moments since being granted the concessions, taken a much tougher approach to illegal miners to show the community it was acting in good faith.

“But that never happened,” Tenorio says.

Under Ecuador’s mining law, concession holders can be fined and even have their tenements stripped for allowing “third parties who are not legally authorised to do so” to mine within their areas of operation.

Maria del Mar Heredia, a legal director at international law firm Dentons, says that in reality matters are not that straightforward.

A hillside showing illegal mining in 2025 CREDIT: JAMES ROSS

“Simply being the titleholder doesn’t automatically make you responsible for illegal mining taking place within your concession,” says Heredia, speaking broadly about the country’s legal context. “In a certain way, you need to establish that you are not involved in it, and that it’s beyond your control.”

That depends on whether a company co-operates with authorities, the mitigating actions it takes, and whether it complies with permits and environmental reporting requirements.

Even then, Heredia says Ecuador’s mining regulator, ARCOM, does not have the resources or technical capacity to investigate, prosecute and sanction much of the wrongdoing.

Heredia points to the controversial mining tax introduced by the Ecuadorian government last year, designed to help fund the regulator’s illegal mining fight. Only about 10 per cent of concession holders have paid it, but Heredia says ARCOM isn’t chasing non-payers.



“On top of that, half the authorities are under threat. What often happens is that officials turn a blind eye and don’t report anything because they are either facing threats or are themselves profiting from the situation,” she says.

Hanrine maintains it took appropriate action and requested administrative protection after observing illegal miners within its concessions in late 2017. The company says it still cannot carry out exploration in the area and is not responsible for the illegal miners’ environmental damage.

“Any suggestion that Hanrine knowingly condones or participates in illegal, environmentally harmful or abusive conduct is false and categorically rejected,” Hanrine said.

‘DEAD DOGS DON’T BITE’

As the stalemate between villagers and Hanrine continued after the company’s arrival, tensions escalated.

Accounts from local villagers, which were backed in a judicial council report, accuse Hanrine staff of trespassing on private land. On one occasion, workers attempted to build a road without permits through a farm, damaging a waterfall the local family owners planned to turn into a tourist attraction.

Local anti-mining advocates say they have been abused, harassed, assaulted and threatened. One claims he was beaten by Hanrine workers while riding a motorbike with his elderly mother, who defended herself from the alleged assailants with a hose. Another received death threats. “Dead dogs don’t bite,” she was told.

At one point in 2020, almost 200 people, including members of the Awa Indigenous community, set fire to two Hanrine camps. Chants of “The people united will never be defeated” echoed as the tents burnt. Two months later, some 150 villagers who had marched to Hanrine’s camp on the outskirts of town to demand the company remove its machinery from the parish clashed with police and security forces.

In 2022 Ecuador’s national assembly granted an amnesty to 22 locals. The charges stemmed from protests and disputes over territorial rights over to their opposition to Hanrine. The amnesty followed a petition from environmental and rural land corporation APT Norte, which had been raising the alarm about Hanrine’s treatment of anti-mining activists.

Tensions boiled over again in January 2023, after locals blocked roads with rocks and debris to prevent military and police personnel travelling with a Hanrine convoy from setting up camp in El Triunfo.

Security forces arrested two people in the ensuing chaos, including a disabled elderly man who told this masthead he was thrown to the ground and stomped on by officers before being handcuffed and detained for five hours.

“I was a little traumatised,” he says. “All this time I have been alive and they arrest me in this way.”

Hanrine has now largely abandoned the parish, but locals are again grappling with the illegal miners who invaded its concessions.

Chicaiza is now working with the military to dismantle illegal mines, controlled by Colombian guerrilla outfits that splintered from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC). The mines have previously been under the thumb of local thugs, petty criminals and a feared prison gang known as Los Lobos (The Wolves).

This masthead travelled to El Triunfo, the last outpost before the steep climb to the illegal mines, last year during an Ecuadorian military operation that sent the illegal miners and guerrillas into hiding.

Some fled across parish lines, others sheltered in improvised miner hostels and bars around La Merced de Buenos Aires.

Armoured vehicles and military trucks lined the road. Soldiers in army fatigues carrying automatic weapons rested in demolished buildings, once used by the illegal miners. The remains of makeshift shelters burned nearby.

The environmental devastation caused by the illegal operations inside Hanrine’s concessions was obvious. Dozens of pitheads covered in plastic sheets scarred the ridges around the community. Tailings spilled down the mountainside, where miners set up ziplines to winch supplies.

The 2025 operation destroyed processing plants hidden in the forest, and seized explosives, Colombian guerrilla uniforms, ammunition and hundreds of sacks filled with gold-bearing rock. But it represented only a temporary win.

The illegal miners know the army doesn’t stick around. The parish is a small part of the unit’s jurisdiction, which also includes gang strongholds like Esmeraldas and parts of the volatile Colombian-Ecuador border.

Resources are stretched and explosives used to dismantle mines are scarce. When the troops peel off, the illegal miners re-emerge. It’s a game of cat and mouse they have played for years.

Heredia, the Dentons lawyer specialised in mining contracts, believes it will take years to eradicate illegal mining in Ecuador.

“There’s a lot of work to be done – and that goes hand in hand with security issues the country will have to address,” she says.

‘A MONSTER OF MANY HEADS’

On the 10th floor of a tower with sweeping views of the business district in Ecuador’s capital, Quito, a special unit inside the office of public prosecutions sorts through stacks of documents. Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny’s smash hit Voy a Llevarte Pa’ PR plays from speakers. Manila folders containing hundreds of pages of police reports, photographs and other evidence are perilously stacked on desks and chairs, and in cardboard boxes on the floor.

The unit, based in a small, unassuming corner office, investigates crimes against nature - including illegal mining.

Ecuador, in 2008, became the first country to constitutionally recognise the rights of nature, a move rooted in the Indigenous concept of “sumak kawsay”, which loosely translates as “good living” and refers to the right of communities to live in an ecologically balanced environment.

Environmental lawyer Yuly Tenorio inspects documents in Ecuador’s capital, Quito, relating to court cases over illegal mining in La Merced de Buenos Aires. Photo: James Ross.

Yuly Tenorio has come to the office to follow up a series of investigations into La Merced de Buenos Aires. They include allegations of water pollution, missing bags of seized gold-bearing rock, and claims that Hanrine carried out drilling works without the right permits.

She says most reports of crimes against nature in La Merced de Buenos Aires were filed by locals. She questions what Hanrine has done, besides obtaining administrative protection, to report and prevent illegal mining.

“There are no reports from the mining company against illegal miners. It’s all us,” Tenorio says. “Or, at least, we haven’t found out about them.”

Hanrine’s decision to challenge in the Constitutional Court the new mining oversight fee does not help its image with locals. Other miners also opposed the measure, which is subject to several constitutional challenges.

Hanrine’s general manager, Carlos de Miguel, has previously claimed the company has denounced illegal mining since 2017, “back when there were only about 60 illegal miners working on a small scale”, and says he has been “within metres of the illegal miners” during military operations to dismantle them.

He has also accused local environmental groups in La Merced de Buenos Aires of failing to denounce illegal miners and being complicit “behind the scenes”, a claim Tenorio and anti-mining activists in the parish strenuously deny.

“We have pursued everything from administrative injunctions to criminal complaints, alongside dozens of formal requests and tireless meetings with every single authority, yet to no avail,” de Miguel told local media outlet El Oriente last year.

Despite years of clashes with locals, violence, environmental issues and strong opposition, there is no sign Hanrine will back off.

Locals certainly worry the company could attempt to enter its concessions again. Their message for Gina Rinehart is to give up. She is not welcome.

“One day she will depart from this world, and where will all her wealth and ego go?” Sulema Armas, farmer and mining opponent from La Merced de Buenos Aires, says.

Research by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime, an independent Swiss policy research institute, shows illegal mining in Ecuador has exploded in recent years, fuelled by soaring gold prices, weak enforcement, dysfunctional institutions and widespread corruption.

In 2018, there were fewer than 60 illegal mines in the country. That number, according to the research, had ballooned to more than 600 by 2024.

Illegal mining is estimated to have produced exports worth more than US$1.3 billion in 2024, turning illicit gold into the main source of income for organised crime networks. Ecuador’s Chamber of Mining estimates about half the gold exported out of the country is illegally mined.

Unlike cocaine, which can be spoilt and degraded, gold is impervious to heat, water and weather. It is also easy to launder. Once it enters the legitimate supply chain, it’s almost untraceable.

“It’s a monster of many heads,” former Ecuador interior minister Mónica Palencia told the media last year. The market is so lucrative, she said, that “you remove a backhoe loader and they purchase another”.

Illegal miners in La Merced de Buenos Aires crawl into narrow, muddy galleries to extract the rock, which is then transported out of the mountain using a network of mules and steel pulley systems for processing.

Ecuadorian soldiers and firefighters retrieve a dead body from the illegal mines in La Merced de Buenos Aires in June 2026. Photo: Ecuadorian Army.

Some ore is processed in rudimentary plants along the Lita River, using toxic chemicals like cyanide to separate the metal from the rock. The rest is processed in other provinces or in countries like Colombia, where “there’s no God or law”, as one official source, unauthorised to speak publicly, put it.

Toxic run-off is released into waterways running through farmland and through forests teeming with bears, monkeys and armadillos.

La Merced de Buenos Aires township is nestled between subtropical forests and the grasslands of the paramo, a high-altitude alpine tundra ecosystem that acts like a giant sponge by soaking up the run-off from the mountains and slowly releasing it into the lands below. This allows rivers to flow all year round and unique wildlife to thrive in the primary forests around them.

Sandro Armas, the president of BUPROE, an environmental group based in the parish, says water analysis carried out by the group has identified traces of heavy metals in the Lita River, which flows through his farm on the outskirts of La Merced de Buenos Aires township. The water is often cloudy and reeks of chemicals.

“It fills me with sadness and indignation,” he says. “We need to take care of the environment and the water because it’s life. If we destroy what gives us life, we are killing ourselves slowly with our own hands.”

Sandro Armas, a farmer and the president of local environmental group BUPROE, says heavy metals believed to come from illegal mining operations have been detected in the Lita River Photo: James Ross.

Armas has repeatedly reported the pollution at great personal risk, but no remediation work has been undertaken. At times, he’s had to report his own family members for collaborating with illegal miners. He worries about the welfare of the Awa community living downstream, and farmers relying on irrigation.

Alfonso Cantincus is the president of the Awa in Palmira de Toctemi. He says wild animals and cattle often wind up dead after drinking water from the Lita River, one of only two rivers flowing through their territory. Cantincus says the fish have also disappeared.

“They drink the water and die,” he says. “I am worried about my people. With pollution comes illness. I do not want that to happen to our community.”

Hanrine maintains it has enjoyed a “long-standing friendship based on mutual respect” with the Awa community, and says it has reverted IMBA 5, the concession encroaching into the Indigenous group’s territory, to the government over its lack of potential.

The Awa fear further mining, by Hanrine or the illegal miners, could potentially pollute their only remaining river, the San Francisco.

“Mining pollutes, legal or illegal,” Cantincus says. It’s unwelcome in their ancestral lands.

World.title: When it comes to cruising, Australians choose one region above all others
World.content:
InspirationCruises When it comes to cruising, Australians choose one region above all others Brian Jonhston October 10, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. According to the Cruise Lines International Association, Australians took 1.16 million cruises in Australian, New Zealand and South Pacific waters last year, making it by far our most popular cruise region and representing 80 per cent of the Australian cruise market. The number increased 8 per cent from the previous year. That might be because passenger age is falling – the average is now 47 – and the average length of cruise itineraries is shortening to accommodate short-break options. International uncertainty is also encouraging domestic cruising. Celebrity Edge in Sydney. A recent survey of Norwegian Cruise Line guests found that cruisers are primarily motivated by relaxation and local cultures, which the South Pacific and New Zealand provide without the need for long-haul pre-cruise flights. Looking for a budget cruise in our region? Carnival has four ships here this summer, operating Queensland and South Pacific itineraries from Brisbane and Sydney.



A fifth ship, Carnival Adventure, arrives after summer (in March 2027), to home port for a month in Melbourne, with most sailings focused on South Australia. 



Premium and luxury ships don’t stay here as long. Rather, they call at a few Australian ports as they relocate between Asia and/or the South Pacific, although generally, they linger to operate several Sydney-Auckland runs. Viking will do just that. In addition to New Zealand cruises from Sydney, Silversea is sailing Sydney-Melbourne and Regent Seven Seas from Sydney to Darwin. All three companies have two ships here. Also with two ships each, Azamara is taking in a wider range of destinations over multiple itineraries, while Oceania is notably sailing in to or out of Perth and along the West Australian coast. Azamara Quest in Melbourne. The cruise line is taking in a wider range of destinations over multiple itineraries. At the small ship level, Coral Expeditions’ three ships offer a comprehensive range of sailings. The company has ramped up West Australian itineraries to destinations such as the Abrolhos Islands, Coral Coast, Ningaloo Reef and South West Capes.



And finally, some cruise lines are just teasing us. Crystal Serenity has a single ship sailing Auckland-Brisbane, and Ponant’s Le Soleal sails Bali-Cairns and Cairns-Dunedin. Lines such as Cunard and Disney won’t be appearing at all, and familiar favourite Quantum of the Seas is sailing its last hurrah in Australia. Still, there’s plenty of choice, so jump in before the ship sails. EVERYONE ASKS Is it OK to arrive in port on departure day? While most cruises won’t depart until late afternoon, it would be unwise to arrive the same day if flying internationally, and especially if relying on journeys with flight connections.



Even single, short-haul flights can be cancelled or delayed, particularly in places such as Europe during the summer high season. Related Article Cruises A record number of Australians are cruising, but they’re facing a problem Call me paranoid, but I wouldn’t even rely on traffic conditions on the day you board if the ship is any distance from the airport or your hotel. Any delay could result in missing your cruise departure. The cruise line won’t compensate you, and nor might your travel insurance, depending on the cause. Arriving after a flight with an hour to spare might be construed as a foreseeable problem. Quite apart from logistics, most cruises depart from key cities such as Barcelona, Vancouver or Singapore that offer much to see and do, so why sail away so soon after you arrive? Most arrival ports are worth an overnight, if not two or three. Finally, cruises can be more tiring than you might think, especially if you’ve signed up for lots of shore excursions. You’ll enjoy them more if you’ve given yourself a couple of nights to get over your jet lag before boarding.
