World.title: My local cafe calls cronuts by another name. Should I correct them?
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Q: My cafe sells delicious cronuts, but advertises them as “cro-donuts”. Should I correct them? I’ve been thinking about this for seven years. M.M., Preston, Vic



Photo: Illustration by Drew Aitken

A: The cronut (croissant-doughnut) is one of those fusion-type pastries that have become very popular, along with the crookie (croissant-cookie), the duffin (doughnut-muffin) and the lame-o-nutbag (a lamington-churro-doughnut-baguette. Actually, I just made that up, but I think it could take off. Investor inquiries welcome!)

So if the owner of your cafe is calling it a “cro-donut”, they may not understand the concept of portmanteaus – combination words (or combords) – which would explain why the cafe may also be listing frap-cappuccinos (frappuccinos) and frog-yoghurt (frogurt) on their break-lunch (brunch) menu. Or maybe the owner does know the correct name for a cronut, but got sick of explaining it to customers – or they were threatened with legal action by lawyers from Cronut Global Pastry Industries, who issued a “cease and delish” order.

Either way, I totally get how confusing-signage (confignage) can cause mental anguish. There’s a glass-and-mirror shop near my house with a sign that says: our glass is warrantied against breakage forever, then, in tiny print underneath, “Conditions apply” – and I’ve lost many a night’s sleep wondering, “What conditions? Like if you dropped a marshmallow on it?”

World.title: Strong earthquake in Central America sparks Pacific tsunami fears
World.content:
A large quake has struck the Central American country of Panama, briefly prompting fears of a Pacific tsunami.

It hit at 6.56am NZ time in the south of the country, measuring magnitude 7.7 at a depth of 33km. It was initially reported as magnitude 8, downgraded to 7.6 then adjusted to 7.7.

The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) and GNS Science initially said it was assessing whether the quake had created a tsunami that could affect New Zealand.

"Based on current information, the initial assessment is that the earthquake is unlikely to have caused a tsunami that will affect New Zealand," it said about half an hour later.

There were no immediate reports of damage in Panama, Reuters reported, with television footage showing people evacuating buildings.

There were warnings of potential tsunami across Central America and in Columbia and Ecuador.

The quake was felt in the capital, Reuters reported, and in Costa Rica.

World.title: Country Life: A little place in Taranaki, blooming around the world
World.content:
Eric Lander's eye for on-trend colours has helped him turn a struggling Taranaki sheep farm into a large orchid nursery which sends off exotic blooms to top florists in New York and around the world.

The 80-year-old still works a full day at his four large greenhouses, brimming with cymbidium orchids, their colours ranging from blood red, bronze and orange to lime green and yellow, trained up elastic thread to keep their stems as straight as possible for discerning overseas markets.

The orchids are trained up threads of elastic to keep the stems as straight as possible RNZ/Sally Round

Lander Orchids are grown in four large greenhouses in view of Mt Taranaki RNZ/Sally Round

Lander has been growing orchids since 1980 when he was searching for a way to improve the income from what was then a struggling sheep farm, not far from Hāwera.

"I was looking for something different to sort of boost the finances, and my sister took me along to visit an orchid nursery up in Whakatāne and I looked at it and I thought, oh, well, I might be able to do that."

His orchids could even be found in New York's Trump Tower at one stage, Lander told Country Life.

Audio player for " An eye for an orchid " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/country/1824421%2Fcountry-life-a-little-place-in-taranaki-blooming-around-the-world

An eye for an orchid Country Life Download MP3 13m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

He exports 95 percent of the flowers and in 2025 sent off more than 3000 boxes via his Auckland-based wholesaler, carefully cut, inspected and nestled in sheep wool.

Wendy Holt is among a small team which picks and packs the orchids twice a week from late May to early November.

"Especially when they go to America and we get the really big ones, you think what do they do with them? How do they display them? Who has them? I guess it's like hotels and that, big hotels … big corporate businesses, I suppose."

Blooms being packed for export RNZ/Sally Round

This yellow variety is among the 30,000 plants nurtured at Lander Orchids RNZ/Sally Round

Adjusting the elastic on each of the 30,000 plants at least once a week is another task, Lander said.

"We need them straight, otherwise they won't fit into the boxes, and the buyers want them straight too.

"It's quite a job."

Breeding and growing orchids is a long game, involving decades of selection involving Lander pollinating by hand to get the colours he thinks his customers will like.

"It takes seven years before you've got a production plant and then if it's a good one, you can keep it, but if it's a bad one, you throw them all out."

"That's the only way you get exclusive varieties."

Taranaki orchid grower Eric Lander RNZ/Sally Round

Eric Lander has a good feel for the colours that will meet the market RNZ/Sally Round

A recent stroke has affected Lander's sight and he relies on his team to inspect for tiny pests, but it hasn't affected his discerning eye for colour.

"You can see a good apple or a bad apple, you know, it's the same thing, but somehow I've got judgment that most people don't have about what will sell, especially overseas."

Lander feels pride and a sense of achievement in the business, Lander Orchids, now nearly half a century old - "A little place in Taranaki away from everywhere and me that never grew anything before.

World.title: US tsunami warning center issues possible threats for Pacific
World.content:
A large quake has struck the Central American country of Panama, prompting fears of a Pacific tsunami.

It hit at 6.56am NZ time in the south of the country, measuring magnitude 8 at a depth of 33km.

The U.S. Tsunami Warning Center latest issue said a possible tsunami threat to Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Marianas from the distant earthquake.

It adds that a threat to American Samoa from this earthquake is still under investigation.

Earlier, the Center said a tsunami threat exists for parts of the Pacific located closer to the earthquake. but it is still too early to determine whether there is a possible tsunami threat to Hawai'i.

World.title: Country Life: Former Wellington zookeeper helps Europe's rescue bears
World.content:
Winter is closing in at a forest in Bavaria, and former Wellington zookeeper John Pickard is giving the resident bears there a helping hand to hibernate.

He works at a bear sanctuary run by the German charity Gewerkschaft für Tiere eV, where 11 bears live on 11 hectares in fenced off enclosures on a reforested block once used by the German Army during the Cold War era.

Several of the bears are ex circus animals, and others have come from Eastern Europe where they were used as money earners after the collapse of communism, Pickard told Country Life.

Audio player for " The Kiwi among bears in Bavaria " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/country/1824379%2Fcountry-life-former-wellington-zookeeper-helps-europe-s-rescue-bears

The Kiwi among bears in Bavaria Country Life Download MP3 8m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

"They've been in private ownership, terrible little cages, boxes, even cages in the corner of restaurants.

"One was going to be made into a dancing bear. She's had all her teeth cut off flat."

There are several bear sanctuaries in Germany, and Pickard said it was good to see the number of bears needing rescue were declining.

Rescue bear Lucy, one of the bears Gnadenhof für Bären in Bavaria, run by the charity Gewerkschaft für Tiere eV Gewerkschaft für Tiere eV

"The last circus bear that was in Germany was here. He got confiscated. The circus had left him on the side of the motorway in a parking area in his wagon unattended for several days, and that was reported to the local council and they confiscated them and sent them to us."

Pickard is on his second stint looking after the bears since starting at Gnadenhof für Bären not far from Munich in 2011.

"The first thing is to get them back into a natural yearly rhythm. Most of them haven't been allowed to hibernate and so we do that, mostly… with the diet."

As winter draws near, the bears are being fed 16 kilograms of food to prepare them for their long winter sleep.

Pickard said it took them a long time to drop behaviours forced on them living in cages.

"They often have that stereotype behaviour that you see of bears in zoos where they're pacing backwards and forwards and things like that, and it reflects the size of the cage they came out of usually."

Pickard, 70, lives on site and starts the day off making up the feed and giving it to the bears at close range while remaining protected behind the wire.

"It's a very active job. I could say it's almost starting to wear me out. I've only got six months to go, I'll make it," he laughed.

The basic diet is a mixture of vegetables, fruit and nuts, with bread "good for weight gain" in the run up to winter.

Sometimes hunters drop off a deer carcass for the bear's weekly serving of meat.

Pickard learnt a lot about bears during a year at the zoo in Cologne and was involved in the successful breeding of sun bears at Wellington Zoo.

With many years under his belt observing the mammal, he has contributed papers on bear behaviour for zoology publications.

"It's a challenge to me, being able to work with an animal like this and being able to get on with them without being actually in contact with them.

"Understanding them, basically, and being able to read their behaviour because when you look at stuff about brown bears, it often says that they don't really signal their behaviour very much.

"Well, I disagree with that. If you work with them long enough, you can read them."

World.title: Young people in Auckland's new Henderson electorate feeling disenfranchised
World.content:
Audio player for " Young people in new Auckland electorate need more to believe their vote matters " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1811435%2Fyoung-people-in-auckland-s-new-henderson-electorate-feeling-disenfranchised

Young people in new Auckland electorate need more to believe their vote matters Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Young people in Auckland's new Henderson electorate say more needs to be done to encourage them that their vote matters.

The electorate has been reformed with new boundaries - covering Henderson, Rānui, Swanson, Lincoln, Massey, Western Heights, and parts of Te Atatū and Upper Harbour.

Just 56 percent of those aged 18 to 24 years old are enrolled to vote in the electorate, compared to 62 percent nationally.

The Green's Alika Wells, Opportunity's Almo Wong, the National Party's Angee Nicholas, independent Kay Luv and ACT's Nick Peirce, all in the running to become Henderson's local MP.

Also in the running is Labour's Phil Twyford, who's been the MP for the old Te Atatū electorate since 2011.

Checkpoint spoke to some young people who live in the electorate.

They said the enrolment rates were low because many felt disenfranchised.

Another said, "Maybe because some of us just don't really care about politics these days. And we don't really know anything about it."

For the issues most important for young people ahead of the election..at the top of the list was unemployment.

Henderson local Fred said many of his friends have been struggling to find work in Auckland.

"To be honest, employment, it's like, really hard to find a job. I was lucky, you know. I managed to get a job with the Defence Force, but not everybody's this lucky, so [there's] heaps of unemployed. A lot of my mates as well, some lost their jobs, some can't even get a job."

Nursing student Angie said high unemployment rates made her feel uneasy.

"I've studying nursing and I'm thinking about like how right now there's not a lot of jobs going around."

Others told Checkpoint the cost of living was what they were most worried about.

"I'm poor each day. It's just a struggle to get by each week ... I'm a student.

"With gas and just especially groceries, everything's pretty much skyrocketing."

Those Checkpoint spoke to also said politicians are failing to engage with young people.

Fred said he was reminded to enrol to vote by his parents.

"For young people finding it hard to vote it's just lack of word. Not a lot of people are hearing about it. I think that's what's holding young people back."

"I feel like it would be better if, say, 16-year-olds were able to vote just early on. I don't think there's anything wrong with that adherently," another said.

Another said, "At least if it was just talked about more because I think [for] a lot of people it's just really overwhelming or a really daunting thing to like get into."

But they all agreed, that more needed to be done in encouraging young people that their vote matters.

The overall enrolment rate is at 91 percent, but for young people aged 18 to 24 it is just over 62 percent.

In 2023, 77 percent of people aged 18 to 24 were enrolled to vote.

Last week, the Electoral Commission's Karl le Quesne told RNZ the Electoral Commission had been visiting schools to try and get the enrolment rate up.

They had also been working with community groups and youth groups.

"We'd like it to be a lot higher," he said.

The 2026 general election will be held on 7 November.

Under the new rules, eligible voters must enrol or update their details by midnight on 25 October to vote, with voting places opening for advance voting on 26 October.

World.title: Independent grocer plans to open more than 20 stores in five years
World.content:
Independent grocery retailer Paddock to Pantry is planning a $25 million expansion which would see it open more than 20 stores over the next five years.

The family-owned business, which has built much of its business around online grocery deliveries, said it planned to open roughly one new store every three months.

Its first new outlet is due to open in Kinloch, near Taupō, in December, with sites on the East Coast and in South Auckland expected to follow early next year.

A licensing application lodged with Taupō District Council confirms Paddock to Pantry is seeking to operate a grocery store at 140 Kenrigg Road in Kinloch.

It said around 90 percent of its sales currently came from e-commerce, but expected that to fall to about a third within five years as it expanded its store network.

The company currently operates two physical stores, alongside its nationwide online supermarket business.

The spending programme includes about $10 million for new stores, a proposed 5000-square-metre distribution centre and an expansion of its delivery fleet.

The new openings would be a mixture of smaller stores of around 500 square metres, to larger footprints as big as 1800 square metres.

Business manager John Kennerley said the company was targeting communities with limited supermarket choice and ultimately wanted to become the country's third-largest grocery retailer.

Kennerley describes himself as a co-founder of Paddock to Pantry and business manager of it and The Meat Box.

World.title: Are you feeling 'politically fatigued' by the election?
World.content:
Audio player for " Are you 'politically fatigued' by the election? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1811892%2Fare-you-feeling-politically-fatigued-by-the-election

Are you 'politically fatigued' by the election? Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Are you politically worn out?

There's still 29 days to the election, but with a barrage of policy announcements every day, some people may feel like they have hit a wall.

Political fatigue syndrome is a real condition, where voters become exhausted and disenchanted, and feel that their vote won't make any difference.

Associate professor of psychology at Auckland University, Danny Osborne, specialises in political psychology.

He told Checkpoint that it was natural for voters to become somewhat disconnected throughout the lead up to any election.

"I think there's definitely a bit of fatigue at the moment, partly due to just the constant barrage of policies that are leaking out at the moment."

Osborne said that policies being announced on a daily basis could lead to people quickly becoming overwhelmed.

"There's reasons for doing it this particular way. You're able to dominate the headlines for the given day when you release a new policy, [but] at the same time, the downside to that is voters do get a bit fatigued in the lead up to the election."

Evie Richardson

Mudslinging between politicians was another major turnoff for voters, Osborne said.

"When parties and politicians go negative, it does lead to this decline in political efficacy and sense that you can do something about the upcoming election."

Checkpoint took to the streets of Auckland's Onehunga to see how voters were feeling in the lead to up the election.

One man said while he was interested in politics, he had been seeing almost "too much" about the election campaign.

"I don't watch the debates, it just doesn't seem to have a lot of point to it, they just sort of slug it out."

In terms of what the parties were offering, he said he thought the options to vote for were good, but that the minor parties were holding too much power.

One woman told Checkpoint she wasn't "very political" and thought she was somewhere it the middle when it came to being engaged with the campaign.

"I'm not really listening to loads ... I know who I'm going to vote for, and that's about it."

She said apart from the Green Party, she felt there wasn't much difference between all the parties.

Her sentiment was echoed by other voters.

Evie Richardson

"I don't think any of the major parties are giving any big bright ideas," another man said.

Another woman, who told Checkpoint she was a university lecturer working in health care, said she had been thinking about the election a lot.

She said she was worried about the low engagement she was seeing among her students.

"It's just priorities, they're just trying to survive, we barely have students showing up to lectures, let alone [voting], they're trying to survive, get food, petrol, it's just the whole cost of living."

She said she felt a big change was needed after this election.

"We have to be hopeful, otherwise we'll just be crying all the time."

Another man told Checkpoint he hadn't really thought much about the election yet, and had been too busy to look into what the parties were offering.

"I think we're going to be stuffed either way."

Osborne said the way for people to stay engaged was to talk to friends and colleagues about what was happening, and trying to keep up with the news on a daily basis.

He said voters needed to remember that the MMP system meant their vote would be sure to make a difference in the outcome of this election.

"It's important for voters to remain optimistic that although maybe your party isn't going to be a major party who gets in, you can still influence the outcome of an election by voting for whichever party is best representing your policies."

Voters felt most valued when politicians reflect and support policies that are relevant to people, Osborne said.

"The cost of living crisis is impacting everyone, and it's really hard to tell voters to stay informed with politics and read the news ... when you're worried about putting food on the table."

"I think the ways that politicians can perhaps break through that barrier is by consistently talking about the policies and explaining how your policies are going to improve people's lives."

World.title: As it happened: Election campaign, 9 October
World.content:
Party leaders traded barbs and weighed in on fresh calls for a fireworks ban as the second week of the election campaign neared its end on Friday.

NZ First wants ban on backyard fireworks

On Friday morning, NZ First launched a fresh push for a ban on backyard fireworks - despite the leaders of National and Labour shooting the idea down in Tuesday's debate.

The party wants to ban the public sale and private use of fireworks, blaming them for frightening animals, starting fires and causing havoc for emergency services.

In a statement, a spokesperson said the legislation was already written and ready to be introduced to Parliament within the first 100 days of the next government.

Leader Winston Peters said fireworks could lead to animals being seriously injured.

"A lot of people making comments have never seen the damage to animals like to dogs and cats and particularly horses...cut to the bone and having to be put down because of the injuries they've sustained being panicked by fireworks."

Peters said National, Labour and ACT were against the ban because they considered it a "freedom issue".

"Yes it's a freedom issue - until you do enormous damage to someone else's property or pets, and that's what's happening around the country."

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong campaigns in Auckland on Friday. BLESSEN TOM / RNZ

'I don't believe him': Opportunity on Luxon ruling them out

Opportunity has bluntly addressed National's continued insistence it will not work with the party, with leader Qiulae Wong saying "I don't believe him".

"I think he would rather be in government than in opposition, I assume," Wong told media while campaigning in West Auckland on Friday.

"There are many things we could work with National on, I think the five bottom lines are realistic for them to commit to."

Wong also brushed off the latest Taxpayers' Union-Curia poll, which showed the party failing to reach the 5 percent threshold needed to get into Parliament.

"We're really encouraged that the general trend is up, and most polls have us well clear of the 5 percent. But obviously, we take nothing for granted and we're out working hard to shore up as many votes as possible" she said.

National leader Christopher Luxon in Feilding. Sanele Chadwick/RNZ

National woos farmers with low-cost loans for water storage

National is promising to lend farmers up to $300 million to help them store more water, as it targets the rural vote in this year's election.

The party said it wanted to make it easier for farmers to collect rainwater when there was plenty of it, then use it to grow crops and feed livestock when conditions turned dry.

National leader Christopher Luxon and agriculture spokesperson Todd McClay unveiled the campaign policy at Feilding's annual Rural Day event.

The day also included the beloved Gumboot Relay, which a number of National MPs and candidates took part in - but not party leader Christopher Luxon.

ACT's leader visited Christchurch on Friday, taking time to tour the city's new stadium. RNZ/Nathan McKinnon

ACT wants agriculture back in year 11 science curriculum

The ACT Party is calling for agriculture to remain a standalone subject in the Year 11 school science curriculum - after the coalition took it out.

Its agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard said he was "gutted" to learn of the move and warned it would send the wrong message to students.

"We've got all these other subjects at Year 11. Why not agriculture and horticulture?" he said.

"They have dance at Year 11. I think agriculture is slightly higher to the importance of New Zealand than dance is."

Hoggard added, with a chuckle: "David might disagree with me on that one."

ACT leader David Seymour appeared on the seventh series of Dancing with the Stars in 2018. He finished 5th.

Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins visits AUT School of Nursing in Auckland on 9 October. RNZ/Russell Palmer

Chris Hipkins in war of words with Winston Peters

Labour leader Chris Hipkins has fired back at Winston Peters after the New Zealand First leader declared he should "be behind bars" given the decisions he made about Covid-19 vaccinations.

In an interview with independent broadcaster Chris Lynch on Friday, Peters unleashed the extraordinary attack on the former Covid-19 Minister: "How can he even be a candidate for Parliament? How can he be a leader right now?"

Asked to respond during a visit to AUT School of Nursing in Auckland, Hipkins told reporters Peters' campaign rhetoric was getting "more and more divisive, more and more desperate".

"Winston Peters shouldn't even be in Parliament," Hipkins said.

Discussing Opportunity, Hipkins said any Labour supporters considering voting for the Opportunity Party would be "giving [their] vote away", given the risk it could side with National.

"You're basically letting someone else make the decision about who the government should be," he said.

"If you want a change, you need to vote for change."

World.title: Litchfield fireworks help Australia to ODI victory over Bangladesh
World.content:
A Phoebe Litchfield masterclass has ensured Australia remains undefeated in 22 ODIs at Allan Border Field after seamer Megan Schutt joined an elite club of bowling greats.

Opener Litchfield's 77 off 57 deliveries ensured Australia polished off the meagre 166 all out set by Bangladesh in just 25.4 overs for the loss of three wickets.

Litchfield combined ramps, glides, clips, exquisite drives, lofted pitching wedges, reverse hockey thumps and thunderous wallops in another knock that confirmed she is unique in world cricket and an absolute joy to watch.

The left-hander was unstoppable in racing to her 12th ODI half-century.

All-rounder Annabel Sutherland, player of the match, finished the chase with 26 not out after earlier taking four wickets.

Australia pace bowler Schutt earlier snared her 150th ODI wicket in a probing opening spell to put the hosts on top.

Stand-in captain Tahlia McGrath invited the visitors to have first use of the surface and Schutt struck with the first ball of the innings, a vicious lifter that had opener Fargana Hoque edging to slip.

A Schutt inswinger trapped Sarmin Sultana (four) in front and from that moment the bowlers kept a vice-like grip on the run rate and picked up steady wickets to dismiss Bangladesh with the fourth ball of the final over.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

The wicket of Sultana was the milestone 150th for Schutt. Only legendary speed demon Cathryn Fitzpatrick (180) and current all-rounder Ellyse Perry (166) have more wickets for Australia in the format.

Schutt finished with 2-19 from her 10 overs with medium pacer Sutherland (4-30) proving a handful when she hit the pitch hard.

Spinners Ashleigh Gardner, Georgia Wareham and Alana King bowled with class.

The visitors had several cameos but nothing substantial. No.3 Sharmin Akhter made a classy and breezy 24, captain Nigar Sultana (29 off 86 balls) was brave but stodgy.

Veteran all-rounder Ritu Moni (45 off 63) showcased her experience and nous and was the best of a mediocre bunch.

Schutt has relished playing at AB Field throughout her career, where she now has 20 wickets.

The quick was initially left out of the ODI side in February against India before a quad injury to Kim Garth opened the door for a recall.

Schutt took 5-19 at AB Field on that occasion to provide a timely reminder of her talents.

McGrath, usually a vice-captain, has been elevated to lead due to injury to regular skipper Sophie Molineux and rotated her bowlers with panache.

The opener of three ODIs at the same venue, Friday's clash is the first match of the summer on home soil for Australia's victorious T20 World Cup side since lifting the trophy in July.

AAP

World.title: Anthony De Ceglie steps down as Perth Bears CEO
World.content:
Anthony De Ceglie, the inaugural chief executive of the Perth Bears, has decided to step down, the rugby league club announced today.

Mr De Ceglie, a former Seven West media executive, was appointed in May 2025 to help put the club together ahead of its entry into the NRL next year as the 18th team in the competition and the first from Western Australia since 1997.

"I'm extremely proud of what the hard-working Perth Bears team has achieved in the past year," Mr De Ceglie said in a statement.

"I have no doubt that the Perth Bears will continue to grow and grow, and become a behemoth of the national sporting stage."

Anthony De Ceglie held several senior roles at Seven West Media before joining the Bears. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

The Perth Bears have not said why Mr De Ceglie is leaving.

It had been reported that the board was seeking to have him replaced.

Mr De Ceglie's decision to leave the club comes after the departure of former head of football David Sharpe, who quit in April.

Club chair Ben Morton thanked Mr De Ceglie.

What awaits the NRL in Perth? This weekend marks the final NRL game in Perth before the city has its own team in the big league and as the beginning of forever looms, rugby league in the west is ready for its close-up.

"I thank Anthony for his leadership of the Perth Bears in our startup phase and we will now turn our attention to the leadership of our organisation as we enter the next phase of our story," he said.

Perth Bears general manager of football Gareth Holmes will act as chief executive until a permanent appointment is made.

Mr De Ceglie was previously the director of news and current affairs at Seven West Media, a role he held after overseeing Western Australia's flagship newspaper.

Channel 7 holds the rights to the AFL, while rival Channel 9 has the rights to the NRL.

World.title: Bad light stops play with Renshaw on the brink of drought-breaking milestone
World.content:
Bad light has stranded Matt Renshaw four runs shy of his first Test half-century in more than 3,500 days on day one of the opening Test between Australia and South Africa in Durban.

Play was stopped after just 65 overs were bowled on day one, with Renshaw unbeaten on 46 off 115 alongside captain Pat Cummins (33*).

If Renshaw can reach 50 it will be his first time past the milestone in Tests since March 2017, but that wait is nothing compared to Nic Maddinson, who was handed his first Test cap in a decade when the teams were announced on day one at Kingsmead.

The 34-year-old replaced Cameron Green in the XI but was elevated to open alongside Travis Head, sending Renshaw back down to the middle order.

Maddinson's first Test dig since 2016 lasted 33 balls and yielded no runs as he and Head (9) fell to leave Australia struggling after electing to bat.

Marnus Labuschagne (37) and Steve Smith (25) the first of the day's repair jobs before Labuschagne was trapped LBW by WIaan Mulder with the last ball before lunch, and Smith edged Marco Jansen to third slip three balls and 45 minutes later.

Renshaw walked to the crease at 4-84 and saw Alex Carey (14) and Beau Webster (4) come and go before finding a willing partner in Cummins, who made it through to an early stumps with him.

Look back at all the day one action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in our ScoreCentre.

World.title: Wallabies must 'walk the walk' if 40-year-old curse is to end
World.content:
Arriving in Auckland ahead of the opening Bledisloe Cup Test in 1999, Wallabies great David Wilson cut a confident figure.

"We're certainly not intimidated by the All Blacks at all," said Wilson, who was acting as Wallabies captain in the absence of an injured John Eales.

Wilson was not being boastful, cocky or showing false bravado, as he had reason to declare the Wallabies were not scared of the All Blacks.

They had won all three Bledisloe Cup Tests the previous year, with the clean sweep including a famous 27-23 victory in Christchurch.

The Wallabies were also enjoying a 10-match winning streak under coach Rod Macqueen, so it was no surprise self-belief was high when they took the field on a chilly July evening at Eden Park.

What followed was later described in the Australian media as a "wake-up call" for the Wallabies.

The All Blacks stunned the Wallabies in the opening 1999 Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park. (Getty Images/Allsport: Nick Wilson)

They were outclassed in an error-ridden 34-15 defeat, having trailed 22-3 at half-time, with a rabid home crowd — most of whom were wearing black — doing their best to put the Wallabies off their game.

"When the Wallabies play the All Blacks in New Zealand, the contest is between a team and a nation," Spiro Zavos wrote in The Sydney Morning Herald at the time.

Given the Wallabies won the Rugby World Cup later that year, the loss was a blip on the radar.

But it did provide a salient lesson: self-belief can only take you so far when you play the All Blacks in New Zealand, as it means nothing if you cannot execute your game plan.

Wallabies upset Boks in Perth The Wallabies manage to overcome four late yellow cards to defeat world champions South Africa 42-38 in a pulsating Test in Perth.

Fast-forward to 2026, and the Wallabies find themselves faced with the same challenge as they prepare for tomorrow night's Bledisloe Cup Test, which will also be played at Eden Park.

Despite having lost their past 11 Tests against the All Blacks, expectation among the Wallabies squad is rising as they look to extend this season's six-match unbeaten run.

They posted a 42-38 victory over the Springboks in Perth a frotnight ago, while last year's stunning 38-22 defeat of the two-time defending world champions at Ellis Park is still fresh in their collective memory.

But as the 1999 Wallabies learned, confidence counts for little if you do not deliver on the field when you play the All Blacks.

"Belief is strong, but belief won't just cut it," Wallabies openside flanker Fraser McReight said earlier this week.

"We have to go out there and perform."

Eden Park 'hoodoo'

McReight would be mindful of how many times the Wallabies have made the trek to New Zealand in a buoyant mood, only to return to Australia with tail between legs.

Not since 2001 have they defeated the All Blacks in their own backyard.

Eden Park has particularly been unfriendly across Bledisloe Cup history, as the Wallabies have not triumphed over the All Blacks at the venue in 40 years.

Convincing defeats in 2008 (39-10), 2015 (41-13) and 2019 (36-0) stick out in the memory as each came a week after the Wallabies lowered the All Blacks' colours on home soil.

The Wallabies have lost 24 straight Tests to the All Blacks at Eden Park, although the New Zealanders have not been defeated by any team at their spiritual home since 1994.

Fraser McReight has stressed the Wallabies need to deliver on the field. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Suggestions of an Eden Park "curse" or "hoodoo" have resurfaced this week, as they always do whenever the Wallabies play in Auckland.

The New Zealand Herald even published an explainer on its website under the headline: A dummies' guide to the Wallabies' Eden Park hoodoo against the All Blacks — 40 years without a win.

A dictionary definition of the word hoodoo featured in the article for good measure.

Wallabies name Bledisloe Cup squad The Wallabies have kept Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the wing for Saturday night's Bledisloe Cup Test at Auckland's Eden Park, with Isaac Henry named in the centres.

Whether Wallabies coach Les Kiss was reading is unknown, but he maintains the run of losses has not been discussed inside his squad.

"It isn't front and centre for us in terms of what we're about," Kiss told reporters.

Instead, the Wallabies have hinted they are flipping the script.

"You can look at it two ways," McReight said.

"We're really trying to win and get the win over here … but they're also defending it [their winning record] and that has to play [on] their psyche as well.

"That's probably how we're trying to frame it."

It has been a talking point among the All Blacks, as coach Dave Rennie revealed when he announced his match-day squad on Thursday.

"No-one wants to be part of the first team for a long time to lose at Eden Park or lose the Bledisloe," said Rennie, who was sacked as Wallabies coach at the beginning of 2023.

"All sides, who come here, want to be seen to break the [Eden Park] record, so they'll [the Wallabies] be highly motivated. We're well aware of what's coming."

Dave Rennie and the All Blacks know the challenge they are facing. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

The All Blacks do not just have an envious home record at Eden Park to protect — they are also hoping to avoid four straight Test defeats.

After winning the series opener against the Springboks in Rugby's Greatest Rivalry, Rennie's side crashed to three consecutive losses.

Not since 1998 have the All Blacks dropped four Tests in a row, and the players do not need to be reminded New Zealand's rugby public only tolerates winning.

Is this the Wallabies' best chance to defeat the All Blacks on their own turf in more the two decades?

That is debatable.

The Wallabies have expressed confidence though, just as their predecessors did in 1999.

But McReight and his teammates are also aware talk is cheap.

"We don't just want to talk the talk," he said.

"We want to walk the walk and be able to deliver."

World.title: Dal Santo quits as St Kilda AFLW coach in winless season
World.content:
St Kilda's disastrous AFLW season has led to coach Nick Dal Santo stepping down after six seasons in charge, ahead of an independent review of the football program.

With four rounds to go until the end of the regular season, the Saints sit at the bottom of the AFLW ladder with eight losses from as many games.

St Kilda's percentage is a league-worst 37.2. The team is averaging 23 points per game in attack, while conceding an average of 62 points a game.

St Kilda kick solitary point St Kilda were 90 seconds from failing to score in their AFLW clash against the Western Bulldogs, as Essendon's first win of the year leaves the Saints as the only winless team in the league.

The situation reached a critical point after last weekend's game, where the Saints lost by 30 points to the Western Bulldogs in Ballarat.

Ashleigh Richards kicked a point at the 17-minute mark of the final term, for what proved the team's only score of the game.

This meant the Saints avoided becoming the first team in AFLW history not to score in a full game.

In a club announcement on Friday, St Kilda confirmed Dal Santo's decision.

Saturday's (home) match against Collingwood will be Dal Santo's final game as senior coach.

"Nick has made a significant contribution to our AFLW program across six seasons and will always be an important part of our football club," St Kilda CEO Carl Dilena said.

"His care, commitment and leadership have been unwavering, and we thank him for everything he has given to the program, including leading the team to its maiden finals appearance last season."

Winless AFLW coaches under pressure Umpiring, teams without a win and big risers: These are the topics fans are talking about midway through the AFLW 2026 season.

Dal Santo was quoted in the statement saying he was proud of "where we've been able to take this program", but that he had been giving thought to whether continuing was the right decision for him and the club.

"It's been a privilege to coach this group and help shape its formative years in the competition.

"I have a strong love for this club. I wanted to contribute to women's football, and with a daughter of my own, it's great to see a pathway for young females with football ambitions.

"I'm looking forward to finishing my time as coach alongside the group this weekend and wish them every success for what comes next."

St Kilda confirmed that football administrator and executive Brad Lloyd from Apogee Sports would lead an independent review into the program.

Lloyd has previously led reviews at AFLW clubs Richmond and Carlton.

World.title: The mixed fortunes of Australia's last South African touring party
World.content:
The members of Australia's touring party from the 2018 South Africa series have endured various fortunes in the eight years since.

Some have seen their careers go to new heights, while others struggled to recapture their form from before the ball-tampering saga.

Others never featured for Australia again.

As Australia plays its first Test in South Africa since 2018, here is a look at where everyone from the previous tour ended up in the years that followed.

Steve Smith

Steve Smith is no longer Australia's Test captain, nor is he at the peak of his powers, but he still remains the best batter in the team. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

It is somewhat of an indictment on where Australian cricket has gone since the last South Africa tour that Smith is still by far the team's best batter.

Although, a glass-half-full view might suggest that it is a sign of Smith's incredible longevity.

While he is not at the peak of his powers like he was on the last tour, Smith is still the trump card in the line-up and will be the wicket South Africa's bowlers most covet.

Smith has retired from all white ball formats and is primarily a Test cricketer at the international level.

David Warner

David Warner was not quite able to recapture his best form at the Test level following his suspension in 2018. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

Arguably Australia's main antagonist in 2018, Warner last represented Australia at the T20 World Cup in mid-2024.

Following his ball-tampering suspension, Warner never quite recaptured his form, particularly in the Test format.

Warner averaged 48.63 in Tests prior to the 2018 South Africa tour and finished his career averaging 37.28 in 38 Tests afterwards.

He is now a T20 gun for hire in various competitions around the world.

Cameron Bancroft

Cameron Bancroft (left) famously fronted the press conference alongside Smith where Australia admitted to tampering with the ball using a piece of sandpaper. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

Bancroft's international career suffered the most out of the three players banned from the 2018 tour, having been the man caught by the Supersport cameras trying to hide a piece of sandpaper from the umpires.

The right-hander has played just two Tests since. The last of those came in 2019, and his Test career looks just about done.

Still just 33, Bancroft remains a prolific domestic run scorer, and ranked third in terms of runs in the Sheffield Shield last year. He has 33 first class centuries to his name.

Joe Burns

Joe Burns enjoyed a few more years of Test cricket for Australia before going on to represent Italy. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Burns was one of the players drafted into the Australian XI for the final Test in 2018 after the suspensions of Smith, Warner and Bancroft.

He enjoyed a productive 2019 at the Test level before playing the last of his Tests for Australia on Boxing Day in 2020.

Burns later became a T20 specialist for Italy, averaging 45.16 in eight matches across 2024 and 2025 to help the Italians qualify for their maiden T20 World Cup this year, but was left out of Italy's World Cup squad.

Pat Cummins

Pat Cummins has gone on to captain Australia in multiple formats since the 2018 series, where he was only just returning from a series of back issues. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Cummins's Test career was in its infancy in 2018, having just returned to the side following years of injury issues.

Since then he has become one of the finest all-format bowlers as well as Australia captain.

Under Cummins's tenure, Australia has won an ODI World Cup and the ICC Test Championship, both in 2023.

He has been named in the Test Team of the Year on four occasions, and was named Test Cricketer of the Year in 2019.

Peter Handscomb

Peter Handscomb has played fleetingly in Australia's Test side since 2018, and is seen as somewhat of a spin specialist. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Another player who came in for the final Test in 2018, Handscomb has forever been on the periphery of Australia's Test side.

Handscomb was famously the man who told the Australian team that they'd been caught ball tampering, after chatting to then-coach Darren Lehmann on a walkie-talkie while flipping an Aussie rules football in between his hands.

Considered a specialist in spinning conditions, Handscomb has added just seven Tests to his career since the 2018 series, but is an outside chance to feature again in India next year after recently being added to the Australia A side.

He was the leading scorer in the last Shield season, scoring 724 runs at an average of 34.47 in very bowler-friendly conditions.

Josh Hazlewood

Josh Hazlewood is one of the few Australians who has seen his career have an uptick following the 2018 South Africa tour. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Hazlewood enjoyed some of his best years as a Test bowler following the 2018 tour.

The right-arm paceman averaged 25.77 with the ball prior to that series and has seen that average dip to an elite 21.17 in the years that have followed.

Hazlewood is still prolific when he is able to get on the park, but his body has given him problems over the last few seasons.

The 35-year-old was restricted to just four Tests last year, but still took 16 wickets at an average of 17.93.

Jon Holland

Jon Holland played just two Tests for Australia after not featuring at all during the 2018 South Africa tour. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Holland was one of the players who didn't play a single Test during the last South Africa tour, and has mostly remained on the outer since.

His two Test appearances following the 2018 tour yielded just four wickets at an average of 75, and he was unsurprisingly surpassed in the spin pecking order.

Nevertheless, Holland continued to enjoy his time in domestic cricket, helping Victoria claim a Sheffield Shield title in 2018–19.

Holland's first class career ended in 2023 when he was let go by Victoria after 95 Shield appearances.

Usman Khawaja

Usman Khawaja completely reinvented his Test career as a prolific opener before retiring from international cricket at the start of this year. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

Khawaja played all four Tests as Australia's number three in 2018, but his struggles in that series were no indicator of what was to come.

After being left out of the Test side in 2020 and 2021, Khawaja returned for the New Year's Test in 2022 and had an incredible stint as one of Australia's openers.

Khawaja scored eight of his 16 Test centuries after his return in 2022 and averaged 48.05 as an opener, one of the best marks by an Australian.

He retired from Test cricket following Australia's Ashes triumph against England last summer and is now a T20 specialist for domestic leagues after also retiring from Shield cricket.

Nathan Lyon

Nathan Lyon still has a stranglehold on the sole spinner spot in Australia's full-strength Test XI. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Lyon remains a mainstay in Australia's first-choice Test XI, just as he was in 2018.

Despite being the oldest player in Australia's team, no spinner has been able to claim Lyon's spot as the non-pace bowling option alongside Starc, Hazlewood and Cummins.

Lyon's body has slowly begun to show signs of aging in the past few years, and he played just two of the five Tests against England in last summer's Ashes.

His performances in the Bangladesh Tests suggest he won't be an automatic selection in South Africa.

Mitch Marsh

Mitch Marsh retired from Test cricket after last featuring in the 2024 Boxing Day Test, but is now Australia's T20 captain. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Marsh played all four Tests against South Africa in 2018, but struggled to kick on from that series in the years that followed. He was the man with the ball in hand when the ball-tampering storm erupted.

He had a strong 2023, scoring a century and four 50s to end the calendar year with an average of 67.50, but managed an average of just 18.86 the following year and saw his Test career come to an end after Boxing Day.

Marsh has since retired from Test cricket but remains in Australia's ODI and T20 sides, captaining the country in the shortest format.

His name gets mentioned with regards to a Test return every once in a while, but that ship appears to have sailed with Australia well-stocked with all-rounder options.

Shaun Marsh

Shaun Marsh did not feature again in Australia's Test XI once Smith and Warner returned from their suspensions. (AAP Image: Dan Himbrechts)

The other Marsh brother also played all four Tests in the 2018 series, but struggled thereafter.

Marsh was relied upon heavily during the suspensions to Smith, Warner and Bancroft, but did not play another Test once the trio were cleared to return.

He played his last first class match in 2023 and his last T20 in the BBL at the end of 2024.

Marsh is one of 10 former international cricketers involved in the CLT10, India's first luxury-format indoor cricket league.

Glenn Maxwell

Despite being a key member of Australia's white ball teams, Glenn Maxwell never played another Test match after 2017. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Maxwell has not played a single Test since 2017 but remains a white ball superstar.

He played a key role in Australia's T20 World Cup and ODI World Cup wins, in 2021 and 2023 respectively.

He retired from ODIs in 2025 but still plays for Australia in the T20 format and is considered one of the most dangerous short-form players in the world.

With less international cricket on his plate, Maxwell is a gun for hire for domestic T20 leagues around the world.

Tim Paine

Tim Paine captained Australia after the ball-tampering scandal, before being forced to resign under controversial circumstances himself. (Getty: Ryan Pierse)

Paine was thrust into centre stage following the sandpaper debacle on the 2018 tour, captaining Australia in the final Test of the series in Smith and Warner's absence.

The Tasmanian keeper retained the captaincy even when Smith returned, and eventually led his country in 23 Tests.

Paine's reign as captain came to an end when he resigned in November 2021 after explicit messages he'd sent to a co-worker in 2017 resurfaced.

He ended his playing career at all levels in 2023 and took up coaching. Currently he is the head coach of Pakistan Super League side Multan Sultans.

Matt Renshaw

Matt Renshaw has only recently returned to Australia's Test side after spending years in the wilderness. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Renshaw was among those drafted into the Australian side for the final Test of the 2018 series in Johannesburg.

He played three more Tests in 2023, including one against South Africa, but managed just nine runs in four innings.

Renshaw received a Test recall earlier this year against Bangladesh, but managed just eight in his sole innings at the crease.

The left-hander has been most effective for Australia at the T20 level, where he averages 38.83 at a healthy strike rate of 125.94.

Jhye Richardson

Jhye Richardson's body has stopped him from enjoying the Test career many believed he was destined to have. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

Richardson has been the nearly man of his generation of Australian cricketers.

He did not feature in the 2018 Tests, but made his debut the following year, shining with six wickets in two Tests.

However, repeated injury issues halted his once-bright career, allowing him to play just two Tests in the last seven years.

He currently features in Australia A's Tests against India A. If his body holds up, he should be back in Test calculations in the not too distant future.

Chadd Sayers

Chadd Sayers's one Test appearance came during the final Test of the 2018 South Africa series. (Getty Images: Lee Warren)

Sayers was another one of Australia's inclusions for the Johannesburg Test in 2018, and it wound up being the only Test he would ever play.

A prolific Shield performer in the lead-up to the South Africa series, a knee injury ruined his 2018–19 season.

Sayers continued to play for South Australia and eventually retired from first class cricket at the end of the 2020–21 season.

Following his retirement, Sayers spent some time as a runner for SANFL side Woodville-West Torrens.

Mitchell Starc

Mitchell Starc remains the spearhead of Australia's bowling attack despite approaching 37 years of age. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Starc's career has gone from strength to strength since 2018, and he remains one of the most feared new ball bowlers in world cricket.

Nearly 37, Starc is as fast as ever and remains an integral part of Australia's Test line-up.

At the end of the 2018 series, Starc had taken 182 wickets at an average of 28.17 in 43 Tests.

Since then, he has taken a further 263 wickets at an average of 24.70 in 64 Tests, and his career mark of 445 Test wickets is the most by any left-arm bowler.

World.title: Bates dedicates historic Bathurst lap to late mum after stunning qualifying
World.content:
Zach Bates has dedicated his historic Bathurst lap to his late mother after becoming the first driver in the current era to break the 2:04 barrier at Mount Panorama.

The 22-year-old from Canberra was a class above the field during Friday's qualifying session, topping the time sheets in his Matt Stone Racing Chevrolet with a 2:03.938, the first and only driver to break the 2:04 barrier in the Gen3 era which began in 2023.

Bates, who was Craig Lowndes's co-driver in the Team 18 entry last year, will head into tomorrow's shootout as the favourite and will be the last driver on track.

Bates dedicated the moment to his mother, who died in 2025.

"I can't believe it; I am speechless," he said.

"Whole credit to the crew behind me. The boys and girls have been working so hard.

"This is for my mum who passed last year. We've had a pretty average year, the whole family. So this is definitely a highlight."

The top 10 from Friday's qualifying session will battle on Saturday for pole position in the Top 10 Shootout.

Brodie Kostecki will have a chance to set a new Bathurst record tomorrow in the shootout, striving to become the first driver to secure four consecutive pole positions at Mount Panorama.

Two cars miss qualifying after crashes in practice

Ryan Wood crashes during the third practice session of the 2026 Bathurst 1000 at Mount Panorama. (Supplied: Supercars)

Ryan Wood/Jaxon Evans (number 2 Walkinshaw TWG Racing, Toyota) and Rylan Gray/Tony D'Alberto (Dick Johnson Racing, Ford) will start from the back of the field on Sunday after missing out on Friday's qualifying session.

Both entrants suffered crashes during practice earlier on Friday, with the damage unable to be fixed in time for the following practice session or qualifying.

Wood clipped the inside wall on the entry to Forrest's Elbow, which sent his Toyota into the outside barrier with force.

The force of the impact was reportedly recorded at 42 G-forces, with the Kiwi later cleared by medics at Bathurst.

"The boys will work pretty hard and that's what I feel stink about. It's given them so much work that they really didn't need," he said.

"Kudos to our team — they do everything by the book. To have a 42G impact like that and be able to walk away is pretty good."

Wood qualified fourth for last year's Bathurst 1000, but watched from the sidelines on Friday.

D'Alberto crashed in the final minutes of the session at The Dipper, with his number 38 Dick Johnson Racing entry taken back to the garage on the back of a tow truck.

World.title: Piastri hopes for better in Singapore as fading challenger promises 'all-out' attack
World.content:
Following a difficult weekend in Malaysia, Oscar Piastri is hoping McLaren will enjoy better results and have a more competitive car in Singapore.

Piastri finished sixth at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, after his team sent him out on slick tyres in wet conditions to start the race, forcing the Australian into the pits as the race began.

The McLaren driver was able to fight his way back through the field, at times showing strong pace, but said sixth was the best result the team could hope for.

Verstappen ends drought with win, Russell retires with five laps to go Max Verstappen's long wait for another Formula 1 race win is finally over, and the drivers' championship race might be over, too.

"We know we've not been as competitive as we would have liked the last couple of weekends,: Piastri said in Singapore ahead of this weekend's racing.

"In Malaysia, I think sixth was more or less what we could've done."

McLaren enjoyed a mid-season resurgence, with Piastri's teammate claiming back-to-back wins in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Norris won those races from pole position, and then again was fastest in qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix in September.

But the reigning constructors' champions were not realistically in contention for wins, but did show promise at times.

It is that inconsistency during weekends which has hurt McLaren in 2026, and something Piastri is hoping can be improved to end the season, starting in Singapore.

"At certain points in [Malaysia], we looked very quick. On my second hard [tyre] stint, and Lando as well on his soft [tyre], we were more or less the quickest cars on the track at one point.

"It's in line with the rest of the year — if you can get the car into the right window, it's very quick.

"But we've struggled to get it there for a lot of the last two weekends. Hopefully we can make things a bit easier this weekend."

Russell cops grid penalty, promises 'all-out attack'

George Russell's dream of a maiden F1 world title is hanging by a thread, after the Briton suffered a power unit failure with five laps remaining last weekend in Malaysia.

Following his retirement, Russell is now 84 points adrift of teammate and championship leader Kimi Antonelli, with a maximum of 183 points left in the championship.

If Antonelli is able to outscore Russell by 16 or more points this weekend, then he can mathematically win the title as early as the following round in Austin, Texas.

To make matters worse for Russell, he will start Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid, after being forced to take on new power unit components which exceed the yearly limit for a driver.

This comes directly on the back of last weekend's power unit failure which ended his race early.

With an improbably steep mountain to climb to maintain a glimmer of hope in the title race, and starting from the back of the field for Sunday's race, Russell has promised to throw everything at this weekend.

"All-out attack; just trying to enjoy the weekend," he said.

"Obviously, if you could choose where to take the penalty in the season, this [track] would be probably the second bottom of the list after Monaco. But unfortunately, just with how things have panned out, we have no choice but to take it here."

Antonelli started 19th for the Italian Grand Prix at Monza after taking on new power units, but drove one of the finest races in recent memory to claim a remarkable victory.

Hopes for Russell to replicate that are slim, with the Marina Bay street circuit tight, slow, and notoriously difficult to overtake on.

Tech.title: Nikon microscopic video competition winner disqualified for using generative AI
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Nikon says the video that originally won first place in its Small World in Motion contest “did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI.” BBC reports that the original first place video from Dr. Ning Xu claimed to show “tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.” Nikon said last week that it was reviewing the video following skepticism online about its authenticity.

In a comment on LinkedIn, Dr. Xu admitted to using AI for the video: “An unsupervised neural-network method was subsequently used for AI-assisted post-processing to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images from the super-resolution optical imaging.”

Dr. Xu’s video has now been disqualified and appears to have been removed from Nikon’s website. A video from Nguyen Nam Nhat now holds first place, according to the contest’s updated rankings. Following the incident, Nikon says it plans to “revisit rules and evaluation procedures for future competition entries.” It also noted in its statement on the contest that the decision to disqualify Dr. Xu’s video “should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent.”

Amazon has the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra in black with 256GB of storage discounted to $949.99, a healthy discount from its usual price of $1,399.99. Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Some users are reporting that the new Kindles have a light leak issue that is especially apparent when using dark mode. The latest base-model Kindles have a flush bezel that gives them a sleek appearance and looks great… as long as you keep the lights on. But things can change once you turn down the lights and turn up the brightness on the e-reader.

In some cases, users see shadows around the edges of the screen, or even visible LED strips. The issue appears to affect both the plastic and aluminum models in all colors. Some minor glowing around the edges might be a byproduct of the combination of front lighting and a flush screen. Good e-Reader says that Amazon is aware of the issue and has confirmed that a manufacturing issue may have led to defects in the current batch of Kindles. However, when contacted by The Verge, the company declined to provide an on-the-record statement.

Tech.title: Microsoft tries to spark new life into Windows
Tech.content:
When Microsoft released Windows 11 five years ago, it felt like an operating system that was still being renovated, a work in progress. You’d think by now that those renovations would be complete, with Microsoft turning its attention to Windows 12. Instead, Windows 11 feels like it’s here to stay, forming the foundation for Microsoft’s next big ambition: transforming Windows into an agentic OS.

At a Windows and Surface event this week, Microsoft laid out its plan to bring AI agents to Windows, including hybrid intelligence that lets Windows take advantage of free local models instead of expensive cloud ones. “I think today is the day we’ll start talking and thinking about the frontier ecosystem taking maybe slightly different contours,” said Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

After trying to sell businesses on a new Copilot last month, Nadella took a similar approach for his vision of agents and hybrid intelligence for Windows. It was so similar that when he mentioned the security, identity, and management aspects of Microsoft’s platform for securing agents, it almost seemed like he was pitching businesses again instead of AI developers, creatives, and just regular Windows users.

After a somewhat dizzying start, Windows chief Pavan Davuluri appeared onstage to try and explain why agents and hybrid intelligence are so important for Windows users. There were demos of GitHub Copilot coding locally without expensive cloud tokens; a long list of models that can now run locally; examples of agents like OpenClaw, Hermes, and Perplexity; and even deeper integration of Copilot in Windows.

I wasn’t fully convinced by any of these demos, though. I wanted to see what practical benefits local AI models could actually deliver for regular Windows users, instead of just the AI builders or developers Microsoft is trying to win over right now. Those are the people who could help turn its agentic OS vision into reality, though, and many of them are using a MacBook Pro instead of Windows. Microsoft’s answer to tempt them across to Windows? The Surface Laptop Ultra.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is the home for Microsoft’s agentic OS push. Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips power the device, and there’s enough raw GPU power to get AI models exceeding 120 billion parameters running locally. “We built it for developers and creators that push the limit of performance and want portability with exceptional craft,” said Davuluri.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is the flagship RTX Spark device, though there are also similar laptops from Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, and MSI. Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra starts at $2,599, and some RTX Spark PCs can run all the way up to an eye-watering $6,999. Much like the very top of the MacBook Pro line, you’d have to really need 128GB of unified memory to spend that kind of money. For many AI builders it might just be worth it, though, especially if you can save thousands in token costs.

For the rest of us, Microsoft had very little to show. A new Windows Search interface looks like it could be one of the best additions to Windows 11 in years, though. Microsoft has totally redesigned search to make it not only more modern, but a heck of a lot faster than before. I’ve gotten to the point where I disable the Bing results in Windows Search, but this new UI now surfaces results in-line and lets you use search more like a launcher.

I wasn’t expecting some grand unveiling of Windows 12 at this event, but I was hoping to hear a lot more about why RTX Spark laptops really do matter. “This is the future we’re building: agents that can work securely on your behalf, intelligence that moves seamlessly between local and cloud, and devices that become more capable than ever before,” said Davuluri.

The problem is Microsoft is still in the early stages of this future it’s betting on for Windows. We had Copilot Plus PCs two years ago, with a big focus on the NPU chips inside that were supposed to revolutionize how consumers use everyday AI on a laptop. They haven’t done that yet, with only a handful of photo, video, and productivity tools making use of the NPU. Microsoft’s Recall feature was supposed to be the star of the NPU show, but the privacy concerns and delayed launch made it totally irrelevant instead.

Nvidia’s presence and GPU dominance may well make RTX Spark a bigger success story than Copilot Plus PCs, but these machines are targeting a niche audience for now. If Microsoft and its partners want to move beyond selling them as MacBook Pro competitors, they’ll eventually need to bring the same capabilities to less expensive, less powerful devices and demonstrate practical reasons for regular Windows users to care. The difference is that RTX Spark PCs are aimed at people who have a much more immediate reason to care about local AI: developers and creators who need to run large models and can potentially save substantial amounts of money by doing so.

For Microsoft, though, it’s the creators and builders that matter most right now. AI agents running in the cloud on Linux virtual machines could spark a wave of desktop Linux app compatibility we’ve never seen before. Microsoft needs to counter that threat by making Windows more agent-friendly.

That might explain why Nadella and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spent so much time reminiscing about the early days of the PC and graphics at this event. Microsoft isn’t ready to give up the PC dominance and app compatibility it has spent decades building. But it knows that the way people use computers is changing, and that Windows can’t rely on its historical advantages forever.

Perhaps that gets to the heart of why Microsoft seems to be scrambling to embrace AI agents and hybrid intelligence in Windows. It needs to make sure that, even as computing shifts beyond the traditional PC, Windows remains at the center of it all.

I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there.

Tech.title: Frances Haugen hopes The Social Reckoning will inspire more whistleblowers
Tech.content:
Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen was mostly unfazed watching Oscar-winning actress Mikey Madison play a character named after her in The Social Reckoning, except for one thing: the wrist warmers.

In Aaron Sorkin’s new thriller, the fictional Haugen — who, like her nonfictional counterpart, leaks thousands of documents to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz — habitually dons the accessories. It’s a character quirk that reflects real life, where they’re a way to deal with the effects of a vasoconstrictive disorder. “I’ve figured out lots of ways to minimize how much of an obstruction this is,” she tells The Verge in an interview. “But having to watch myself wear wrist warmers for two hours, I came out of it being like, ‘Oh my god, this is really disruptive. Like, how have I successfully not thought about this for like seven years?’” With The Social Reckoning appearing in theaters Friday, Haugen hopes Meta’s CEO might watch it and have a similar moment of recognition with his own counterpart: a callous, robotic character played by Jeremy Strong. “I hope Mark Zuckerberg watches the movie and has as much of a knee-jerk emotional response as I had on that regarding, ‘Do I really want to live this life anymore?’”

Strong’s version of Zuckerberg has become sick of taking criticism for content moderation and fact-checking decisions as he prepares for congressional testimony, and waves off concern for design choices that his staff believe will stoke anger on the platform. “It’s very possible that Mark has learned to not see how distorted his world has become,” Haugen says. “My hope is that holding that mirror up, if he does ever watch the movie, that it gives him the gift of perspective, so he at least has a chance to choose.”

“I hope Mark Zuckerberg watches the movie and has as much of a knee-jerk emotional response as I had”

Five years since she went public as the figure behind the Journal’s Facebook Files, Haugen hopes that the film can remind viewers about the breadth of information they uncovered and “humanize the whistleblowing experience.” While she says her mother may take issue with Madison’s young, brunette character being shorter and less blonde, she’s happy the fictional Haugen stands apart from her. “We want as many people as possible to see themselves in Mikey’s character,” she says. If someone at a frontier AI lab becomes “so unlucky that they find themselves in a place where they need to blow the whistle,” she hopes they’ll connect with the fictional Haugen and “be like, ‘Oh, I actually have a duty to my common human beings and fellow citizens to do that.’”

One of Haugen’s most tangible impacts was providing evidence in lawsuits that claim Meta harmed young users, culminating in a $17 billion settlement earlier this year. But as the movie reminds viewers, child safety wasn’t what initially motivated her. In fact, documents about Instagram’s impact on teens were among the last she collected before resigning, because she worried clicking around too far outside her own subject area of civic integrity would raise alarms. “The collective memory of ‘What exactly was I complaining about?’ has shifted,” Haugen says. “Only about 10 percent of what I brought out was about kids.”

Revelations about how the algorithm pushed users toward extremist groups, special content moderation privileges for elite users, and other issues “kind of disappeared into time,” she says. Meta declined to comment on the movie but has previously said the documents Haugen disclosed were cherry-picked and flatten decisions the company has had to make amid difficult tradeoffs.

“We want as many people as possible to see themselves in Mikey’s character”

Still, Haugen has since engaged frequently on policy around social media and kids, much of that in Europe and Australia, where movement seemed more likely than in the US. While she says she’s “not a prohibitionist” when it comes to social media, she believes Australia’s youth social media ban pushed Meta to implement what she calls “‘yeah, duh’ features” to combat the threat. “I don’t think the first line of defense is you ban kids off social media,” she says. “But the problem is that platforms have shown repeatedly that they’re not particularly interested in making these spaces safe for kids, and Facebook particularly has shown they only improve safety for kids when they’re scared.”

Meta has aggressively moved to silence another recent whistleblower, former public policy director Sarah Wynn-Williams, taking legal action to stop her from promoting her memoir about her time at the company, Careless People. But Haugen says she sees Meta’s action against Wynn-Williams as an “outlier,” in part because her retelling relied much more on personal narrative than Haugen’s reams of documents. Before Haugen’s character obtains the documents, “there’s a scene in the movie where the Jeff character tells the Frances character, ‘You didn’t give me evidence, you gave me a story,’” she says. “And because a lot of what [Wynn-Williams] is saying is dependent on her personal credibility, Meta very, very desperately needs no one else who had access to that same information to ever come forward.”

As hype over artificial intelligence overtakes Meta and the rest of Silicon Valley, Haugen says conversations around industry regulation and public dissent are already much further along in AI than they were at a similar point with social media. Though she says some proposals seem “simplistic or misdirected,” like a pause on development, she’s encouraged that “we see people engaging, and we did not see people even engaging four years into social media.”

Reflecting on her own decision to go public as a whistleblower, Haugen tells The Verge that she took a pretty dispassionate approach. She knew Meta could cause financial hurt, but says she didn’t worry too much about that. “I’m a Quaker and I don’t take a lot to be very content and happy,” Haugen says. “They can only take as much from you as you let them.”

YouTube, Twitch, Meta, and X aren’t saying whether they’ll allow the US government to livestream an execution on their platforms. The four companies didn’t respond to The Verge’s requests for comment after an unnamed Pentagon official said yesterday that the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of a mass shooting at a Texas military base in 2009, will be livestreamed.

Two platforms responded to The Verge’s inquiries. Jamie Favazza, a spokesperson for TikTok’s US operations, pointed to the platform’s policies banning “shocking and graphic content,” including “the moment of someone’s death.” Kick, a platform known for taking a hands-off approach to content moderation, confirmed that such a livestream would violate its policies. “If this was livestreamed on KICK, it would breach our Community Guidelines,” Kick spokesperson Audrey FitzGerald writes in an emailed statement to The Verge.

Tech.title: LumenUs helps automate tedious paperwork in times of grief
Tech.content:
When Sara Tashakorinia’s husband died in a car accident eight years ago, the last thing she needed was the roughly 570 hours of paperwork it takes, on average, to settle a loved one’s affairs. But for millions of people each year, this is their reality: a crushing loss, followed by a soullessly mundane avalanche of tedious administrative work.

“The day your loved one passes away, you also get this honorary badge of a project manager for a project you had no idea about, trying to navigate something and learn something when you literally have zero information,” Tashakorinia told TechCrunch.

After years of volunteering to help others navigate what she had to learn on her own, it occurred to Tashakorinia that AI might be able to help — not with the complex, messy experience of grieving and healing, but with the least human parts of the process, like finding the right tax forms, filing insurance claims, and shutting down bank accounts.

The result is LumenUs, the grief care platform that Tashakorinia founded last year to relieve grieving families of some of the administrative burden.

“I think going through it, your threshold of pain is so high, and you’re so lost that you don’t really realize, why do people treat you this way? Why was I left with a stack of paperwork, and why was the funeral home charging me a 300% markup on a casket?” Tashakorinia said.

While Tashakorinia hopes LumenUs will eventually support people throughout the lifelong grieving process, the startup will initially focus on people in the immediate aftermath of a death. When people initially join the platform, they go through an onboarding process in which they share information about the nature of their particular situation.

“We are asking very specific questions to understand the legal and financial means, and their state of mind, and this is only to personalize who they are, and then personalizing what happened,” Tashakorinia said.

From there, the platform organizes tasks by urgency, helping users decipher what needs to be done immediately and what can wait. In some cases, this can even help people discover that they’re entitled to money that can help ease the financial burden of death. In fact, billions of dollars in life insurance benefits go unclaimed because people don’t know they’re available.

“We are using AI to automate as much as we can to save time during this process, and give it back to [users],” she said.

Tashakorinia has a background in cybersecurity, which is sure to prove essential for building a product that asks people to share so much sensitive personal and financial information. She is building LumenUs alongside co-founders Sajad Mirzaei, a former engineer at Google and Box, and Larry Keeley, an innovation scientist, professor, and entrepreneur. The team is also consulting with clinicians and social workers while testing the product.

LumenUs, a participant in this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 — the annual showcase of promising early-stage startups at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco — will launch in early access in October.
