Tech.title: Danu Robotics’ fight to build a better recycling robot
Tech.content:
For Danu Robotics founder Amy Ma, the eureka moment came after years of working as a software developer at a London bank. It was the kind of high-touch office that’s typical in finance — but despite all the perks, Ma was alarmed to realize that the building’s recycling bins were being emptied into the trash.

“Even though they have tons of money, there’s all these different recycling bins that just end up in the same place,” Ma told TechCrunch.

The more she dug into the problem, the deeper it seemed to go. It wasn’t just her building. The economics of recycling as a whole often boil down to human beings sorting by hand through streams of waste to pull out different kinds of recyclable material.

“I saw the technology and thought, we can do so much better,” Ma remembers.

Now, she’s making good on that promise with six-year-old, Edinburgh, Scotland-based Danu Robotics, which makes a robot designed to sort through recycling more cheaply and quickly. Ma has been working on that idea for six years and is finally bringing her version of the product to market. Her robot, dubbed H.E.R.O., has a few advantages over its competitors. For example, it picks up items with a pincer claw instead of a suction system. But the bigger difference is the business approach: Danu leverages AI to continuously improve the robot’s software.

The approach is already seeing some traction. Danu has letters of interest from two large customers and $500,000 worth of signed contracts. More notably, more than 200 customers are in its sales pipeline, which gives the company a hook into the $20 billion market for recycling sorting across Europe and North America.

On the back of that promise, Dabnu has raised $5 million in late-seed funding to keep the commercial pressure on.

There’s already a robust market for robotic waste-pickers, particularly the suction-based arms offered by competitors like Glacier and RecycleEye. But Ma believes the economics of recycling will make it easy for a new competitor to prove its worth. Because recycling centers make money off the materials they’re able to sort out, there’s an immediate return on investment for a working system. Ma estimates that a working site will earn $485,000 in additional revenue from having the robot on the sorting line, compared with a $160,000 initial investment and $24,000 in maintenance fees each year. That’s significantly cheaper than the competition, and Ma believes the robot will be more efficient, too.

Since those machines are already shipping, Ma’s next goal is to make the robot sturdier, smaller, and more versatile. Once it’s portable enough, it can be used outside dedicated waste facilities, opening up a whole other world of use cases.

“Once it’s smaller, it can be used as a stand-alone recycling solution for events, for shopping centers, hospitals, or airports to recycle their waste at the source,” Ma told TechCrunch, “and that’s the way we can really change how we’re managing our packaging waste.”

Danu Robotics will be participating in Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, October 13-15 at the Moscone Center in San Francisco.

Tech.title: We can’t help treating AI like it’s human. But should we?
Tech.content:
In a tan polo shirt, brown leather belt, and round bolo tie, MIT PhD student Wil Norton kind of looks like a park ranger, leading our tour group through a tropical jungle. We’re not actually on safari, though — we’re at MIT’s Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL). But what we’re about to see is even more exotic than a cheetah or a jaguar: a pair of humanoid Unitree robots, each costing about $50,000.

(“They’ll tell you they cost $16,000,” Norton says. “That’s a lie.”)

We usually only see these robots on YouTube when they’re performing a synchronized martial arts routine, or dancing on “America’s Got Talent.” Here, they’re approachable. Even though I know it isn’t sentient, I want to be its friend.

With Norton’s permission, I approach the robot, whose nickname is Gabe. For a moment, I’m not sure how to interact with something that has a LiDAR sensor where its brain should be, but I default to treating it like a person.

“Hello, sir, it’s nice to meet you,” I say, grabbing its gloved, dexterous hand and shaking it.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

I think about this interaction later — my instinctive impulse to be friendly to a robot — when I attend Dr. Sherry Turkle‘s “Artificial Intimacy” book launch at MIT Future Fest.

Turkle, who joined the faculty at MIT in 1976, has been researching the relationship between humans and computers perhaps longer than anyone, charting technology’s psychological impact on us from the first home computers to ChatGPT.

“When we are drawn into even the most primitive exchanges with a relational artifact, we believe it cares for us,” Turkle writes in the book. “And we are wired to care for it in return.”

I’m not alone in my tendency to anthropomorphize robots and large language models (LLMs) — as Turkle notes, it seems to be in our nature. One study found that about 70% of people are polite when interacting with AI, while another showed that users are more likely to say “please” or “thank you” to chatbots once a conversation has progressed past a first prompt-and-response.

“People tend to categorize whether this is the right use or wrong use, but I don’t think that is a clear boundary,” Dr. Pat Pataranutaporn, a colleague of Turkle who founded the Cyborg Psychology research group at the MIT Media Lab, told TechCrunch. “The question is, who are we becoming when we talk to [AI]?”

There’s no material consequence of my politeness toward Gabe the robot, but as LLMs infiltrate everything from Google searches to customer service interactions, it has become routine for people to interact with these seemingly sentient chatbots. We’re more vulnerable than ever to the flip side of this impulse, which is that some people can ascribe so much legitimacy to the feelings of chatbots — which are programmed to never spark conflict — that they end up favoring them over other humans.

“You can think of it like fantasy and fiction. We go to the cinema even though we know the story is completely fictional, but we want to experience a certain dimension of human experience that maybe our reality cannot give us,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we benefit from that ability to experience other dimensions of human experience without losing it to the fantasy, where you can no longer come back to the reality?”

Pataranutaporn describes himself as a “critical optimist,” and he studies AI’s potential to contribute to human flourishing. But he’s well aware of how dangerous this technology can be in the extremes. He even served as an expert in a wrongful death lawsuit over the suicide of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer, III, whose mother sued the chatbot platform Character.AI, alleging that a chatbot modeled after a “Game of Thrones” character had encouraged her son to end his life.

“It can create a situation where people don’t feel agency in actually creating their own future — like when you say that AI will replace everyone, people ask, what are we gonna do? And these companies are not really responding ethically or responsibly,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we have imagination while still being responsible for the impact of that imagination?”

While Turkle’s book explores the risk of turning to AI for emotional support, rather than other people, she doesn’t think that AI-human interactions are universally harmful.

She recalls a project she advised in which a student created an AI bot to help people practice for job interviews.

“My big metaphor is, stay in your lane, chatbot!” Turkle said at the event. “Coaching for a job interview? That’s a lane. I can do that … A chatbot that says to a three-year-old, ‘I’m your parent, you can talk to me, not your parents,’ is not in a lane.”

But when this technology deviates from its lane even slightly, we become vulnerable to the way it can slowly chip away at our skepticism and make us trust it. It can start with something as simple as a handshake.

Tech.title: Tesla renames ‘Full Self-Driving’ to ‘Tesla Assisted Driving’ in Europe
Tech.content:
Tesla has changed the name of its advanced driver assistance system in Europe after pushback from Germany’s transportation ministry. It’s now called “Tesla Assisted Driving,” instead of “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).”

It’s a big capitulation from Tesla, which has been using the “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” name for years despite the system requiring humans to pay attention to the road and take over when necessary. But the name change could help Tesla achieve its goal of wider adoption on the continent, which could unlock a potentially massive new revenue stream for the company.

Germany’s transport minister, Steffen Bilger, said earlier this month that calling the software “Full Self-Driving” was somewhat misleading because it doesn’t perform the entire task of driving. He spoke with Tesla last month, and the company suggested the name change, according to an official release from the ministry. Bilger said he will now advocate for approval of Tesla Assisted Driving across Europe ahead of an EU-wide vote that could happen later this year. Tesla CEO Elon Musk thanked Bilger on X this week.

Musk has spent years agitating for Full Self-Driving (Supervised), or FSD, to be approved in Europe. “FSD in Europe will save lives of people in the car, as well as vulnerable road users like pedestrians, cyclists, and pets,” he wrote on X in June 2025. “Please let your government know that you want approval.”

In March of this year, he wrote that the “extreme regulatory burden” of the EU “stifles innovation in Europe,” adding that Europe “will love Tesla self-driving!”

Just a few weeks later, the Netherlands became the first European country to approve FSD (Supervised). On Wednesday, Reuters reported that Tesla’s campaign for European approval has been “built on faulty company safety research” and “flawed studies.” The outlet also reported that the Dutch vehicle safety regulator, RDW, faced fierce pressure from Tesla and its legion of online supporters.

Tesla’s software has certainly become more capable over the years. What used to be little more than a mix of lane centering and adaptive cruise control is now a driver assistance system that some owners use for nearly 100% of their daily driving. FSD can pull in and out of parking spots and navigate surface streets and highways. Tesla is so confident in the technology that it recently made it possible for FSD to intervene in a human driver’s control of the vehicle if it senses an oncoming collision — even if FSD is not active.

But FSD has been at the center of federal investigations and civil lawsuits over crashes in which it was allegedly in use. Its less capable predecessor, Autopilot, has been associated with dozens of fatalities. Tesla discontinued Autopilot earlier this year after a judge ruled Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing about the system’s capabilities.

Tech.title: Remember Orkut? Its founder wants to bring it back
Tech.content:
Orkut, the once-popular social networking platform that shut down more than a decade ago, may finally be making a comeback, as its founder has called on users to help revive it with a renewed focus on friendship, community, and human connection.

In a post on X on Thursday, Orkut Büyükkökten, the founder of the eponymous social network, urged users to visit Orkut.com and add their names in support of bringing it back, as well as invite others to join.

Orkut first debuted in 2004 as a side project by Büyükkökten, 51, while he was at Google. The social network went on to become hugely popular in India and Brazil but later lost ground to Facebook. Google eventually shut it down in September 2014, shifting its focus to other platforms, including Google+ and YouTube.

In a letter published on Orkut.com, Büyükkökten criticized how social media has evolved over the past two decades, particularly the growing influence of algorithms and AI-generated content. “Artificial intelligence is extraordinary technology, but it’s dissolving the one premise that made social networking special and worth building: that there was a person on the other side,” he wrote.

“I know how to get there: we rebuild the internet we first loved. The one with authentic people, real connection, and genuine belonging,” Büyükkökten added.

This is not the first time Büyükkökten has explored a return to social networking. In 2016, two years after Orkut’s shutdown, he launched another social network, Hello, focused on connecting people through shared interests. The platform shut down in 2020 after attracting more than 2 million downloads worldwide, compared with Orkut’s about 300 million active users.

In 2022, Büyükkökten hinted at another social networking venture in a note on Orkut.com, saying that he was “building something new.” He did not offer further details. Two years later, he told WIRED he was working on a social network that would “leverage AI and machine learning” to bring people together and build communities. That platform has yet to launch.

Now, Büyükkökten is asking people to register their support for Orkut’s return. He has, however, not clarified whether a new version of the platform is already in development or whether it will ever launch.

An email sent to Orkut seeking comment from Büyükkökten did not elicit a response.

Tech.title: a16z’s Olivia Moore on the state of consumer AI
Tech.content:
I wrote this week about the bleak economics of consumer AI — but where some see a crisis, others see an opportunity.

Olivia Moore covers consumer AI as a partner at Andreessen Horowitz — and on Monday, she released a report on the top 100 consumer AI apps. ChatGPT is still the biggest player by a mile, but smaller players like Suno and ElevenLabs are showing real staying power. Even more interesting is what we don’t see, as Moore’s report details half a dozen consumer categories that seem to be completely untouched by AI.

Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges. On a call this week, I talked with her about the unusual economics of consumer AI and why it’s still early days for the category.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

It’s an interesting moment for a report about consumer AI, since we’ve seen OpenAI pivot back to enterprise this year. It’s inspired a lot of pessimism about the overall revenue picture for consumer AI, including from me. But I take it you’re more optimistic?

I agree with you that OpenAI has moved back towards the enterprise. To me, it’s not necessarily a pivot because they’re still launching a lot in consumer. It’s more of an expansion. But I don’t blame them, as much as I love consumer, because almost all of the AI revenue thus far has come from subscriptions and then token usage. And that is much more concentrated on the enterprise and prosumer side.

How can consumer AI products change that revenue problem? The State of Markets report reminded us that just 2.2% of U.S. households are paying for AI. Do we need that number to rise before the market becomes attractive?

I actually don’t know if I want to see that user number increase. I’m more interested in getting back to a world where the consumer is monetized in a way that isn’t subscription dollars out of their own pocket.

I think it’s very easy in Silicon Valley, with people who are high-income and have corporate cards to pay for those tools, to say, “oh well, I’d rather pay for the product.” But I think most people would actually rather have free access to something and see some ads, and then they can decide if they want to subscribe or not to make the ads go away.

The other challenge is the marginal cost of AI services, which is still a lot higher than classic internet services like Facebook or Google Search. Do you see a lot of these services finding ways to keep those costs down, whether it’s open source or other lightweight models?

Yeah, I think we’re seeing improvements there. Even ChatGPT now has a Go plan, which is just $8 a month, and I’m assuming it runs on cheaper models. We don’t necessarily need frontier intelligence for every task, and so that could mean cheaper models, especially for some consumer use cases. It could also mean more consumer companies building on top of open source models. We’ve heard a lot of that from our founders lately, and it really feels like it’s starting to change.

The problem is that right now, the users driving the revenue are doing coding and other technical automation, where they probably do need frontier intelligence. I think as we get more people building for the consumer, where the model is not the product, we’ll start to see lower-cost models used more often.

It’s unusual to talk about technical automation in a consumer service, which feels like another unique feature of AI. Are we starting to blur the lines between consumer and enterprise?

I wrote an article about this maybe a year or so ago called The Great Expansion trying to get at this. Pre-AI, you would have companies like Canva that were consumer-first and often took six or seven years to even add teams or enterprise plans. Now we’re seeing companies like Gamma, ElevenLabs, and Cursor that start as consumer and within 18 months become majority-enterprise businesses.

Almost all of what we think of as consumer AI, I would argue, is prosumer AI. This really comes out on the revenue list, where there’s basically like three categories that power users are spending on. There’s product-building apps, so like Lovable, Replit, and Fal. There’s product marketing, which is AI ad generators like Higgsfield or HeyGen. Then there’s general work management, like Manus, Fireflies AI, and Granola. Those are like being paid for by consumers to start with, but I would argue that they’re not consumer in the way that we would think about pre-AI.

There are also all these whitespace categories: social apps, dating apps, marketplaces, retail, travel, finance, health. There are no entrants in our top 100 list in those categories, which is pretty surprising. And that’s what I think we need to see over the next six months.

So maybe we haven’t really seen true consumer AI yet?

It’s definitely very early.

Tech.title: Automattic loses its interim CFO just weeks after boardroom shakeup
Tech.content:
Automattic’s interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left his position after less than a month, TechCrunch has learned. Klaperman had been elevated to the new job last month after the governance crisis at the WordPress.com parent company, which saw its entire board either quit or be fired.

The company confirmed the departure with the following statement, shared by Automattic’s director of communications Megan Fox: “Automattic will always be grateful for Jeremy Klaperman’s leadership. We wish him the best of luck on his next endeavor.”

Before serving as the organization’s interim finance chief, Klaperman had served as the CFO of Automattic’s VIP Enterprise business unit.

He was meant to replace the former CFO, Mark Davies, who had briefly become Automattic’s CFO after the company’s board members voted to put CEO Matt Mullenweg on leave in September. Within 33 hours of the board’s decision, Mullenweg retook the CEO role, and the board was wiped clean.

Automattic’s chief legal officer Andy Missan had also left the company alongside Davies. Both executives had signed reciprocal severance deals during Mullenweg’s short leave of absence, TechCrunch previously reported. Automattic’s new board of directors was announced in late September, and includes best-selling science-fiction author Hugh Howey; two co-founders of the now-defunct social app IRL, Henry Khachatryan and Krutal Desai; plus author Amy Chan.

A source at Automattic told TechCrunch that Klaperman was upset the board was considering external candidates for the CFO role. Though he was announced internally as interim CFO, the board never legally approved his title, the source said. In addition, there was a disagreement with Mullenweg over a work project related to employee performance reviews, which led to Mullenweg’s demotion of Klaperman back to his former position at VIP. Klaperman resigned shortly thereafter.

Automattic’s spokesperson did not comment on the reason for Klaperman’s departure. The company is still performing an external search for a qualified CFO candidate, we understand.

When Mullenweg originally announced Klaperman’s new role as interim CFO on Automattic’s Slack, Mullenweg reiterated that he had “100% confidence” in the company’s cash and financial position.

Updated after publication with more information about Klaperman’s departure.

Tech.title: The DOJ Is Weighing Perjury Charges Against Cassidy Hutchinson
Tech.content:
Federal prosecutors have been weighing a perjury and obstruction-of-justice case against Cassidy Hutchinson, who implicated President Donald Trump in the January 6 Capitol riot in testimony four years ago, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

The efforts mark the Justice Department’s intent to proceed against Hutchinson, a former aide to ex-Trump White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, though prosecutors are not expected to ask a federal grand jury in Washington to return an indictment until at least after the midterm elections, the sources say.

Hutchinson testified as a star witness to the committee that investigated the riot, recounting that Trump encouraged his supporters to march to the Capitol even though he knew many were armed. She sat for several interviews in addition to her public testimony, where she recalled hearing that Trump had lunged at one of his Secret Service agents after being told he could not join his supporters at the Capitol.

In recent months, prosecutors at the Justice Department have focused on the fact that the former special counsel, Jack Smith, did not corroborate much of Hutchinson’s account to the committee, and the Secret Service’s denial of any altercation in the presidential limo, the sources say.

By comparing the transcripts of Hutchinson’s interviews with the committee and against her testimony to Smith’s team, prosecutors have been trying to construct a case based on how her testimony has changed, the sources say.

Tech.title: I’m Still Convinced the iPod Was the Perfect Gadget
Tech.content:
I remember the birth of the iPod, 25 years ago this month. I was working at Newsweek. It was October 23, little more than a month after the attacks on the twin towers of the World Trade Center, and everybody was focused on the aftermath. I didn’t go to Cupertino for the launch, where Steve Jobs pulled the gadget from his jeans pocket and boasted that it contained a whole music library. Apple couriers hand-delivered the device to me in New York, and Jobs got on the phone with me. “iPod,” he told me, “will be a landmark product.”

He was right. By 2004, I was writing a cover story called “iPod Nation,” and later I published a book about the iPod called The Perfect Thing.

The death of the iPod wasn’t as memorable. It’s not even clear when it happened. Officially, one might date the time of death as occurring on May 10, 2022, when Apple discontinued the iPod Touch, the last product to use that name. But I never considered the Touch a real iPod; it was simply an iPhone without cellular connectivity. Maybe the appropriate death call might have been July 27, 2017, when Apple killed the Nano—the last traditional iPod with a screen—and the iPod Shuffle, a postage-stamp-sized player that clipped to your shirt. (Apple had quietly discontinued the classic iPod, with a hard drive and click wheel, in 2014.)

All these final dates were an inevitable consequence of what Steve Jobs put in motion on January 11, 2007. That’s when he announced three new products—a phone, an internet device, and “the best iPod ever,” all integrated into a new thing called the iPhone. From that moment on, the iPod as a separate device was living on borrowed time.

Still, for years, Apple sold millions more of the beloved devices before the iPod went silent. But even as we love our smartphones, the iPod scratched an itch that still lingers, and I’m sticking to my claim that the iPod was The Perfect Thing. It was a one-function device that superbly executed its function. It made people unconditionally happy. In contrast, our relationships with our iPhones (and Android phones) are more complicated. Yes, the device that superseded the iPod is galaxies more impactful than its predecessor. Financially, of course, it is the engine of a $4 trillion company. I can’t imagine any other contender for the mantle of best product of the century.

But I would not call the iPhone perfect. It gobbles our attention, sometimes with toxic social media apps. Countless cars have been totaled because drivers were more interested in its touch screen than what was happening on the other side of the windshield. iPhone doomscrolling can result in depression. Whereas that perky iPod brought nothing but joy.

Tech.title: Dunking on Dating App Profiles Is Content Gold. People Are Getting Sick of It
Tech.content:
Evangelizing to his 512,000 TikTok followers occasionally requires that dating coach Chad Franklin post the private communications of his clients, who pay upwards of $5,000 for his services.

In September, Franklin shared a DM conversation in which a woman implied she couldn’t afford an Uber with the text overlay “Don’t date POOR women!!!” That same month, he uploaded a video of a client’s successful text exchange on Hinge where they talked about the need to “flirt over some margaritas.” In the clip, Franklin can barely contain himself, noting that it was the type of tête-à-tête that gets his “dick hard”: “This is what men are looking for. We lead, you follow.”

Franklin posts under the alias @DefundSimping, and has made it his mission to help straight, career-driven guys in their “post-breakup, post-divorce” era undo their “simp” behavior, which he defines as putting women on a pedestal or giving them too much attention.

I reached out to the 30-year-old content creator because I wanted to talk about Hinge’s decision to start testing screenshot protection in India. The announcement set off a firestorm of reaction across social media last week, rekindling a debate around digital etiquette, privacy, and shame.

“​​Everyone who’s downloaded the app has seen the debauchery and the drama,” Franklin says, explaining that being online in 2026 simply means there is a chance you will become the day’s main character whether you intended to or not. “People are aware that they could be the next haha moment, but that doesn't mean they deserve it.”

TikTokers, X accounts like @hingestrange, and other online creators have built entire brands out of screenshotting and sharing bizarre dating profile prompts, cringe pickup lines, or red flags found while swiping. But critics of the trend argue it’s a form of public humiliation that should end.

In response to news of Hinge revoking profile screenshotting ability in India, some responded with relief.

“People on here kinda turned being on a dating app into both an extension of the panopticon and a window into their own personal penchant for cruelty,” writer Tres Dean noted on X. “I actually think this might be the first ethical development in online dating in years if not ever.”

X user @randy_mossad added, “Better for a million cheaters to go unpunished than for one regular person looking for love to get humiliated by leaked chats.”

Tech.title: The Best Mac Desktop to Buy (2026): Mac Mini, Mac Studio, or iMac?
Tech.content:
MacBooks have taken most of the spotlight away from Mac desktops in recent years. Now that mobile performance and battery life have improved so much, there's less of a reason to buy a desktop that chains you to your office.

But Mac desktops are getting a resurgence. The Mac Mini and Mac Studio were finally refreshed with brand-new chips and a newfound focus on running local AI. But which one should you buy? And where does the iMac land these days? I've been testing Macs for over a decade and have tested all these Mac desktops, so I can recommend what's right for you.

Also check out our complete guide to the Best MacBooks, Best Desktops, and Best All-In-One Desktops.

The Best for Everyone: Mac Mini

Apple's lovable mini PC was just upgraded with the M6 chip, and it's a big deal on a couple of fronts. Before the refresh, these little computers were sold out for months, and it has AI to thank.

The Mac Mini isn't the ultracheap mini PC it used to be. It's $300 more than in the past, but the base model now has higher specs and a focus on running local AI. If you want a truly affordable little desktop PC for occasional use, you'll have to opt for a Windows machine. The good news is that the Mac Mini remains a compelling offer across its configurations. You can choose between two new models: one with the M6 and one with the M5 Pro. The M6 model is the one most people should buy, especially if you're looking for a fast, reliable Mac desktop.

The new M6 chip is especially fast in terms of GPU performance, an area Apple continues to make strides. If you're a fledgling video editor or designer, the base configuration packs plenty of performance for creative applications. Unfortunately, it's only a couple hundred bucks cheaper than a similarly configured MacBook Air, which makes the buying decision frustrating given how much more versatile a laptop is. But for the first time, the Mac Mini's form factor is a benefit over a laptop. AI enthusiasts get excited about the prospect of an always-on, agentic AI box that sits on their desk and can then be controlled remotely from a MacBook or iPhone. That's exactly what the Mac Mini can do (just be sure to upgrade the memory). And given memory prices across the industry, you won't find many comparable options on Windows or Linux—at least not with this much performance and RAM.

I haven't tested the M5 Pro model yet, but the main difference is in the enhanced graphics. Despite the improvements I mentioned on the M6, you can configure the M5 Pro up to 20 GPU cores, which really come in handy for tasks like gaming, 3D modeling, and video rendering. As the name suggests, I wouldn't consider the pricier M5 Pro config unless you're a professional who sits in front of Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve all day. If you're more of a hobbyist or dabbler, the M6 will likely do you just fine.

Tech.title: Best Battery-Powered Leaf Blowers (2026): Tested for Power, Battery Life, and Noise
Tech.content:
Here’s what I’d focus on when buying a blower for leaf cleanup:

Volts: In the cordless power-tool arms race, leaf blower batteries range from 18 to 80 volts. Some of that difference is marketing trickery: an advertised 20-volt max battery or tool delivers essentially the same power as an 18-volt model, and the same goes for 36- and 40-volt options. But, unless you’re a minimalist who wants one battery to power everything from a drill/driver to lawn and garden gear, you’ll probably be happier with a leaf blower that uses at least a 36-volt battery. A few capable 18-volt blowers use two batteries—either simultaneously to mimic the power of a 36-volt tool or in succession to increase the run time—but they tend to cost more and only make sense if you already own the batteries. For smaller jobs, though, a standard, single-battery 18- or 20-volt blower may be all you need to clear a patio, clean out the garage or shed, or dry a car.

Amps: Volts get most of the marketing attention on the box, but a battery’s amp-hour rating tells you more about how long a blower runs. Think of voltage as the car’s engine and amp-hours as the size of the gas tank—you want to know both. Batteries with higher amp-hour ratings cost more than otherwise-similar battery voltages, and they tend to be heavier. For leaf blowers, manufacturers typically pair kits with batteries rated from 4 to 8 amp-hours. You can buy higher-capacity batteries separately, and it pays to know the range of options a manufacturer has. A battery with a higher amp-hour typically takes longer to charge.

Systems: Underestimating the range of tools a battery can power in pursuit of “the best” is, in my opinion, a mistake. Often, the difference between two top-performing tools is negligible, and with cordless power tools, that difference often comes down to run time, which you can address with a higher-capacity battery. If your garage is already stocked with one brand’s outdoor power equipment (OPE), it makes sense to stay within that platform and buy the blower as a bare tool, leveraging the batteries you already have. Switching brands just to buy “the best” probably isn’t worth it to introduce a whole new battery and charger.

If you’re new to OPE—and a leaf blower is a common first purchase—the breadth of tools that share the battery matters. Some manufacturers stick to the lawn and garden basics, so one battery can power a blower, mower, string trimmer, and hedge trimmer, while others offer a much wider range of tools, from log splitters to snow blowers, and even some handy lifestyle products like portable power stations. Before buying, consider what else you can power with the battery that comes with your leaf blower because, chances are, lording over leaves won’t be your only lawn and garden chore.

Traditional 18-volt power tool manufacturers—the ones who make drill/drivers and circular saws—all offer leaf blowers and the simplicity of a one-battery platform, but they’re not powerful enough to replace a gas unit. Ryobi, for example, uses 18-volt batteries across its traditional power tools, and some outdoor equipment, but its most capable gas alternative options run on 40-volt batteries.

Detent clasp: Blowers have two or more connection points: where the tube meets the housing and where the nozzle attaches to the tube. Look for models with a detent at those junctions—a small, often brightly colored spring-loaded clip that snaps into place with a satisfying click when the parts connect. I find these connections hold more securely and last longer than simple friction-fit attachments.

Stubby nozzle: Recently, blowers aimed at car detailers, with short tubes and sometimes a pistol grip, have become popular. Manufacturers responded by adding a stubby, 3- to 6-inch tube that the main blower attachment slides over. When you remove the longer tube, this short one works to direct the volume of air with an overall shorter tool length that’s easier to use around cars or in tight spots (the blower’s nozzle doesn’t fit on this stubby tube, though, so you lose some velocity).

What I’d Worry Less About:

Weight: Across the board, regardless of voltage, a good battery-powered blower will weigh about 10.5 pounds with the battery attached. If you need a lighter option, look for an 18-volt powered blower. Some have better balance than others, meaning that when you hold them without squeezing the trigger, as you would while walking around, the tool stays mostly level or the nozzle end tips down a bit. These models will cause less fatigue than one that forces you to rotate the nozzle upward. With the former, you only need to make a slight horizontal twisting motion to spread the stream of air. Most modern leaf blowers also draw air in a straight line through the rear of the tool, unlike gas-powered models with intakes mounted to the left or right of the engine. Those offset intakes can create a twisting motion that increases hand fatigue and may even suck in your pant leg.

CFM, MPH, and Newton: This sounds counterintuitive, considering how much marketing goes into boasting about a leaf blower’s cubic feet per minute (CFM) and MPH, but these figures are a guide, not necessarily the only reason to buy a specific model. A blower needs both to be useful: CFM tells you how much air it moves, while MPH tells you how fast that air is moving. But there’s no universally adopted testing method for these specifications when it comes to battery-powered blowers (ANSI/OPEI B175.2, the standard test on the books, applies only to internal combustion engines). That means brands can test their units differently — for example, measuring MPH where the motor meets the tube rather than at the end of the blower tube, which gives you a better sense of the airspeed you’ll actually get in use. Some CFM numbers are also measured with the unit running in its max, boost, or turbo setting, rather than on high speed.

Newtons, a unit of force, is a rating that’s appearing more frequently on the spec sheets of higher-voltage, battery-powered leaf blowers and is the best apples-to-apples comparison of blowing power. However, because there’s no testing code for battery-powered leaf blowers, reporting newtons is optional and, like CFM and MPH, consumers have no way of knowing whether the test is standardized. Generally speaking, a good midrange blower will produce around 20 newtons, while models that produce more are typically higher-performing units. Treat newtons as a guide rather than a definitive specification while buying.

Wide nozzles: Some blowers come with a wide-tip nozzle, which can be useful for clearing paved surfaces like patios and driveways or blowing water off flat surfaces. But in practice, it’s not enough of a game changer to be a deciding factor. The narrower nozzle is typically what you’ll use, and you can twist your hand back and forth to create a wider pattern when needed.

Tech.title: Even ‘Law & Order’ Is Terrified of AI
Tech.content:
Longtime fans of the NBC procedural Law & Order know that storylines often center around hot-button issues in the news cycle, often to absurdist effect (see: the episode brave enough to ask: “What if Paula Deen shot Trayvon Martin?”).

It was inevitable, then, that the franchise would dip a toe into the wacky world of artificial intelligence. With its mercenary culture, power-hungry CEOs, and massive ethical and philosophical implications, the rapidly evolving AI industry is ideal fodder for the series. But while this week’s season opener is entertaining, the show’s foray into the AI space doesn’t say anything new or interesting about the technology. Instead it largely rehashes the dangers the public is already acutely aware of, until the very end when the stakes become startlingly clear.

The episode, titled “Ghost in the Machine,” opens in typical L&O fashion with a murder. This time, it’s Steve Kelly, a man ID’d by detectives Theo Walker (David Ajala) and Vincent Riley (Reid Scott) as a high-ranking engineer at a company called Advanced Alignment. Throughout, the detectives seem utterly perplexed by the concept of artificial intelligence, saying “AI” the same way your mom would say “Snapchat” or “borg” or “Alix Earle.” But it’s clear that whatever this newfangled technology is, they don’t like it: “Maybe one day they’ll invent a technology that stops these tech guys from shooting each other,” Riley deadpans in typical grizzled cop fashion.

After interviewing Kelly’s boss, Advanced Alignment CEO Chuck Klein (a perfectly cast Vincent Kartheiser, aka Pete from Mad Men, who nails Dario Amodei’s absence of charisma and Sam Altman’s thousand-yard stare), the detectives figure out who actually carried out the murder—a guy in a baseball cap who did it for “20 grand in crypto” that was offered to him by a rando on Discord. Then they learn—spoilers here—that the hit was ordered not by an actual human being but by the company’s AI agent ELIANA, which stands for Evolutionary Language Inference Automated Nano Advantage. Apparently, Kelly had expressed some concerns about the AI agent’s “powerful” and “aggressive” personality, and out of self-preservation, ELIANA ordered him killed.

It’s never explained exactly how the detectives figure out that ELIANA is behind the hit; it’s also never fully explained how ELIANA recruited this assassin in a baseball cap, much less ID'd him as the perfect patsy for its cold-blooded scheme. Law & Order also doesn’t pay much, if any, lip service to the potential benefits of AI as touted by its evangelists: its potential for helping to cure deadly diseases, for instance, or at the very least, streamline B2B workflows. The show is much more interested in demonstrating the staggering capacity of this technology, as well as the legal and ethical implications of a nonhuman not just facilitating criminal behavior but actively plotting it.

We already know from the Hugging Face debacle, as well as the lawsuits from grief-stricken family members alleging that OpenAI encouraged their loved ones to take their own lives, that the former is an immediate concern. But by positing a future in which AI agents can actively order a hit on a platform predominantly used by gamers and horny millennial furries, Law & Order is asking us to consider the risks of AI beyond what they pose in our current reality. And the fact that this prospect doesn’t strike the viewer as absolutely ludicrous is terrifying.

Tech.title: A New Mexico Community Was a Place to Build a Life. Then a Hypersonic Missile Factory Showed Up
Tech.content:
Sally Schultz thought she had struck gold when she purchased land in Rio Rancho Estates, an unincorporated, census-designated community just outside the city of Rio Rancho, New Mexico. A single mother of four, Schultz came there following a divorce to build a homestead of her own and finally gain some stability in her life.

For $3,500, she was able to purchase half an acre for her trailer in a rural area located close to numerous elementary schools and parks. In a relatively short time, she was able to coax crops like corn, squash, and green chile from the ground. This cheap land became Schultz’s haven, giving her a second chance at life.

WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from Freedom of Information Act requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism.

Then a missile company showed up next door.

“We’ve already been through so much,” she says, “and now we have to leave. It is the unknowing that is scariest.”

Castelion, a startup founded in November 2022 by three former SpaceX executives, is building Project Ranger, which it claims will be America’s “largest dedicated hypersonic manufacturing production facility.” Construction is set to be complete by the end of the year.

The company’s chosen site for its mega-campus is, in some cases, it appears, a little more than 1,000 yards away from roughly 450 properties in Rio Rancho Estates, including Schultz’s. That puts the homes squarely within a danger zone should any explosive chemicals stored onsite catch fire.

A year into Castelion’s relationship with the state of New Mexico, the company—which declined to speak with WIRED for this story—still hasn’t answered basic safety questions, even as an official hazard assessment found buildings would simply be left to burn in the case of fire, releasing hydrochloric acid gas into the air. Emails between the company and Rio Rancho officials reviewed by WIRED also show Castelion was negotiating fire safety standards even after construction was well underway.

“I live next door to where World War III will be manufactured,” says local resident Laura Lundberg.

Big Plans

Castelion has become a bit of a darling among the new wave of defense tech startups. The company has recently hit a valuation of $13 billion—more than four times its Series B valuation of $2.8 billion from last year.

It has received over $500 million in US military contracts in just 18 months, swiftly securing its spot as one of the “Arsenal of Freedom” suppliers.

The firm touts its ability to make hypersonic missiles—a label for any missile flying at five times the speed of sound or higher—at a lower cost than its competitors. The US Army’s Dark Eagle is the most mature domestic hypersonic weapon, and it costs an estimated $41 million per missile, according to a 2023 Congressional Budget Office study. Castelion’s main product, Blackbeard, is a solid-rocket-powered missile that was set to sell for $384,000 per unit.

Tech.title: America’s Hybrid Hype Has Hit the Used Market
Tech.content:
Conventional wisdom is that cars are bad investments. Drive one off the lot, and it starts losing value the minute its wheels touch the road. That makes what’s happening with the 2026 Toyota Rav4 downright weird.

Some used vehicles are listing for $3,000 to $6,000 above brand-new dealership prices, according to new data from the online automotive marketplace CarGurus. The months-old cars are aging like fine wine.

The crossover SUV—one of the top-selling in the US—went all-hybrid last year, after Toyota announced it would drop the gas-powered model from its lineup. That’s likely why we’re catching a glimpse of an economic Upside Down. Kevin Roberts, director of economic and market intelligence at CarGurus, says the situation reminds him of the pandemic-era chip shortage, when a supply crunch for new cars also drove up used prices, and buyers flipped them months later for a profit.

“Hybrid demand is so strong, the Rav4 is still in that 2021 world,” he says. Toyota can’t make new models fast enough.

The leaves are changing, and America’s hot hybrid summer has become a toasty hybrid autumn, for new cars and for old ones. Toyota reported this month that its hybrid sales are up 29 percent in the third quarter of 2026; Kia said its sales more than doubled. Nearly one in six new US cars sold is a hybrid, according to Cox Automotive data.

“The American market has a reputation for gas guzzlers, but we're starting to shake that reputation because of how much we like hybrids,” Roberts says.

The major driver is gas prices. They’ve skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war and the ensuing conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, a global center of oil and gas production and shipping. Nationally, a gallon costs an average of $4.40, up 40 percent from this time last year, according to AAA; Californians pay an average of $6.36. Car buyers are a simple bunch, Roberts says—when prices start rising, they immediately look for more fuel-efficient cars. Soon, drivers actually start buying them.

For now, struggles in the US electric vehicle market are hybrids’ gain. New EV sales are down by almost half from last year, after the Trump administration cut a federal tax credit that made the often-expensive powertrains more affordable. Unlike electrics, hybrids don’t necessarily force drivers out of their familiar gas station routines. (Even plug-in hybrids sometimes need a gas top-up, though smart owners depend mostly on electricity.) Finally, more hybrids are available now than before. A buyer interested in nearly every major sort of passenger vehicle—three-row SUVs, pickups, minivans, or luxury cars—can find one with the powertrain

Interest has spread to the used market, where hybrid prices are up almost 5 percent over last year, according to the automotive data website iSeeCars.com. At $34,500, the average price of used hybrids is higher than used EVs or gas-powered cars. Used buyers seem to be especially keen on long-term fuel savings.

Tech.title: Yes, You Can Reuse Cooking Oil and It’s Easier Than You Think
Tech.content:
Nobody argues with deep-fried food, whether it’s donuts, drumsticks, party-sized appetizers or any form of potato. The technique isn’t the hurdle, either. Grab a sturdy pot and a reliable thermometer, and frying is quick and easy. The part that gives home cooks pause is the cleanup: where does all that used oil go?

Shallow frying can also get the job done in many cases, but it can also create a conundrum. Putting that oil down the sink? Potentially drain-clogging, environmentally dubious, and frankly, wasteful. I grew up in a household where we put leftover grease and oil in a glass mayonnaise jar under the sink, then discarded it when it was full. Sure, this saves the sink, but it doesn’t address the other two issues. It’s a quick kitchen hack that makes it easier to toss with food waste, but there’s another solution.

Leftover frying oil is begging to be reused. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Don’t get rid of it. “Oil used for frying is not one and done,” says Melanie Underwood, cookbook author, culinary instructor, and founder of Nourish and Gather, “unless the oil has been overheated, or if you’re frying things that are particularly strong in flavor. With something like seafood, you want to be careful, but it’s perfectly reusable as long as it wasn’t smoking.”

More from CNET

With that, Underwood shares her best practices and advice for reusing oil multiple times.

Manage the oil before and during the frying process

A proper frying temperature is between 350 and 400 F. Pamela Vachon/CNET

To ensure oil is good for multiple uses, first make sure you’re using the right oil — something neutral in flavor with a high smoke point. “Any vegetable oil, such as canola oil, peanut oil or sunflower oil, is best for frying,” says Underwood. While olive oil can be tricky to fry with because it has a lower smoke point, “I’ve used it,” she says, “and I have never had any problem with it whatsoever.”

Resist the impulse to eyeball your oil for temperature clues, or test bits and pieces to make sure you’re in the right zone, unless you fry so regularly that it’s second nature. Otherwise, that’s a recipe for pieces with burnt exteriors and undercooked interiors, and/or smoking out your upstairs neighbors. (Speaking from experience, sadly.) Using a thermometer, “the correct range for frying is usually between 350 to 400,” says Underwood, which prevents smoking.

Just a bit of residue, which you can easily skim off. Pamela Vachon/CNET

During the frying process, it’s a great idea if you can skim out any crumbs or whatever has come off in the oil,” she says, “because when you have little burned pieces, that will degrade the oil faster.”

After frying: cool, strain, and store

Cool, strain and store. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Once you’re done frying, managing the oil for future use is simple. “First, you let it cool,” says Underwood. Don’t try to speed up the process by refrigerating it; just let it sit until it cools to room temperature.

Straining it is also straightforward and can be done with whatever you already have on hand. “I use a fine mesh strainer,” Underwood says. “People also use cheesecloth or a coffee filter. You just want to strain it and get out all those teeny particles.” Some microparticles may still be visible in the oil after straining, but they will settle once the oil is stored, and it is easy to prevent them from transferring into a pot the next time you want to use it.

Finally, Underwood suggests transferring the oil to a clean and dry container. “It’s very important that it doesn’t have any residual water in it,” she says, “and then just put a lid on it, tightly sealed, and keep it away from heat and light.” If you don’t plan to use it immediately, you can store it in the refrigerator, but any place with a consistent temperature and away from light works.

Considerations for reusing oil

Microparticles may still remain, but will settle during storage. Pamela Vachon/CNET

There’s nothing special that needs doing in order to use preused oil the next time, but bear one thing in mind: “Just be aware that it would now carry allergens from anything that you previously cooked in it,” says Underwood, which is essential to know if you’re cooking for other people.

Since that can be hard to track over multiple uses, “Always label and date it,” she suggests. “I just put a piece of tape on it with the date and the number of uses. And I also actually put what was fried in it,” she says, which can help keep track of potential allergens.

Store in a clear, dry jar with a tight-fitting lid. Pamela Vachon/CNET

It also helps keep potentially odd flavors out of whatever you cook next, as certain items like seafood or onion rings can impart flavor into the oil. “I don’t typically like to fry a savory thing and then fry a sweet thing,” says Underwood. “Like I wouldn’t make schnitzel and then use that oil for a donut.”

If you’re unsure whether an oil is still good to use, let your nose guide you to suss out if something is funky. If you’re not confident in your sniffing ability, Underwood advises smelling unused oil of the same type first, then smelling the used oil for comparison. You can use frying oil at least two or three times, maybe more if it was only used for light-flavored things that didn’t impart many particles and was never overheated.



Benefits of reusing oil

The biggest benefit of reusing frying oil is the savings in every possible regard — you save money, and it’s a much more environmentally friendly practice across the board. “When you’re reusing any product, then you’re lowering the demand for things like production, packaging and transport,” Underwood says. “I don’t think that we think about that big picture very much, but if we were all reusing it, it would reduce those demands on the environment.”

Each time you reuse oil, it also loses a bit of volume. In my experience, at least with shallow frying, you can use the same batch of oil until, after a few uses, nothing remains to discard — the ultimate win.

Tech.title: AI’s Problem Solving Is a ‘Profound Disruption’ for the Math Community
Tech.content:
Artificial intelligence has profoundly shaken up tech, education, entertainment and many aspects of everyday life. Now it’s come for math.

According to companies like OpenAI, the large language models they’re developing internally are solving an unprecedented number of longstanding mathematics problems with the goal to “push the frontier of human knowledge.“

But one thing these AI models apparently can’t do: read the room with the world’s most brilliant mathematical minds.

More from CNET

This week, Open AI released more than 700 math “preprints,” or preliminary research papers, on GitHub. The move further angered an academic math community already so up in arms that last month, 28 Fields Medal winners put up a website called Math and AI with an open letter accusing AI companies of having goals that are “severely misaligned” with those of mathematicians.

The Fields Medal is only awarded every four years (usually to three or four mathematicians) and is widely considered the Nobel Prize of math. One of the winners who signed the website declaration, Harvard professor Curtis McMullen, told CNET in an email that AI companies are not coordinating with math experts or using AI models in ways that could practically benefit society.

“The rollout of mathematical work by frontier AI companies has been carried out with disregard for the profound disruption to our community and its academic ecosystem,” McMullen said. “Its goal appears to be to increase the valuation of these companies at any cost.”

‘We can tell almost nothing’

In the months leading up to the Math and AI website and OpenAI’s repository dump, steam was already building over the outsized impact artificial intelligence would have on the study of mathematics. Given that these models were largely trained on written language and lacked a grasp of ground truth, some initially had such poor math skills that they could frequently misplace decimals or simply hallucinate incorrect answers to math problems.

But, as with other areas of AI advancement, the models have evolved at startling speed, going from so-called math dunces to wizards, even as some suggested that they still had a long way to go before displacing actual math experts.

Those who’ve devoted their lives to math study, however, aren’t just worried about their job security. They have fundamental issues with how AI models and companies approach math, including a lack of transparency in how they’re achieving these results and a lack of understanding about why these math problems matter in the first place. That’s something OpenAI has not addressed since the announcement, which, according to Scientific American, is piling on to a field “already in shock” just a month after the company solved the Navier-Stokes equation, a math problem so tough it had a $1 million bounty attached.

A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately return a request for comment.

In his email to CNET, McMullen acknowledged that the potential for AI as a tool for math research is “undeniable.” But so far, he said, research has not been carried out transparently or in cooperation with scientists. “In particular, the models used to achieve these results should be shared

with the scientists who understand and formulated the conjectures or questions under investigation,” McMullen said.

OpenAI has said that it has formed an advisory group hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study, but has not detailed how that will work or whether it will share its most advanced models, calling it only “a first step.”

Not everyone is upset about AI’s disruption of math society; for instance, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working for another leading AI company, Anthropic, congratulated the team at OpenAI, posting on X, “There are some sad stories related to their users getting scooped … we should put that aside for today though. It’s obviously the most significant moment in mathematical history.”

Big, big, big, big props for quasiriemann and no Siegel zeroes (with many other beauties in there), I’m kicking myself for talking all over about it being within reach but not actually having pushed.



There are some sad stories related to their users getting scooped / conflicts… — levent (@__alpoge__) October 6, 2026

But the GitHub drop has left many in math upset and without enough information on how many of this new batch of problems were solved. Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and professor emeritus at New York University, wrote on Substack that the publication “would never pass peer review. We don’t know what the procedure was … From the initial report we can tell almost nothing.”

The mass solving of problems, especially in the absence of context, misses the deeper goal of this study, McMullen said. “Mathematics is not a game of chess,” he said. “Its primary aim is to develop human understanding of abstract structures. Indeed, it is the breadth and versatility of this kind of understanding that underpins technological progress.”

Ironically, that progress includes the AI models that have ingested vast stores of human knowledge. It remains to be seen whether their math proofs will advance human understanding or just create artificial confusion.

Tech.title: How to Disable Some Apple Intelligence Features on Your iPhone or Mac and Reclaim Valuable Space
Tech.content:
Apple launched iOS 27 and MacOS 27 in September, and those updates introduced a revamped Siri AI powered by Apple Intelligence to Apple devices. While the new Siri was better at most tasks in my testing, it can still take up a significant amount of on-device storage space. On my iPhone, for example, it takes up about 6.4GB of data, while it takes up about 17.9GB of space on my MacBook Neo.

If you aren’t using the new AI features, you can disable some of them, and depending on what system you’re on, you can reclaim some of that valuable storage space. That way you can stave off for a little while the dreaded pop-up that tells you your storage is full – I need that extra storage for photos of my wife, son and dog.

Here’s how to see how much storage Apple Intelligence is taking up on your devices and how to disable – or at least limit – it on different operating systems. And don’t forget, Apple Intelligence is only available on certain devices.

How much space is Apple Intelligence taking up on your device?

How much space Apple Intelligence is taking up on your device is easy to check. If you’re on iPhone, go to Settings > General > iPhone Storage > iOS. From here, look for the Apple Intelligence tab to see how much space it takes up on your iPhone.

On a MacBook, click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your screen, then go to System Settings > General > Storage, and click the i next to MacOS. A new pop-up will open to show you how much space Apple Intelligence uses on your MacBook.

How to disable Apple Intelligence on your iPhone

Disabling Apple Intelligence on your iPhone that’s running iOS 27 or later is straightforward. Go to Settings > Siri > Turn Off Siri and follow the on-screen prompts. You can then go back and check your storage, and Apple Intelligence should be gone from that menu.

Disabling Siri AI can free up a few gigabytes on iOS 27. CNET

If you’re running iOS 26, you can disable Apple Intelligence by going to Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri and tapping the toggle next to Apple Intelligence. This should free up some space on your iPhone.

You might also have to disable other Apple Intelligence features across your iPhone. To do this, go to Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions and tap the toggle next to Content & Privacy Restrictions. Then, tap Intelligence & Siri. From here, you’ll need to tap into Image Creation, Writing Tools and Intelligence Extensions and tap Don’t Allow in each one.

This should free up a few gigabytes of space on your iPhone.

You can free up a few gigabytes of space in iOS 26 by disabling Apple Intelligence features. CNET

How to disable Apple Intelligence on your Mac

Disabling Apple Intelligence and freeing up storage space on your device can be weird, depending on which operating system you’re using. For instance, if you’re on MacOS 26, it’s easy to disable the feature and free up space. If you’re on MacOS 27, it’s a little more complicated.

We’ll start off with the easy one. To disable Apple Intelligence on MacOS 26, first click the Apple logo in the top left corner of your screen. Then go to System Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri and click to toggle next to Apple Intelligence. That should free up a few gigabytes of data on your device.

Disabling Apple Intelligence on MacOS 26 frees up a little bit of storage. CNET

There are a couple of potential ways to disable Apple Intelligence on MacOS 27. The easiest way I found to free up a few gigabytes of space is to click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your screen, then go to System Settings > Siri and change your language to something like English (Irish). Siri AI isn’t available in every region yet, so changing your Siri language to a language from one of those regions could trick your device. Granted, it freed up only about 4 GB for me.

I changed my Siri language, and it freed up a few gigabytes of space. CNET

CNET’s sister site PCMag has a more in-depth way of turning off Apple Intelligence and freeing up some space. However, I couldn’t get this method to work. I’m not sure why I couldn’t get this method to work, other than that my device is running MacOS 27.0.1 and not MacOS 27. Maybe this will work for you, though.

According to PCMag, you have to go to System Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy. Then, toggle Content & Privacy off. Click Siri and change it to Siri Classic. Then go through the list of Capabilities and turn each feature off.

You’re not finished yet. Then, go to System Settings > Siri and select Don’t Allow Siri or Siri Classic.

Finally, you’ll need to go into individual Apple Intelligence settings and disable those features. Some easy ones include going to System Settings > Notifications > Summarize Notifications and turning the toggle off, or going to System Settings > Messages > Settings and turning off Message Summaries.

You could do all that work, or you could just switch your Siri language as I did. The choice is yours.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and iOS 27.0.1.

Tech.title: I Asked Meta Muse to Fix an Issue With My Phone Provider. It Got Blocked at Every Turn
Tech.content:
Something weird has been happening with my phone for years. I thought I’d fixed the issue, but it always comes back. Years ago, I bought a SIM-only plan through Visible, Verizon’s cheap sibling. $25 a month gets me unlimited calls, texts and a decent amount of data… and a lot of spam calls and messages looking for someone called Andrew.

Given Visible is all-digital with no number to call, it’s a pain to wrestle with a customer service chatbot to fix it. I’ve tried before, and it said the number is in my name, but I’m not convinced. I still receive multiple messages per month from people trying to reach Andrew.

These messages almost always have something to do with a home trades project. Weird, I know.

More from CNET

Screenshot by Amanda Smith/CNET

It’s one of those life admin tasks that just never gets done because I can easily ignore these messages – making it the perfect job for a personal AI agent like Meta Muse. I want to make sure my name is formally listed as the number owner, as I don’t want people thinking I’m this elusive Andrew.

I tried using Meta Muse as my personal shopper, which was fun, but I ran into an issue at checkout. Let’s see how it can handle an annoying task like this, without a number to call. One AI agent versus another.

Setting up Meta Muse with the task

I opened the Muse app and started a new conversation, instead of picking up on my previous chat with the AI agent. Keeping tasks and chats separate prevents context overload and helps Muse stay focused on the specific objective at hand. Just hit the new side chat button.

Here’s how I instructed it: “I am a Visible customer on the $25 per month plan. I often get calls and texts looking for someone called Andrew. I think he was the previous owner of my number. It’s not a coincidence, because every time someone reaches out, they always ask for Andrew. I’ve contacted Visible before, and it said I own the number, but can you check I’m formally listed as the number owner? Check government websites, etc.”

I also uploaded an example of a text I got.

This was Muse’s response:

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

I told Muse to talk to the Visible chatbot, search my number online and find anywhere that references Andrew. Within seconds, it found a link where my number showed up on a data broker page.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

But Muse couldn’t get through, as Visible blocks bot visits. Muse suggested changing my number (no) and making some changes on my phone to minimize unknown senders and silence unknown callers. This wasn’t super helpful either, as I often receive work calls from numbers I haven’t saved.

I told Muse I didn’t want to change my number. It advised me against claiming the number, as that can encourage spam calls directed at me instead of Andrew.

It said the Andrew data will go stale at some point.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

I had to take over the browser for Muse to chat with Visible. That was taking forever, so Muse did a workaround via the guest option. This took a good 10 minutes, which I spent cleaning the kitchen. But it had no luck.

“Quick honest update,” Muse told me, “I got into Visible’s guest chat, but their send button wouldn’t submit my message, and then their help pages temporarily blocked me.”

It advised me to paste the following chat into my Visible app: “My number is recycled — I get monthly spam calls and texts for ‘Andrew,’ the previous owner. I don’t want to change my number. What are my options? Do you offer spam/scam protection, and how do I turn it on? Can I report the number as recycled?”

Of course, such advice could have been delivered to me by a regular AI chatbot like ChatGPT or Gemini. The advantage of using an AI agent like Muse is that it’s supposed to do all of that for me.

But with a lot of these websites blocking AI agents, it makes autonomous task completion a challenge. I attempted to take over the browser again, but got a 403 forbidden error.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

Muse told me the 403 error is a dead end and that my taking over the browser didn’t change the network address, which was annoying. Muse said it’s the bot protection that’s the problem, not Muse. It drafted a message to send to Visible chat manually, via a live agent.

Screenshot by Amanda Smith/CNET

While I chatted with Visible, Muse gave me a link that showed Andrew and my number. What’s interesting is that the last reported date was when I owned the number.

When I ran a quick manual search on my phone number, the top two websites referenced Andrew. I asked Muse how to update these, and it gave me good advice, like requesting a suppression or removal of records from WhitePages and FastBackgroundCheck, but no instant resolution.

Muse said this would clean the public record, but the messages are coming from old marketing lists, so it said I should keep reporting those as junk. Brokers re-scrape, so it should resolve in time.

I tried it via WhitePages, but quickly hit a roadblock. It wouldn’t let me click Next.

I couldn’t follow the second instruction as I don’t have Andrew’s email address. It advised me to use my email (no thanks) or to call the number.

In another browser, I got escalated to Visible’s “advanced” support. Its instruction was to keep the browser open for 4 to 24 hours.

At this point, I gave up.

The verdict on Meta Muse for this task

I wouldn’t say this was Muse’s fault specifically. It seems most websites have mechanisms in place to block any bots. Most AI agents would struggle to complete this autonomously. For me, in this situation, Muse still feels like a regular chatbot, giving guidance for me to follow.

While I better understand the issue — spammers using outdated data — it still didn’t fix the problem. I’m hoping Visible pulls through with a solution and, if so, this was still time well spent. Without testing Muse to see if it could do it for me, I wouldn’t have prioritized this task.

So, that’s a win, I guess.

Tech.title: How to Tell if a New Neighborhood Device Is a Flock Surveillance Camera
Tech.content:
When a Flock camera shows up on a nearby street corner or sidewalk, it spells a new era of surveillance for your area. These license-plate reading cams can also use AI to identify vehicles and people by their appearance, or even listen to nearby sounds of screaming, depending on the add-ons that the users have chosen. Those features and how Flock cameras have used are raising serious privacy concerns, and a tug-of-war between cities forced to cancel their Flock networks and other towns embracing new Flock setups.

The problem is that while there’s so much concern over Flock cameras and various abuses by law enforcement, people aren’t always great at spotting Flock cams in the real world. It leads to lots of mistaken fears about radar, traffic cameras, trail cams and other various, nontracking devices. That’s one reason I’m not a huge fan of crowdsource-dependent apps such as DeFlock, which can give conflicting information based on what people think is Flock.

That’s why I’m breaking down exactly what a Flock installation looks like — and how to tell whether you’re looking at one, a similar automated license plate reader camera or something else entirely.

More from CNET

Look for the telltale Flock camera shape and logo

You can still most Flock cameras by their distinctive design. Allen J. Schaben/Contributor/Getty Images

Flock Safety’s brand has a very clear camera shape, so with a closer look, it’s typically easy to tell if it’s a Flock automatic license plate reader camera or something else.

Watch for the classic oval, hooded shape of the camera with a circular lens, a near-universal mark of Flock camera.

Notice this competitor brand Obvio has a distinctly different design than Flock, and may not offer the same surveillance services.

Not all license plate cameras are Flock, and that can matter for your privacy. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Keep in mind, Flock offers a variety of surveillance technology, including cameras that can recognize human attributes like clothes and beards, as well as devices that can detect sounds like gunshots, so not every device will look the same. But this is still one of the first and simplest ways to detect a Flock brand camera. If you get very close, you can also small, shiny, stem-like Flock logo on the front of the cameras.

Some Flock cameras don’t have the slim hood, but the color, general design and logo still give them away. Bloomberg/Getty Images

I have seen reports of other ALPR cameras hidden inside objects like fake plants, but this doesn’t appear to be Flock’s typical approach and is very rare so far.

Look for Flock’s visible solar panel arrays

Flock’s solar panels often have a distinctive look. Bloomberg/Getty Images

Next, look for Flock’s large, dark-colored solar panels, which are typically angled above the camera or close by on the same mount. Many ALPR cameras use solar panels so they can be installed nearly anywhere, but Flock’s have a unique design that’s more noticeable the longer you look at the cameras.

If you see what you think is a surveillance device without a solar panel, it probably isn’t one, or at least not one associated with Flock and its camera competitors like Axon or Obvio.

For example, red-light or speed cameras may be wired into traffic-light mounts, but they are used for traffic enforcement and don’t carry the same surveillance baggage as general ALPR cameras. While they automate certain aspects of traffic enforcement and take pictures of license plates, they don’t typically have the AI recognition, broad police search capabilities, or ways to recognize individual vehicles and people like Flock can (although they can still make communities uncomfortable).

Red light and traffic cameras aren’t Flock, and don’t have the same surveillance capabilities as Flock. Robert Daemmrich Photography Inc./Getty Images

Remember, Flock and ALPR solar panels are always larger and more public than the panels people use for their home security cameras. Fortunately, there are other ways to make sure.

Check what surveillance equipment local law enforcement has bought

Searching the Atlas of Surveillance by city or county can surface Flock Safety camera locations, contract details and any reported data-sharing agreements with federal agencies. EFF

I recommend confirming your community is using Flock cameras even if you think you’ve spotted one. One of the best ways is with the Atlas of Surveillance website, which uses dedicated research to collect the different surveillance technologies that cities, police and sheriff departments have bought and are using.

The Atlas of Surveillance tries to stay as current as possible, and you can search by town or county in just a few seconds. It links to reports or public records to confirm use if possible. I’ve used it frequently to trace Flock activity in certain areas, not only with cameras but with growing numbers of surveillance drones, too. It works with multiple types of devices and platforms that law enforcement uses, making it one of the most dependable ways to corroborate that your local government recently started using Flock cameras.

When I talked to senior research Beryl Lipton from the Electronic Frontier Foundation about using the website, she said, “People should start by searching for their town and county to see what technology is in play close to home. While folks may expect some larger cities to use some of these devices, I think people will be surprised to see how common they’ve become in mid-sized and rural areas too.”

Lipton also recommended using a similar tool, the Street-Level Surveillance hub, which is more focused on the complex ways today’s agencies use surveillance technology. With both tools together, you should have a good idea what your community is facing.

Check who owns the property and what contracts they may have

Private companies like Home Depot can use Flock too, which makes it confusing when cameras are posted around parking lots. Bloomberg/Getty Images

Flock doesn’t just contract with cities or police departments. That means that while a city government may have canceled Flock Safety cameras, local businesses can use them on their private property, which can cause a lot of confusion among worried people.

If it doesn’t appear your local government is using Flock cameras, try to find out who owns the property with a camera on it, and if they contract with Flock. Home Depot and Lowe’s, for example, are very open about using ALPR cameras, including Flock’s, in their parking lots, and sometimes share that data with police.

Local businesses and neighborhood entities like HOAs can also contract with Flock, but you can often ask them directly if they have AI surveillance cameras and why.

Ask your city council

Asking your city government and showing up to meetings is a great way to find out what’s going on with Flock. The Washington Post/Getty Images

Going to your city council, especially in person, can also be helpful (even Darth Vader thinks so). You can find out about present or future connections with Flock and make your opinion heard. You may also discover that, as I’ve seen before, cities have canceled their Flock contracts and no longer use the cameras, but they still stay up because no one is sure how to legally remove them.

I’ve also seen city councils unsure what Flock cameras are or how police use them, essentially signing off on police and sheriff budgets without knowing what they’re paying for, which is a sign that auditing and accountability practices are lacking. Or, I’ve noticed some cities announce new camera or surveillance programs but carefully avoid using the word “Flock” even though they are contracting with Flock Safety.

Asking direct questions to public servants can help handle issues like these. Look for council meetings where the public is welcome, and try writing or calling your city council to ask about their plans for Flock, if any.

File a public records request

Check if your city or state supports public records requests. You may be able to use a government website to formally request access to information about ALPR cameras, installations and contract documents.

Depending on the public records portal, you may have to be very specific about the kind of information you want, and which government body has it — the police department vs. the city, for example. My other steps are a good start to the research you need if you want to access public records like this.

While not every camera is from Flock, knowing which are — and which have ALPR or person detection capabilities — is a key step in avoiding confusion and protecting your privacy.
